Request-to-schedule trace · DOH HFEP

One facility request can be followed across the hearing and the three schedule stages. In the September 2 DOH hearing, Rep. Audrey Zubiri asked DOH to review the “Moolog Bagong Filipinas” health-center allocation, cited as ₱2.7 million against a ₱19 million request. The NEP schedule contains the closest identifiable row, “Damulog, Bukidnon Bagong Pilipinas Health Center.” The name differs, so this is a candidate identity match supported by the municipality and facility name, not an exact string match.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

HFEP shortfall, utilization, reversions, and FY2027 catch-up funding

Members raised a reported HFEP shortfall of about 15 billion, low or delayed utilization, unused equipment, uneven construction standards, and hospital-specific infrastructure gaps. DOH said the shortfall reflected the difference between requested and granted funding, acknowledged the need to synchronize construction and equipment, and cited stronger project-management systems, site-readiness rules, local investment plans, and catch-up planning. Members also sought additional funding for hospitals in Negros Occidental, Northern Mindanao, Region 12, and other localities, while the agency discussed referral networks, phased construction, alternative equipment financing, and hospital prioritization. The committee highlighted 26 percent combined infrastructure and equipment disbursement, a proposed FY2027 catch-up amount of roughly 14 billion, and lower proposed capital outlay of 14.5 compared with 22.3 in the prior GAA. The chair required DOH to submit utilization and catch-up data by Friday, September 11th and prioritized funding information by Wednesday at 12 noon. The hearing was terminated and the proceedings on House Bill No. 10858 were suspended, leaving the FY2027 HFEP amount dependent on the requested submissions.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much HFEP funding had been allocated, released, utilized, delayed, or reverted; why infrastructure and equipment remained incomplete; and how much FY2027 funding was justified by a catch-up plan. Members also asked how HFEP and related hospital investments should be prioritized, standardized, and monitored before the committee acted on the proposed budget.

DOH said HFEP implementation should be governed by omnibus guidelines, site readiness, local health investment plans, and stronger project management linking construction, equipment, personnel, and operations. The agency acknowledged implementation and utilization problems, committed to submit historical utilization, reversion, release, and catch-up data, and said the FY2027 request should be based on historical performance and current project needs.

Outcome The committee did not settle the appropriate FY2027 HFEP amount. It required DOH to submit historical utilization, reversions, implementation, equipment, and catch-up information, plus prioritized and hospital-specific funding lists, before the committee and plenary deliberated further.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

DOH proposed budget reductions and priority funding requests

Members questioned how substantial reductions in medical assistance, HFEP, commodities, hospitals, emergency preparedness, and other programs would affect service delivery. DOH said it would rely on primary-care expansion, payment reform, procurement improvements, and efficiency measures, while requesting additional support for PhilHealth benefits, zero-balance billing, hospitals, and selected commodities. The committee raised specific concerns about a reported medical-assistance reduction from about 51 billion to about 24 billion, lower capital outlay from 22.3 to 14.5, and a possible additional hospital zero-balance-billing requirement of about 11 to 12 billion, although some transcript figures were unclear. Members also sought support for specialty hospitals, a regional hospital and outpatient department, senior-citizen flu vaccination, maternal care, primary-care facilities, and national hospital data systems. DOH committed to submit corporate-budget figures, prioritized funding lists, hospital-by-hospital zero-balance-billing needs, and equipment-financing information. The issue remained subject to further committee deliberation within limited fiscal space.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 reductions would affect medical assistance, hospital operations, medicines, immunization, HFEP, commodities, and zero-balance billing. It also sought to identify priority additions to the DOH and PhilHealth budgets, including capital outlay, primary care, and hospital-specific needs.

DOH said it would manage the reductions through primary-care expansion, payment and procurement reform, efficiency measures, and better hospital and financial-data systems. It maintained that additional support was needed for PhilHealth benefit expansion, zero-balance billing, hospitals, and selected commodities, but acknowledged that fiscal space was limited and several requested amounts required further breakdown or documentation.

Outcome The committee did not settle the adequacy of the reduced FY 2027 DOH budget or the final funding level for zero-balance billing, hospitals, HFEP, and capital outlay. DOH committed to submit the requested budget, hospital-prioritization, and equipment-financing information for further committee deliberation.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

Zero-balance billing and MAIFIP coverage for DOH and LGU hospitals

Rep. Brian Yamsuan and Rep. Edgar Erice questioned how zero-balance billing could continue after the proposed MAIFIP reduction and other DOH budget cuts. The DOH described a prospective, rules-based payment model and said PhilHealth packages would form the first tier, with MAIFIP providing complementary assistance. The agency cited R51 billion dollars falling to about R24 billion in MAIFIP, while another committee member noted that the 20 26 General Appropriations Act had a dedicated zero-balance-billing amount that was not clearly identified in the 20 27 National Expenditure Program. Vice Chair JC Rahman Nava then asked whether coverage would apply to all DOH hospitals and expand to LGU hospitals; the agency referred to 300 plus LGU hospitals and said a special provision was needed. The agency also said about 85 percent of LGU-hospital bills were already covered by PhilHealth, with the remaining 10, 15 percent to be addressed through expanded packages and MAIFIP. The committee accepted the agency's stated direction but left the sufficiency and final legal and budgetary basis of the expansion as matters requiring follow-through.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how zero-balance billing would be financed in FY 2027 after reductions in MAIFIP and related DOH programs. It also asked whether the coverage would apply to all DOH hospitals and be expanded to LGU and other non-DOH government hospitals, and how PhilHealth packages would complement MAIFIP.

The DOH said zero-balance billing would operate through complementation: PhilHealth packages would cover the first tier, with MAIFIP addressing the remaining eligible costs. The agency indicated that coverage was intended to include DOH hospitals and 300 plus LGU hospitals, but acknowledged that a special provision was needed for 20 27 and that expanded PhilHealth packages and rules for outliers were still being negotiated.

Outcome The agency stated that MAIFIP would complement PhilHealth and that the intended coverage would include DOH hospitals and 300 plus LGU hospitals, subject to a 20 27 special provision. The adequacy and dedicated identification of funding remained a concern, with PhilHealth package expansion and the final budget authority not fully settled.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

Vaccine procurement delays, coverage, and the FY2027 immunization budget

Rep. Brian Yamsuan asked about the FY2027 immunization budget, which an agency official stated as 6855000000, and about vaccine scheduling and essential-medicine procurement. Vice Chair Julienne Baronda challenged the DOH to justify additional funding while suppliers had an ongoing portfolio of about 15 billion and asked for delivery percentages and statuses for major vaccine and medicine procurements. The DOH reported awards or notices of award for several vaccines but acknowledged procurement delays, bid changes, and incomplete visibility over delivery percentages; Baronda requested a supplier-by-supplier performance matrix and the chair required a full report. Rep. Girlie Veloso cited coverage of almost 4 out of 10 children not being fully vaccinated and received a DOH plan focused on community outreach, trust-building, last-mile services, forecasting, cold-chain management, and digital records. Members then pressed the DOH over flu-vaccine delays, including the failure to procure for 20 25, emergency vaccination of only 2500 individuals, and planned coverage of 25 percent to 50 percent of senior citizens versus a cited 75 percent standard. The DOH committed to early procurement and the chair indicated that another small purchase could be made, but members said the explanation was insufficient.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the DOH had sufficient FY2027 funding and a reliable procurement system to deliver vaccines on time, particularly childhood, influenza, pneumococcal, HPV, rabies, and other priority vaccines. Members also asked how the DOH would address low childhood coverage, vaccine hesitancy, supply-chain weaknesses, and delayed flu vaccination for senior citizens.

The DOH said procurement delays were driven largely by bidding failures, procurement procedures, inadequate forecasting, and timing challenges for a vaccine with a one-year shelf life, rather than by a lack of vaccine availability. It said it was moving to early procurement, clearer terms of reference, stronger supply and cold-chain management, improved forecasting and digital information systems, community-level outreach, and a strategy targeting 25 percent of senior citizens annually, while acknowledging that coverage remained inadequate.

Outcome The DOH explained the procurement delays and outlined corrective strategies, but members remained dissatisfied with the flu-vaccine record and low coverage. The DOH was expected to submit procurement-performance information, pursue early procurement, and consider another small purchase; the underlying delivery and coverage problem remained open.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

Essential-medicine and TB-drug procurement, stockouts, and expirations

Rep. Brian Yamsuan asked how DOH would schedule immunization procurement and match essential medicines to local needs; the agency cited the approved FY 2027 immunization amount of about 6.86 billion and described bidding, centralized procurement, and inventory-management measures. Deputy Minority Leader Percy Sandania raised HIV test-kit and TB-drug stockout risks, and DOH said HIV procurement was nearing post-qualification and that the TB award was expected within the month or by the following month; the committee required a regional TB balance and risk report covering the suspended 3225000000 procurement. Rep. Caroline Agyao questioned medicine overstocking and expirations, and DOH said it was improving electronic inventory visibility and forecasting. Vice Chair Julienne Baronda questioned major vaccine and TB procurements, citing an ongoing portfolio of about 15.4 billion and a procurement pipeline of about 21.68 billion, and demanded a supplier-by-supplier performance matrix. Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron sought an updated Yakap medicine list, while Vice Chair Anna York Bondoc criticized delayed flu vaccine procurement and obtained a commitment for another small purchase. The issue therefore landed with agency follow-up commitments and requested documents, rather than a fully resolved finding.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DOH could procure essential medicines, TB drugs, vaccines, and HIV test kits on time while maintaining accurate inventories and preventing stockouts, overstocking, and expirations. Members also asked for supplier-by-supplier performance data, regional balances, and corrective measures for delayed or failed procurement.

DOH said procurement was governed by terms of reference, bidding, post-qualification, and other statutory procedures, while harder-to-procure vaccines, anti-HIV medicines, and TB medicines were centralized. The agency said it was improving inventory visibility and forecasting, reviewing the Yakap medicine list, pursuing delayed awards, and applying supplier-performance remedies, but several deliveries and requested data remained pending.

Outcome The agency gave partial explanations and several procurement-status updates, but the committee required additional reports on TB stocks, expired medicines, inventory, and supplier performance. Flu vaccine procurement remained a point of dissatisfaction, while the promised data submissions and corrective actions were left for follow-up and plenary consideration.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

YAKAP medicines, Gamut pharmacy access, and benefit expansion

Rep. Miro Quimbo and Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron supported Yakap while raising implementation, medicine-list, and pharmacy-access concerns. PhilHealth said it was reviewing the list, including medicines that were unavailable or obsolete, but was not prioritizing differential reimbursement between hospital and retail pharmacies. Rep. Rachel Singson pressed for a solution in provinces without Gamut pharmacies; PhilHealth discussed FDA-regulated mobile pharmacies, alternative licensing, and possible action within 30 days. Chair Mika Suansing cited the reported 20000 allocation per patient and encouraged future expansion subject to actuarial and fiscal review. PhilHealth and DOH committed to submit a prioritized list of possible benefit and funding changes and a hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the additional request, including about 12 billion as spoken in the transcript.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Yakap medicine list remained relevant and whether beneficiaries could access Yakap medicines in areas without Gamut-accredited pharmacies. It also examined possible changes to pharmacy reimbursement, the reported 20000 allocation per patient, and priorities for expanding PhilHealth benefits.

PhilHealth said it was reviewing and rationalizing the Yakap medicine list using provider feedback and was not currently prioritizing differential reimbursement between hospital and retail pharmacies. For areas without Gamut pharmacies, it was pursuing FDA rules for mobile pharmacy outreach, considering alternative pharmacy licensing, and supporting further Yakap expansion subject to actuarial review, available fiscal space, and program calibration.

Outcome The medicine-list review and access problems were acknowledged, but differential pharmacy reimbursement and alternative accreditation remained under study. PhilHealth and DOH committed to follow-up coordination and to submit prioritized funding and hospital-level information; Yakap expansion was encouraged but not decided.

DOH · 2026-09-07 · committed

PhilHealth and private-hospital payment, billing, and reimbursement rules

Members questioned DOH and PhilHealth on private-hospital payment terms, balance billing, professional fees, claims processing, and the treatment of hospital and physician charges. The agency said it was moving toward direct negotiations, rules-based global payments, and selective advance payments, with hospitals expected to provide no-balance-billing beds and include physicians in the payment arrangements. Reported figures included payment processing in about 15 to 20 days, a 10 percent no-balance-billing bed requirement, a 15000000000 HFEP shortfall, and estimated unallocated PhilHealth-related collections of about 199 billion in total. The agency also committed to guidelines by October 2026, provider-network targets by end-2027, an HMO complementation agreement, and studies or reports on billing and HFEP concerns. The issue was not fully resolved because specific payment terms, professional-fee safeguards, and remittance and billing reforms remained under development.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DOH and PhilHealth would pay private hospitals and physicians, including payment timing, advance or global payments, professional fees, claims processing, and safeguards against balance billing. Members also asked how private-provider networks, PhilHealth benefits, and hospital contracting would ensure timely, transparent, and affordable care.

DOH and PhilHealth said they were moving toward negotiated, rules-based and potentially global-budget payments rather than relying exclusively on fee-for-service reimbursement. Advance payments would be piloted selectively in exchange for no-balance-billing beds, predictable professional-fee arrangements, and lower patient out-of-pocket costs; provider networks would be built with LGUs and private providers, but several implementation guidelines and billing issues remained under study.

Outcome The agency answered the committee's principal questions by outlining negotiated and global-payment models, selective advance payments, no-balance-billing conditions, and provider-network targets. However, the payment terms, professional-fee controls, private-hospital invoice rules, remittance delays, and several implementing guidelines remained subject to study, negotiation, or future reports.

Professional-fee regulation and transparency in health-care billing

Rep. Miro Quimbo requested a written DOH update on professional-fee regulation, citing the growing share of professional fees in medical expenses and asking what legislative authority the department needed. Rep. Brian Yamsuan later asked how the DOH would address professional-fee controls amid a reported budget decrease stated as "50 per 53 percent" and zero balance billing. The agency discussed primary care, provider negotiations, fee-for-service, rent-seeking behavior, and a shift toward rules-based global payments, but did not give a detailed billing-control system. Yamsuan specifically sought safeguards against abusive or duplicate billing and a way to reconcile charges. The agency later said that professional fees should be transparent and accountable and that a mechanism should be established, while also mentioning "15, 20 days," whose context was unclear. The matter remained open pending the requested written update and more specific mechanisms.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOH could regulate, monitor, and require transparency for professional fees charged in government and private hospitals. It also sought mechanisms to prevent abusive or duplicate billing and to clarify what legislative tools or institutional arrangements the DOH needed.

The agency indicated that it was considering provider negotiations, a shift away from fee-for-service, and rules-based global payments to reduce rent-seeking and control payment incentives. It also agreed in principle that professional fees should be transparent and accountable and that a mechanism should be established, but it did not specify the mechanism, enforcement authority, or implementation timetable.

Outcome The agency acknowledged the need for transparent and accountable professional-fee practices and referred generally to provider negotiations, global payment arrangements, and a future mechanism. The requested written update and the specific regulatory, billing-verification, and enforcement arrangements were not provided in the transcript.

Hospital capacity, specialty facilities, and regional hospital development

Members raised concerns that hospital capacity and infrastructure had not kept pace with statutory bed expansions and patient referrals. Ferrer sought phased additional funding for Negros Occidental, while Suntay questioned the absence of capital outlay for specialty and large tertiary hospitals such as East Avenue Medical Center. Lagbaf reported severe overcrowding at Northern Mindanao Medical Center, including 760 to 780 patients against 692 beds and emergency-room utilization of 403 percent; DOH cited delayed releases, infrastructure lag, and the need for a stronger referral network. Baronda pressed for action on Western Visayas Medical Center and its cancer center, and the chair required a full report. Hernandez sought additional funding for a regional hospital and outpatient department, while DOH indicated that a 100-bed regional hospital could cost more than 1 billion and recognized the need to support conversion of SokSargen General Hospital. DOH also committed to flood-response planning, standardized hospital data systems, equipment-financing analysis, and a hospital-by-hospital breakdown of additional funding requests before plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 budget would adequately expand and staff DOH hospitals, specialty facilities, and regional referral networks. Members also asked how DOH prioritized capital outlay, addressed overcrowding and delayed construction, and would support hospital conversions and flood-resilient infrastructure.

DOH said hospital and specialty-facility funding should be based on catchment-area needs, referral networks, hospital development plans, project readiness, and equipment and staffing requirements. The agency acknowledged infrastructure and data-system gaps, supported interim referral and private-hospital arrangements, and undertook to submit catch-up plans, reports, financial models, and hospital-level funding priorities.

Outcome The committee did not finally resolve the requested hospital-expansion and capital-outlay increases during the hearing. DOH was directed or undertook to submit hospital-level funding priorities, development and catch-up plans, and reports before plenary, leaving the amounts subject to further committee deliberation.

Pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing localization

Deputy Speaker Serge Memon raised the risk of renewed foreign medicine-supply disruptions and asked how the government would support local pharmaceutical manufacturers. The DOH cited negotiated rates, procurement-volume shifts, DTI manufacturing provisions, and the Clark pharma hub as possible incentives, and said an ITRM vaccine study was underway. Memon argued that a 6 year tax holiday was insufficient and pointed to Malaysia's 70 percent government-purchase market share, suggesting at least 50 percent sustainable support for manufacturers. TS Miron separately urged the government to establish vaccine fill-and-finish capacity using imported bulk vaccine. He said the arrangement could save billions, but the agency made no specific commitment to establish the facility or adopt the proposed procurement targets.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what the DOH planned to do to support local pharmaceutical manufacturing and reduce dependence on foreign medicine suppliers. It also considered whether the government should develop domestic vaccine fill-and-finish capacity and adopt stronger procurement or market incentives.

The DOH stated that it was considering incentives for local pharmaceutical suppliers, including negotiated rates, procurement-volume shifts, DTI manufacturing-plant provisions, and the Clark pharma hub. It also said an ITRM study on vaccines was underway, but it did not provide a specific commitment to establish a government fill-and-finish facility or adopt the proposed procurement shares.

Outcome The DOH presented general incentive and procurement approaches and noted an ongoing vaccine-related study, but no specific fill-and-finish project, procurement-share policy, or implementation timetable was adopted during the exchange. The proposals remained for further consideration.

FDA medicine-registration backlog and regulatory-fee policy

Rep. Caroline Aguil raised the recurring FDA registration backlog and requested data covering at least 50 widely used generic medicines, with separate counts for principal CPRs, related CPRs, and CLIDPs or “baby CPRs.” The FDA director general said the agency would provide information for the past 4 years and reported a total backlog of 19000 applications, including almost 15000 in CDRR. A member identified by the chair as DS Baron proposed 2 years of provisional registration for certain products, automatic renewal of medical devices, and use of the FDA's retained income of about 2 billion through a DBM business plan. The member also objected to a regulatory-fee increase described as 1000 percent and sought its deferral. The FDA said it would revisit the policies, and the chair required an update, but the proposed reforms and fee deferral remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the scale and composition of the FDA's medicine-registration backlog, including the distinction between principal CPRs and related or “baby” CPRs and CLIDPs. Members also asked whether policy reforms, additional manpower, use of retained FDA income, provisional registration, and fee-policy changes could reduce the backlog and improve access to generic medicines.

The FDA acknowledged a current backlog of 19000 applications, including almost 15000 in CDRR, and committed to provide data for the past 4 years. The director general said the FDA would revisit its policies, including the reforms raised by the members, to align them with the mandate to make medicines available to the public.

Outcome The FDA answered the headline backlog question and committed to submit historical and disaggregated data. It also undertook a policy review, but no decision was recorded on provisional registration, automatic device renewal, use of retained income, or deferral of the fee increase.

Questions and agency response

It also asked about delayed PhilHealth fund allocations, HMO complementation, and the timeline for integrating medicines into the field health system.

DOH said provider networks should be organized around province-wide or citywide systems led by LGUs, with private providers complementing public capacity and patients routed to appropriate accredited facilities. It reported ongoing work on private-bed guidelines, initial HMO complementation agreements, and discussions with DBM and DOF on delayed PhilHealth-related allocations, while maintaining that benefit expansion should continue.

Outcome DOH provided implementation targets and undertook further work on private-bed guidelines, LGU networks, HMO complementation, and medicines integration. The delayed PhilHealth allocations and the precise status and cause of the outstanding funds were not fully resolved during the exchange.

Health data systems and national capacity planning

Vice Chair Javi Benitez asked how a national data repository could track patients, diseases, beds, hospital capacity, and budget needs, and how primary-care expansion could reduce out-of-pocket spending. The DOH said it was developing a repository integrating Yakap and eventually inpatient records, while targeting 60 percent Yakap enrollment by 20 28 and at least 50 percent by that year in its more cautious projection. Officials said the country lacked around 3000 primary-care facilities, that 52 percent had a Gamut provider, and that around hundred 20000000000 in reimbursements could ideally go to primary care; the amount was unclear as spoken. The secretary said 800000000000 was an aggressive health-care requirement, cited a projected PhilHealth payout of 420000000000, and said additional subsidies and reforms were necessary. Deputy Speaker Albee Benitez then raised fragmented DOH hospital data systems and lower capital outlay, with the DOH reporting 22.3 previously approved versus 14.5 proposed for 20 27. The DOH committed to standard reporting and to provide equipment-financing and financial-modeling information.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOH would build an integrated national health data system, use it to plan capacity and reduce out-of-pocket spending, and expand primary-care access. It also asked whether DOH hospitals could standardize their data systems and how the agency would address lower capital-outlay funding for equipment.

The DOH said it was pursuing a national health data repository integrating Yakap outpatient records and eventually inpatient records, while standardizing hospital financial and operational reporting. It said primary-care expansion and lower out-of-pocket spending required additional subsidies, efficiency reforms, value-based payment, expanded Yakap and Gamut coverage, and a mix of public and private providers; it also supported examining pay-per-use, PPP, and other equipment-financing arrangements.

Outcome The DOH answered the data, primary-care, and capital-outlay questions and undertook to standardize hospital reporting and provide equipment-financing information. The broader funding requirement and the timeline for achieving national coverage remained dependent on additional subsidies, efficiency reforms, and future implementation.

The DOH committed to submit those materials, leaving the requested effectiveness comparison for follow-up.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOH funded and administered drug-treatment and rehabilitation programs, including which programs were voluntary, compulsory, or court-referred and what safeguards protected informed free consent. Members also sought a facility- and program-level budget breakdown, beneficiary costs, and comparisons with alternative harm-reduction models.

The DOH characterized drug use and related illness as a medical and potential epidemic issue, supported treatment and rehabilitation centers, and said it was expanding primary-care, health-promotion, and community-based responses. It agreed to provide historical budget data, implementation reviews, and cost-per-beneficiary and alternative-model comparisons.

Outcome The DOH answered the facility-count and budget questions but did not provide the requested beneficiary-cost analysis or alternative-model comparison during the hearing. It committed to submit the requested budget breakdown, implementation review, and comparative cost information.

Questions and agency response

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

DICT budget utilization, unobligated funds, payables, and project bottlenecks

Rep. Romeo Momo and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned DICT's low utilization, unobligated balance, payables, project delays, and manpower capacity. Members cited about 61.7 percent obligation and 22 percent disbursement for 20 25, a 9 percent 20 26 obligation figure, and an unobligated balance of about 20.5 billion, while DICT reported a 24 percent BUR and said it had released 89 percent of downloaded funds. DICT attributed delays to the 85 percent BUR threshold, late fund downloads, extended implementation periods, procurement cycles, World Bank rules, and insufficient personnel; DBM had approved 115 of about 500 requested positions. Members also pressed DICT to clarify its claim of 100 percent DepEd school connectivity and to identify unpaid e-government service providers, while DICT agreed to submit lists and reports. Rep. Iris Marie Montes raised the Philippine Digital Infrastructure Project, and DICT acknowledged two failed biddings and a 6-month delay but projected BUR shares of 3.03 by September, 45 percent by October, and 80 percent by December. DICT also confirmed that a COA-directed UIS GDA payment for services rendered without a renewed contract had already been paid and said current contracts would be handled more strictly.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DICT could efficiently utilize its existing and proposed appropriations, identify the causes of unobligated funds and unpaid obligations, and explain project implementation delays. Members also asked whether DICT had sufficient manpower and procurement capacity to deliver connectivity and digital infrastructure projects.

DICT said its reported BUR was 24 percent as of June, rather than the 9 percent figure attributed to COA, and said it would reconcile the difference with COA. The agency attributed weak utilization and project delays to late fund downloads, an 85 percent BUR threshold, project implementation periods extending into the following year, manpower shortages, unusual procurement cycles, and World Bank procurement rules. DICT said it had paid the COA-directed UIS GDA claim, would submit lists and reports on payables and unpaid providers, and was taking steps to accelerate procurement and project execution.

Outcome DICT provided competing utilization figures and explanations for delayed implementation, but the discrepancy between the 9 percent COA figure and the 24 percent DICT/DBM figure remained subject to reconciliation. The agency undertook to submit multiple lists and reports and to accelerate procurement, while the project delays, payables, and detailed coverage claims were not fully resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

Questions and agency response

Outcome DICT's explanation established that PDIP had suffered two failed biddings and was about six months behind its original schedule, but the agency said procurement adjustments with the World Bank were underway and projected implementation through December. DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Government data centers, cloud subscriptions, and data sovereignty

Members questioned DICT about the location and security of government data, the use of foreign cloud services, and the adequacy of domestic data-center capacity. DICT said about 80 percent of government data was outside the Philippines and that some eGov storage was in Singapore and the United States, while its first Subic facility held only about 60 racks. DICT estimated that complete sovereign data-center infrastructure would cost around 20 billion, with a return on investment in about 4 to 5 years, and said unified data management could yield roughly 50 to 60 percent savings. Officials said cloud subscriptions were procured through competitive bidding, eGov used AWS for about 80 percent of its public-cloud service, and migration would occur gradually. The department also said eGov was government-owned, its source code was maintained by DICT, and underlying data remained decentralized with the responsible agencies. DICT committed to issue EO 119 guidelines, develop government-wide data standards, convene an oversight committee, and submit procurement and infrastructure information, but no firm localization timetable was established.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish where government data was stored, how data sovereignty and localization would be implemented, and whether DICT had sufficient domestic data-center capacity. Members also asked about the cost of foreign cloud subscriptions, the proposed cost and savings from sovereign data centers, procurement safeguards, cybersecurity, and the timetable for moving critical government workloads locally.

DICT said EO 119 would establish a risk-based classification and residency framework under which top-secret and other sensitive national-security data would remain in the Philippines, while lower-classified data could be contracted out within Philippine jurisdiction. DICT acknowledged substantial reliance on foreign cloud services but said it was building domestic capacity, reducing duplicated data, using encryption and decentralized agency control, and gradually migrating workloads to locally owned and managed sovereign data centers.

Outcome DICT acknowledged that much government and eGov data remained on foreign public-cloud infrastructure, while presenting domestic sovereign data centers as the long-term solution. The department committed to issue EO 119 guidelines, develop standards, provide procurement information, and progressively migrate data, but the hearing did not settle the precise 2027 infrastructure requirement or a firm timetable for full localization.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Cybersecurity program funding and protection of government systems

The Chair framed cybersecurity as a national-security responsibility and asked whether the proposed program would measurably protect government systems, critical infrastructure, and Filipino data. DICT reported NSOC monitoring of 99 agencies and about 6.7 billion security alerts, while proposing expanded VAPT, private-sector certification, professional registration, and cybersecurity laboratories. Rep. Presley de Jesus questioned overseas cloud storage, data-center capacity, encryption, and control of eGov data; DICT said data was decentralized, used double-layered encryption, and could be localized through a projected investment of about 20 billion with estimated savings of 50 to 60 percent. Rep. JP Pagianos asked what protection would result from the 1094000000 cybersecurity program after reported website compromises and an eGov disruption; DICT answered that the budget covered currently protected agencies but not the whole country or all critical infrastructure. DICT and CICC said they were investigating a reported Department of Labor portal incident, while the NPC described expanded breach monitoring and faster registration validation. The committee received commitments for reports, targets, procurement records, case figures, and regional validation, so the issue was not fully resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DICT's cybersecurity program would provide measurable protection for government systems, critical infrastructure, and Filipino data, especially after reported government-portal compromises. It also examined whether data localization, cloud arrangements, privacy enforcement, and agency responsibilities were sufficient to reduce cyber risks.

DICT said its cybersecurity approach combined NSOC monitoring, encryption, decentralized data custody, agency assistance and training, VAPT, private-sector certification, professional registration, and proactive breach monitoring. It acknowledged that the proposed cybersecurity budget was sufficient for agencies currently covered but insufficient to protect the entire country and all critical infrastructure, and it said data localization and consolidation could reduce costs and duplication.

Outcome DICT presented existing cyber-monitoring, encryption, training, VAPT, and privacy-monitoring measures, but acknowledged that the proposed cybersecurity funding would not protect the whole country or all critical infrastructure. Several measurable targets and documents, including cybersecurity outcomes, procurement records, eGov usage data, case figures, and regional validation, were left for submission or follow-up.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

eGov PH sustainability, operating costs, personnel, and service continuity

DICT presented eGov as a widely used, government-owned platform with about 61 million downloads, 56 million verified users, more than 1.2 billion eGovDX transactions, and 1,332 integrated services. The chair and Representative Richard Gomez asked whether the in-house system could survive changes in administration; DICT said continuity was assured but that low government salaries threatened staffing and that a Magna Carta for IT professionals was needed. Members also challenged DICT over unobligated funds, payables, an outage attributed to an unexpected surge in usage, and the lack of precise information on unpaid providers. DICT said local data sovereignty would require about 20 billion, while unified data management could produce roughly 50 to 60 percent savings against cloud costs of 30 to 40 billion. The agency reported that eGov data were decentralized, encrypted, and integrated through eGovDX, although much cloud storage remained in Singapore and AWS accounted for about 80 percent of eGov cloud services. Members requested written reports on usage, connectivity, payables, school and SUC coverage, regional targets, and data infrastructure, while DICT committed to additional legislative, standards, cybersecurity, and digital nomad visa work.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DICT's in-house eGov platform could remain operational across administrations, whether it had sufficient personnel and funding, and whether its usage, cloud arrangements, cybersecurity, and data infrastructure were sustainable. Members also asked what measurable connectivity and digital-service outcomes would result from the FY 2027 budget.

DICT maintained that eGov was a government-owned, in-house platform with guaranteed institutional continuity, but said sustained operations depended on adequate funding and competitive compensation for IT personnel. It supported moving toward sovereign local data infrastructure, standardized and decentralized data exchange, stronger cybersecurity capacity, and continued congressional support, while acknowledging that several requested lists, targets, cost reconciliations, and timelines remained to be submitted.

Outcome The committee received DICT's assurance that eGov was government-owned, in-house, and capable of administrative continuity, but accepted that staffing, compensation, cloud costs, and service-continuity funding required further action. Multiple written submissions and legislative follow-up were requested; the precise unpaid obligations, SUC coverage, end-to-end usage, regional targets, local-data migration cost and timeline, and full budget reconciliation remained open.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

National ID integration, social-media registration, and online age verification

Minority members Renee Co and Antonio Tinio questioned whether national-ID-based social-media registration would be effective, privacy-protective, and compatible with rights, particularly after DICT and NTC acknowledged limits in SIM registration. DICT said the national ID could provide a stronger identity and age-verification record, with Roblox targeted for compliance by October and Meta engagement continuing before the end of the year. Members also pressed DICT and NTC on fake IDs, scam complaints, the number of acceptable IDs, and the proposed reduction from 17 IDs to 3. The NPC and DICT acknowledged unresolved risks involving data minimization, surveillance, data sovereignty, and access to government databases. DICT linked the issue to data localization, citing about 92 million digital national IDs, an estimated 20 billion data-center requirement, potential savings of 50 to 60 percent, and continuing reliance on foreign cloud services during migration. The committee obtained commitments for a position paper, procurement and budget information, implementing guidelines, technical standards, an online-gaming age-verification standard, and continued consultation, but the broader policy remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DICT could technically and legally integrate the national ID into social-media, SIM, and online-gaming age and identity verification, and whether such integration would be effective, privacy-protective, and enforceable. Members also examined the related use of national ID and government data systems, data sovereignty, cloud storage, and cybersecurity.

DICT supported using the national ID as a higher-confidence source for identity and age verification, potentially linked through PSA systems and APIs while limiting the information disclosed to platforms. DICT said implementation remained technically and legally complex, required public consultation, stronger platform compliance, data-minimization safeguards, data localization, interoperable standards, and cybersecurity controls. It undertook to develop standards, submit position papers and procurement information, recommend online-gaming age-verification standards, and pursue migration toward Philippine data centers.

Outcome DICT answered the technical and policy questions but did not establish that social-media registration or national-ID integration had been fully implemented, tested, or accepted by all stakeholders. The matter remained subject to public consultation, platform compliance, proposed SIM-registration amendments, technical standards, implementing guidelines, and multiple promised submissions.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Online scams, child safety, and technology-facilitated abuse response

The chair raised complaints about harmful online content, including 197 Facebook links, and directed DICT and CICC to review and report on them while asking Meta to explain its dispositions. Representative Ann Matibag pressed for timelines and mechanisms requiring Meta and Roblox to comply with Philippine law and protect children; DICT committed to Roblox compliance by October and described interagency threat-monitoring operations. Members questioned whether SIM registration had reduced scams, and DICT and NTC acknowledged gaps, supported stronger national-ID verification, and committed to submit a position paper on limiting IDs and SIM ownership. The committee also examined a hacked portal, NPC spending and privacy-monitoring targets, and 47446 online-lending complaints. NPC explained that additional funding would expand breach monitoring and registration capacity and agreed to provide specific online-lending case numbers. The issue landed with several agency commitments, but major enforcement and legislative questions remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DICT and its attached agencies had effective, enforceable, and privacy-compliant mechanisms to address unlawful online content, scams, child exploitation, technology-facilitated abuse, and data breaches. Members also examined whether platform compliance, SIM-registration controls, interagency response, and privacy-enforcement targets were adequate and funded.

DICT said existing mechanisms could coordinate platform compliance, law-enforcement response, scam investigations, and child-safety interventions, but acknowledged that SIM registration had not fully achieved its objectives and that stronger ID controls might require legislation. DICT and attached agencies undertook platform engagements, operationalized the CICC threat-monitoring center, supported national-ID verification, expanded privacy monitoring, and agreed to submit or provide requested materials.

Outcome The agencies answered the operational questions and made commitments on complaint review, Roblox compliance, an ID position paper, breach investigation, and NPC case data. However, stronger Meta enforcement, legislative limits on acceptable IDs and SIMs, and concrete enforcement results for online-lending complaints remained open.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · unresolved

Digital Workforce Hub renewal and beneficiary expansion

Representative Sarah Elago questioned the renewal of the Digital Workforce Hub, its public cost, whether it was locally developed, and the sharp increase in beneficiaries targeted for 2027. Undersecretary Aguirre said the platform had cost 60000000 in the current year and that renewal was estimated at 40000000, with an unlimited-user license. He described a free platform that matched CVs to jobs, identified skills gaps, and directed users to training and micro-credentials. Aguirre said the platform was localized for the Philippines but originally developed by a Singaporean entity. He attributed the increase from 94778 beneficiaries in 2026 to 631251 in 2027 to the shift from face-to-face to online delivery and broader implementation through LGUs and other partners. The rationale was stated, but the transcript did not show detailed supporting metrics or a final resolution of the target's validity.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the public cost and development status of the Digital Workforce Hub renewal, and why the target number of digital-economy beneficiaries would rise sharply from 2026 to 2027. It also sought the expected reach and benefits of the platform.

DICT said the Digital Workforce Hub would be renewed for an estimated 40000000 and could serve an unlimited number of users under the procured license. The agency said the platform was localized for the Philippines but originally developed by a Singaporean entity, and that the higher beneficiary target reflected online delivery, toolkits, and expanded implementation through partner institutions.

Outcome DICT provided the renewal cost, described the platform's functions and partnerships, clarified that it was localized rather than wholly locally developed, and attributed the higher 2027 target to online and partner-based implementation. The transcript did not show a further challenge, document submission, or separate validation of the beneficiary projection.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

National Privacy Commission funding, enforcement, and performance

Members questioned DICT and the NPC on whether national-ID-based social-media verification could protect privacy after SIM registration had fallen short of its promises. DICT said the Philippines could be the first country to integrate a sovereign ID into a social-media platform, while the NPC said data minimization, database security, lawful processing, and public consultation were necessary. DICT described data-sovereignty safeguards, including encryption, contractor qualification, and keeping sensitive government data in the Philippines, and committed to issue implementing guidelines and procurement information. Rep. Dino also questioned data-center spending, including a cited historical budget of about 8.7 billion and a disputed 20 27 figure, while DICT said about 700 million had been spent on the first Subic data center. Rep. Pagianos challenged the NPC's increase from about 440 million to 505 million despite lower stated targets; the NPC said the funds would expand breach monitoring from 20 to 50 websites and accelerate controller registration from 7 days to 3 days or 1 day if possible. The NPC attributed 83000000 in unused funds mainly to a delayed fit-out and committed to provide online-lending case numbers, while regional connectivity validation and the final privacy framework remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the National Privacy Commission and DICT had sufficient funding, enforcement capacity, and safeguards to protect personal and government data. Members also asked whether proposed national-ID-based social-media verification, data-sovereignty rules, privacy enforcement, and breach monitoring would produce measurable results and respect privacy rights.

DICT and the NPC maintained that national-ID-based verification and data-sovereignty measures could be implemented with data minimization, security, consultation, encryption, contractor qualification, and lawful processing safeguards. The NPC defended its increased 20 27 request as funding for expanded breach monitoring, faster registration validation, and more registered controllers, while explaining that unused funds were mainly linked to a delayed and ultimately abandoned fit-out contract.

Outcome The agency answered the committee's principal policy and funding questions but left several implementation matters for consultation, guidelines, and documentary submissions. The NPC defended the additional budget, explained the unused funds, and committed to provide online-lending case data; privacy safeguards and the final design of national-ID-based social-media verification remained unresolved.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · unresolved

Disaster communications and connectivity restoration

Caroline Agyao asked DICT how it would provide emergency communications and rapidly restore connectivity in calamity-prone and commercially underserved areas. She sought details on deployable assets, activation time, operational sites, maintenance costs, 2027 coverage, and funding for school and community power supplies. DICT cited improved availability of about 60 percent in affected areas, telecommunications-provider availability of 99.8 percent, and a contractual restoration period of 72 hours. The agency also described longer contracts, a nationwide project covering about 5,400 schools, and a DepEd partnership to install solar-powered Starlink. The committee did not receive clear answers to all requested budget and operational figures, so the issue remained unresolved despite the agency's described projects and commitments.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what DICT programs, assets, funding, and response times would support emergency communications and rapid connectivity restoration in calamity-prone areas. It also asked how many sites and schools had reliable connectivity, how DICT would serve communities without commercial signal, and whether schools could maintain links during disasters.

DICT said it was strengthening disaster communications through deployable assets, telecommunications and satellite arrangements, longer service contracts, and a nationwide school-connectivity project. It presented Starlink, including solar-powered installations with DepEd, as a resilient option for schools and remote communities, while stating that managed-services contracts required restoration within 72 hours.

Outcome DICT provided a general operational response, citing a 72-hour restoration requirement, longer contracts, coverage of 5400 plus schools, and solar-powered Starlink for resilient school connectivity. The transcript did not show a precise response to the requested budget amounts, site counts, per-site maintenance costs, or funding for power-supply units.

DICT · 2026-09-07 · committed

DICT IT staffing and compensation capacity

Rep. Romeo Momo questioned DICT’s low absorptive capacity, citing a 61.7 percent obligation rate, 22 percent disbursement against obligations, and a disputed June obligation figure of 9 percent versus DICT’s reported 24 percent. DICT attributed implementation difficulties partly to funding-release requirements and manpower constraints, saying it had about 1700 JOs or SOs, had requested about 500 positions, and received about 115 additional positions. The committee then asked whether the in-house eGov super app could continue across administrations; DICT said continuity was assured but required adequate staffing and funding, particularly more competitive IT salaries. DICT cited developer salary grades of 12, 15, and 17, IT salary grades of 20 and 22, and programmer pay of around 50 to 60000, with a maximum range of around 59000 to 89000 a month. Rep. Richard Gomez and the chair committed to pursuing legislation on IT salary grades and a Magna Carta for IT professionals. The utilization discrepancies and project-implementation figures remained unreconciled, but legislative and administrative follow-up was undertaken.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DICT had sufficient budget-utilization and manpower capacity to implement its growing appropriations and sustain systems developed in-house, particularly the eGov super app. It also examined IT salary levels and whether legislative action, including a Magna Carta for IT professionals, was needed to retain technical personnel.

DICT said implementation capacity had been constrained by staffing, outdated organizational and staffing structures, and the inability to offer compensation competitive with the private sector. It maintained that the eGov app could continue across administrations because it was developed in-house, but said sustained funding, adequate personnel, and legislative action on IT compensation and a Magna Carta for IT professionals were needed.

Outcome DICT’s continuity assurance for eGov was accepted as conditional on resolving personnel and funding needs. The COA-versus-DICT utilization figures and the unimplemented-project amounts were not reconciled during the hearing, while legislative action on IT compensation and a Magna Carta was committed for follow-up.

THE JUDICIARY · 2026-09-07 · committed

FY2027 Judiciary budget proposal of about 86.27 billion

Justice Estuesta presented a proposed FY2027 Judiciary budget of about 86.27 billion, compared with about 70.611 billion under the FY2026 General Appropriations Act. He detailed proposed allocations for the Supreme Court and lower courts, PET, Court of Appeals, Sandigan Bayan, and Court of Tax Appeals, and sought about 5.344 billion in further augmentations, including court-complex requirements and sheriff hazard pay. Representative Roman Romulo asked whether DBM had commented on the proposal and whether the amount would support the Judiciary's programs; the Judiciary said it had not received DBM's comments and that funding all programs was its goal. Patal also questioned electronic discovery procedures, and the Judiciary said electronic evidence rules were still under review, with privacy, relevance, materiality, and forensic issues requiring consideration. Representatives Jan Rurik Padiernos and Biloso expressed support, with Padianos conditioning support on measurable performance and accountability. The committee invited augmentation letters by Wednesday before lunch, promised consideration subject to fiscal space, and then terminated the hearing.

Questions and agency response

What was the Judiciary's proposed FY2027 budget, how was it divided among the courts, and what additional augmentations or program-related funding did the Judiciary seek? The committee also sought to establish whether DBM had reviewed the proposal, whether the budget would support the Judiciary's programs, and how electronic discovery reforms were progressing.

The Judiciary supported its proposed FY2027 budget of PHP 86271000000 and said the amount was intended to fund all planned programs. It additionally sought 5344000000 in augmentations, including court-complex requirements and sheriff hazard pay, while electronic-discovery procedures remained under review through revisions to the rules on evidence.

Outcome The committee terminated the hearing after the Judiciary presented its original proposal and requested further augmentation. Additional funding remained subject to the courts' Wednesday submissions, subcommittee review, and available fiscal space; DBM comments and finalized electronic-discovery protocols were not yet available.

THE JUDICIARY · 2026-09-07 · committed

About 4.3 billion MOOE increase for case backlogs

Rep. Renee Co asked how much of the roughly 4.3 billion MOOE increase would directly clear backlogs, particularly in lower courts reporting first-half disposal rates of about 65 to 69 percent. Justice Estuesta answered that the funds would support case-flow management, ICT systems, monitoring through the CMO data hub, and lower-court personnel upgrading, but he did not give a specific backlog-allocation amount. He reported 4 6300 judge vacancies, or 16.7 percent of authorized positions, and undertook to pursue funding measures while the Judiciary was asked to submit staffing lists. Rep. John Tracy Cagas raised delays in election cases and obtained an assurance that a time-bound election protest would hopefully be resolved before the next election. The agency also committed to look for funding for a Davao Sur House of Justice at 150000000, while Rep. Charah Jain Ilago’s request for detailed spousal- and child-support outcomes was only partially answered. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos supported the budget subject to measurable reductions in delays and stronger accountability.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much of the roughly 4.3 billion MOOE increase would directly address case backlogs and speed case processing, particularly in first-level courts. It also examined whether staffing and judicial vacancies were limiting disposition rates and whether the Judiciary had measurable steps to reduce delays.

The Judiciary said the MOOE increase would support case-flow management, monitoring through the CMO data hub, ICT and digital systems, and the upgrading and reclassification of lower-court personnel. It also said judge vacancies were constrained by the lack of NOSCAs and promised efforts to secure funding and accelerate time-bound election cases, but it did not provide a specific amount of the MOOE increase dedicated solely to backlog reduction.

Outcome The Judiciary explained the systems and personnel measures that would support case disposition but did not identify a specific portion of the 4300000000 MOOE increase dedicated to clearing backlogs. Staffing data and commitments on election cases and the Davao Sur facility were noted, while the support-case outcome data requested by Rep. Ilago remained incomplete.

THE JUDICIARY · 2026-09-07 · committed

Funding and NOSCAs for newly created courts and plantilla positions

Rep. Renee Co asked how the proposed budget increase would reduce case backlogs and how many judge and court personnel positions remained unfilled in newly created courts. Justice Estuesta said staffing depended on NOSCAs, reported 4 6300 judge vacancies, and said the Fiscal Autonomy Act could provide a solution after the 120-day DBM period. The chair pressed the Judiciary to complete the IRR and use its fiscal autonomy, while Justice Marquez said approval would be pursued in September October and that the Judiciary could program positions for funding. DBM described a proposal including 46 family courts worth 541103000 and stated that it had no opposition to the Judiciary's legal authority. Justice Villanueva reported 135 courts requiring about 1.4 billion in additional funding and committed to submit the relevant requests and amounts. The chair directed that the FY 2027 budget consideration focus on NOSCA requests for which the 120-day period had elapsed, leaving broader implementation pending.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how funding and staffing would address vacancies in newly created courts, including the number of unfilled judicial and court personnel positions and the status of required NOSCAs. It also pressed the Judiciary and DBM on whether the Fiscal Autonomy Act allowed the Judiciary to proceed with staffing and funding without waiting for DBM action.

The Judiciary said staffing newly created courts depended on NOSCAs under the prior process, but it recognized that RA 1 2 2 3 3 and the Fiscal Autonomy Act could allow programming and funding positions after DBM failed to act within 120 days. The Judiciary committed to pursue the IRR, identify eligible courts and positions, and submit additional funding requirements, while DBM stated that it had no opposition to the Judiciary's authority under the law.

Outcome The matter was left with a commitment by the Judiciary to submit the NOSCA and funding information for the 135 courts and to pursue implementation of the Fiscal Autonomy Act. The chair limited immediate budget consideration to requests meeting the 120-day condition, while the broader timing of the IRR and staffing of all newly created courts remained open.

The Chair framed the budget discussion around the 138 unorganized courts and the Judiciary’s continuing reforms under SPJI. Justice Estuesta presented a proposed Judiciary budget of about 86.3 billion and described digital, infrastructure, case-disposition, and justice-sector convergence milestones supporting the 2022–2027 plan. Rep. Sarah Elago asked whether SPJI was on schedule and how it integrated gender and development; the Judiciary answered that the plan was on track and cited gender-sensitivity training, gender-fair language, gender-neutral comfort rooms, legal-feminism research, and a digital GAD corner. The Judiciary also discussed justice zones and a Justice Sector Convergence Program, but the proposed amount was garbled and inconsistent in the transcript. Rep. Jay Vergara requested detailed digitalization figures after being told that Supreme Court digital infrastructure totaled about 5.21 billion, and the agency undertook to provide them. Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. supported an adequate budget increase, citing nearly 99 percent obligation of available allotments and improved GAD-budget utilization.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Judiciary’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations was on schedule, how its reforms were being funded, and whether gender and development commitments were integrated into the plan and budget. Members also examined digitalization and justice-sector convergence funding, including whether the Judiciary could absorb additional resources.

The Judiciary stated that SPJI was on track and that its 2027 budget was designed both to sustain current reforms and to support transition to the next Chief Justice. It said gender responsiveness had been institutionalized through training, gender-fair language, gender-neutral facilities, legal-feminism research, a digital GAD corner, and related justice-sector initiatives, while additional digitalization details would be submitted separately.

Outcome The Judiciary’s SPJI was presented as on track, with gender responsiveness described as institutionalized through multiple programs and facilities. Members expressed support for additional resources, but detailed digitalization figures were left for submission and the Justice Sector Convergence Program amount remained unclear in the transcript.

Judicial security and protection of judges and legal professionals

Rep. Renee Ko raised concerns about attacks, threats, and killings involving judges and legal professionals, citing 35 security operations and the Judiciary's proposed increase of 15000000000. The Judiciary said its Office of the Judiciary Marshals was still being staffed, lacked sufficient manpower for independent investigations, and relied heavily on the PNP and NBI. Rep. Ko requested information on extrajudicial killings, attacks, and threats covering 2025 through 2026 before plenary deliberations. The Judiciary said Supreme Court committees were revising the rules on Amparo, Habeas Data, and other remedies, and hoped to pass them before November 6, within the next 2 months. The chair directed submission of the requested materials but ruled that internal drafts could only be provided after approval.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the extent of threats, attacks, and killings involving judges and legal professionals; the Judiciary's capacity to investigate and protect them; and whether updated protective-writ rules, including the writ of Kalayaan, were being developed and could be submitted before plenary deliberations.

The Judiciary said the Office of the Judiciary Marshals was responding to security risks involving judges but was still being staffed and lacked sufficient manpower for independent investigative work. It said the Judiciary therefore relied heavily on the PNP and NBI, while Supreme Court committees were revising the rules on Amparo, Habeas Data, and other remedies as part of the strategic plan for judicial innovation.

Outcome The Judiciary committed to provide the requested information and materials, while the chair ruled that still-internal draft rules could not be demanded. The status of the proposed budget increase and the Judiciary's independent investigative capacity remained dependent on further submissions and staffing support.

Election-case disposition and delayed Supreme Court resolutions

Rep. John Tracy Cagas raised concerns about Supreme Court election cases that remained pending, including matters that had been unresolved for almost a year. The Chair emphasized that election cases required expedited handling because elected officials were limited to three terms and a three-year term. The court administrator said three Supreme Court members were aware of the time-sensitive petitions and assured the committee that the election protest would hopefully be resolved before the next election. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why election-related cases before the Supreme Court remained unresolved and whether the Court could adopt a faster procedure given the time limits of elected terms. It also sought an assurance that the relevant cases would be resolved within a timeframe meaningful to the next election.

The Judiciary explained that election petitions under Rules 64 and 65 follow a process requiring comments from the parties, collation of pleadings, assignment, and division deliberation. The court administrator stated that three Supreme Court members were aware of the petitions' time-sensitive nature and gave an assurance that the election protest would hopefully be resolved before the next election.

Outcome The Judiciary explained the ordinary procedural steps for election petitions and assured the committee that Supreme Court members were aware of the time-sensitive nature of the cases. The committee requested the supporting case details after the hearing, while the broader request for a formal fast-track procedure was not shown as finally resolved.

THE JUDICIARY · 2026-09-07 · resolved

Electronic service of process and preliminary-investigation access

Roman Romulo asked whether electronic notarization could reduce the distance and inconvenience of personal appearance. A Judiciary official said applications for electronic notaries public had opened on August 10, 20 26, and that the Supreme Court had established a legal framework for electronic documents and online submissions through JEPS. Rep. Patal then raised the risk that a respondent in a criminal case could have proceedings move forward after only one side had been heard, effectively denying preliminary investigation. The Judiciary answered that personal service was generally required, with substituted service allowed only under specified conditions and documented by the sheriff or process server's return. The official said strict verification was required before a defendant could be declared in default. Rep. Patal suggested the issue might be one of implementation, and the official agreed.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether electronic notarization and other innovations could address the inconvenience of personal appearance, and whether service of process in criminal cases could protect a respondent's right to preliminary investigation. It also examined whether deficient service could result in cases proceeding in court without the respondent having an opportunity to be heard.

The Judiciary said electronic notarization and electronic document submission were already supported by a Supreme Court legal framework, with ENP applications opened on August 10, 20 26. On service of process, it maintained that strict requirements for personal or properly justified substituted service, documented through a return by the sheriff or process server, protected defendants before default or further proceedings.

Outcome The Judiciary answered that existing Supreme Court rules imposed strict safeguards on service of process and verification before a defendant could be declared in default. Rep. Patal indicated that the remaining concern might be implementation, but no further corrective action or document submission was committed to in the excerpt.

THE JUDICIARY · 2026-09-07 · informational

Electronic notarization and remote access to judicial services

Roman Romulo asked why electronic notarization could not be used more broadly to reduce distance and personal-appearance burdens. A Judiciary official said applications for electronic notaries public had opened on August 10, 20 26, and that the Supreme Court had established the legal framework for electronic documents, with submissions also made through JEPS. Patal then raised concerns about service of process in criminal cases and the possibility that a respondent would effectively be denied a preliminary investigation if only one side's account reached the court. The Judiciary answered that personal service was required for personal actions, with substituted service allowed only under specified conditions and documented through a sheriff's or process server's return. The official said these safeguards had to be verified before a defendant could be declared in default. Patal suggested the remaining issue might be implementation, and the official agreed; no further action or funding commitment was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether electronic notarization could address the distance and personal-appearance burdens associated with notarization, and whether remote or alternative service of process was legally permissible in criminal cases. It also examined whether existing procedures adequately protected defendants from proceedings based on one-sided service or notice.

The Judiciary stated that it had already established a legal framework for electronic documents and had opened applications for electronic notaries public. It also maintained that service of process in relevant cases was governed by strict rules requiring personal service or properly documented substituted service before default could be declared.

Outcome The Judiciary provided an informational answer that electronic notarization and electronic-document procedures already had a legal and operational framework. The service-of-process concern was answered by reference to existing strict service and documentation rules, but no separate implementation measure or budgetary action was agreed upon.

THE JUDICIARY · 2026-09-07 · resolved

Preliminary-injunction bonds and judicial jurisdiction

Rep. Eli San Fernando raised questions under Rule 58, Section 4(b), about whether approval of an injunction bond was required before a preliminary-injunction writ could issue. A Judiciary official explained that the injunction was an ancillary provisional remedy and that the bond protected the adverse party against damages from implementation. The member tested the rule using a hypothetical bond of x amount, and the official confirmed that the bond was a prerequisite. The exchange was summarized as no bond, no injunction. The official further discussed jurisdiction and stated that a decision could be appealed, while an interlocutory order could be challenged under Rule 65 certiorari; parts of that discussion were unclear.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to clarify whether approval and posting of an injunction bond was a prerequisite to the issuance of a writ of preliminary injunction, and what remedy was available for a court order issued in an interlocutory matter involving jurisdiction.

The Judiciary official stated that approval of the requisite injunction bond is a prerequisite to issuance of a writ of preliminary injunction, because the bond secures potential damages to the adverse party. The official also indicated that final decisions may be appealed, while interlocutory orders may be challenged through Rule 65 certiorari, although the jurisdiction discussion was partly unclear.

Outcome The agency confirmed the bond requirement in the formulation that no bond means no injunction. The discussion also identified appeal and Rule 65 certiorari as possible remedies depending on whether the order was a decision or an interlocutory order, but the jurisdiction portion was not fully developed.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

Classroom backlog, construction, repairs, and capital-outlay cuts

Members repeatedly challenged DepEd’s proposed facilities funding against a classroom backlog variously cited at about 142000 to 165000 and against substantial repair and disaster-damage needs. Secretary Angara said the FY 2027 plan would complete 700 classrooms but supported a broader target of roughly 4000 to 5000, while PPP arrangements targeted 16000 classrooms and repairs were funded at about 5 billion. He attributed delivery problems to absorptive capacity, procurement timing, rising construction costs, DPWH and LGU implementation, and the two-year construction cycle, while citing early procurement and decentralization as corrective measures. Members raised district shortages, delayed buildings, missing furniture, earthquake damage, remote-area costs, and possible GAA-PPP duplications. The Secretary committed to prioritize affected districts, coordinate with DPWH and LGUs, submit or provide project lists, and consider additional funding, while Rep. Rodriguez moved for a possible 20000000000 augmentation. The central funding and backlog issues were not finally resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DepEd’s proposed FY 2027 facilities funding would materially reduce the classroom backlog, address repairs and disaster damage, and be implemented efficiently through DepEd, DPWH, LGUs, and PPP arrangements. Members also pressed for the actual classroom targets, construction costs, procurement timelines, furniture provision, and transparency of project locations.

DepEd said the FY 2027 facilities allocation was insufficient to eliminate the nationwide backlog, but represented an effort to expand construction, repairs, LGU participation, PPP delivery, early procurement, and regional implementation. The agency acknowledged persistent delays, rising construction costs, disaster-related damage, and absorptive-capacity constraints, and sought higher infrastructure funding through the budget process.

Outcome The committee received DepEd’s explanation that the 700 figure covered classroom completions, while the broader FY 2027 construction target was roughly 4000 to 5000 classrooms, with repairs funded at about 5 billion and PPP targeting 16000 classrooms. Members sought higher appropriations, priority lists, transparency, and district-specific action; several commitments were made, but the backlog, funding reduction, project duplication, and delivery delays remained unresolved.
