DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

FY2027 DepEd budget reductions and MOE falling to 174 billion

Members, led by Rep. Edgar, Rep. Nelson Legacion, Rep. Antonino Roman III, Rep. Elmer Catulpos, and the Chair, questioned reductions in DepEd's FY 2027 proposal, especially MOE falling from 207 billion to 174 billion and capital outlay declining sharply. Secretary Angara acknowledged that the reductions would shorten school feeding from 180 days to 120 days, reduce classroom construction, limit laptops to 50000 teachers, and affect per-learner funding and other services. He attributed much of the decline to the unusually high FY 2026 congressional-stage allocation and said DepEd had requested about 1.1 trillion from DBM. The Chair said a net budget increase of about 41.3 billion was largely absorbed by a roughly 57.8-billion increase in personal services, leaving about a 16-billion reduction in MOE and capital outlay. The committee also examined utilization, carryover funds, classroom implementation, voucher safeguards, and the effects on feeding and inclusive education. DepEd agreed to submit a reprioritized list, and the committee committed to consider restoration or augmentation, but no final adjustment was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why DepEd's proposed FY 2027 budget reduced maintenance and other operating expenses (MOE), capital outlay, and several core programs despite persistent classroom, learning, feeding, and teacher-support needs. Members also asked what the reductions would mean for service coverage and whether Congress should restore or augment the affected programs.

DepEd acknowledged that the FY 2027 proposal reduced MOE, capital outlay, feeding days, classroom construction capacity, and some program coverage, largely because FY 2026 funding had been increased during the congressional stage and because the agency's larger request was not adopted. The agency maintained that the cuts would have concrete effects on feeding, classrooms, learning materials, and other services, and asked Congress to restore or augment priority items while offering to submit a reprioritized list.

Outcome The committee did not accept the reductions as a settled policy choice. DepEd was asked to submit a reprioritized list, while the committee indicated that it would consider restoring or augmenting feeding, inclusive education, ARAL, mental-health, classroom, and other priority programs; the final funding outcome remained open.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

ARAL learning-recovery funding, including the requested 16000000000

Rep. Salvador Pleyto asked where ARAL funding appeared in the FY 2027 NEP and raised the need to compensate teachers and tutors fairly. DepEd answered that the NEP contained a 0 allotment, while it had proposed about 9.98 billion for implementation and 3.5 billion for tutor and teacher remuneration; the agency also reported coverage of about 6.7 million learners and substantial reading improvements. Iris Marie Montes separately pressed for the amount devoted to foundational literacy and numeracy, and Secretary Angara gave a ballpark estimate of at least 10 billion, or about 4 percent of the DepEd budget's learning systems and curriculum strand. Rep. Audrey Zubiri cited the prior 8.9 billion ARAL GAA budget, the reported results, and an estimated 1500 peso per-learner investment in supporting a request to increase funding to 16 billion. DepEd explained that the NEP exclusion reflected the treatment of prior congressional insertions rather than a rejection of the program. The committee expressed support but requested a reprioritized list from DepEd, so the final ARAL funding level remained pending.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the FY 2027 funding actually included in the NEP for the ARAL learning-recovery program, the amount DepEd requested, and the program's funding and tutor-compensation requirements. Members also asked whether ARAL was producing measurable improvements and what would happen if its requested funding was not restored.

DepEd stated that the FY 2027 NEP contained a 0 allotment for ARAL even though the program had received congressional funding previously. The agency sought substantial funding for ARAL implementation, including tutor compensation and learning-recovery interventions, and argued that reported learning gains demonstrated the program's effectiveness and justified restoration or augmentation.

Outcome The committee supported restoring or augmenting ARAL, but no final appropriation was adopted in the hearing. DepEd committed to submit a reprioritized list for the committee's consideration, leaving the requested funding unresolved pending budget review.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

Teacher hiring, shortages, promotions, and career progression

The chair and several members examined DepEd's plans for teacher hiring, promotion, tutoring, and training. DepEd proposed about 12.09 billion for career progression, targeting more than 135000 promotions, but Secretary Angara acknowledged that about 100000 qualified teachers remained in the promotion backlog, leaving about 35000 effective new promotions. Rep. Tinio also elicited that the proposal had 0 funding for new teacher hiring despite a reported shortage of 14274 teachers and 58000 vacant teaching items. Rep. Pleyto sought fair compensation for ARAL tutors, and DepEd cited a proposed ARAL package of about 9.98 billion, including 3.5 billion in total teacher and tutor remuneration. Members further questioned teacher preparation, values education, mental-health staffing, and AI training; DepEd cited about 3 billion for teacher training, 2.9 billion for school counselor associates, and no FY 2027 AI line item. The hearing left additional hiring and ARAL support to the budget process, with commitments to reiterate promotion policy, monitor AI results, and pursue possible training partnerships.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DepEd's proposed resources would address teacher shortages, qualified applicants awaiting appointment or promotion, fair compensation for additional tutoring, and meaningful career progression. Members also asked how teacher training, including AI and values education, would prepare teachers for changing instructional needs.

DepEd said the proposed budget prioritized career progression and training but contained 0 funding for new teacher hiring, despite a reported shortage of 14274 teachers and 58000 vacant teaching items. The agency supported fair compensation for ARAL tutors, sought funding for the program, and said it would continue teacher training, values education, and AI capacity-building while working through the budget process and available partnerships.

Outcome The committee received answers on the promotion targets, promotion backlog, vacant teaching items, ARAL tutor compensation, and teacher-training initiatives. The central issue of 0 FY 2027 funding for new teacher hiring remained open, while DepEd's requests for ARAL and possible additional support were left to the succeeding budget process.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

School counselor staffing and school-based mental-health funding

Members raised the shortage of licensed guidance counselors, the over-3000 vacancies, and the difficulty of recruiting professionals because of the master's-degree requirement. DepEd said it was hiring 10000 school counselor associates, had shortened the hiring period to 30 days, and had received over 20000 applications. The FY 2027 proposal funded 1800 positions, while DepEd requested 39000 positions and calculated that 11400000000 would be needed for a meaningful first tranche. Deployment would prioritize schools with high bullying or mental-health incidence, larger enrollment, congestion, and senior-high-school implementation, while maintaining equitable distribution. Members also pressed for greater mental-health funding and cautioned against relying excessively on security measures and potentially traumatic active-shooter drills. DepEd committed to provide progress and deployment data and described scholarship, training, social-emotional learning, and psychological-first-aid initiatives, but the requested funding increases were not finally resolved in the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how many guidance counselor and school counselor associate positions DepEd had, how many were vacant or funded, whether qualified applicants were available, and how the positions would be deployed. Members also examined the funding needed for school-based mental-health services and the balance between mental-health interventions and school-security measures.

DepEd said the FY 2027 proposal funded 1800 school counselor associate positions, while the department was requesting substantially more to move toward one counselor associate per school. It said hiring for the 10000 existing items was underway, with over 20000 applicants, and that deployment would prioritize need, bullying and mental-health history, school size, and senior-high-school implementation while maintaining equitable nationwide distribution.

Outcome The committee received DepEd's explanation of the counselor staffing gap, the ongoing hiring process, the applicant pool, and the proposed deployment criteria. The department's larger requests and the final level of mental-health funding remained subject to the budget process, while DepEd committed to provide hiring and deployment information.

Classroom safety, bullying, violence, and learner protection

Members raised bullying, school violence, online harms, learner-rights implementation, and the need for mental-health and counseling personnel. DepEd said more than 30000 of over 36000 schools had functioning Child Protection Committees, all schools had learner formation officers, and hiring for 10000 school counselor-associate positions was underway after more than 20000 applications. The issue landed with ongoing implementation and reporting commitments, rather than a fully resolved determination of funding adequacy.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DepEd would prevent and respond to bullying, school violence, and online harms; protect learners; and fund school security and mental-health measures. Members also asked whether counselor vacancies, Child Protection Committees, reporting systems, drills, and related policies were adequately staffed, implemented, and monitored.

DepEd said learner protection required a combined approach involving Anti-Bullying Act implementation, Child Protection Committees and learner formation officers, mental-health and counseling personnel, school-community participation, reporting systems, and proportionate security measures. The agency acknowledged major staffing and funding constraints, said hiring and policy work were ongoing, and undertook to provide several reports, verify materials, reiterate protections against coercive activities, and coordinate with other agencies on online violence.

Outcome The committee received DepEd's explanations of its anti-bullying, counseling, reporting, drill, and security measures, but significant staffing and funding gaps remained. DepEd undertook to submit reports, verify questioned materials, reiterate learner safeguards, and provide regional and district hiring data.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

Textbook, instructional-material, and furniture procurement backlogs

Rep. Edgar and other members questioned the reduction in textbook and instructional-material funding and pressed DepEd on whether procurement would translate into delivery, particularly in remote schools. Secretary Angara said DepEd had procured all 105 curriculum titles and was pursuing a one-textbook-per-learner goal, but acknowledged delivery delays, including delays of 1 year. Rep. Amato and civil-society questions highlighted classroom and repair backlogs, while DepEd cited a backlog of roughly 142000 classrooms, more than 350 LGU partners, and a request for 98000000000 in infrastructure funding. DepEd said early procurement, regional or decentralized procurement, and PPP and LGU participation would improve absorptive capacity and delivery. Rep. Catulpos separately cited a drop in textbook procurement from about 19 billion to 6 billion and questioned the FY 2027 classroom target. DepEd did not resolve the funding and delivery concerns, and it undertook to verify whether a questioned grade 1 material was officially authorized.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DepEd’s proposed FY 2027 procurement and infrastructure allocations would reduce backlogs in textbooks, instructional materials, classrooms, and related facilities, particularly in last-mile and poorer schools. Members also asked how DepEd would address delayed delivery, underutilization of funds, procurement decentralization, and the age appropriateness and authorization of learning materials.

DepEd said it had made significant progress in textbook procurement, including procuring all 105 curriculum titles, but acknowledged that timely delivery—especially to last-mile schools—remained unresolved. It attributed delivery and utilization improvements to early procurement, decentralization, regional procurement, and expanded participation by LGUs and PPP partners, while seeking larger infrastructure funding to address the classroom backlog.

Outcome DepEd provided progress figures and identified procurement reforms, but members’ concerns about the sharp FY 2027 textbook reduction, delayed delivery to last-mile schools, classroom targets, and transparency of allocations remained open. Verification of the questioned grade 1 material was deferred to DepEd’s regional offices.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

Computerization, connectivity, and digital-transformation funding

The committee questioned DepEd's reduced Computerization Program, the funding for 50000 teacher laptops, undelivered computer packages, school connectivity, and the absence of a dedicated AI appropriation. Secretary Angara said prior computerization deliveries had been completed and that DepEd would improve tracking through early procurement and decentralization. He reported 99 percent internet coverage, 460 schools without internet, an aspiration for 100 Mbps minimum bandwidth, and a goal of reaching 10 to 12000 schools with AI tools from about 3000 schools. DepEd described AI applications for hazard mapping, teacher support, administrative work, and learner reading assessment, while warning that safeguards and teacher training were necessary. Angara said over 1000000 faculty and students had been trained and that 115000000 had been carved out in 20 26 for an AI research center, but there was no AI line item in the 20 27 budget. Members expressed support but left funding adequacy and the scale-up of digital services for the continuing budget process.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DepEd's proposed computerization, connectivity, and digital-transformation funding would address prior delivery and absorptive-capacity problems, expand meaningful school and learner access to computers and the internet, and support responsible use of AI. Members also asked what specific AI uses, training, bandwidth, monitoring, and funding were in place.

DepEd said prior computer-delivery problems had been addressed and that it was improving tracking, early procurement, and regional decentralization to raise absorptive capacity. It supported expanding computer laboratories, internet bandwidth, teacher training, and carefully safeguarded AI applications, but acknowledged that the 20 27 budget contained no AI line item and that connectivity quality and access remained uneven.

Outcome The agency answered that computer deliveries had been completed and described measures to improve procurement, tracking, connectivity, teacher training, and AI deployment. The committee received the explanations, but the adequacy of the reduced computerization funding, the 20 27 teacher-laptop allocation, bandwidth gaps, and the absence of a dedicated AI line item remained matters for the budget process.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

Inclusive and special-needs education funding

Representative Sandania questioned the apparent reduction of special-needs education funding from about 1 billion to 850 million and proposed restoring or increasing the allocation. DepEd said the comparison was affected by congressional insertions in the prior budget and appealed for an additional 541.5 million to support staffing, facilities, equipment, schools, and multidisciplinary-team capacity-building. The agency said 81.6 million would construct six Inclusive Learning Resource Centers, bringing the projected total to 38 against a target of 1,642, and reported 10.8 million for learner-support-center enhancement. Representative Caroline Agiau sought additional funding for disability assessments and assistive devices, but the transcript did not provide the requested counts of learners awaiting assessment or lacking devices. The committee later identified a shortfall of about 190 million to reach FY 2026 levels for the group of programs that included SNED and requested a reprioritized list. The matter therefore landed with DepEd commitments for further submissions and with funding augmentation left for committee consideration.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 funding for special-needs and inclusive education was sufficient to implement the Inclusive Education Act. Members asked what additional funding would cover, how many Inclusive Learning Resource Centers could be built, and whether DepEd could provide adequate assessment, assistive-device, staffing, and learner-support services.

DepEd said the apparent reduction in special-needs education funding reflected the exclusion of prior congressional insertions from the NEP, rather than a change in the program's importance. The agency supported additional funding for staffing, facilities, equipment, teacher and multidisciplinary-team capacity-building, Inclusive Learning Resource Centers, and related inclusive services, and sought congressional consideration of its appeals.

Outcome The issue was left for budget consideration rather than finally resolved. DepEd committed to provide additional learner-support-center information and a reprioritized list of requests, while the committee indicated that it would consider restoration or augmentation of SNED and related inclusive-education funding.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

School feeding, ECCD, and learner nutrition programs

Rep. Edgar flagged a 55 percent reduction in school-based feeding, and Secretary Angara said the proposed funding would support only 120 days rather than 180 days and would reduce coverage, including universal feeding for Grade 1. DepEd linked feeding to weight gain, attendance, and improved learning, and said ECCD responsibilities were shared with DILG, LGUs, DSWD, and the National Nutrition Council, with DepEd focused on curriculum and participation in the ECCD Council. Rep. Zubiri supported increasing ARAL funding from about 9 billion to 16 billion after DepEd reported that 6.7 million learners were covered and 4.5 million advanced reading levels. The committee chair questioned whether the 26 billion 2026 feeding allocation was being utilized, and DepEd reported 45.8 percent current utilization, with school-year carryover and higher historical rates. DepEd said it would submit a reprioritized list of priority programs, and the committee agreed to consider restoration or augmentation before the budget moved forward.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed reductions would affect school-based feeding, including the number of feeding days, learner coverage, and nutrition and learning outcomes. Members also asked how DepEd's ECCD responsibilities related to day-care feeding and malnutrition response, and whether funding for ARAL and other foundational-learning programs should be restored or augmented.

DepEd stated that school feeding was strongly linked to improved weight, attendance, and learning outcomes, especially during the early years, and that the proposed level would reduce both the feeding cycle and coverage. The department supported restoring or augmenting funding for feeding and ARAL, sought an amendment to the school-feeding law, and offered to submit a reprioritized list of requests.

Outcome The issue was not finally resolved in the hearing. DepEd explained the operational consequences of retaining the lower school-feeding allocation and committed to submit a prioritized restoration and augmentation list, while the committee undertook to consider the requests.

Voucher programs and senior-high-school beneficiary controls

Rep. Edgar questioned a reported 100 percent reduction in senior-high-school voucher assistance and sought clarification of the FY 2026 and FY 2027 amounts. Secretary Angara said the consolidated voucher program, including JDVP and ESC, was PHP 38000000000, about PHP 3000000000 below the prior year. Rep. Montes asked whether the allocation would cover unpaid obligations to private participating schools; DepEd said the backlog was less than 10000000 and that the FY 2027 voucher budget was 38000000000. Secretary Angara described five validation layers, payment holds, post-audits, inspections, and end-of-year enrollment checks, and reported one conviction and four filed cases. The issue ended with members recognizing that the safeguards were expected to minimize, but not entirely eliminate, recurrence.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the FY 2027 funding level for senior-high-school voucher programs, including whether appropriations were adequate to cover obligations to participating private schools. It also examined whether DepEd had controls to prevent ghost beneficiaries, fictitious claims, and payments for learners who were not actually enrolled.

DepEd said the consolidated FY 2027 voucher budget was 38000000000, while the unpaid balance to participating private schools was less than 10000000. Secretary Angara maintained that five validation layers, payment holds for unresolved discrepancies, post-audits, on-site inspections, end-of-year enrollment checks, and criminal cases had substantially strengthened controls against ghost beneficiaries and fictitious claims.

Outcome DepEd provided the requested voucher figures and described strengthened controls, including five validation layers and enforcement actions. The committee did not order a separate submission or resolve the apparent discrepancy between Rep. Edgar's reported reduction and DepEd's consolidated funding explanation.

DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

Teacher loans, APDS payroll deductions, and take-home pay

Rep. Adrian Amato raised teacher financial literacy, loan support, and the possibility of an annual allocation, while Secretary Juan Edgardo Sonny M. Angara said DepEd would examine the proposal and work with him. Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. then questioned the legal basis and welfare effects of allowing APDS loans for up to 7 years, including the number of teachers with multiple loans and their average and median take-home pay. Secretary Angara said the arrangement was voluntary, complied with the GAA protection for 5000 in net take-home pay, and could give teachers longer repayment periods and lower payments. Rep. Nazal cited a reported rate of 3.5 percent per month, roughly 42 percent per year, and asked about lender oversight. DepEd stated that accredited lenders were subject to a 9.6 percent per annum ceiling, while higher-rate lenders were probably not accredited and fell outside DepEd's police power. The requested loan and take-home-pay data and specific legal basis were not resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DepEd legally authorized APDS automatic payroll deductions for loans of up to 7 years, whether extended loan terms helped teachers or prolonged indebtedness, and what teachers' take-home pay was after deductions. Members also questioned the interest-rate ceiling and DepEd's ability to police nonaccredited lenders.

DepEd said the 7-year APDS loan option was voluntary, was offered at teachers' request, and complied with the GAA protection requiring 5000 in net take-home pay to remain untouched. It stated that the interest ceiling for accredited lenders was 9.6 percent per annum, while lenders charging 3.5 percent monthly were not accredited, and acknowledged that DepEd did not have police power over such lenders.

Outcome DepEd explained the voluntary nature of the 7-year option and stated the 5000 take-home-pay protection and 9.6 percent interest ceiling. The requested data and fuller legal explanation were not provided in the exchange, leaving those issues open.

Outcome The National Museum's proposed MOE and exhibition augmentations were identified as priorities, and members expressed support, but no appropriation or committee ruling was made in the transcript. DepEd · 2026-09-07 · committed

AI, curriculum reform, and teacher capability development

Members questioned DepEd's readiness to use AI, train teachers, upgrade the curriculum, strengthen GMRC and Values Education, and prepare learners for future work. Secretary Angara said AI could support teachers and personalized learning but required safeguards, age-appropriate introduction, teacher training, and stronger connectivity. DepEd cited about 3 billion for teacher training, 150 million for its eCare AI research center, and 115 million in 2026 AI-center research funding, while acknowledging no dedicated AI line item in the 2027 budget. Officials described GMRC teacher training for grades 1 to 10, values integration across subjects, and curriculum additions involving life skills, AI, and future skills. Members manifested support for DepEd's budget, and the agency agreed to monitor AI's effects and share relevant GMRC survey results.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DepEd would fund and implement AI, curriculum reform, teacher capability development, GMRC and Values Education, and future-skills preparation. Members also asked how AI would be used without weakening critical thinking, creativity, or human-centered education.

DepEd supported carefully governed AI adoption to assist teachers, personalize learning, analyze administrative and operational problems, and build future skills. It maintained that teacher training, appropriate age-based safeguards, connectivity, and continued curriculum and values-education work were necessary, and acknowledged that the 2027 budget contained no dedicated AI line item.

Outcome The agency answered the members' policy questions and secured expressions of support, but AI funding remained partly unresolved because DepEd acknowledged there was no dedicated AI line item in the 2027 budget. DepEd undertook to monitor AI results and share relevant GMRC survey findings.

DOT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Tourism infrastructure, access roads, and interagency project priorities

Members questioned whether priority and emerging tourism destinations had adequate roads, visitor facilities, and related infrastructure, and whether DOT's promotional work was matched by national investments. DOT said promotions and infrastructure required equal resources, but road construction generally remained with DPWH through TRIP, while DOT funded facilities and coordinated with DPWH, DOTR, TIEZA, and local governments. DOT disclosed that 28 Tier 2 projects worth approximately 6.02 billion were proposed, but continuing and new TRIP projects were not included in the FY2027 NEP. Members also discussed a proposed 1.64 billion augmentation, a Region 6 allocation of about 50.8 million, and roughly 5.2 billion for TIEZA multiyear projects. DOT committed to destination inventories, regional planning, and follow-up on unresolved environmental and infrastructure matters, while the committee requested a list of TIEZA's ongoing multiyear projects.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether priority tourism destinations had adequate roads, facilities, and basic services, and whether DOT, DPWH, DOTR, TIEZA, DBM, and local governments were coordinating their investments. Members also asked how projects would be funded, continued, and prioritized across emerging, high-potential, and regional destinations.

DOT said infrastructure and promotion required equal attention, but responsibility for infrastructure was distributed among DOT, DPWH, DOTR, TIEZA, and local governments. DOT funded destination facilities and planning, coordinated through regional and convergence programs, and sought to record unfunded priorities in regional tourism development plans; it did not itself build access roads. The agency acknowledged that several proposed road and Tier 2 projects were not included in the FY2027 NEP and that further coordination and funding decisions remained necessary.

Outcome The committee received DOT's explanations and several funding figures, but the absence of DPWH TRIP funding in the FY2027 NEP and the lack of a clearly identified formal interagency master list left major infrastructure priorities open. DOT undertook coordination, destination inventory, planning, and document-related follow-up, while members expressed support for budget augmentation and requested continuity funding for multiyear projects.

DOT · 2026-09-07 · committed

TIEZA funding, travel-tax resources, and multiyear infrastructure projects

DOT presented about 1.64 billion in additional requests for its attached agencies, including about 1.31 billion for TIEZA infrastructure projects, while warning that travel-tax abolition could create funding implications. TIEZA said around 300 personnel could be affected if the travel tax were abolished. DBM said no FY 2027 national government subsidy tied to the proposed abolition was included because the measures had not been enacted, but TIEZA could use available collections and other resources. A minority member sought a tourism-destination inventory and received the Secretary's commitment. Howard Gintu raised the Region 6 allocation, clarified at 50800000 pesos after conflicting figures, and questioned the continuity of TIEZA's multiyear projects. TIEZA said almost all projects were multiyear and cited around 5.2 billion pesos for 2027; Gintu requested a project list for possible committee support.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much additional funding DOT's attached agencies, particularly TIEZA, were requesting; how travel-tax abolition could affect TIEZA resources and personnel; and whether ongoing tourism infrastructure projects, including projects in Region 6, had secure multiyear financing. Members also sought destination inventories and a list of ongoing TIEZA projects to support possible appropriations.

DOT and TIEZA presented travel-tax resources as important to tourism infrastructure and other priority programs. DBM said no national government subsidy requested in connection with proposed travel-tax abolition was included because the measures had not been enacted, but TIEZA could use available travel-tax collections, its corporate operating budget, and potentially other authorized sources. TIEZA stated that almost all of its projects were multiyear and that the 2027 amount was around 5200000000 pesos.

Outcome The committee received explanations that travel-tax abolition had not yet resulted in a DBM subsidy because the bills remained pending, while TIEZA could use available resources and other authorized funding sources. The destination-inventory request was met with a commitment, but the requested list of ongoing TIEZA projects and the final protection of multiyear-project financing were not resolved during the excerpt.

Questions and agency response

It sought 82330000 in additional funding, requested restoration of its prior funding level, and undertook to pursue unfunded requests such as Terra Madre Asia Pacific through DBM and other available funding channels.

Outcome The committee heard the DOT's request for additional funding and received support from Representative Rodriguez for augmentation, although no final committee ruling on the augmentation appears in the transcript. Terra Madre Asia Pacific remained outside the approved FY 2027 proposal, but the DOT committed to pursue DBM approval and identify funding options.

DOT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Tourism promotion, domestic and international marketing allocations

The DOT presented 1000000000 for its FY 2027 branding campaign and said the campaign would combine international visibility with conversion into travel and spending. Members supported additional funding but questioned competitiveness, private-sector counterparts, infrastructure needs, and whether promotion could be separated from broader tourism reforms. On domestic and international marketing, the DOT stated that 60 percent of the branding allocation would target international markets and 40 percent domestic travelers, serving 13 key markets. It cited 69 percent growth for China, around 29 percent for Vietnam, around 30 percent for India, and a 17 percent South Korea decline addressed through 50000000 in campaign funding. The DOT also cited a training allocation of 198752000, pesos, while a member referenced 230000000 for training. The discussion ended with support for the budget, but without final action on the augmentation or a definitive destination-investment road map.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOT would allocate limited tourism-promotion resources between domestic and international markets, and whether the allocations were tied to measurable returns. Members also asked how branding, celebrity or influencer campaigns, training, and destination investment would support tourism competitiveness.

The DOT said the 1000000000 branding campaign would combine global awareness-building with conversion into travel and spending, while prioritizing international markets because of their value per peso. It stated that 60 percent would go to international marketing and 40 percent to domestic marketing, with targeted campaigns for 13 key markets, selected use of influencers or celebrities, and continued investment in training, infrastructure coordination, and destination development.

Outcome The DOT explained the international-versus-domestic allocation as 60 percent to international marketing and 40 percent to domestic marketing, with targeted spending for 13 key markets and 50000000 for South Korea. Members generally supported augmentation, but the record did not establish final approval, a completed Tourism Promotions Board request, or a fully developed destination-investment road map.

DOT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Domestic travel affordability, airfares, and possible fuel subsidy

Rep. Perci Cendaña raised the affordability of domestic travel and asked how the DOT would respond to volatile fuel prices, limited aircraft capacity, and infrastructure gaps. The DOT said island routes were expensive because turbopropeller aircraft carried only about 70 to 80 seats and airport limitations restricted supply, while larger aircraft and runway improvements could lower costs. It said a fuel subsidy modeled on Vietnam's program could help but was still finalizing the proposal and gathering data. Cendaña requested the DOTR's airport-improvement commitments and the DOT's FY 2027 contingency plan, while another member cautioned that affordability claims required actual investment and reforms. Rep. Elmer Catulpos later asked whether Filipinos traveled abroad because neighboring countries were 20 to 30 percent cheaper; the DOT answered that domestic tourism remained the backbone of the industry and cited 80 percent of tourism income as domestic. The matter landed with agency follow-up commitments and remained open pending the requested documents and subsidy details.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why domestic airfares remained high, whether the DOT had a plan to make domestic travel more affordable—including a possible fuel subsidy—and how infrastructure, tourism promotion, and competitiveness measures would address the problem. Members also sought to clarify whether Filipinos were choosing foreign travel because neighboring destinations were cheaper and how the DOT balanced domestic and international marketing.

The DOT said domestic airfares were primarily pressured by fuel costs, demand and supply, limited aircraft capacity, and airport infrastructure constraints, particularly for island destinations. It supported continued airport improvements, was gathering data and finalizing a possible fuel subsidy proposal, and intended to use targeted tourism promotion, training, accreditation, branding, and private-sector partnerships to improve competitiveness.

Outcome The DOT explained the structural and fuel-related causes of high domestic airfares and said airport improvements, airline support, and a possible fuel subsidy could help, but the subsidy proposal was still being finalized. The issue remained open pending the DOT's contingency plan, DOTR facility commitments, and further data on the proposed subsidy.

DOT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Travel-tax abolition and its effect on DOT personnel and projects

The committee first asked about personnel consequences of abolishing the travel tax, and DOT said around 300 travel-tax personnel would be affected, with some terminated and others receiving separation incentives. A committee member also sought alternative financing for tourism, heritage and related projects. Representative Sergio Dagooc then asked DBM why TIEZA's requested subsidy and tourism-infrastructure funding were not augmented. DBM said the FY 2027 subsidy was not included because abolition bills remained under deliberation, but TIEZA could use available funds totaling about 2.355 billion, including the stated unobligated allotment and unreleased operations figures. DOT described its sustainable-tourism convergence program, which had conducted 13 trainings for 417 participants. The Secretary committed to the requested tourism-destination inventory, while no specific budget augmentation or deadline was resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the personnel consequences if the travel tax were abolished and how tourism infrastructure and related projects would be financed without that revenue. It also asked whether TIEZA could receive augmented funding and whether DOT would prepare an inventory of tourism destinations.

DOT and DBM indicated that abolition of the travel tax would affect around 300 travel-tax personnel, with some terminated and others offered separation incentives. DBM said no requested FY 2027 national-government subsidy for TIEZA was included while abolition bills remained pending, but TIEZA could use available travel-tax collections and other funds for priority tourism projects; DOT also committed to support the requested destination-inventory effort.

Outcome DBM explained that the requested FY 2027 TIEZA subsidy was not included because travel-tax abolition measures remained pending, while identifying TIEZA funds and other financing avenues that could be used for tourism projects. The destination-inventory issue resulted in a general commitment from the DOT Secretary, but no specific augmentation or submission deadline was settled.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOT and its attached agencies would develop dive tourism while protecting marine ecosystems and ensuring environmental sustainability. PCSSD cited partnerships and coordination with marine-science, environmental, and DENR-related institutions, while the DOT said promotions and infrastructure required equal effort to support a sustainable industry.

Outcome The committee received the agency's explanation of PCSSD's environmental partnerships and program standards, but the DOT's specific role in protecting marine sanctuaries and the data on dynamite-fishing incidents remained subject to a later response. The agency also stated that promotions and infrastructure should receive equal priority.

DOT · 2026-09-07 · committed

Outbound travel, foreign arrivals, and tourism competitiveness

Rep. Perci Cendaña raised the effects of fuel prices, airline capacity, and airport limitations on domestic travel costs and asked for DOTR commitments and a 2027 contingency plan. The DOT attributed high island-destination airfares to limited supply and infrastructure, and said it was finalizing a fuel-subsidy proposal while pursuing airport improvements, training, accreditation, branding, and private-sector partnerships. Rep. Elmer Catulpos then asked whether Filipinos were choosing neighboring countries because they were 20 to 30 percent cheaper, citing 7650000 outbound Filipinos and 5870000 foreign tourists; the DOT responded that domestic tourism remained the backbone, with 134000000 domestic tourists in 2024 and roughly 6000000 to 6480000 foreign arrivals in 2025. The DOT said 80 percent of tourism income came from domestic tourism and 20 percent from inbound tourism, while international marketing received 60 percent of the branding allocation and domestic marketing 40 percent. It identified 13 key markets, cited growth in China, Vietnam, and India, and said 50000000 was being used to address a 17 percent South Korean decline. The agency also discussed influencers and homegrown talents such as SB19 and cited a 230000000 pesos training budget for 2027; requested documents and the fuel-subsidy proposal were not shown as delivered.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why domestic travel remained costly and how the DOT would improve tourism competitiveness amid fuel-price pressures, infrastructure constraints, and a limited budget. Members also asked whether outbound Filipino travel and changes in foreign-tourist arrivals reflected cheaper competing destinations, and how the DOT was allocating and targeting its marketing resources.

The DOT said competitiveness depended on airline support, airport and runway improvements, strategic prioritization, private-sector participation, targeted international marketing, and stronger worker training and accreditation. It maintained that domestic tourism remained the industry's backbone, while international campaigns would focus on 13 key markets, including efforts to reverse the 17 percent South Korean decline.

Outcome The DOT answered the questions with its planned airport coordination, competitiveness, training, branding, and market-specific strategies, but the transcript did not show submission of the requested DOTR commitments or 2027 contingency plan. The issue therefore remained open on the requested documents and on whether the proposed interventions would reverse cost and arrival trends.

Agency unavailable · 2026-09-03 · unresolved

PSA civil-registration funding and organizational capacity

The bill sponsor sought funding for a modernized civil registration system, including digitization, expanded access, and anti-fraud safeguards. The PSA supported the bill and said the existing civil-registration law dated to 1931, but requested a stronger civil registration office under Section 6. It said the PSA and local civil registrars lacked sufficient capacity to expand registration services and protect records from fraud. The DBM answered that any office creation or strengthening would require its usual evaluation and review under the government optimization program. It also recommended using "existing retirement laws" and clarified that the legal service in Section 61 referred to the PSA's existing legal service. The organizational and funding issues remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee was considering whether the substitute bill and its funding should provide for a stronger Philippine Civil Registry Office within the PSA, given the need to expand services and protect records from fraud. It also sought to establish how the proposed organizational changes would be evaluated by the DBM and how the bill's legal-service provision should be interpreted.

The PSA supported the substitute bill but maintained that the civil registration office and the capacities of the PSA and local civil registrars needed to be strengthened to expand access and combat fraud. The DBM did not reject the organizational provision but said any creation or strengthening must undergo DBM evaluation and the government optimization program, and it requested clarification of the retirement-law and legal-service language.

Outcome The PSA's request for a stronger civil registration office and greater organizational capacity was placed on the record, but the DBM said the proposal remained subject to its evaluation and the government optimization program. DBM also placed proposed drafting clarifications on the record; no final decision on the requested strengthening or funding was stated.

10% PSA registration-income retention for immediate operations

Questions and agency response

The DBM official maintained that DBM preferred the one-fund concept because it would provide flexibility during budget preparation and would preserve more resources for the General Fund. However, DBM deferred to the committee's decision on allowing PSA to retain 10% of generated income and did not object on the record to the committee's approval.

Outcome The committee approved the revised motion excluding the proposed deletion of Section 78, so the 10% PSA income-retention provision was retained. The agency estimated the 10% at 1,139,000,000 based on 2025 revenue, while the broader policy concern about setting a precedent for other earning agencies was left as a caution rather than resolved.

Disaster risk financing, DREAM Funds, and insurance structure

Rep. Joseph Lara sponsored the DRFI framework, citing annual disaster-related asset losses of about 177 billion and an equivalent of about US3.5 billion dollars. OCD supported the measure but asked that its relationship with the existing DREAM Funds be clearly defined and protected against duplication. DOF supported prearranged financing, multilayered risk financing, and parametric insurance, while the Insurance Commission sought clearer boundaries over government assets, existing institutions, asset prioritization, and claims guidelines. Treasury objected to creating a special fund because of the regular budget process, trust-receipt treatment of insurance proceeds, and the one-fund policy. DBM recommended calling it a program funded through a GAA line item and requiring DBM review of positions. The committee adopted those amendments and approved the measure, although a member's parametric-insurance clarification received a garbled and unclear response.

Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish how the proposed disaster risk financing and insurance framework would complement existing DREAM Funds and government insurance arrangements, and whether the proposed financing mechanism should be a special fund or a program. It also sought to clarify the respective roles of the Insurance Commission, Department of Finance, Bureau of the Treasury, DBM, and the proposed DRFIB.

The agencies supported the DRFI substitute bill but sought clearer boundaries and implementation rules. OCD supported the framework as complementary to the DREAM Funds; DOF supported prearranged financing and parametric insurance; the Insurance Commission requested clarification of coverage and government-insurance responsibilities; Treasury opposed creating a special fund under the one-fund policy; and DBM recommended treating the mechanism as a program funded through a GAA line item.

Outcome The committee adopted the agency-backed amendments, converting the proposed DRFI special fund into a program, subjecting implementation to DBM guidelines, and requiring DBM evaluation and approval of positions. It then approved the DRFI measure subject to those amendments; the precise response to the parametric-insurance clarification was left unclear in the transcript.

Local-government performance incentives and SGLG funding

Rep. Albert Garcia sponsored a bill establishing a data-driven performance-measurement system for local governments and linking improvements to performance-based rewards. Questions and agency response

The committee was determining how the proposed performance-measurement and meritocracy system would apply to local governments and barangays, including the treatment of national government agencies. It also examined whether the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) fund, barangay performance-based bonuses, DBM approval requirements, and the 2% operating-fund cap should be retained or amended.

DBM supported adjusting the bill to remove national government agencies from its scope while retaining DBM approval for additional positions, coordinating with DILG on barangay performance bonuses, and preserving and harmonizing the SGLG fund provisions. DBM also supported retaining the 2% SGLG-fund operating provision, subject to drafting harmonization and style.

Outcome The committee approved the amendments and then approved the measure subject to those amendments and style. The approved package removed national government agencies, retained the SGLG fund provisions, preserved the 2% phrase, and added DBM approval and DILG-DBM coordination requirements.

DFA FY2027 budget request, allotment classes, and utilization

The DFA presented an FY2027 request of about 35 billion, while its stated net level for the department and attached agencies was 35,170,000,000, 17% above the 2026 net. Maintenance and other operating expenses accounted for 54% of the request, personnel services for 39%, and capital outlay for 7%; major items included next-generation passport funding, the International Commitments Fund, ATN and legal assistance, ICT, and the building fund. The agency reported an 80% 2025 BUR and close to 53% utilization in the first half of the current year, attributing lower performance to delayed retrofitting, transferred ATN functions, deferred building projects, and changing passport demand. Members requested detailed spending and program documents, particularly for the Security Council campaign, ATN Fund, ICT, and ePassport allocations. Rodriguez supported placing 250,000,000 for cybersecurity and restoring 300,000,000 to the building fund, while the Foreign Service Institute sought MXN 6,500,000 for HMO coverage. The committee left the additional funding requests for written submission and subsequent consideration, with a deadline set for the following Wednesday.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the DFA and attached agencies’ FY2027 funding requirement, the distribution of that request across allotment classes, the reasons for the increase, and the department’s utilization performance. Members also examined specific funding needs for passports, ICT and cybersecurity, buildings, consular operations, HMO, and permanent positions, and identified documents or augmentations to be submitted for further consideration.

The DFA presented the FY2027 request as necessary to sustain overseas and consular services, implement the next-generation passport, strengthen ICT and cybersecurity, maintain overseas properties, and support foreign-policy operations. It reported strong physical performance but acknowledged utilization constraints and committed to submit requested budget, expenditure, and program documents.

Outcome The DFA’s proposed budget was presented and supported, but several augmentations and requests remained subject to written endorsement and later committee or plenary consideration. The agency committed to submit the requested ICT, ePassport, ATN, campaign-expenditure, and wish-list documents.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

Assistance to Nationals and Legal Assistance Funds for overseas Filipinos

The committee asked the DFA to clarify ATN and LAF coverage, appropriations, utilization, eligibility rules, and approval authority after the DMW assumed responsibility for more OFWs. The DFA said 1,000,000,000 was appropriated annually for the ATN Fund from 2022 to 2025 and reported 2,884 ATN beneficiaries from January to July 2026, including 387 repatriation beneficiaries. It also cited welfare assistance of dollars 559,000,000, medical assistance of 20,000,000, and shipment of remains of 40,000,000, although some wording and currency attribution were unclear. The DFA said it generally did not deny qualified requests and that its office handled recommendations below 20%, while the Secretary approved amounts above that threshold. Members requested the ATN guidelines and detailed ATN and LAF utilization records, including balances, expenditures, approvals, rejections, nonqualifications, and beneficiaries. The DFA also described ongoing coordination on distressed seafarers and safe passage through embassies, MWOs, DMW, the IMO, and bilateral channels.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the Assistance to Nationals (ATN) Fund and Legal Assistance Fund (LAF) were allocated, utilized, and administered, including which overseas Filipinos remained covered after the creation of the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW). It also sought beneficiary, expenditure, approval, rejection, eligibility, and utilization data, as well as the DFA's continuing assistance to distressed OFWs and seafarers.

The DFA said ATN and LAF assistance remained available to distressed overseas Filipinos within the DFA's mandate, particularly in countries without MWOs and for categories such as tourists, students, pilgrims, permanent residents, and dual citizens. It said qualified requests were generally approved rather than denied, while the DMW increasingly handled OFWs as more MWOs opened.

Outcome The DFA explained the division of responsibility between the DFA and DMW and supplied partial ATN utilization and beneficiary figures. The committee requested additional ATN and LAF records and guidelines; the requested documentation was not submitted during the hearing.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

Consular-service expansion, satellite offices, and passport access

Rep. Niko Raul Daza supported the DFA budget and cited the funded forty third consular office in Katarman, Northern Samar as an example of service expansion. The DFA reported 42 consular offices, more than 1.5 million passports processed, and 35 passport on wheels activities as of 08/31/2026. Rep. Eulogio Rodriguez asked the DFA to account for distance, isolation, travel costs, and accessibility in underserved provinces and specifically raised a possible satellite office in Catanhuanes. The DFA said it was assessing existing and proposed offices under operational, fiscal, geographic, DBM, and Executive Order 45 criteria, while studying a satellite model and offering passport on wheels in the interim. Bukidnon and Virac-Catanhuanes requests, consular vehicles, and facility funding remained under review. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported an additional building-fund request of about 300 million and other DFA requests, subject to written submissions and further budget consideration.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DFA was expanding access to consular services, particularly for provinces without a consular office, and whether new, satellite, or mobile facilities could address geographic isolation and travel costs. It also examined the funding and administrative requirements for proposed offices, vehicles, buildings, and related consular infrastructure.

The DFA said it was conducting a nationwide assessment of existing and proposed consular facilities, balancing demand and accessibility against proximity, operational viability, fiscal sustainability, DBM guidance, and Executive Order 45. It had no established satellite-office model but was studying a smaller Catanhuanes facility, while offering passport on wheels as an interim option; requests for Bukidnon, Virac-Catanhuanes, vehicles, and additional building funds remained subject to review and coordination with DBM.

Outcome The DFA answered the accessibility and satellite-office questions and committed to provide a written status update and coordinate with DBM, while offering passport on wheels as an interim service. The proposed permanent facilities, vehicle requests, and funding augmentations were supported in principle but remained subject to DBM review and subsequent written budget action.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

ePassport budget of 5,500,000,000 and procurement breakdown

Assistant Secretary Emilio Fernandez presented passport funding as a major component of the DFA's proposed budget, including 2,800,000,000 for initial next-generation-passport funding and PHP 5,800,000,000 for passports overall. Representative Antonio Tinio then questioned the separate proposed ICT allocation of 956,610,000 and asked what the agency was actually purchasing. The ICT official described a shift toward large-scale capital assets, cited 511,000,000 in ICT projects, and identified the ePassport and passport appointment system among the covered systems. Tinio requested a year-by-year breakdown of ePassport services, providers, and procurement for 2025 through 2027. The DFA committed to provide the list and said the passport database was maintained by a third-party government printer at its facility in Lima, Batangas. The spending breakdown remained pending, so the issue landed as committed rather than fully resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the DFA proposed a large ePassport allocation separate from its ICT expenditures, and how the passport budget would be divided among services, providers, and related procurements. It also sought clarification on the location and security of the passport database.

The DFA said the passport allocation included implementation of the next-generation passport, while ICT expenditures supported broader cybersecurity, digital-transformation, infrastructure, and consular systems. It said the ePassport database was maintained by a third-party government printer at the provider's facility in Lima, Batangas, and undertook to submit the requested multi-year procurement and provider breakdown.

Outcome The DFA answered the database-location question and committed to submit the requested breakdown of ePassport services, providers, and procurement by year. The composition and justification of the 5,500,000,000 allocation were not fully examined on the record.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

ICT budget of about 956.6 million, cybersecurity, and data privacy

Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the DFA's proposed ICT spending of about 956.6 million and sought utilization data and a detailed breakdown of the separate ePassport budget of about 5.5 billion. The DFA explained that ICT spending had shifted toward major capital assets and identified cybersecurity, data privacy, digital transformation and consular systems as priorities. It said current ICT projects totaled 511,000,000 and committed to submit a year-by-year and provider-by-provider breakdown. In response to questions about passport-data security, the DFA said the passport database was maintained on a server at the Apo production facility in Lima, Batangas, rather than in an external cloud. Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro and an ICT official sought cybersecurity funding, with the transcript containing an unclear initial reference to 10,000,000 followed by "Billion," while 250,000,000 was ultimately placed on the record as the minimum request. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez and the chair supported further consideration of the request, subject to a written, signed and endorsed wish list.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DFA's proposed ICT expenditures and ePassport budget were allocated, how much had been utilized, and why the proposed ICT amount had increased. It also sought assurances about cybersecurity, passport-data privacy and sovereignty, and considered additional funding requests for cybersecurity and related ICT capital outlay.

The DFA said the proposed increase in ICT spending was a deliberate shift toward enterprise-grade capital assets needed for cybersecurity, data privacy, digital transformation and critical consular systems. It maintained that substantial cybersecurity funding was necessary because of repeated attacks and the sensitivity of passport data, and committed to submit Rep. Tinio's requested ICT and ePassport breakdown.

Outcome The ICT and cybersecurity issues were not finally resolved through a detailed budget reconciliation. The DFA committed to submit the requested breakdown and written wish list, while the committee signaled support for considering 250,000,000 for cybersecurity and restoring about 300,000,000 to the building fund.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

Passport data storage, sovereignty, and cloud-security arrangements

Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the proposed ICT allocation of about 956.6 million and asked why it had increased, as well as what the capital spending would acquire. The DFA attributed the increase to cybersecurity, data protection, digital transformation, infrastructure resilience, and support for passport and other consular systems; it cited ICT projects of about 511 million. Tinio then contrasted the ICT allocation with the separate ePassport budget of about 5.5 billion and requested a 2025–2027 breakdown by services and providers. The DFA committed to submit the requested list. Tinio also asked where passport data was stored and how its privacy, security, and sovereignty were assured. The DFA said APO maintained the database and data center at the passport plant in Lima, Batangas, and confirmed that the database was in-country, although the exchange about cloud hosting remained unclear.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the DFA proposed 956,610,000 for ICT expenditures, how that amount related to the separate 5,500,000,000 ePassport budget, and what the funds would acquire. It also sought to determine where Filipino passport data was stored and how the DFA could assure its privacy, security, and data sovereignty.

The DFA said its increased ICT spending was a deliberate shift toward enterprise-grade capital assets focused on cybersecurity, data protection, digital transformation, and related systems. It stated that the passport database was maintained by APO at the passport production plant in Lima, Batangas, and characterized the database as being in-country, although the transcript leaves the cloud-service clarification unclear.

Outcome The DFA stated that the passport database was held on an APO-maintained server at the passport production plant in Lima, Batangas, and therefore was in-country. The requested budget breakdown was committed for submission, but the transcript did not fully resolve the cloud-hosting and broader data-sovereignty implications.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

Foreign-service allowances, HMO, and permanent-position requirements

Assistant Secretary Emilio Fernandez reported that the DFA's foreign-service allowances accounted for about 9.9 billion and that about 345 million was set aside for terminal leave benefits. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez then asked for the DFA's priority wish list, which included a special lease provision, cybersecurity funding, building-fund augmentation, and consular vehicles. DFA officials identified 250 million as the reduced cybersecurity request and sought an additional 300 million for the building fund. The Foreign Service Institute requested HMO coverage amounting to MXN 6.5 million for almost 100 personnel, and the VFA Presidential Mission requested 13 permanent positions requiring a little less than 3 million in additional PS. Rodriguez supported the requests and undertook to work for them, while the chair required a signed and endorsed wish list by the following Wednesday. The permanent-position request and DBM-dependent funding actions were not finally resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

What recurring personnel and operating support did the DFA and its attached agencies need for foreign-service allowances, HMO coverage, cybersecurity, facilities, vehicles, and permanent positions? The committee also sought to determine which requests could be supported in the budget and what documents or further DBM action were required.

The DFA sought continued support for foreign-service allowances and additional resources for cybersecurity, building-fund restoration, consular vehicles, HMO coverage, and permanent positions. It committed to coordinate with DBM on funding matters and to submit the requested written wish list and special-provision language, while the permanent positions remained subject to future DBM processing.

Outcome The committee expressed support for the DFA's existing budget and the identified wish-list requests, including the HMO request and proposed funding augmentations. The permanent positions remained subject to a future request and DBM processing, while the written wish list and special-provision language were still to be submitted.

DFA · 2026-09-03 · committed

West Philippine Sea diplomatic protests and China provisional arrangement

Rep. Perci Cendaña asked the DFA to explain the written Philippines-China provisional arrangement for RORE missions, its negotiating authority, and whether it limited Philippine activities in the exclusive economic zone. Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said it was an exchange of notes limited to Ayungin Shoal, without prejudice to Philippine positions under UNCLOS and the 2016 arbitral award, and focused on information exchange for daily necessities. She committed to making the arrangement's details available, and reported 16 RORE missions without incident over two years. Rep. Brian Poe asked about diplomatic protests, and DFA officials reported 39 protests in 2026 and 296 from 2022 to 2026, while noting that diplomacy could take time to produce results. In the second round, Rep. Antonio Tinio challenged Chinese Embassy statements concerning construction materials and the arbitral award; the DFA denied that construction materials were covered by the arrangement and said it raised concerns through diplomatic channels. The complete text and the DFA's response to each public embassy statement were not fully resolved in the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the scope, legal character, operational effect, and disclosure status of the Philippines-China provisional arrangement for rotation and resupply missions in the West Philippine Sea. It also examined the DFA's diplomatic protests against China and its response to public statements by the Chinese Embassy in Manila.

The DFA stated that the provisional arrangement was a limited exchange of notes for information exchange and the safe conduct of RORE missions at Ayungin Shoal, covering the reprovisioning of daily necessities and not requiring Philippine permission from China. It maintained that the arrangement was without prejudice to Philippine sovereignty, territorial claims, UNCLOS position, or the 2016 arbitral award, and said it had responded through diplomatic channels to Chinese positions and statements.

Outcome The DFA clarified the arrangement's stated scope and said it did not contain a restriction on construction materials, but the complete terms were not disclosed in the hearing. The committee recorded the secretary's undertaking to share the arrangement's details, while questions about the DFA's public response to individual Chinese Embassy statements remained only partly answered.

Questions and agency response

The DFA stated that geopolitical issues were the reason the Philippines failed in its UN Security Council bid. Outcome The DFA supplied the total appropriation, obligated amount, and utilization rate and attributed the loss to geopolitical issues. The requested category-level expenditures and post-campaign accountability assessment were not provided in the exchange, leaving those matters open.

Critical Minerals Agreement review and US-Philippines economic relations

Rep. Renee Co asked the DFA to submit the Critical Minerals Agreement or MOU with the United States and clarify whether the DFA had reviewed it. The DFA said the DENR led the agreement, with DTI and BOI involved, and that the DFA did not possess the document. DFA officials said the DENR and DTI had assessed the economic aspects, so the Office of International Economic Relations did not conduct a separate economic review, although the DFA concurred with the agreement. The agency said the arrangement could support value-added processing of copper and nickel, technological know-how, investment protection, and participation in chip, artificial-intelligence, and electric-vehicle applications. Rep. Co emphasized that the agreement had implications beyond one bilateral relationship and that the DFA should consider consistency with related agreements. The secretary committed to requesting the MOU from the concerned agency, but the scope of the DFA's review role remained partly unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the DFA had reviewed the Critical Minerals Agreement or MOU between the Philippines and the United States, what role it played in clearing or assessing the agreement, and whether it could provide the committee with a copy. It also sought clarification on the agreement's broader implications for US-Philippines economic, trade, and political relations.

The DFA said it did not possess the Critical Minerals Agreement and had not conducted a separate economic review because the DENR and DTI were the lead and more competent agencies on the agreement's economic aspects. It said the DFA nevertheless concurred based on the lead agencies' assessment and considered the arrangement beneficial to Philippine processing capabilities and US-Philippines relations.

Outcome The DFA did not provide the MOU during the hearing and said it would have to request the document from the concerned agency. The DFA's review role remained limited in the agency's account to being consulted or giving concurrence, while the broader question of the extent of its language and international-agreement review was not fully resolved.

Rep. Brian Poe asked how the DFA was assisting Filipinos affected by the Nepal crisis and sought an update on Sam De La Cruz’s remains. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DFA was assisting Filipinos affected by the Nepal crisis and whether it could secure the repatriation of Sam De La Cruz’s remains from Somalia. It also examined the scale, beneficiaries, approval rules, and documentation governing the Assistance to Nationals (ATN) Fund.

The DFA said it was coordinating through its regional diplomatic posts, honorary consul, international organizations, and local authorities to assist Filipinos affected by the Nepal crisis and identify the missing Filipino. It remained committed to pursuing the return of Sam De La Cruz’s remains and said ATN assistance was governed by a 2019 department order with defined approval authorities.

Outcome The Nepal assistance and ATN utilization information were presented, while the Sam De La Cruz case remained dependent on renewed diplomatic engagement with Somali authorities. The DFA committed to pursuing the remains case and was asked to submit the ATN Fund guidelines.

FY2027 CHR budget reduction and restoration request

CHR Chairperson Richard Palpalato presented an original FY 2027 proposal of about 2.75 billion against a 2027 NEP allocation of about 1.27 billion, describing an almost 53% reduction and the elimination of capital outlay. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez sought restoration of the 74,000,000 Tier 1 reduction and asked the CHR to identify its highest-priority Tier 2 items; Palpalato identified preventive monitoring, mandatory expenses, productivity, capacity building, information systems, and international participation, with the exchange pointing to a package of roughly 200 million to 250 million. De Lima and Aris Montes separately supported restoration and received answers on the CHR’s monitoring and gender-ombud functions, while Salazar said the 592,000,000 trust fund remained with the Bureau of the Treasury and had not been released. In response to the NGO caucus, Palpalato reiterated the 2,749,000,000 proposal, the roughly 1.27 billion NEP amount, the 53% reduction, and a 34,000,000 MOOE cut, although some figures in that exchange were unclear. The committee required a consolidated, prioritized wishlist with the Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission by September 9, and the hearing was terminated without a final restoration decision.

Questions and agency response

What was the extent and effect of the reduction in the CHR’s FY 2027 proposed budget, and which Tier 1 and Tier 2 items did the committee seek to restore or augment? The committee also sought to establish how the reduced funding would affect the CHR’s statutory and constitutional functions and requested a prioritized written wishlist.

The CHR said its original FY 2027 proposal of 2,749,000,000 was reduced by almost 53% in the NEP, with capital outlay eliminated and MOOE reduced. It asked Congress to restore the reduced funding and support prioritized Tier 2 requirements for preventive monitoring, mandatory operating expenses, productivity, capacity building, information systems, infrastructure, and related mandates.

Outcome The committee did not finally resolve the restoration amount during the hearing. Members expressed support for restoring the CHR’s reduced funding and increasing it for prioritized Tier 2 requirements, while the CHR committed to submit a written, consolidated and prioritized wishlist.

Tier 2 priority requests and written funding list

Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez supported restoring the CHR’s reduction and asked for the first three Tier 2 priorities in writing. In response to the NGO caucus, Palpalato said the CHR had no administrative or programmatic oversight over NTF-ELCAC or the Support to the Barangay Development Program, but needed resources for field monitoring, investigations, assistance, and human-rights education in vulnerable communities. The committee required a consolidated, prioritized CHR and Human Rights Violations Victims Memorial Commission wishlist by September 9, and the CHR agreed to comply.

It also sought clarification on the CHR’s resource needs for monitoring the Support to the Barangay Development Program and requested a prioritized written wishlist.

The CHR maintained that its proposed Tier 2 funding was needed to expand preventive visitation and torture prevention, cover mandatory central and regional office expenses, improve productivity and information systems, build local human-rights capacity, and support infrastructure and institutional roles. Outcome The CHR answered the committee’s questions about its ranked priorities and committed to submit a written, consolidated wishlist, including the amounts and priorities requested by the committee. The possible restoration or augmentation was not finally approved in the hearing and remained subject to committee review and fiscal space.

CHR · 2026-09-03 · committed

Capital outlay reduced to zero

The CHR chairperson said the FY 2027 NEP was reduced mainly because it contained no capital outlay, affecting the commission’s proposed infrastructure, ICT, facilities, and vehicle requirements. The deputy minority leader asked how zero capital outlay would affect mandate delivery, and the chairperson answered that it would constrain ICT infrastructure, facilities, and regional-office workplaces. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez and Vice Chair Sia Agyong supported restoring or substantially increasing the CHR budget, with Rodriguez specifically identifying retrofitting, ICT, buildings, and vehicles. Rodriguez requested a written list of the CHR’s highest priorities, and the chairperson committed to submit it by the next day. Representative Reneko linked funding needs to jail visitation, torture prevention, rapid response to red-tagging, and digital evidence capabilities; the CHR provided a total protection-program figure of 323,278,000 but did not provide the exact jail-visitation allocation. In the later NGO-caucus exchange, the chairperson restated the proposal as 2,749,000,000 and the NEP as 1,272,000,000, and cited a capital-outlay amount transcribed unclearly as “ND152 million.” The issue was left for subsequent budget amendments rather than finally resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed zero allocation for capital outlay would affect the Commission on Human Rights’ infrastructure, ICT capabilities, regional offices, transportation, and delivery of its constitutional mandate. Members also sought the restoration of the capital outlay and clarification of the related Tier 1 and Tier 2 funding requests.

The CHR stated that the absence of capital outlay would constrain ICT infrastructure, facilities, retrofitting, regional-office workplaces, software, and transport vehicles, thereby limiting mandate delivery. It sought restoration of the capital-outlay component and broader support for its Tier 2 infrastructure and digital-capability requests.

Outcome Members broadly supported restoring or substantially increasing CHR funding, including the eliminated capital-outlay component, but no restoration was formally approved in the transcript. The CHR committed to submit a written priority list, while the capital-outlay issue remained subject to subsequent budget amendment deliberations.
