CHR · 2026-09-03 · committed

Case backlog and capacity to resolve investigations

Leila de Lima asked which CHR mandate faced the greatest resource constraints and whether the commission had case backlogs. CHR identified prevention as the most resource-constrained mandate and reported that it had resolved 95.8 percent of a historical backlog of about 28,000 cases, leaving roughly 1,200 pending. De Lima and Antonio Tinio separately pressed CHR on drug-war investigations; CHR cited 493 cases for reinvestigation, 289 cases investigated or concluded by the task force, and 140 cases for resolution, with delays attributed to lack of evidence, noncooperation, missing documents, and reprisal risks. CHR committed to prioritize the 140 cases within the year and submit a written update before plenary. An NGO caucus raised regional staffing and workload concerns, and CHR acknowledged that Regions 4-B, 7, and the Negros Island Region remained affected by manpower and geographic constraints. CHR agreed to submit regional personnel figures, but the additional staffing and FY 2027 appropriation required remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the extent of CHR case backlogs, the status and resolution rate of investigations—particularly drug-war cases—and whether CHR had sufficient personnel and resources to discharge its mandates. It also asked what additional data, staffing, and reports CHR would provide and what targets it could commit to meet.

CHR said it had substantially reduced its historical backlog, reporting a 95.8 percent resolution rate, but acknowledged continuing pending and regional-office backlogs. It attributed delays—especially in drug-war reinvestigations—to lack of evidence, noncooperation, missing police documents, reprisal risks, staffing shortages, and geographic barriers, while committing to prioritize 140 drug-war cases within the year and submit written and staffing updates.

Outcome The committee received CHR's reported backlog and drug-war investigation figures and obtained commitments to resolve 140 drug-war cases within the year and submit written case and staffing updates. The broader question of whether CHR had adequate staffing and what additional FY 2027 appropriation was required remained open.

Jail visitation and monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty

CHR Richard Palpalato reported that the commission visited 960 facilities in 2024, 985 in 2025, and 617 during the first semester of 2026, but could reach only about one third of 2,920 detention facilities with existing resources. He said DBM had provided 16,000,000 and 19,000 for the expanded visitation program, although the context of the 19,000 figure was unclear, and requested 108,223,700 under Tier 2 for visitation and torture prevention. Representative Reneko supported restoring the budget and pressed for more frequent jail visits, rapid-response legal teams for red-tagging, and digital-forensics capabilities. The CHR gave 323,278,000 as the total protection-program allotment but did not provide a separate jail-visitation or red-tagging amount. Leila de Lima asked which mandate faced the greatest resource gap, and the CHR identified prevention because it shared funding with protection and lacked a dedicated allocation. The CHR agreed to submit rapid-response guidelines, while funding restoration and digital evidence resources remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had sufficient funding and personnel to conduct regular visitation and preventive monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty. Members also asked how the CHR's prevention mandate was funded, including jail visitation, torture prevention, rapid response to red-tagging, and related investigative capabilities.

The CHR stated that prevention services, including visitation and monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty, were its most resource-constrained mandate because they lacked a dedicated budget and shared resources with protection services. It maintained that additional funding would permit more frequent and wider facility coverage, earlier risk identification, corrective recommendations, and torture prevention.

Outcome The need for additional funding for jail visitation and prevention services was presented and supported, but the exact dedicated jail-visitation allocation was not supplied during the exchange. The CHR committed to submit rapid-response guidelines, leaving the requested funding restoration and the digital-forensics funding question unresolved.

A committee member asked whether the CHR had a dedicated program for digital privacy, online harassment, cyberbullying, misinformation, and artificial-intelligence risks. CHR chairperson Richard Palpalato said the Commission had focal officials, research, policy monitoring, and protection activities concerning emerging technology and human rights. Representative Reneko later connected red-tagging to online campaigns, doxing, and deepfakes and asked about rapid-response protocols and funding for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, and secure databases. The CHR cited a broader protection-program allotment of 323,278,000 but did not identify a separate digital-evidence allocation. The CHR agreed to submit guidelines or related materials, while the specific digital-capacity funding question was left unanswered.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had programs, funding, protocols, and operational capacity to address digital privacy violations, online harassment, cyberbullying, misinformation, artificial intelligence risks, and digitally enabled red-tagging. It also asked whether the CHR had digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, secure databases, and systems to preserve digital evidence.

The CHR stated that it had institutional activities on emerging technology and human rights, including focal officials, research on artificial intelligence, monitoring of gender-based violence and disinformation, and protection-related work involving technology. However, it did not state a specific budget for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring systems, or secure digital-evidence databases; it only identified the broader protection-program allotment of 323,278,000 and agreed to submit requested guidelines or related material.

Outcome The CHR described existing emerging-technology and human-rights activities and provided the broader protection-program figure, but it did not answer with a dedicated amount for digital-forensic tools, cyber-threat monitoring, or secure database infrastructure. The request for guidelines was accepted for submission, while the digital-evidence funding question remained open.

CHR · 2026-09-03 · committed

NTF-ELCAC and barangay development-program monitoring

Rep. Reneko supported restoring the CHR budget and sought funding for jail visitation, rapid-response legal teams, and digital evidence capabilities in response to red-tagging. The CHR said its total protection-program allotment was 323,278,000 but did not identify a separate red-tagging allocation, and it agreed to submit relevant recommendations and guidelines. Rep. Leila de Lima asked about resource gaps, case backlogs, drug-war investigations, ICC membership, and NTF-ELCAC oversight; the CHR reported that 95.8 percent of about 28,000 backlog cases had been resolved, with around 1,200 pending, and identified 493 drug-war cases for reinvestigation. The CHR supported rejoining the ICC but said it had no formal oversight over NTF-ELCAC, limiting its role to monitoring compliance and investigating violations. An NGO caucus then asked about the roughly 740 million Support to the Barangay Development Program and the safeguards and resources needed in vulnerable communities. CHR Richard Palpalato said additional demands would involve more field monitoring, investigations, protection, documentation, and human-rights education, and reiterated the agency's tier-two resource proposal.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether CHR had sufficient resources and authority to monitor, investigate, and respond to human-rights risks associated with NTF-ELCAC and the Support to the Barangay Development Program. It also examined CHR's response to red-tagging, its position on ICC membership, relevant case backlogs, and safeguards or additional resources needed in vulnerable communities.

The CHR stated that it had no administrative, programmatic, or formal oversight function over NTF-ELCAC or the Support to the Barangay Development Program because these were executive-branch functions. It could nevertheless monitor government compliance with human-rights obligations, investigate alleged violations, and would require stronger regional-office capacity for field monitoring, complaint handling, investigations, protection, documentation, and community engagement in vulnerable areas.

Outcome The committee received the CHR's clarification that it could monitor and investigate human-rights violations connected with NTF-ELCAC and the Barangay Development Program but could not exercise formal oversight over them. The need for additional regional capacity and tier-two funding was reiterated, while specific red-tagging allocations and safeguards were not fully resolved.

CHR · 2026-09-03 · resolved

ICC reengagement and human-rights implications

The deputy minority leader asked whether the CHR would lead advocacy for the Philippines’ reengagement with the ICC. The CHR said it supported rejoining the ICC and the Rome Statute and had issued statements, policy recommendations, public-information materials, and an EJK report concerning ICC-related developments. The member urged the CHR to speak more visibly for victims and against false narratives surrounding the ICC proceedings involving former president Rodrigo Duterte. Leila de Lima later asked about the status of drug-war investigations and the CHR’s ICC position. The CHR reported 493 cases for reinvestigation and described the task force as having concluded “208 289” cases, an unclear figure, while citing lack of evidence, hostile conditions, noncooperation, and unavailable police documents as obstacles. The CHR unequivocally maintained that rejoining the ICC and Rome Statute would provide an additional assurance of accountability for human-rights violations.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the CHR’s position and actions regarding the Philippines’ possible reengagement with the ICC and return to the Rome Statute. Members also asked how the CHR was investigating drug-war killings and communicating its human-rights position in relation to the ICC proceedings.

The CHR stated that it consistently supported the Philippines rejoining the ICC and the Rome Statute, viewing this as an additional guarantee of accountability for human-rights violations. It said it had advocated this position through statements, recommendations, policy papers, public-information activities, and monitoring, while continuing to investigate and reinvestigate drug-war cases.

Outcome The CHR gave a clear and consistent answer that it supported the Philippines rejoining the ICC and the Rome Statute and described its related advocacy and investigative work. The issue was informationally resolved, although the transcript did not record a separate committee ruling or action on reengagement.

It said limited resources required adaptation but that additional, dedicated funding would strengthen compliance monitoring and the discharge of special mandates.

The deputy minority leader questioned whether the CHR had adequate funding for job-order personnel and capital outlay, and said a motion would be made to restore capital outlay. The member also pressed the CHR to be more vocal on victims' rights and the ICC proceedings; the CHR cited its public statements, monitoring role, victim assistance, and the reopening of 493 cases, with 140 for disposition. Representative Reneko sought additional funding for jail visitation and cited a priority grant of 108,000,000, while the CHR said limited resources had restricted visit frequency and reported a total protection-program allotment of 323,278,000. The CHR described a three-pillar national protection mechanism for human-rights defenders involving early warning, protection services, and monitoring, but funding and implementation details remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the CHR had sufficient resources and operational capacity to protect human-rights defenders, victims, and persons deprived of liberty, including through jail visitation, legal assistance, rapid response, and digital evidence preservation. Members also asked how the CHR was addressing red-tagging, gender-based violence, case backlogs, and the proposed national protection mechanism.

The CHR said protection work was constrained by limited operating and capital-outlay resources, affecting jail-visit frequency, regional operations, and infrastructure. It presented its protection program, existing victim and witness services, and a proposed three-pillar national protection mechanism for human-rights defenders, but did not identify exact allocations for rapid-response legal deployment, digital forensic capabilities, or jail visitation.

The Commission undertook to submit rapid-response guidelines; restoration of capital outlay and additional protection funding were supported by members but were not shown as finally approved.

CHR · 2026-09-03 · unresolved

Martial-law reparation trust-fund interest and release status

Rep. Leila de Lima asked whether about 597.7 million in martial-law reparation trust-fund interest had been released in fiscal year 2026 and sought the status of the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund. CHR Executive Director Lorette Salazar answered that the trust fund remained intact with the Bureau of the Treasury and that no amount had been released because the commission had not made a request. She said a request to the DBM would be necessary before any release. Salazar identified the fund as sourced from the 10,000,000,000 reparations fund, said distribution of reparations was complete, and described 592,000,000 as intended for memorialization. The exchange did not resolve the discrepancy between the reported interest amount and the agency's stated trust-fund amount.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether 597,742,802.78 in martial-law reparation trust-fund interest had been released during fiscal year 2026, why the corresponding provision was absent from the proposed 2027 budget, and the current status of the 10,000,000,000 reparation fund.

The CHR said the trust fund remained intact with the Bureau of the Treasury and that no amount had been released because the commission had not requested funds. It said the reparations distribution was complete and that the remaining trust-fund balance was for memorialization purposes.

Outcome The CHR answered that no release had occurred and that the trust fund remained with the Bureau of the Treasury, while stating that reparations distribution was complete and the remaining balance was for memorialization. The difference between the reported 597,742,802.78 interest amount and the 592,000,000 amount cited by the agency was not explained, and no release or follow-up submission was committed during the exchange.

CHR · 2026-09-03 · unresolved

CHR program allocations for personal services, MOOE, and Arleap

Sarah Elago and the committee reviewed the CHR's proposed allocations for personal services, MOOE, Arleap, and its protection, promotion, policy, and jail-visitation programs. The agency reported a stated total of about 1.27 billion, along with program allocations and participation figures for community dialogues and promotion activities. Elago asked whether activities represented expansions and how human-rights education could be institutionalized; the agency cited regional dialogues and partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher educational institutions, and law schools. An NGO and civil-society representative then asked for the CHR's total proposal, the NEP recommendation, the shortfall, the reasons for reductions, affected expenditures, operational consequences, and requested augmentation. Richard Palpalato cited a proposal of about 2.75 billion, an NEP amount of about 1.27 billion, a stated 53% reduction, a capital-outlay figure of "ND152 million," and an MOOE reduction of 34,000,000. The excerpt ended without a complete answer on the DBM rationale, all operational effects, or the requested augmentation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the CHR's proposed FY 2027 budget was distributed among personal services, MOOE, Arleap, and core programs, and how those allocations supported community dialogues and human-rights education. It also asked what budget the CHR proposed to the DBM, what the NEP recommended, the resulting shortfall, and the operational effects of reductions or exclusions.

The CHR presented its proposed allocations for personnel services, MOOE, Arleap, and its protection, promotion, policy, and jail-visitation programs. It said regional offices conducted community dialogues and described partnerships with DepEd, CHED, higher educational institutions, and law schools to advance human-rights education. On the FY 2027 reduction, the CHR attributed the MOOE decrease to a reduction in the ISSP and identified effects on capital outlay, but did not clearly answer every question concerning DBM's reasons, operational consequences, or requested augmentation.

Outcome The committee received the CHR's program allocations, participation figures, partnership information, and partial explanation of the FY 2027 reduction. Public Transport Modernization Program funding and continuity

Members led by Rep. Carl Legaspi, Rep. Renee Co, Rep. Lim, Rep. Chan, Rep. Rodge Gutierrez, and Rep. Bonispares questioned the sharp reduction in PTMP funding and its effect on operators, commuters, vehicle supply, and program continuity. DOTr said the reduced 2027 amount would support only limited operations, ground preparation, route rationalization, industry consolidation, stakeholder support, and monitoring, while seeking congressional help for subsidies and service contracting. The agency reported a 1,500,000,000 unobligated amount in one update, and explained that the 2026 1,500,000,000 budget had only recently received its cash allotment. Members also challenged inconsistent consolidation figures, including the agency's correction from 86.23% to 83.64%, and requested updated franchise and unit data. The Secretary committed to written explanations within the following week, while other questions on utilization, passenger demand, GPS transmission, reporting baselines, and passenger infrastructure were not fully answered. The issue therefore landed with agency submissions and congressional efforts to restore funding still pending.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the sharply reduced FY 2027 funding would allow the Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP) to continue, including subsidies, route rationalization, consolidation, service contracting, and support for operators and commuters. Members also sought explanations for prior unobligated funds, current utilization, vehicle and consolidation data, and the department's plans to address financing distress and passenger needs.

DOTr said PTMP remained necessary but acknowledged that implementation and utilization had been problems. It said the reduced 2027 allocation would sustain limited operations and ground preparation, while the department intended to pursue equity subsidies, support for distressed transport groups, and congressional restoration or augmentation of PTMP, fuel subsidy, and service-contracting funds.

Outcome The committee did not accept the reduced PTMP funding as sufficient and members repeatedly indicated that they would seek restoration or augmentation of PTMP, fuel subsidy, service contracting, and related active-transport funds. DOTr committed to written explanations and updated consolidation data, but questions about utilization, passenger-capacity effects, route viability, GPS compliance, baselines, and the full continuity plan remained unanswered.

Active transport, bike lanes, and Safe Pathways funding

Members Renee Co, Rep. Lim, Rep. Chan, Rep. Rodge Gutierrez, the Ways and Means Committee chairman, and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the sharp reduction in active-transport, bike-lane, and Safe Pathways funding. The proposed amount was cited variously as 33,900,000 or 33,000,000, compared with about 105 million in the prior year, while another presentation described a reduction from 1,100,000,000 to 33,000,000 or 34,000,000. DOTr said the proposed amount would support only about six kilometers in one exchange and 33 kilometers of Class One bike lanes in another, while DBM cited 2.66% utilization of the 60,000,000 2025 allocation and limited absorptive capacity. DOTr attributed delays to LGU partnerships and tranche-based downloading, and said it would complete procurement for a sidewalk project funded at more than 60 million and use the remaining 34,000,000 with an LGU. Members sought restoration, convergence with DPWH, clearer congressional oversight, and a report on 3,800,000,000 appropriated from 2022 to 2026. The issue remained unresolved as to the final 2027 appropriation, but the agency made implementation and reporting commitments.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why active-transport, bike-lane, and Safe Pathways funding had been sharply reduced, whether the proposed amount could deliver meaningful infrastructure, and whether low utilization justified the reduction. Members also asked how projects were being implemented with LGUs, what oversight and monitoring would apply, and whether funding should be restored or amended.

DOTr and DBM attributed the reduced active-transport and Safe Pathways proposal primarily to limited fiscal space and low utilization or absorptive capacity, while DOTr said LGU partnerships and tranche-based downloading had delayed liquidation and disbursement. DOTr maintained that active-transport implementation was coordinated with, rather than formally devolved by policy to, LGUs, and undertook to accelerate procurement, use remaining funds, improve monitoring, and submit a progress report.

Outcome The reduction was not restored during the hearing. DOTr and DBM defended the proposed amount on fiscal-space and utilization grounds, while members continued to press for restoration and better oversight; DOTr committed to implementation steps and a progress report, leaving the adequacy of the 2027 funding unresolved.

EDSA Busway zero FY2027 allocation and operating support

Rep. Carl Legaspi first raised concern that the EDSA Busway had a proposed budget of about 1.79 billion but received zero allocation, alongside a sharp reduction in public-transport modernization funding. Rep. Claudine Botisdalim and Rep. Lim then asked what the zero line item would mean for busway operations, maintenance, safety, accessibility, and station rehabilitation. DOTr officials said maintenance, security, accessibility equipment, and station improvements remained necessary, and Senior Undersecretary Pastor identified a FY2027 request of about 1.7 billion to rehabilitate 12 more stations and facilities. Pastor also cited ridership rising from 90,000 to 190,000 passengers per month at one renovated station. Rep. Lim appealed for the full request, while Rep. Rodge Gutierrez later supported restoring transport programs and examining convergence arrangements. The hearing did not record a committee decision restoring the allocation, leaving the issue unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the EDSA Busway had no FY2027 line-item allocation and whether the absence of funding would disrupt its operations, maintenance, safety, accessibility, and rehabilitation. Members also sought clarification on the amount needed to sustain and improve the busway.

DOTr officials did not indicate that the EDSA Busway would cease operating. They described continuing maintenance, safety, accessibility, security, and station-rehabilitation requirements and identified 1,700,000,000 as the FY2027 request to rehabilitate 12 additional stations and facilities. The agency also said EDSA Greenways had been pivoted to other projects because it was not progressing as expected.

Outcome DOTr identified 1,700,000,000 as the FY2027 requirement for rehabilitation of 12 additional EDSA Busway stations and facilities, and members supported restoring or funding the request. No committee ruling or confirmed restoration of the zero FY2027 allocation was recorded.

PTMP consolidation, franchise data, and route capacity

Congresswoman Renee Co raised conflicting fleet data and argued that modernization may have removed about 171,000 PUJ units and roughly 34,000,000 in daily passenger capacity, while the agency attributed the decline mainly to route rationalization and authorized-unit limits. She also questioned nearly 9 billion in PTMP funding and cited 1.6 billion in unobligated 2022 funds; the Secretary committed to submit written explanations and a budget report within the next week. Congressman Bonispares challenged the reported 86.23% franchise-consolidation rate, and the agency corrected it to 83.64% while promising more detailed franchise and provisional-authority data. He also questioned how a 176 million FY 2027 request could sustain a program previously associated with amounts including 1,500,000,000, 2,500,000,000, and 1,000,000,000; the Secretary maintained that the program would continue but acknowledged implementation problems. Civil-society questions sought route-demand testing, GPS compliance, modernization baselines, staffing data, and passenger infrastructure, but several received no precise answer. The issue therefore landed with documentary commitments but material data and accountability questions unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the actual number of public transport units and franchises before and after modernization, whether consolidation reduced passenger-carrying capacity, and how route rationalization affected authorized units. It also examined PTMP funding utilization, the basis for the proposed FY 2027 allocation, and whether the program would continue with adequate data, monitoring, and passenger infrastructure.

DOTr and LTFRB officials said the reduced unit counts were substantially attributable to route rationalization and authorized-unit limits, not solely to modernization. They maintained that PTMP would continue, but acknowledged implementation and utilization problems, proposed to use newly downloaded cash authority for subsidies, and undertook to submit updated consolidation, franchise, and budget-utilization data.

Outcome The agency explained that route rationalization and authorized-unit limits contributed to lower vehicle counts and acknowledged that PTMP implementation had been problematic. Updated fleet, franchise, consolidation, and unobligated-fund documents were committed, but the passenger-capacity calculations, GPS reporting rate, route-demand assessment, modernization baseline, and passenger-infrastructure responsibilities remained unanswered or insufficiently supported.

Unobligated and underutilized transport-modernization funds

Rep. Renee Co questioned the loss of transport capacity and cited unobligated PTMP amounts, including nearly 9 billion and 1.6 billion in 2022; DOTr attributed lower vehicle counts to route rationalization and acknowledged that earlier funding required further explanation. The secretary committed to submit a written PTMP report from 2018 through 2025 within the following week. Other members challenged reductions in PTMP, fuel subsidy, service contracting, EDSA Busway, and active-transport funding; DOTr said limited fiscal space, delayed releases, and weak absorptive capacity contributed to the reductions and sought congressional help to restore funds. The agency described the proposed PTMP budget as about 177 million, including financing, route rationalization, consolidation, stakeholder support, and monitoring activities, and said a 1 billion NCA would fund subsidy support. DBM cited 2.66% active-transport utilization for 2025, while DOTr attributed low utilization partly to tranche-based LGU releases and committed to accelerate procurement and submit progress data. Civil-society questions on passenger-demand testing, GPS validity, modernization baselines, passenger infrastructure, and staffing were read into the record, but several answers, especially the GPS percentage and staffing figures, remained incomplete.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why transport-modernization and related public-transport appropriations were unobligated or underutilized, and whether reduced FY2027 funding would impair PTMP continuity, fuel subsidy, service contracting, active transport, and passenger infrastructure. Members also sought updated consolidation, utilization, and monitoring data and asked whether the agency would provide documents or seek restoration of funds.

DOTr attributed low utilization and reduced proposed funding primarily to limited fiscal space, delayed or tranche-based releases, and implementation or absorptive-capacity problems. It nevertheless stated that PTMP would continue through a policy pivot, subsidy support, and requests to restore service contracting, fuel subsidy, active transport, and other reduced lines.

Outcome The committee did not resolve the causes and extent of historical PTMP unobligated funds or the adequacy of the reduced FY2027 allocations. DOTr and LTFRB undertook to submit updated data and reports, while members manifested support for restoring or increasing several programs.

Rep. Lim questioned the effects of reduced or zero funding for the EDSA Busway, fuel subsidy, active transport, and public-transport modernization. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 budget would affect the EDSA Busway, fuel subsidy, active transport, public-transport modernization, and service contracting. Members also asked whether DOTr intended to restore zeroed-out support for transport operators and drivers, particularly amid an oil crisis and financial pressure on modernized jeepney cooperatives.

DOTr said the 2025 fuel-subsidy allocation had been downloaded to the LTFRB and fully disbursed, subject to an unclear administrative deduction. Agency officials said the proposed allocations could sustain only limited modernization and active-transport activities, attributed the reductions to limited fiscal space, and sought congressional help to restore fuel subsidy, service contracting, modernization, and active-transport funding.

Outcome The agency answered how the 2025 fuel subsidy was used and identified limited proposed funding for modernization and active transport. However, restoration of the zeroed-out fuel-subsidy and service-contracting lines, and significant increases for active transport, modernization, and the EDSA Busway, remained subject to congressional action.

North-South Commuter Railway funding, utilization, and completion

Committee members first sought the status of relocation for 637 affected families and were told that none had yet been relocated, although site construction and inspection were ongoing. The DOTr right-of-way official gave April 2027 as the target for completion and was asked to submit detailed relocation and turnover data. Chairman Franz Pumaren questioned whether inadequate funding could affect NSCR utilization. Representative Bong Son Dai then examined the NSCR allocation of about 123.8 billion, foreign-assisted project utilization, right-of-way acquisition, and the financing gap; the DOTr reported an NSCR funding total of about 67 billion, an obligation rate of 89.89%, and a disbursement rate of 47.94% as of June 2026. The Department said the first phase was targeted for December 2027, the Clark demonstration run for June 2028, and revenue operations toward Clark for the last quarter of 2028. The financing gap and a firm full-project completion date remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the North-South Commuter Railway (NSCR) had adequate and usable funding, including foreign-loan and GOP counterpart financing, and whether obligations and disbursements were keeping pace. Members also asked about right-of-way constraints, relocation, utilization, and the realistic dates for partial and full operations.

The DOTr said NSCR implementation was progressing but depended on continuing foreign-loan proceeds and GOP counterpart funding, with right-of-way acquisition being prioritized. It reported high obligations but substantially lower disbursement for NSCR and gave operating targets of December 2027 for the initial segment and the last quarter of 2028 for revenue operations toward Clark.

Outcome The Department provided utilization, financing, right-of-way, and operating targets, but the hearing did not resolve the funding gap or establish a firm full-project completion date. Relocation information was to be submitted to the committee, with April 2027 given as the resettlement target.

Metro Manila Subway and other railway completion targets

Rep. Bong Son Dai questioned the scale and utilization of railway appropriations, emphasizing that the North-South Railway and Metro Manila Subway together represented about 191.3 billion and roughly 76% of the DOTr-OSEC expenditure program. DOTr officials reported an 82 obligation rate as of July 2026, 33 billion in June and July disbursements for foreign-assisted NSCR and subway projects, and 89.89% obligations against 47.94% disbursements for NSCR as of June. They said about 90% of NSCR and subway right of way had been acquired, while funding remained incomplete, including only 26 billion of a 47 billion GOP counterpart requirement. The agency targeted December 2027 for initial NSCR partial operations, June 2028 for a demonstration run, late 2028 for revenue operations, and around 2031 for Metro Manila Subway operations. Rep. France separately questioned whether the PNR South Long Haul investment was justified, and a PNR official cited current ridership of about 1,600 daily and projected ridership of 20 to 25,000 under the original alignment. PNR committed to submit written data and justification before plenary consideration.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 railway allocations were being utilized effectively, whether right-of-way and counterpart-funding constraints could be managed, and when the North-South Commuter Railway and Metro Manila Subway would reach operations. It also asked whether the proposed PNR South Long Haul investment was financially justified and requested supporting ridership and investment data.

The DOTr said railway implementation was progressing, with high NSCR obligations, substantial recent disbursements for foreign-assisted projects, and most NSCR and subway right of way acquired. It maintained targets of December 2027 for initial NSCR partial operations, roughly the last quarter of 2028 for NSCR revenue operations after a June 2028 demonstration run, and around 2031 for Metro Manila Subway operations; PNR officials continued to support rehabilitation and requested additional capital funding for South Long Haul.

Outcome The DOTr provided indicative completion and operations targets, utilization figures, and right-of-way status, but funding gaps and counterpart-fund requirements remained concerns. The PNR South Long Haul question was committed for further review through a written submission before plenary consideration.

LRT-2 capacity and improvement funding

Rep. Renee Co raised LRT-2's record ridership of 250,578 passengers and cited 197,000,000,000 in proposed rail transport funding for improvement. The agency said the Gen Four train sets were financed through an ODA loan and described LRMC revenues, including about 31 billion in total revenues, about 14 billion for rehabilitation, and about 6 billion in 2015 operating expenses. Rep. Renee Co also questioned LRMC's responsibility for leaks, flooding, cleanliness, and other service failures; the administrator cited 121,000,000 in outstanding penalties. The agency undertook to submit NNIC revenue and passenger-service-charge data, while Rep. Renee Co said she would submit a formal written request. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed rail transport investment would address LRT-2's rising ridership and limited train capacity. It also examined the financing and use of rail revenues, responsibility for LRT-1 service deficiencies, and whether additional revenue and passenger-service data would be submitted.

The agency said LRT-2's principal challenge was its aging train fleet, with trains more than twenty-two years old and insufficient capacity during peak periods. It stated that Gen Four train sets were ODA-loan financed, that LRMC revenues were being used for system rehabilitation and operations, and that LRMC could be penalized for concession-agreement violations.

Outcome The agency explained that aging LRT-2 trains were the main capacity constraint and confirmed that additional train procurement was part of the budget proposals, but it did not provide a clear capacity projection or directly resolve the public-debt question. Revenue, accountability, and NNIC data matters were left for written submissions and follow-up.

Ozamis City Airport modernization funding

Representative Inviu Aminal raised Ozamis City Airport modernization as a regional and presidential priority targeted for completion by 2028. DOTr officials confirmed that the project had received no DOTr funding from 2023 onward and cited limited fiscal space and low obligation or utilization rates as possible reasons. The secretary mentioned about 300 million in connection with the proposal, while the implementing authority confirmed a ballpark modernization requirement of about 2.1 billion. The agency also cited 169 million for site acquisition, a transcribed phase-one amount of 303,300,000,000, and 891,000,000 for the FY2027 phase-two asphalt overlay. The secretary declined to commit to a specific final FY2027 amount without board consultation and undertook to get back to the committee, leaving completion funding unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Department of Transportation had recognized Ozamis City Airport modernization as a priority and whether the FY2027 proposal contained funding for it. Representative Inviu Aminal also asked what funding could be provided through the end of the President’s term to complete the project by 2028.

DOTr officials said the airport had no DOTr funding from 2023 onward, attributing the absence to limited fiscal space and, potentially, low obligation or utilization rates. The implementing authority identified 2027 phase-two funding of 891,000,000, but the secretary said the department could not commit to a specific 2027 amount without consulting and obtaining approval from the relevant board and undertook to get back to the committee.

Outcome The hearing established that the project had lacked DOTr funding from 2023 onward and that the implementing authority cited 891,000,000 for the FY2027 phase-two asphalt overlay. The department did not commit to the final FY2027 amount or full completion funding and undertook to consult the relevant board and report back.

Chairman Franz Pumaren asked MARINA to confirm the cyber incident, identify system accountability, and explain the effect on seafarer-document processing. Questions and agency response

It also sought an explanation for reports that seafarers were being charged substantially higher amounts for fast-track processing.

MARINA said the cyber incident had not resulted in data loss and that operations had resumed through a temporary and controlled system. It said the system required a technology refresh and disaster-recovery capability, while the alleged fast-track charges would be investigated.

Outcome MARINA answered that DICT was investigating the cyber incident and that the agency needed funding for system modernization and recovery capability. The alleged fast-track charges remained under investigation, with MARINA committed to provide a report.

NLEX flooding mitigation and alternative transport routes

Rep. Anna York Bondoc raised the severe NLEX flooding and traffic disruption, reporting delays of about ten to twelve hours over roughly 10 kilometers. Vince Dizon cited short-term measures including raising the pavement by about point six meters northbound and point five meters southbound, flood walls, dredging, floodgates, sheet piles, and heavy-duty pumps. He also said TRB had issued NLEX a notice to explain, was studying possible reimbursement, and had sought toll-free passage and proactive advisories. Bondoc pressed for alternative expressways or viaducts, unfinished bridges and bypass roads, and public transport options because McArthur Highway and railway access were flooded. Dizon said the agency would coordinate with other officials and ask its planning office to study additional rail infrastructure, while identifying elevated public transport as a long-term solution. Bondoc also requested full Coast Guard support and cited the clearing of 15,000 items or material, although the transcript's description of that figure was unclear. The issue landed with agency commitments and further coordination, but without a complete resolution of the alternative-route and public transport gaps.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DOTr and other agencies would address recurring NLEX flooding and severe traffic disruptions, including immediate flood-control measures, alternative roads and bridges, public transport options, and longer-term elevated or rail infrastructure. It also sought clarification on the status of related PPP infrastructure and support for emergency responders.

DOTr, through Vince Dizon, said NLEX flooding required coordinated short-, medium-, and long-term action involving TRB, NLEX, DPWH, and other agencies. The agency supported immediate road, drainage, floodgate, pumping, and information measures, while identifying elevated public transport and whole-of-government coordination as longer-term requirements; several route and rail proposals still required further coordination or study.

Outcome DOTr described immediate NLEX flood-control, drainage, pumping, toll-management, and information measures, while longer-term viaduct, bridge, floodway, and elevated public transport proposals remained subject to coordination, feasibility work, or DPWH action. The public transport and alternative-route concerns were therefore not fully resolved during the exchange.

It said the classification framework included three local societies and seven international IACS members, denied favoritism, and reported that an increase in passenger insurance coverage had been drafted for submission to the MARINA Board.

Outcome The agency answered that Orient was still suspended but not blacklisted and that its appeal remained pending, but the committee did not receive a fully developed justification for the classification society's treatment. DAR · 2026-09-02 · committed

Land acquisition and distribution balances and the 2027 target

Secretary Estrella reported accelerating land-title distribution, including 410,179 titles covering 556,088 hectares under the Marcos administration as of 08/12/2026. Members questioned whether the 2027 target of about 20,000 to 22,000 hectares was adequate, and DAR acknowledged that the target was constrained by the DBM budget ceiling and was not enough. The civil society representative highlighted conflicting LAAD balances of 147,493 hectares, about 700,000 hectares, and 563,076 hectares; Secretary Estrella said 750,000 hectares was the more accurate figure and suggested DAR might reduce it to 500 or a little less during the year. DAR said much of the larger balance related to partializing collective CLOAs rather than entirely new acquisitions. The agency also described its balance-cleansing process under MC 4 series of 2014 and said it was reviewing the policy to impose stricter, Secretary-level controls. DAR committed to provide official LAAD figures and Agrarian Reform Fund utilization data, but the committee did not resolve which balance should govern the 2027 budget.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish DAR's actual land-acquisition and distribution balance, the figure underlying the President's 2027 title-distribution directive, and whether the proposed funding and targets were sufficient. It also examined how DAR cleanses the LAAD balance, reports accomplishments, and addresses land titles affected by legal or documentation problems.

DAR maintained that the practical balance was 750,000 hectares, while distinguishing land still requiring acquisition from parcels being processed through SPLIT and partialization of previously distributed collective CLOAs. It attributed the limited 2027 LAAD target and funding proposal to the DBM budget ceiling, acknowledged that existing landowners' compensation balances remained, and said it was reviewing the rules for deleting or cleansing land from the LAAD balance.

Outcome DAR identified 750,000 hectares as the more accurate practical balance, but the record also retained the conflicting figures of 147,493 hectares, about 700,000 hectares, and 563,076 hectares. The agency attributed its 20,000-hectare target and limited funding request to the DBM ceiling and agreed to provide official balance, accomplishment, and fund-utilization data; the underlying balance and adequacy of funding remained contested.

DAR · 2026-09-02 · committed

LAAD funding, land deletions, and the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance

A civil society representative questioned DAR's conflicting LAAD balances, which ranged from 147,493 hectares and 563,076 hectares to about 700,000 hectares and a response referring to 750,000 hectares. The representative challenged DAR's 20,000-hectare target, the deletion of land from the balance, and the agency's ability to preserve the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance. DAR said it was following MC 4 series of 2014 but was reviewing and seeking to amend the deletion process, including possible centralization under the Secretary. On funding, DAR attributed its proposal to the DBM ceiling and cited about 7 billion in landowners' compensation, including 2.2 billion in cash, while the representative presented substantially larger amounts for completing the balance. DAR agreed to publish official LAAD figures and requested one or two days to submit missing ARF utilization data. It also reported 135,884 validated collective CLOA-equivalents, 1,481,491 hectares, 1,075,672 beneficiaries, and 330,497 e-Titles, but the central balance and funding questions remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which LAAD balance DAR was using for budgeting, the legal and procedural basis for deleting land from that balance, and how DAR could meet the legislated 5,400,000-hectare balance. It also sought official accomplishment, funding, and utilization data supporting DAR's reported figures.

DAR said it was using existing procedures under MC 4 series of 2014 to validate and remove low-priority or legally problematic landholdings from the LAAD balance, but was revisiting and seeking to amend those procedures. The agency attributed its proposed funding to the DBM budgetary ceiling, cited 2,200,000,000 as the cash portion of a reported 7,000,000,000 landowners' compensation balance, and agreed to publish official LAAD figures and submit missing ARF data.

Outcome DAR provided partial explanations and some accomplishment figures but did not resolve the conflicting LAAD balances, establish a definitive legal basis for deletions, or provide the requested ARF utilization data during the hearing. It undertook to publish official LAAD figures and submit the missing ARF tally within one or two days.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the SPLIT project remained a DAR priority, whether its World Bank loan had been exhausted, and whether the project could be completed before the loan expired. DAR stated that SPLIT remained a priority for 2027, was proceeding at full speed, and had not exhausted its World Bank loan. The agency acknowledged that the DBM-imposed ceiling was insufficient for its preferred coverage, while reporting continuing work on collective-CLOA parcelization, shapefiles, and digital titles.

Outcome DAR confirmed that SPLIT remained a priority, that the World Bank loan had not been exhausted, and that the project was scheduled to expire on 12/31/2027. The committee was not given the requested regional output or loan-disbursement figures in the transcript, and the adequacy of 2027 funding remained a concern, with DAR undertaking validation and further submissions.

Outcome The committee received answers on the backlog, the 30% cash and 70% bond structure, Land Bank’s role, and the zero utilization of the 2026 allocation pending OP approval. DAR undertook to provide a supporting list of pending compensation payments.

PBBM Bridges foreign-assisted project and FY2027 loan treatment

Rep. Antonio Tinio asked whether the PBBM Bridges project was financed by a Republic of Korea loan and how its proposed funding of about 1.4 billion would be reflected in the FY 2027 budget ceiling. The foreign-assisted-projects undersecretary answered that the total loan package was 22 billion and said the loan contract was scheduled for final signing on Monday. Rep. Salvador Plato separately asked whether the project was grant-funded or ODA, and a DAR official answered that it was ODA. Rep. Rep. Tim Cayton asked about selection criteria and a Nueva Vizcaya crossing; DAR cited validation, farmer beneficiaries, food security, and economic internal rate of return, after reviewing 1,200 locations and approving "three fifty" sites as transcribed. The financing reconciliation and definitive 2027 schedule were not resolved, but DAR made implementation and follow-up commitments.

Questions and agency response

Agrarian debt condonation and land-tenure security

Secretary Conrad Estrella III presented debt condonation as a central DAR and presidential priority under Republic Act No. 11,953 and said the statutory 06/30/2026 completion deadline had been met. DAR reported about 703,000 certificates distributed, covering about 901,246 hectares, while the identified statutory scope involved approximately 57,760,000,000 in agrarian debt; some debt figures in the transcript were inconsistent or unclear. Representative Leila De Lima asked whether SPLIT and its World Bank loan remained priorities, and Estrella answered that SPLIT was proceeding at full speed, the loan was not exhausted, and the project would expire on 12/31/2027. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status and completion of DAR’s agrarian debt-condonation program, including the number of beneficiaries and obligations covered, any exclusions, and the remaining distribution of certificates. It also examined whether the SPLIT project and World Bank financing remained priorities for FY 2027 and whether the proposed land-tenure-security funding was sufficient.

DAR stated that debt condonation under Republic Act No. 11,953 had been completed within the statutory deadline, with only final certificate distribution in the BARM area remaining. It also stated that SPLIT remained a priority for FY 2027 and that the World Bank loan was not exhausted, but acknowledged that the DBM-imposed land-tenure-security funding ceiling was insufficient for DAR’s preferred coverage.

Outcome The agency answered that debt condonation was substantially completed, with only final distribution in the BARM area remaining, but the committee requested validation and further explanation regarding allegedly excluded beneficiaries. Outcome DAR provided a partial answer identifying targeted farm-input support, machinery and equipment coverage, and an expected service reach of around 26,980 people. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DAR was adequately monitoring and enforcing agricultural land-use rules, including illegal conversion, renewable-energy projects, agricultural inactivity, and premature conversion. Members also asked for data on land conversion, ARB land status, and DAR's implementation of related programs and mandates.

DAR said it monitored and called out illegal agricultural conversions, communicated with local governments, and reported that some parties returned to the proper procedure and complied. On renewable-energy-related conversion, DAR said it would defend its mandate and contest the validity of eminent-domain exercises affecting agricultural land and farmers. DAR also stated that the penalty for agricultural inactivity and premature conversion was strictly implemented.

Outcome DAR answered that it monitored illegal conversion, enforced the inactivity and premature-conversion penalty, and would defend farmers against disputed renewable-energy-related land takings. Detailed conversion and implementation data were requested for later submission, leaving the data-verification aspect pending.

FY2027 DAR budget, utilization, and support-services allocation

The committee reviewed DAR’s FY2027 proposed allocation and its utilization of prior appropriations. The chair cited a proposed net budget of about 14.691 billion and identified allocations for land tenure security, agrarian justice, and beneficiary development and support. Secretary Conrad Estrella III reported support-services accomplishments and utilization rates, including a 47% obligation rate and 70% disbursement rate for FY2026 as of June. He presented the FY2027 net as 16,935,000,000, with about 7.066 billion for personnel services and 8,610,000,000 for maintenance and other operating expenses, although some transcript figures were unclear or internally inconsistent. DAR committed to complete remaining debt-condonation work, improve implementation and utilization, and continue land, justice, and support-service programs. Representative Sheen Gonzales moved to terminate the briefing, and the chair approved the motion without objection.

Questions and agency response

The committee was establishing DAR’s FY2027 proposed budget, how it had used prior appropriations, and whether the requested resources were aligned with land tenure, agrarian justice, debt condonation, and support-services priorities. It also sought to determine what DAR committed to deliver with the proposed allocation.

DAR maintained that its prior appropriations had supported substantial land-distribution, debt-condonation, justice, and support-services accomplishments. It defended the FY2027 request as necessary to complete remaining condonation work, sustain land distribution, strengthen agrarian justice, and provide productive support to beneficiaries, while acknowledging the need to improve implementation and utilization pace.

Outcome The agency presentation established DAR’s stated budget, utilization record, support-services accomplishments, and FY2027 priorities. The committee then terminated the briefing without a recorded challenge to the agency’s budget figures; remaining implementation commitments were left for agency follow-through.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

DOH FY2027 budget reduction and priority-item restoration

The committee chair highlighted a proposed DOH budget of about 354 billion and described a reduction of roughly 95 billion, or 21.2%, against the FY2026 enacted level. Secretary Mercado said the DOH had requested 837,000,000,000 but received approval for 353,000,000,000, and identified the indirect-member PhilHealth gap, HFEP, and hospital operations as priority restoration items. PhilHealth officials described an indirect-member benefit requirement of about 2.44 or R244 billion dollars against an allocation of 74, with an additional 170 identified as necessary to reach breakeven. Mercado cited PHP19 billion requested for HFEP against PHP14.5 billion provided and about 12,000,000,000 for hospital operations. Rodriguez supported the DOH and PhilHealth budgets and said he would seek the requested increases. The committee also requested rare-disease lists and earmarked-revenue information, but the exact 2027 sin-tax and rare-disease funding figures were not established.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 DOH budget was sufficient to sustain the Department's five pillars, universal health-care commitments, hospitals, facilities, and PhilHealth-related benefits. It also sought to identify the priority items and amounts that should be restored, and to clarify the funding gap for indirect-member premium subsidies and earmarked revenues.

DOH officials maintained that the FY2027 net budget of 353,800,000,000 supported the Department's five pillars, hospital operations, HFEP, primary care, and universal health care. They nevertheless identified major restoration priorities: about 170 for indirect-member benefit payments, PHP15.1 billion as stated for the HFEP shortfall, and about 12,000,000,000 for hospital operations. PhilHealth officials said the 74 allocation was insufficient against an expected indirect-member benefit payout of about 2.44 or R244 billion dollars, and said they would coordinate with DBM on unavailable earmarked-revenue estimates.

Outcome The agency identified the indirect-member PhilHealth benefit gap, HFEP, and hospital operations as the principal restoration priorities, and Rodriguez expressed support and said he would seek increases. The rare-disease funding request and 2027 earmarked-revenue estimates remained incomplete, with documents and coordination left for follow-up.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) cuts, utilization, and reverted funds

Members questioned the reduction of HFEP funding from the DOH request of about 19 billion to an allocation of about 14.5 billion, although the Secretary also gave an inconsistent stated shortfall of PHP15.1 billion. Representative Suntay cited an audit showing only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities operational, or roughly 33 percent, and challenged facility planning and political allocation. The Secretary said site conditions, catchment planning, facility standards, and a rules-based referral network would guide future projects, and undertook to improve compliance and oversight. Representative Garin raised low HFEP obligation and disbursement figures and called for projects to have complete designs, programs of work, budgets, and procurement arrangements before inclusion. Representative Nava said completed super health centers remained unequipped and asked for primary-care standards and the amount of funds reverted to the National Treasury. The Secretary said active construction would be completed before new projects were started, and the Chair directed the DOH to submit reverted-funds data before plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the HFEP allocation was reduced, how effectively HFEP-funded facilities and projects were being used, and whether projects were being prioritized according to health-network needs rather than political requests. Members also asked what funds had been reverted to the National Treasury and whether those funds could be restored or repurposed for health facilities.

The DOH said HFEP allocations should be governed by site conditions, facility standards, catchment-area planning, and a rules-based Universal Health Care referral network rather than by political requests. It acknowledged implementation and utilization problems, said active projects should be completed before new projects were started, and undertook to provide data on reverted funds and develop standards for primary-care and super health facilities.

Outcome The HFEP reduction, low utilization, facility planning problems, and politicization concerns were not resolved during the hearing. The DOH committed to standards, closer oversight, and coordination, while the Chair required submission of reverted-funds data before plenary; the specific reverted amount and any restoration of HFEP funding remained outstanding.

PhilHealth differential benefits for direct and indirect contributors

Perci Cendaña first raised the distinction between PhilHealth’s direct and indirect contributors under universal health care. PhilHealth answered that an approved Board resolution on differential benefits had not yet been implemented because the agency was studying its medical-inflation, database, collection, and operational implications. Eli San Fernando later asked whether the measure had been tested and whether it would disadvantage marginalized indirect contributors. The agency reiterated that it was still studying the policy and committed to examining its implications thoroughly before implementation. PhilHealth cited about 54 billion as earmarked from sin taxes for 2027 and 69.78 billion pesos as the approved 2026 budget, but did not clearly establish that all earmarked revenues would finance indirect-contributor subsidies. The issue therefore remained under agency study, with the allocation question not fully answered.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PhilHealth’s proposed differential benefits for direct and indirect contributors were legally and operationally ready, consistent with universal health care, and supported by sufficient and properly allocated revenues. Members also asked how much excise-tax and other earmarked revenue PhilHealth would receive in FY 2027 and whether those funds would finance indirect-contributor subsidies.

PhilHealth stated that an approved Board resolution on differential benefits existed, but the policy had not yet been implemented because the agency was still studying its operational, fiscal, database, collection, and policy implications. It indicated that 54,000,000,000 was earmarked for PhilHealth from sin taxes in 2027, based on BIR and BOC certification, but did not establish that all legally earmarked revenues were fully allocated specifically to indirect-contributor subsidies.

Outcome The agency confirmed that the Board resolution existed but had not been implemented and remained under study. The committee did not receive a clear confirmation that all legally earmarked FY 2027 excise-tax revenues would be fully allocated to indirect-contributor subsidies.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

DOH-retained hospital operations, MOE, and personnel-service cuts

Representative Antonio Tinio raised concerns that DOH-retained hospitals and some GOCC hospitals faced personnel-services and MOE cuts, including an 8% personnel-services reduction and 112,000,000 pesos in one hospital example and an 11,000,000 MOE cut at the National Center for Mental Health. The DOH said the personnel-services differences reflected unfilled positions, while total plantilla positions remained unchanged; vacancies resulted from noncompetitive salaries and the temporary nature of residency and fellowship posts. On MOE, the DOH cited normative financing, income retention and the need to assess GAA funds alongside PhilHealth and other revenue streams. A majority member moved, and Representative Tinio seconded, a request for hospital-level PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP allocations and MOE utilization. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez later asked about the overall DOH reduction, and the Secretary said the request was 837,000,000,000 against an approval of 353,000,000,000, with the difference stated unclearly as R485 dollars. The Secretary identified the PhilHealth indirect-member gap, HFEP and hospital operations as restoration priorities, including about 12 billion for hospital operations, while the committee left the funding restorations open pending further deliberation and documents.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed FY 2027 budget would affect DOH-retained and government-owned hospitals, particularly hospital operations, personnel services, and maintenance and other operating expenses (MOE). Members also asked whether the apparent cuts were justified by unfilled positions, normative financing, PhilHealth reimbursements, Medical Assistance for Indigent Patients and Families (MAIFIP), or the implementation of Zero Balance Billing (ZBB), and what funding the DOH wanted restored.

The DOH said the apparent personnel-services reductions largely reflected unfilled positions rather than a reduction in the total plantilla, and that vacancies resulted from noncompetitive compensation and the temporary nature of residency and fellowship posts. It said hospital MOE was based on normative financing and should be assessed together with income retention, GAA funding, PhilHealth reimbursements, MAIFIP and ZBB-related financing; it also identified hospital operations, HFEP and the PhilHealth indirect-member gap as priority funding needs.

Outcome The DOH provided explanations for the personnel-services and MOE differences, but the committee requested hospital-level reimbursement, MAIFIP and MOE-utilization data and a comprehensive written explanation of unfilled positions. The committee also identified major restoration priorities, but no restoration was approved during the excerpt.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Hospital staffing shortages and unfilled plantilla positions

Members raised the inability of hospitals to operate at their intended levels because plantilla positions remained vacant despite available facilities and equipment. DOH said vacancies stemmed from noncompetitive salaries, specialty requirements, limited applicants, and temporary residency or fellowship posts; it reported 6,774 unfilled positions as of July 2026, mostly in DOH hospitals. The committee also questioned whether the country was producing and retaining enough physicians, and DOH cited 82 medical schools, about 5,600 annual physician passers, and a garbled figure of 'seventeen ninety seven' temporary migrant doctors annually. Representative Renee Ko challenged mental-health budget reductions and shortages of psychiatrists and other professionals, while DOH cited MH-GAP training, hotline expansion, salary-grade adjustments, and PhilHealth-based income streams. Chair Romeo Momo separately questioned regional allocations and a hospital staffing gap of about 989 personnel, including a request for 185 positions amounting to 212,471,000. The hearing landed on commitments for written explanations, mental-health documentation, hospital visits, and further review, while the broader staffing shortage remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why DOH hospitals had substantial unfilled plantilla positions despite available facilities and hospital upgrades, how personnel-service allocations were determined, and what DOH was doing to address shortages of doctors and mental-health professionals. Members also asked whether medical-education production, migration, compensation, and accreditation rules were contributing to the workforce gap.

DOH attributed unfilled hospital positions to noncompetitive salary grades, stringent specialty requirements, few applicants for some professional posts, and positions structured for temporary residency or fellowship service. It maintained that the overall plantilla and personnel-services budget remained available, while proposing recruitment, revised accreditation and training arrangements, compensation adjustments, PhilHealth income streams, and direct review of affected hospitals.

Outcome DOH explained the vacancies and outlined recruitment, compensation, training, accreditation, and workforce-retention measures, but several hospital-specific staffing and budget questions remained subject to written data, direct review, or future allocation decisions. The committee obtained commitments for written submissions and hospital follow-up, but did not resolve the underlying nationwide staffing gap.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Zero Balance Billing, no-balance-billing beds, and professional fees

Members pressed DOH and PhilHealth on how the President’s ZBB commitment would cover hospital costs and professional fees without leaving patients to seek political assistance. DOH said fixed costs should be covered by hospital MOE and personnel-services funding, while PhilHealth would pay for variable costs and MAIFIP would address outliers. The agency cited a target to reduce out-of-pocket spending from 41% in 2025 to about 37.8% by 2028, while members sought stronger targets and a single-digit outcome. Members also demanded enforcement of the 90% government and 10% private no-balance-billing bed requirements and cited a case involving a 1,000 hospital bill and a 60,000 professional fee. DOH committed to issue private-hospital guidelines within the year, negotiate standardized professional-fee arrangements, improve reimbursement timing, and use PhilHealth or licensing leverage to improve compliance. The committee requested hospital reimbursement, MAIFIP, MOE, and capacity data, but compulsory physician participation and full ZBB enforcement remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the President’s Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) commitment would be financed and enforced, including coverage of professional fees. Members also asked how PhilHealth, DOH hospital budgets, MAIFIP, and private hospitals would be coordinated to prevent patient balance billing and reduce out-of-pocket spending.

DOH said ZBB should be financed through hospital MOE and personnel-services funding for fixed costs, PhilHealth payments for variable costs and ordinary cases, and MAIFIP or other assistance for outliers. The agency supported stronger monitoring, clearer rules for private-hospital no-balance-billing beds, faster PhilHealth reimbursement, and negotiated or standardized professional-fee arrangements, but acknowledged implementation gaps and that private-doctor participation remained partly optional.

Outcome The agency outlined a financing model and committed to guidelines, reporting, negotiations with professional societies, stronger monitoring, and faster reimbursement. However, enforcement of private-hospital bed requirements and compulsory acceptance of MAIFIP by private doctors remained under development rather than fully resolved.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Consolidation and coordination of medical assistance programs

Members pressed DOH and PhilHealth to integrate medical assistance, hospital subsidies, and PhilHealth payments so patients would not have to seek help from politicians or remain liable for unpaid balances. The agency said PhilHealth should be the first payer, with DOH, MAIFIP, PCSO, and other programs addressing outliers, and proposed shared statements of account, one-stop shops, joint contracting, and global payments. Members also challenged politically influenced HFEP and medical-assistance allocations, citing only 200 of 600 HFEP facilities as operational and demanding rules-based distribution. Secretary Edwin Mercado committed to DOH-PhilHealth financial alignment, simpler medical assistance, stronger monitoring, allocation reports, and private-hospital no-balance-billing guidelines within the year. The agency reported a fall in out-of-pocket spending from 44% to 41% and a 2028 target of 37.8%, but said single-digit spending would require additional fiscal resources. The hearing therefore produced several reporting and implementation commitments, while full consolidation and reliable zero-balance billing remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PhilHealth, DOH medical assistance, PCSO, and related hospital-support programs could be coordinated or consolidated to reduce out-of-pocket costs, simplify access, and prevent patients from being left unpaid. Members also asked whether assistance and hospital allocations were being distributed through objective, rules-based systems rather than political channels.

DOH and PhilHealth officials supported greater alignment and a clearer order of payment, with PhilHealth covering ordinary or first-payer obligations and MAIFIP, DOH, PCSO, and other programs addressing outliers. The agency said it was developing one-stop shops, shared statements of account, joint contracting, rules-based allocation, stronger monitoring, and private-hospital no-balance-billing guidelines, but several operational details and data requests remained pending.

Outcome The committee obtained commitments for financial alignment, hospital and MAIFIP allocation data, liquidation and program-breakdown reports, stronger monitoring, and private-hospital no-balance-billing guidelines. The broader question of fully consolidating assistance programs and eliminating political intermediation remained open, with implementation dependent on future guidelines, data submissions, fiscal resources, and coordination among DOH, PhilHealth, LGUs, and providers.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

YAKAP prevention, medical missions, and provider accreditation

Rep. Ian Amatong sought easier, consolidated medical assistance and asked how YAKAP could serve as an integrated primary-care entry point. Rep. Patrin Gorazeta pressed PhilHealth on prevention beyond screening, the low number of GAMOT-accredited centers, expanded medicines, and flexible mental-health and autism-provider accreditation; the agency said it was reviewing standards, considering mobile and outreach pharmacies, and planning unbundling and provider expansion. Rep. Bong Suntay cited roughly 33% operational HFEP facilities, challenged politicized allocation, and alleged abuse of YAKAP through barangay medical missions; Secretary Edwin Mercado and Undersecretary Beverly Ho committed to rules-based allocation and YAKAP 2.0 safeguards. Rep. Jay Vergara asked about YAKAP capacity, with PhilHealth citing 4,423 centers and 17,200,000 assigned beneficiaries, although the transcript also captured 4,426 and an unclear 15.2? figure. Rep. Christopher received confirmation that ambulance transport was covered and asked for strict enforcement of the one-year transfer rule and the three-month GAMOT receipt rule. The hearing ended with commitments and a requested provider list, while alleged abuse and implementation capacity remained subject to follow-up.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether YAKAP was delivering genuine prevention and primary-care services, whether its centers and providers had adequate capacity, and whether accreditation and payment controls prevented abuse. Members also asked how medical missions, GAMOT accreditation, facility planning, and zero-balance-billing arrangements would be corrected or expanded.

The agency maintained that YAKAP was the foundation of primary care and that YAKAP 2.0 would strengthen prevention, patient verification, consent, provider controls, performance-based incentives, and information systems. It also supported more flexible accreditation through mobile pharmacies, outreach arrangements, unbundled packages, professional-society accreditation, and expanded provider training, while developing rules-based infrastructure and assistance procedures.

Outcome The agency provided explanations and undertook multiple policy, accreditation, and control improvements, but the committee's concerns about provider abuse, medical missions, center capacity, HFEP placement, and politicized access were not fully closed. The requested accredited-provider list and several promised guideline and system changes remained for submission or implementation.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

GAMOT pharmacy accreditation and medicines coverage

Rep. Patrin Gorazeta raised the limited reach of GAMOT, reporting only 15 of 47 accredited facilities in her district and identifying pharmacist, space, and licensing requirements as barriers in poorer municipalities. PhilHealth said it was reviewing the standards, considering four accounts per pharmacy, and planning mobile pharmacies and outreach arrangements. She also sought broader medicine coverage, and PhilHealth said thyroid medicines were already in its pipeline. Members later raised alleged YAKAP abuse through barangay medical missions; Dr. Beverly Ho described YAKAP 2.0 safeguards, revised incentives, and planned IT changes, and was asked to provide the accredited-provider list. Rep. Christopher then asked about patient transfers and GAMOT dispensing, and PhilHealth confirmed a one-year transfer rule, three-month receipt validity, and dispensing of only one month's medicines. The hearing produced commitments and requests, but the final accreditation revisions and provider list were not presented in the excerpt.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether GAMOT accreditation requirements were preventing pharmacies and rural health facilities from participating, and whether medicine coverage and dispensing rules were adequate. Members also asked how PhilHealth would address access, provider accreditation, and alleged abuse of YAKAP and related packages.

PhilHealth said it was reviewing GAMOT accreditation standards and considering flexible arrangements such as multiple accounts per pharmacy, outreach services, and mobile pharmacies. It also said medicine coverage was being expanded, provider participation was being widened through package unbundling and other accreditation changes, and YAKAP controls and incentives were being revised to address abuse.

Outcome PhilHealth answered the members' questions and undertook several accreditation, package-expansion, and YAKAP-control reforms. The specific list of accredited YAKAP providers and the final revised GAMOT accreditation standards were not supplied during the excerpt, so implementation remained partly unresolved.
