DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Primary-care and super health-center standards and equipment

Secretary Edwin Mercado presented primary care as a DOH budget pillar and said HFEP covered facilities, infrastructure, and equipment with an allocation of about 14.5 billion. Perci Cendaña questioned the status of 1,823 health centers, and DOH reported 806 HFEP-funded super health centers, including completed, occupancy-ready, operational, and non-operational facilities. Rep. Audrey Zubiri sought additional support for Bukidnon and asked DOH to review the Moolog Bagong Filipinas health center allocation, which was 2,700,000 against a 19,000,000 request. Rep. JC Rahman Nava pressed for clear minimum services and equipment standards, citing two completed but unequipped super health centers that had remained unused for about two years. Secretary Mercado proposed a tiered spoke-and-hub model and committed to standards and a road map, while the Chair directed DOH to submit reverted HFEP-funds data before plenary. The standards, equipment funding, reverted amount, and requested local allocations were not finally resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DOH was setting clear, workable standards for primary-care facilities and super health centers, including the services and equipment each facility should provide. Members also asked whether facilities were geographically and financially supported, and what would happen to incomplete, unequipped, or reverted HFEP projects.

DOH said primary-care access was a core budget priority but acknowledged that licensing requirements had been too stringent and that standards would be revisited. The agency proposed a tiered, spoke-and-hub referral network, with basic primary-care services at the lower level and super health centers providing a higher level of care, potentially including outpatient surgery; it also undertook to coordinate on project deficiencies and submit reverted-funds data.

Outcome DOH outlined a proposed tiered standard and referral-network model but did not provide final service classifications, an equipment plan for the cited unequipped centers, or the amount of reverted HFEP funds during the hearing. The Chair required DOH to submit the reverted-funds data before plenary, while Bukidnon and Moolog funding questions remained subject to coordination and review.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Hospital bed capacity, expansion, and tertiary-care access

Members asked the DOH to explain its hospital bed-capacity baseline, surge requirements, expansion plans, and regional distribution of facilities. The DOH cited efficiency measures, physical-plant expansion, HFEP, referral-network planning, and functional-bed-based staffing, while acknowledging major funding and personnel gaps. The agency reported a request of about 837 billion against an approved 353 billion, requested PHP19 billion for HFEP against PHP14.5 billion, and identified about 12 billion for hospital operations as priorities, although some figures were inconsistent or unclear. Members pressed for greater Mindanao funding, tertiary hospitals in island provinces, implementation of the Basilan Medical Center upgrade from 125 to 500 beds, and completion of ongoing hospital projects. The DOH committed to written responses, study of insulin-pump coverage, adjustments for project completion, and support for legislation authorizing hospital funding or conversion. The issue landed with commitments and follow-up obligations, but important allocation, staffing, timetable, and bed-capacity questions remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the DOH had a systematic plan and sufficient funding to expand hospital bed capacity, upgrade hospitals to tertiary level, and provide equitable access to higher-level care, particularly in underserved and island provinces. Members also asked how hospital projects, staffing, regional allocations, and PhilHealth-supported care would be prioritized and implemented.

The DOH said hospital access should be improved through efficiency measures, expansion of existing physical plants, HFEP-supported facilities, regional referral-network planning, and prioritization based on functional capacity and normative budgeting factors. It acknowledged funding and staffing gaps, supported legislative conversion or renationalization where authorized by law, and said several matters—including the Basilan Level 3 timetable and certain expansion figures—required further clarification or written submission.

Outcome The DOH answered the committee's questions in broad terms and identified funding, staffing, infrastructure, and PhilHealth gaps, but several bed-capacity figures, allocation discrepancies, island-province criteria, and the Basilan implementation timetable remained unresolved. Written reports, further studies, legislative action, and project-level follow-up were required.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Hospital infrastructure site selection and structural safety

Bambi Emano questioned who selected the Northeastern Misamis hospital site, its reported 98% completion in phase two, the change from five stories to three, and the discovery of a fault-line concern in 2025. DOH said the local government had selected the site by donating the land, that the initial hazard map placed it more than two kilometers from the fault line, and that DPWH considered the reinforced or retrofitted three-story design acceptable. Emano disputed the account and requested the hazard map, technical report, and DOH site-selection guidelines. DOH committed to provide those materials and its decision before plenary. Yusop Alano asked about the timeframe and requirements for Basilan Medical Center's Level 3 upgrade; DOH cited a 2025 allocation described as 180 and another 80,000,000 for 2027, while identifying four specialty residency programs and a 500 kVA transformer as requirements. Romeo Momo separately raised DOH's 65.8% disbursement against 93.5% obligations, personnel gaps, regional allocation disparities, and completion funding for ongoing hospital projects. The principal safety issue therefore remained unresolved, but documentary and implementation follow-up was committed.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish who selected the sites for the Northeastern Misamis General Hospital and other hospital projects, whether the sites and structures were technically safe, and whether DOH had adequate plans, funding, equipment, and personnel to complete and operate upgraded hospitals. It also examined the basis for regional allocations and the completion of ongoing infrastructure projects.

DOH said the Northeastern Misamis site had been donated and effectively selected by the local government, while DPWH executed the project and determined the acceptability of the retrofit. DOH said it would review and submit the hazard map, DPWH report, site-assessment guidelines, and its decision before plenary. For hospital upgrades and staffing, DOH said Level 3 status depended on specialty residency programs, functional bed capacity, normative budgeting, and infrastructure and equipment requirements.

Outcome The Northeastern Misamis site-selection and safety questions were not finally resolved during the hearing. DOH committed to submit the hazard map, DPWH report, site-assessment guidelines, and its decision before plenary; Basilan's upgrade requirements and the broader staffing and infrastructure concerns remained subject to implementation and funding follow-up.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Tuberculosis-drug procurement and Global Fund transition

Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked Secretary Edwin Mercado what the DOH had inherited from the delayed TB-drug procurement and whether the procurement failure had been reviewed. Mercado said the process was being pushed forward, with almost 159,000,000 in Global Fund medicines committed and award targeted by the end of September, followed by delivery by the end of October or in November. He confirmed that the FY 2027 budget included 20,000,000 for TB in addition to Global Fund support, including MDR-TB and XDR-TB coverage. Montes then asked whether domestic financing would compensate for the Global Fund's tapering support, and Mercado answered yes while describing an ongoing transition. The delivery timetable was committed, but the procurement-failure review and the long-term financing framework remained insufficiently explained.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what procurement problems the DOH inherited for tuberculosis drugs, when delayed supplies would be delivered, and whether the FY 2027 budget covered TB treatment needs. It also examined how domestic financing would replace declining Global Fund support, including for MDR-TB and XDR-TB.

The DOH said procurement delays were being addressed through a reconstituted directive, an agency-to-agency arrangement, and Global Fund-supported procurement. It stated that the FY 2027 budget included 20,000,000 for TB in addition to Global Fund assistance and that domestic financing would cover the transition as Global Fund support tapered.

Outcome The DOH confirmed a FY 2027 TB allocation and said procurement would be awarded by the end of September, with delivery expected by the end of October or in November. The Global Fund transition framework and the adequacy of domestic financing remained only partly developed, and the review of the earlier procurement failure was not clearly resolved in the exchange.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Vaccine procurement delays and routine immunization supply

Rep. Iris Marie Montes and Rep. Bong Suntay questioned DOH about delayed influenza and pneumococcal vaccine procurement and the failure to make timely awards. DOH attributed the delay to a protest by a disqualified bidder and a change in management, but said the protest had been resolved and procurement was expected by October or early November. Rep. Janette Garin warned that the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine delay could cause infants to miss doses scheduled at one and a half, two and a half, and three and a half months. DOH also reported that the 2026 immunization allotment was 10,200,000,000, with 1,400,000,000 obligated and 164,000,000 disbursed. A DOH official later said OPV and PCV routine vaccines remained affected by bidding and supply problems, with delivery hoped for by October or November and some recent procurement deliverable within thirty days to forty-five days. DOH committed to early procurement for 2027 and catch-up or boosting activities, but complete and timely delivery remained to be verified.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DOH had procured influenza, pneumococcal, polio, and other routine vaccines on time, why procurement was delayed, and how the agency would prevent shortages from affecting beneficiaries. Members also asked about immunization funding utilization, vaccine coverage, and procurement plans for 2027.

DOH attributed the pneumococcal and influenza delays to a bidder protest and the need for an incoming secretary to conduct an independent legal and procurement review. The agency said the disputed procurement had been resolved, delivery was expected by October or November, and early procurement for 2027 had already been directed; it also acknowledged that OPV and PCV routine-vaccine supplies remained affected by bidding and supply problems.

Outcome DOH said the delayed vaccine procurement had been resolved and that delivery was expected by October or November, but the record did not establish that all influenza, pneumococcal, OPV, and PCV needs had already been delivered. Early procurement for 2027 and catch-up vaccination were committed, leaving implementation and timely supply availability to be monitored.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Medicine wastage, expired inventories, warehousing, and logistics

The issue was raised by Perci Cendaña, Deputy Speaker Ferjenel Biron, Rep. Janette Garin, and Rep. Salvador Pleyto. Members questioned the DOH's supply-chain allocation, central warehousing, recurring medicine expiries, double financing, and more than 90,000,000 in undistributed inventories alongside 34,000,000 in expired or nearly expired medicines. Secretary Edwin Mercado attributed the problem partly to paper-based inventory tracking and said about 60% of commodities were already procured regionally, with 40% downloaded centrally. Rep. Garin cited annual expiries of about 50 million in nutrition commodities and 300 million in mental-health medicines and urged redirection of usable stocks to assistance programs. The chair approved a request for data on expired, expiring, and near-expiring medicines, including regional offices, while the DOH also committed to review redirection and double-financing issues.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the scale and causes of medicine expiries and undistributed inventories, including whether procurement, inventory controls, warehousing, and logistics were responsible. It also examined the DOH's supply-chain budget and whether procurement should be regionalized to prevent medicines from remaining in central warehouses.

The DOH attributed medicine expiries and distribution problems primarily to weak, paper-based supply-chain and inventory systems, while also identifying possible double financing between DOH procurement and PhilHealth reimbursement. It supported greater regional procurement, saying about 60% of commodities were already procured regionally, and committed to submit expanded expiry data and examine measures to redirect or better finance unused medicines.

Outcome The DOH acknowledged supply-chain and inventory-control weaknesses, supported continued regionalization of procurement, and undertook to submit comprehensive expiry data covering central and regional operations. The audit-cited inventory amounts and the broader causes of recurring expiries remained subject to the requested reports and further review.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · unresolved

HIV prevention commodities and 2027 NHSP funding

Perci Cendaña questioned whether the 2027 budget could meet NHSP HIV-prevention targets amid shortages of condoms, lubricants, and HIV self-tests. He cited 1,200,000 condom beneficiaries requiring up to about 302.4 million annually, a lubricant shortfall of about 98.7 million, and an unclear HIV self-testing shortfall described as “twenty six to sixty three point nine million.” Secretary Edwin Mercado responded that the DOH would use a two-pronged approach involving Yakap, the OHAT program, and DOH data commodities, including testing. Cendaña then questioned the adequacy of a 10,000,000 regional supply-chain allocation, particularly where geography and logistics differed. The agency gave no substantive recorded response to that final question, and the issue remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the DOH's 2027 allocation would be sufficient to meet the National HIV Strategic Plan (NHSP) targets, particularly for condoms, lubricants, and HIV self-tests. It also questioned whether the proposed regional supply-chain allocations were adequate given differing geographic and logistics requirements.

The DOH stated that HIV prevention and testing would be addressed through a two-pronged approach involving Yakap, the OHAT program, and DOH data commodities. It did not state that the 2027 budget definitively covered the cited commodity gaps and did not provide a recorded answer on whether the regional supply-chain allocations were adequate.

Outcome The DOH offered a general account of its prevention and testing approach, but did not establish that the 2027 funding would close the identified commodity gaps. The logistics-allocation concern received no substantive recorded answer before the chair moved to the next member.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Mental-health budget, hotline demand, packages, and workforce

Congresswoman Kathrin questioned whether Yakap included prevention, whether GAMOT accreditation requirements were practical, and whether mental-health and autism packages could be expanded through simpler provider rules. PhilHealth said its mental-health package had general and specialist tiers, could cover conditions such as bipolar disorder, and was being expanded through more training and providers. Antonio Tinio separately questioned hospital MOE reductions, including an 11,000,000 NCMH cut, while DOH attributed the reductions to normative financing and broader revenue arrangements and agreed to submit hospital-level data. Renee Co pressed DOH on an NCMH cut described as 21% and 311,000,000, despite an estimated 12.5 million Filipinos with mental-health conditions and a decline from 1,500,000,000 in 2025. DOH reported 77,000 cumulative hotline calls since 2019, including 23,000 in 2024, and described MH Gap certification and salary-grade adjustments as workforce responses. The discussion ended with commitments to provide exact budget comparisons, current mental-health initiatives, and implementation details for the 2024–2028 strategic framework.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DOH and PhilHealth's mental-health packages, prevention programs, medicines, and provider-accreditation rules were reaching communities, and whether budget reductions and staffing shortages were impairing service delivery. Members also asked how rising hotline demand, hospital MOE reductions, reimbursements, and the 2024–2028 mental-health strategic framework were being addressed.

DOH and PhilHealth said they were expanding mental-health coverage through general and specialist packages, MH Gap training, school-based prevention, hotline services, and additional provider and reimbursement mechanisms. They attributed hospital and NCMH MOE reductions primarily to normative financing and broader budget comparisons, but acknowledged the need to provide exact data and further details on initiatives and strategic-framework implementation.

Outcome The agency answered the package, hotline, workforce, and financing questions but did not resolve the committee's concern over the scale and rationale of mental-health and hospital MOE reductions. DOH and PhilHealth undertook to review accreditation, expand training and provider capacity, and submit comparative budget and program information.

Health emergency allowances and barangay health-worker arrears

Rep. Eli San Fernando questioned the DOH on the 2027 health emergency allowance and unpaid arrears affecting health workers and BHWs. Secretary Edwin Mercado cited 741,000,000 as the verified amount and said 150,000 claims had been verified, while the member cited a 2026 survey reporting about 5.15 billion in unpaid arrears affecting 47,000 BHWs across 294 cities and municipalities. San Fernando also referenced the September 2025 release of 6,700,000,000 pesos for final payments and challenged the discrepancy between that payment history, the reported arrears, and the DOH's verified figure. Mercado said the reported amount had to be reconciled with DBM and that a grievance committee mechanism would address claims. The Chair directed the parties to share data and sources, but the arrears remained unresolved pending validation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status of the 2027 health emergency allowance budget and the unpaid arrears of health workers, particularly barangay health workers (BHWs). It also sought a credible reconciliation of the reported arrears, the operation of the grievance mechanism, and the data needed to validate the claims.

The DOH said 741,000,000 and 150,000 claims had been verified, while the much larger reported arrears required reconciliation with DBM and further validation. It identified a regional grievance mechanism and data-sharing process as the means to resolve the discrepancy.

Outcome The issue remained open because the committee did not reconcile the reported 5,150,000,000 in arrears with the DOH's verified 741,000,000. Data and source sharing, together with validation through the grievance mechanism and coordination with DBM, were identified as the next steps.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

FDA digitalization, application backlog, staffing, and retained income

Ferjenel Biron raised the FDA's registration problems and asked about fully digitalizing the CDRR and medical device division. The FDA said the system would cost about 217 million in the transcript's marked figure, while the total MOE request was 589,000,000; it also reported retained income of about 2 billion and sought authority to access part of it. Rep. Dette Escudero later asked about the backlog, which the FDA estimated at about 19,000 applications, and linked it to limited manpower and financial resources. The FDA reported total manpower figures ranging from about 1,100 to 1,320, including 101 personnel in the drugs center, and said 124 posts were proposed for 2027. Officials described review timelines, defended digitalization as necessary beyond simply adding staff, and cited retained earnings of approximately 3,200,000,000. The FDA said modernization would significantly reduce the backlog and could be launched within 16 to 18 months after notice to proceed, while Rep. Dette Escudero expressed committee support.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the FDA's application backlog, its staffing and financial constraints, and the budget and retained-income authority needed for digitalization. Members also asked whether modernization would materially reduce the backlog and how long implementation would take.

The FDA said the backlog resulted from rising application volumes, inadequate manpower, and constrained financial resources, and that additional personnel alone would not be sufficient. It sought congressional support for an in-house digitalization system, authority to use retained income through the SAGF, and additional staffing, while stating that modernization would significantly reduce rather than necessarily eliminate the backlog.

Outcome The FDA's need for digitalization, additional staffing, and authority to use retained income was placed before the committee, with congressional support requested. The FDA projected a significant backlog reduction and a 16 to 18 month launch period, but did not assure complete elimination of the backlog.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Family planning, reproductive health, and protection-unit funding

Dadah Kiram Ismula raised birth spacing, postpartum coverage, and the gap between PhilHealth’s projected premium and payout requirements. PhilHealth said its packages supported IUDs, ligation, and vasectomy, but postpartum reimbursement currently covered only six weeks; it cited an original requirement of about 76 billion, a current allocation stated as PHP79, and a maximum projected annual payout of 500 billion. Ismulla requested a draft policy revision within thirty days and the chair requested supporting PhilHealth data. Assistant Minority Leader Sarah Elago then sought data on patient detention and asked for reproductive-health funding details. DOH cited 664,000,000 for family planning and reproductive health, 51,000,000 for protection-unit support in 51 hospitals, and said the amount included sexual-assault investigation kits. DOH undertook to provide breakdowns, review DOST-developed kits, and submit reports on gender and development, HIV policy, cancer control, and anti-detention data; cancer-fund expansion was described as including blood products and nutritional support.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether family-planning and postpartum services were adequately funded and whether PhilHealth’s proposed premium subsidy matched its projected requirements. It also asked for the funding breakdown and planned expansion of reproductive-health, women’s and children’s protection, sexual-assault kit, and cancer-support programs.

DOH and PhilHealth said existing PhilHealth packages supported birth spacing, but postpartum reimbursement currently ended at six weeks. The agencies acknowledged funding and data gaps, stated that reproductive-health and protection-unit funding was available, and undertook to provide detailed breakdowns and requested reports; DOH also said it would review expansion of cancer and sexual-assault-kit support.

Outcome The issues were not fully resolved during the hearing. DOH and PhilHealth were directed or undertook to submit policy revisions, data, and program breakdowns, while the sufficiency of reproductive-health, protection-unit, postpartum, premium-subsidy, and cancer-support funding remained subject to review.

Cancer, rare-disease, and expanded PhilHealth benefit packages

Representative Patrin Gorazeta pressed PhilHealth and DOH on prevention under Yakap, GAMOT accreditation barriers, additional medicines, mental-health coverage and autism providers. PhilHealth said it would review accreditation, expand provider training, unbundle the children-with-disabilities package and develop rare-disease coverage initially for 10 to 15 of 159 diseases. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez highlighted the overall budget gap, including the indirect-member benefit shortfall, the HFEP request and the roughly 12 billion requirement for DOH hospital operations, while the agency said actuarial work for rare diseases was not yet complete. Representative Maximo Rodriguez Jr. sought a larger Mindanao share and asked PhilHealth to study insulin pump coverage for diabetes, which PhilHealth committed to do. Representative Janette Garin raised DOH-PhilHealth double financing and reported roughly 50 million in nutrition commodities and 300 million in mental-health medicines expiring annually; the secretary committed to review alignment, medicine use and simplification of medical assistance. The hearing also produced commitments concerning island-province tertiary hospitals and faster Zero Balance Billing payments, but did not resolve the final funding and implementation requirements.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PhilHealth and DOH could expand and effectively implement benefit packages for cancer, rare diseases, diabetes, mental health, autism and other catastrophic conditions. Members also examined the funding gap, provider and accreditation barriers, medicine wastage, hospital access, and the alignment of DOH and PhilHealth financing.

DOH and PhilHealth stated that they were expanding or preparing to expand coverage for mental health, autism and children with disabilities, rare diseases, catastrophic conditions and diabetes-related care. They also said they were reviewing accreditation standards, aligning DOH and PhilHealth financing, improving provider capacity, and studying additional benefits such as the insulin pump device, but several actuarial, utilization and implementation details remained incomplete.

Outcome The committee obtained commitments to submit the rare-disease lists, study insulin-pump coverage, simplify or realign financing and medical assistance, review medicine wastage, and support island-province hospital legislation. However, the amounts needed for full rare-disease implementation, the final scope of expanded packages, and several utilization and reimbursement problems remained unresolved.

DOH · 2026-09-02 · committed

Out-of-pocket health spending and regional allocation formulas

Secretary Edwin Mercado presented a proposed DOH budget of about 353.8 billion and said government spending had risen while out-of-pocket spending fell to 41.2% in 2025. Rep. Ismula questioned the gap between the requested PhilHealth premium subsidy and the NEP allocation; the agency cited a 76 billion headcount-based requirement, a current allocation spoken as PHP79, and projected payouts reaching 500 billion, although several figures were unclear. Members pressed for greater Mindanao and Bukidnon funding, with Mindanao reported at 15% of the CHD share and Northern Mindanao at about 17.45 billion, while Bukidnon requests substantially exceeded approved amounts. Rep. Rodriguez sought a concrete plan to reduce out-of-pocket spending, and the agency identified a target of about 37.8% by 2028 but said single-digit spending would require more fiscal resources. Members also challenged hospital allocation formulas, utilization, staffing, and no-balance-billing compliance. The agency committed to submit regional and hospital data, study insulin pump and assistance coverage, coordinate on HFEP conditions, and issue implementation guidelines within the year.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed DOH and PhilHealth allocations were sufficient to reduce household out-of-pocket health spending and whether the budget was distributed equitably across regions, provinces, and hospitals. Members also asked how allocation formulas, absorptive capacity, utilization, and health-service gaps affected the proposed amounts.

The DOH said government health spending and PhilHealth's share had increased while out-of-pocket spending had declined, and it identified a Philippine Development Plan target of reducing out-of-pocket spending to about 37.8% by 2028. It maintained that allocations were based primarily on hospital level, absorptive capacity, normative budgeting, utilization, and operational conditions, while acknowledging gaps in PhilHealth financing, provincial disaggregation, and implementation capacity.

Outcome The committee obtained the agency's reported spending indicators, regional shares, and 2028 out-of-pocket target, but did not resolve the adequacy of the PhilHealth subsidy, the Bukidnon allocation, or the formula for regional and hospital funding. The DOH and PhilHealth undertook to provide data, study coverage and financing changes, coordinate on HFEP deficiencies, and issue no-balance-billing guidelines within the year.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

DOE FY2027 budget increase and agency funding priorities

DOE presented a proposed FY 2027 budget of about 5.58 billion, an increase of 25.74%, and attributed it mainly to gray geometry, mobile energy systems, and automation. Members questioned the increase, DOE’s 49% obligation rate, the separate emergency allotment of about 29 billion, and whether the projects would deliver lower rates, fewer outages, and lasting electrification. DOE said the projects would improve energy security, committed to provide fuel-marking data, and described plans for government-controlled strategic petroleum storage. ERC requested more than 700 million, or at least about 200 million plus, to complete distribution-utility rate resets, while NEA sought 7 or 10 billion to cushion electric cooperatives from system-loss elimination. Members broadly supported DOE and ERC, but final restorations and special provisions were left to subcommittee review, DBM consultation, committee action, and plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why DOE’s FY 2027 budget was increasing by roughly 25%, whether its existing and emergency resources were being properly utilized, and whether the proposed funding would improve energy security, electricity reliability, and consumer prices. Members also examined related unfunded priorities, ERC’s request for additional resources, system-loss reduction, and the development of government-controlled fuel reserves.

DOE maintained that its proposed increase was concentrated in three energy-security and modernization projects—gray geometry, mobile energy systems, and automation—and that it did not seek a further increase beyond the proposed budget. DOE supported additional ERC resources for rate resets and a strong regulator, while seeking special provisions and corporate-fund authority for energy-security measures. The agencies committed to provide utilization, fuel-marking, strategic-reserve, system-loss, and ERC funding details, but several requests remained subject to budget-subcommittee, DBM, committee, and plenary action.

Outcome The committee generally supported DOE’s proposed budget and endorsed stronger ERC funding, but did not finally resolve the additional ERC, NEA, DOE special-provision, or reserve-related requests. DOE and ERC were directed to submit detailed information for review by the budget amendments review subcommittee, with DBM consultations and plenary action still required.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

System-loss reduction, anti-pilferage, and electric-cooperative funding

Rep. Chukwish questioned ERC on the VAT treatment of the 12% system-loss charge and when consumers would see changes, while ERC said the BIR process and publication requirements had to be completed. DOE and ERC distinguished technical from nontechnical losses, described four phases of twenty five percent reductions for nontechnical losses, and said cooperatives needed about six months to prepare technical-loss plans. ERC identified November as the earliest hoped-for billing implementation and later clarified that the 7,500,000,000 figure was for nontechnical-loss work, with cooperative assistance to be assessed case by case. Members also pressed for cooperative subsidy reforms, safeguards against rooftop-solar costs being shifted to non-solar consumers, and action on stranded capacity. ERC requested more than 700 million and at least about 200 million for consulting and related operating expenses, while NEA requested 7 or 10 billion to cushion cooperatives; the chair approved the ERC request and the 8.2 reconsideration amount for NEA CTO electrification, although the unit of the latter figure was unclear. The agencies committed to further guidelines, consultations, cooperative assessments, and studies, but final funding and technical-loss obligations remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how technical and nontechnical system losses would be reduced, how their VAT and billing treatment would affect consumers, and how the effort would be financed without shifting costs to consumers or destabilizing electric cooperatives. Members also asked about cooperative subsidies, rooftop solar, stranded costs, and the adequacy of DOE, ERC, and NEA funding.

DOE, ERC, and NEA stated that nontechnical losses, particularly pilferage, should be eliminated through phased enforcement, consumer education, billing improvements, and cooperative support, with a stated objective of zero nontechnical loss and implementation potentially within one year. They said technical-loss reduction required cooperative-specific engineering plans and could not be rushed; funding would be assessed case by case and, where possible, obtained from cooperative earnings, loans, or existing resources rather than additional national funding.

Outcome The agencies provided a phased plan and timetable, including a possible November billing implementation and a one-year objective for eliminating nontechnical losses. Funding, technical-loss targets for private utilities, the final treatment of VAT and stranded costs, and the adequacy of NEA support remained subject to further guidelines, studies, consultations, and budget action.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

ERC budget reduction, restoration, and regulatory capacity

The ERC chair presented a workload that included thousands of decisions and orders, rate resets after more than a decade, and system-loss regulation, while saying the FY 2027 allocation was below the commission's proposal. The ERC sought restoration of more than 700,000,000, or at least around 200,000,000 plus for consultants and related operating expenses. Secretary Sharon Garin and Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported stronger ERC funding, with Rodriguez also referring to a 120,000,000 increase. NEA separately requested 7 or 10,000,000,000 to cushion electric cooperatives from nontechnical system-loss elimination. The committee chair asked for detailed justification and a prioritized list, and the ERC committed to submit a narrative explaining the consultancy requirement and its link to rate resets and system-loss reduction. No final restoration amount was adopted during the hearing; DBM-related special-provision questions were deferred for discussion before plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the ERC's FY 2027 funding was reduced, how much additional funding was needed to sustain its regulatory workload, and whether the requested resources were tied to specific outputs such as rate resets and system-loss reduction. It also sought to determine what documentation the ERC would provide to support restoration or augmentation of its budget.

The ERC said its workload and regulatory responsibilities had expanded substantially, while its available FY 2027 funding was below its proposal. It sought restoration of more than 700,000,000, or at minimum around 200,000,000 plus for consultants and related operating expenses, to complete utility rate resets in 2027 and support system-loss reduction and eventual removal of system-loss charges.

Outcome The committee expressed support for restoring or augmenting the ERC budget but did not record a final appropriation in the hearing. The ERC was required to submit detailed justifications and a prioritized list for review by the budget amendments review subcommittee, while the special-provision issue remained subject to consultation with DBM.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Electricity supply security, alerts, outages, and reserve capacity

The Chair and members examined whether the proposed DOE and ERC resources would prevent future alerts, outages, fuel shortages, and high-cost generation. DOE attributed the Visayas and Mindanao alerts to coinciding maintenance, defective coal-plant equipment, reduced hydropower and biomass output, and forced operation of remaining plants, while proposing up to 250 megawatts of Visayas battery storage and short-term deployment of about 200 to 300 megawatts. Members also questioned Iligan's reduced 8.75 megawatt firm allocation, DOE's 49% utilization rate, the excluded 29,000,000,000 emergency allotment, and the adequacy of government-controlled fuel reserves. DOE and PNOC described plans for a government-owned 1,000,000-barrel tank farm, while the reported national fuel inventory remained largely in private storage. ERC said it would address excess contracted capacity and review reserve-market pricing, but several allocation, outage, CBA, system-loss, and stranded-cost issues remained open. The committee requested written fuel and remittance reports and carried the matters forward for subsequent action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 DOE and ERC resources would improve electricity supply security, reduce alerts and outages, secure fuel and reserves, and prevent consumers from bearing the cost of excess or unreliable generation. Members also asked what immediate and long-term measures would address constrained Visayas and Mindanao supply, plant outages, battery storage, firm-power allocations, and strategic petroleum reserves.

DOE and ERC maintained that the proposed programs would strengthen energy security through resource surveys, mobile energy systems, automation, battery storage, renewable integration, improved monitoring, and strategic fuel reserves. DOE attributed current alerts mainly to coinciding maintenance, defective equipment, reduced hydropower and biomass output, and forced operation of remaining plants, while ERC said market and contract mechanisms could mitigate congestion, excess capacity, and reserve-market costs.

Outcome The committee received explanations and several forward commitments, but the underlying supply-security problems were not fully resolved. DOE and PNOC committed to written reports, battery deployment, plant monitoring, system-loss work, and development of government-controlled fuel storage; Iligan's added allocation, the CBA memorandum, stranded costs, and the full impact of outages remained subject to further action.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Strategic petroleum reserve, fuel storage, and emergency fuel allotments

The Chair framed the energy budget as requiring permanent preparedness after DOE secured more than 178 million liters of diesel for an emergency buffer. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos questioned DOE's separate emergency allotment of 29,860,000,000 and asked how much fuel the government actually controlled. DOE said an additional 29,000,000,000 had been passed to PNOC and would be separately liquidated after the emergency, but it did not provide a clear government-controlled days-of-supply figure. DOE undertook to provide data comparing fuel imports and sales to help assess illicit fuel and fuel-marking gaps. PNOC said it would begin with a 1,000,000-barrel tank farm and later expand it, while Sharon Garin said construction could be completed in a year and a half and would require about 8,000,000,000. Members supported the need for a strategic reserve, but the final government-controlled capacity and the inconsistent later-phase figures were left open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Philippines had a government-controlled strategic petroleum reserve, how much emergency fuel was under government control, where fuel was stored, and how the reserve would be financed and expanded. Members also asked how DOE measured illicit fuel, whether private commercial storage was sufficient, and what documents or infrastructure commitments would follow.

DOE said the emergency fuel allotment was being retained and would be liquidated separately after the emergency ended. It supported a permanent, government-owned strategic petroleum reserve through PNOC, beginning with a 1,000,000-barrel tank farm and expanding through later phases, while acknowledging that current national storage figures largely reflected private commercial facilities. DOE also said it would provide import-versus-sales and fuel-marking data and use cross-agency data analysis to address illicit-fuel gaps.

Outcome The agency committed to developing a PNOC-owned strategic reserve, beginning with a 1,000,000-barrel facility and scaling up, but did not provide a final figure for government-controlled days of supply. DOE also undertook to submit fuel-marking and import-versus-sales data; the extent of government control, the later-phase reserve size, and the financing details remained partly unresolved.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Total electrification and off-grid solar, batteries, and fuel support

DOE presented Mobile Energy Systems and a proposed 2027 allocation of about 600 million for at least 60 units, while members questioned whether much larger resources were needed to close the remaining electrification gap. Rep. Nassal was told that total electrification required roughly 8 to 10 billion annually, compared with receipts of about 2 to 3 billion, although parts of the household and timeline figures were garbled. Rep. Stephen Tan raised an approved but unfunded off-grid solar project, fuel shortages, pole relocation, submarine-cable resilience and solar-plant fees; DOE and NEA undertook follow-up actions. Rep. Jan Chan pressed for targeting high-poverty and geographically isolated areas, while DOE and NEA said Mindanao and disadvantaged areas were priorities but did not provide exact regional allocations. The chair approved reconsideration of additional CTO-electrification funding after NEA confirmed the figures cited for its proposal and grant. A minority member also proposed a 200 million solar-and-battery alternative to line extensions, receiving agreement in principle but no recorded implementation details.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed budget would accelerate total electrification, particularly in off-grid, geographically isolated and high-poverty areas, and whether solar-battery systems could substitute for costly line extensions. Members also asked what funding, fuel support, infrastructure and policy changes DOE, NEA and related agencies would provide.

DOE and NEA supported accelerating total electrification through the Total Electrification Program, Mobile Energy Systems, photovoltaic mainstreaming, solar-home systems and solar-plus-battery projects, while recognizing that funding remained insufficient. The agencies favored targeted deployment in Mindanao, geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, and high-poverty communities, but several site-specific funding, fuel, fee-waiver and infrastructure questions required follow-up.

Outcome The hearing produced commitments to follow up on specific off-grid solar, fuel, pole-relocation, submarine-cable and transmission concerns, and the chair approved reconsideration of additional CTO-electrification funding for Mindanao. The broader funding requirement, exact number and cost of remaining CTOs and households, poverty-targeted allocations, and the proposed 200,000,000 solar-battery provision were not fully resolved in the transcript.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Transmission upgrades, congestion charges, and NGCP reliability

Members raised concerns that inadequate firm power, delayed transmission projects, congestion charges, and NGCP performance were contributing to high rates and reliability risks. PISAM said Iligan's allocation had fallen because Agus and Pulangui dependable capacity declined and committed to evaluate an increase from 8.75 megawatt toward the requested 25 megawatt. DOE and Transco cited planned or proposed connections for Catanduanes and Eastern Samar, a Visayas master plan, storage, and third-party construction, but several projects remained subject to funding and approvals. ERC said LLCC suspension applied only during congested trading intervals and committed to review disputed collections. Transco reported roughly 160,000 right-of-way claims and an estimated 220,000,000,000 settlement cost, with a target to settle 50,000 claims in two years and clear them by 2034. Members also obtained commitments for the PNPP1 feasibility study, NGCP performance and dividend records, and updates on Negros-Panay Line 2 and CNP approval.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether transmission constraints, congestion charges, delayed interconnections, and NGCP performance were contributing to reliability problems and higher electricity costs. Members also asked what DOE, ERC, Transco, NAPOCOR, and NEA would do, and what documents or project updates they would provide.

DOE and its attached agencies said that generation and transmission constraints were being addressed through project prioritization, third-party construction, island and Visayas master planning, storage, system-operations improvements, and coordination with NGCP. ERC maintained that LLCC suspension applied only during specified congested trading intervals and said it would review disputed collections. Several matters, including the Eastern Samar and Negros-Panay upgrades, remained subject to funding, approvals, NGCP implementation, or further study.

Outcome The hearing produced multiple agency commitments to evaluate allocations, submit documents, study or accelerate transmission projects, review LLCC collections, and provide NGCP performance information. However, the major transmission projects and the LLCC dispute remained dependent on approvals, funding, NGCP implementation, or further review.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Electric-cooperative franchises, CBA obligations, and distribution competition

Rep. Perci Cendaña pressed NEA on the suspended electric-cooperative CBA memorandum and asked whether it would be rescinded. NEA said a tripartite technical working group was developing rules and that the memorandum could be rescinded after a September 10 meeting and subsequent resolutions, but Cendaña noted that the same answer had been given the previous year. Rep. DiCasson questioned franchise expirations in 2028 or 2029, the exclusivity of cooperative distribution areas, and the suitability of a private applicant with 5,000,000 in capital compared with a cooperative with about 1,500,000,000 in assets. NEA and DOE said Congress controlled franchise grants, while functioning cooperatives generally merited renewal and franchise holders had to provide the required infrastructure and service. Rep. Sergio Dagooc raised labor demands including grocery allowances of up to 6,000 pesos monthly and laundry allowances of 500 to 600 pesos monthly, which NEA said cooperatives could not afford. ERC said new system-loss rules could support consumers or cooperative infrastructure and committed to propose revisions and consult stakeholders, including Mindanao cooperatives.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOE, NEA, DOLE, and other agencies would resolve electric-cooperative collective-bargaining disputes and whether a memorandum affecting cooperative CBAs would be rescinded. It also examined the necessity of cooperative franchises, the possible entry of private distribution utilities, and whether revised system-loss rules could support cooperatives and consumers.

The agencies maintained that the CBA memorandum was suspended because electric cooperatives had industry-specific circumstances, but said it could be rescinded after the tripartite council adopted resolutions. They supported renewal of functioning cooperative franchises, deferred franchise-grant decisions to Congress, warned that excessive CBA benefits could undermine cooperative finances, and said revised system-loss rules could allow consumer subsidies or infrastructure support subject to stakeholder consultation.

Outcome The CBA memorandum remained suspended, with possible rescission deferred until the tripartite council produced resolutions; Rep. Cendaña remained dissatisfied with the delay. The agencies supported functioning cooperatives and committed to consultation and possible revisions on system-loss rules, but the record did not resolve whether any new private franchise would be granted.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

ERC rate-setting, WESM overcharges, refunds, and consumer protection

The ERC said it had directed refunds of around 71.3 billion and attributed 70 billion to Meralco's delayed rate reset, but Rep. Chukwish sought the exact WESM overcharge and a clearer refund account. The ERC responded with a technical explanation of locational marginal pricing, congestion, line losses, and settlement-surplus allocation, while referring to interim measures, a longer-term market-operator solution, and a third-party audit. Rep. Robert Nassal questioned why consumers paid for projected capital investments before completion and called for independent verification that charges funded useful investments. The ERC said it had shifted to performance-based regulation, using forecast costs, capital expenditure, returns, depreciation, and regulatory-asset-base calculations over four- or five-year periods. The ERC also sought around 200,000,000 plus for consulting services and related MOE to complete all utility rate resets in 2027, and Rep. Rufus Rodriguez said the request was approved according to the chairman. NEA separately requested 7 or 10 billion to cushion electric cooperatives from eliminating nontechnical system losses.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the ERC set distribution-utility rates, including whether consumers were charged for projected investments before completion, and how WESM pricing flaws and market-settlement surpluses would be addressed through refunds. It also examined the ERC's budget needs for completing rate resets and supporting system-loss reduction.

The ERC said it was implementing performance-based, forward-looking rate regulation while limiting recovery to approved asset values, returns, depreciation, and other recognized revenue-requirement components. It maintained that rate resets, WESM settlement measures, audits, and consumer-focused regulation were needed to protect consumers, but the transcript did not provide a clear exact WESM overcharge or refund amount.

Outcome The ERC answered the rate-setting question by explaining its performance-based methodology and said recovery was tied to approved asset values and regulatory-period resets. The exact WESM overcharge and refund requested by Rep. Chukwish remained unclear in the transcript, while the ERC's rate-reset funding request was stated to have been approved according to the chairman.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

System-loss VAT and consumer billing implementation

Rep. Chukwish asked ERC Chair Francis Wang to clarify the treatment of the 12% VAT on system-loss charges and when consumers would see it in their bills. The ERC and DOE said implementation required BIR coordination, publication and effectivity steps, classification of technical and nontechnical losses, and phased work by electric cooperatives. Secretary Sharon said cooperatives would need about six months to prepare technical-loss plans and described 25% reduction stages toward eliminating nontechnical losses, with a possible report in the first half of the following year. Wang later identified September as the target for the BIR and billing-format process and said November was the earliest implementation after resolving September and October issues. An agency official cited 200,000,000 in support of the ERC budget because of the technical demands of the work.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the ERC's position on applying 12% VAT to system-loss charges and when consumers would see the treatment reflected in their bills. It also sought a timetable for reducing system losses and implementing the related billing changes.

The DOE and ERC said the 12% VAT and system-loss billing treatment required coordination with the BIR, classification of technical and nontechnical losses, and a phased implementation rather than an immediate across-the-board reduction. They presented September as the target for the BIR and billing-format process, with November identified as the earliest implementation after resolving September and October issues.

Outcome The agencies provided a target timetable but acknowledged that billing and reconciliation issues remained. The issue therefore landed with an agency implementation plan and November as the earliest stated implementation point, rather than as an immediate consumer-billing change.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Renewable-energy expansion, auctions, and agricultural-land safeguards

The DOE reported that renewable energy had reached about 25.04% of the 2025 generation mix, with 20.7 gigawatts awarded through the Green Energy Auction and another 25 gigawatts planned for auction through 2035. Rep. Presley de Jesus questioned whether failed renewable-energy contracts should be canceled and whether generation costs required regulation; the DOE favored safeguards, reported about 33 contracts totaling about 1.3 gigawatts, and said more than 100 contracts had been canceled or were being canceled. Rep. Marco Anko raised concerns about solar projects and requested hydrological review, to which the DOE committed a report. Rep. Salvador Pleyto asked how renewable targets could be met while protecting about 3,000,000 hectares of agricultural land; the DOE cited possessory-rights requirements, DA coordination, LGU ordinances, and farm-compatible solar development. Rep. Reneko questioned incentives affecting indigenous communities and the environmental classification of waste-to-energy; the DOE cited prior informed consent, emissions safeguards, and the statutory classification but said it lacked authority to reclassify the technology. Several records and policy questions were left for follow-up, so the issue was committed rather than fully resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOE would expand renewable-energy capacity while protecting agricultural land, enforcing renewable-energy service contracts, safeguarding consumers and communities, and addressing the environmental and legal treatment of waste-to-energy projects. Members also asked what safeguards, studies, records, and policy changes the DOE would provide or undertake.

The DOE supported accelerated renewable-energy deployment through auctions and programs including ground-mounted solar, agrosolar, offshore wind, solar on irrigation canals, and waste-to-energy, but said projects had to comply with land-use, permitting, community-consent, contractual, and emissions requirements. It favored safeguards and stronger generator accountability rather than direct generation-cost regulation, and said it could not reclassify waste-to-energy without a change in the law.

Outcome The DOE's renewable-energy expansion plans were presented as supported by auctions, new project types, and consumer-access programs, but questions about agricultural-land protection, hydrological review, contract cancellations, indigenous safeguards, and waste-to-energy records remained subject to further review or reporting. The DOE maintained that it could not reclassify waste-to-energy without legislative action.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Rooftop solar, net metering, and distribution-system cost allocation

Rep. Jay Vergara asked the ERC how rooftop-solar exports, net metering, back-feed, and system losses would affect distribution utilities and whether non-solar consumers could be protected from shifted costs. The ERC said batteries, two-way metering, distribution impact studies, interconnection standards, and future review of the Philippine Grid and Distribution Codes would address the risks; it expected system-loss impacts to be minimal because exported power would be consumed locally. An unclear portion of the exchange referred to a 20-kilowatt capacity and a system-loss document dated 08/26/2026. Rep. Felimon Espares then raised the inability of some electric cooperatives to provide net metering for solar-powered rice mills, cold storage, and residential facilities. DOE Secretary Sharon said most utilities could accommodate net metering and committed to reinforce information and capacity building. The chair directed submission of a report listing capable utilities, leaving the detailed cost-allocation issue not fully resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the ERC evaluates the technical and cost impacts of rooftop solar exports, net metering, back-feed, and system losses, and what safeguards prevent those costs from being shifted to non-solar consumers. It also sought to determine which distribution utilities and electric cooperatives could accommodate net metering, particularly for solar-powered post-harvest facilities.

The ERC said rooftop-solar exports could affect distribution-utility markets, rates, technical operations, and supply quality, but expected local consumption of exported energy to limit impacts on existing system losses. It relied on two-way metering, distribution impact studies, interconnection standards, further code studies, and possible customer investments or refusal of connections above the net-metering threshold. The DOE said most distribution utilities and electric cooperatives could accommodate net metering and committed to check the specific cases and reinforce information and capacity-building efforts.

Outcome The ERC provided a preliminary explanation centered on two-way metering, distribution impact studies, interconnection standards, and future code review, but the transcript leaves the detailed cost-allocation discussion unclear. The DOE and agency officials were directed to check and submit a list or report on utilities capable of net metering.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Catanduanes and island high-cost generation assistance

Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought an emergency subsidy and long-term transmission solution for Catanduanes, where diesel dependence was driving high electricity costs. DOE declined to commit to a subsidy but promised a task force, fuel and electric-cooperative assessment, coordination with NAPOCOR, and work toward a grid connection or other long-term solution. Rep. Stephen James Tan then raised funding for an off-grid solar project, fuel allocation for an island system, pole relocation, a submarine-cable option, solar-plant fee relief, and the Luzon-Visayas transmission upgrade. The agencies cited about 300 million requested for pole-relocation advances, 50 million in a 2026 DPWH allocation, roughly 60 million in donated solar support, and roughly 100,000 a month in fees, while NAPOCOR said one island was operating at eight hours with peak demand stated unclearly as “a 100 kilo 108 kilowatts.” The issues were not finally resolved, but DOE, NEA, Transco, and NAPOCOR undertook follow-up studies, coordination, and presentations.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what emergency assistance, fuel allocation, and regulatory or budgetary mechanisms could reduce high electricity costs and improve reliability in Catanduanes and other island or off-grid systems. It also sought the status and funding of solar, pole-relocation, submarine-cable, and Visayas transmission projects.

DOE and its attached agencies did not commit to a temporary subsidy, saying DOE was not authorized to support one. They instead supported task-force assessment, fuel and system reviews, reduced diesel dependence, grid or submarine-cable alternatives, pole-relocation coordination, and a longer-term Visayas plan based on more self-sufficient island systems.

Outcome The temporary subsidy request was not accepted because DOE said it lacked authority to support it. The matters were left with agency commitments to conduct assessments, coordinate on funding and infrastructure, process or prioritize transmission options, and submit or present further information.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Ancillary services, stranded costs, and excess renewable capacity

A majority member asked the ERC to address stranded costs that could arise when distribution utilities retained excess contracted capacity while consumers shifted toward solar power. The ERC pointed to carve-out provisions in post-2023 power-supply agreements and said it would examine assistance for utilities and captive customers. A member also questioned ancillary charges, stating that about 60 percent of transmission charges were ancillary charges and citing a reserve-market price of 25 pesos per kilowatt hour; the ERC said a lower-price proposal was under consultation. Javi Benitez connected transmission delays in Negros and Panay to possible renewable curtailment involving roughly 1,300 megawatts of projects, with risks described as about 10% and possibly 20% to 30%, while DOE cited 50 megawatts of proposed battery storage in Negros. A minority member pressed for CSP amendments, greater NGCP accountability for ancillary services, and solar-plus-storage in place of uneconomic line extensions, citing 200,000,000 for the proposed funding step. The matters were not finally resolved, but the ERC and DOE undertook further review and reporting.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how stranded costs from excess or curtailed renewable capacity would be allocated, whether distribution utilities and consumers could be protected from those costs, and whether ancillary-service and reserve-market charges could be reduced and made more accountable. It also examined whether transmission constraints were contributing to renewable curtailment and whether solar-plus-storage could substitute for uneconomic line extensions.

The ERC said existing and post-2023 power-supply agreements could use carve-outs or other mechanisms to unload excess contracted capacity, and it was considering a reserve-market proposal intended to lower pricing. DOE said transmission was lagging generation, supported battery storage as an alternative or supplement, and would monitor and report on NGCP transmission commitments.

Outcome The ERC described existing contractual and reserve-market mechanisms for excess capacity and undertook to consider a proposal intended to reduce reserve-market prices. Transmission-related curtailment, ancillary-service accountability, and the proposed CSP and solar-plus-storage changes remained open for further action.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

ER 194 host-community remittances and unresolved claims

Rep. Presley De Jesus asked the DOE for the total ER 194 host-community remittances and questioned the apparent gap in benefits. The DOE reported audited post-remittance figures as of 06/20/2026, including about 1.8 billion for Nordell Luzon and 8 million for the National Capital Region, with specified allocations for electrification, development, watershed rural health, DLF, and water management. The chair required the DOE to submit the audit-based records, and the DOE agreed. The DOE also reported roughly 160,000 pending right-of-way claims and committed to an outsourced settlement program targeting 50,000 claims in two years and all claims by 2034. It estimated the total cost at about 220 billion based on a 2016 zonal valuation, excluding unregistered and public land, but Rep. De Jesus questioned whether that amount was realistic.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much ER 194 host-community benefits had been remitted, including the allocation of post-remittance benefits, and whether the DOE could provide audited records. It also sought to determine the scale, cost, and timetable for resolving pending right-of-way claims associated with transmission lines.

The DOE said audited records showed direct remittances and post-remittance benefits for host communities and agreed to submit those records to the committee. It said the right-of-way backlog would be addressed through nationwide outsourcing, with a target of reducing the claims by 50,000 in two years and clearing them by 2034, but acknowledged that the projected 220,000,000,000 cost was only an estimate based on a 2016 zonal valuation.

Outcome The DOE committed to submit audited remittance records and outlined a settlement program for the roughly 160,000 right-of-way claims. The 220,000,000,000 estimate was challenged by the member and remained subject to validation; the committee did not resolve the underlying claims or funding obligation.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Nuclear-energy roadmap, SMR feasibility, and regulatory framework

Rep. Marco Anko pressed the DOE over the PNPP Unit 1 feasibility study, saying it was needed for House bill eight five six seven and other nuclear-policy decisions. The DOE said the study was controlled under its agreement with KHNP and could not be photocopied or transmitted, but committed to submit the arriving hard copy by Monday and compare and certify it against the DOE-held version. Rep. Tino then asked about the status, technology, cost, and providers for Philippine nuclear development. Secretary Sharon said the country had a roadmap and a target for nuclear energy in the next decade, but was reconsidering SMRs in favor of conventional technology because SMR options appeared limited. She said regulatory organization and implementing rules remained to be completed, and gave indicative costs of 10,000,000,000 for conventional technology and 4,000,000,000 for an SMR. The DOE said development would rely mostly on private funding and that it was exploring providers from Korea, China, Japan, Canada, the United States, and France.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status and availability of the DOE's PNPP Unit 1 feasibility study, including whether the committee would receive the same document held by the DOE. It also asked about the country's nuclear roadmap, the choice between small modular reactors (SMRs) and conventional reactors, regulatory readiness, technology providers, and indicative costs.

The DOE said the Philippines had a nuclear roadmap and still targeted nuclear energy in the next decade, but was reconsidering an SMR-centered approach because options appeared limited and conventional technology might be pursued instead. The agency said regulatory and safety requirements were still being completed, nuclear development would rely mostly on private funding, and technology and provider options remained under study.

Outcome The feasibility-study issue landed on a commitment for the DOE to submit the copy arriving from Korea by Monday and to compare and certify it against the DOE-held copy. The broader nuclear roadmap remained exploratory: the DOE had not settled the SMR-versus-conventional choice, regulatory framework, provider, or financing arrangement.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Strategic energy projects and West Philippine Sea service contracts

Antonio Tinio questioned the DOE about the Energy Secure Philippines program, which he described as having 24 million in funding, and asked whether it included energy storage. The DOE said the activities were mostly technical studies, with a containerized solar-battery system described as providing 10 kilowatts and higher. Tino also raised the ownership and use of fuel-storage facilities, including a 1,000,000-barrel facility announced through the US Embassy; the secretary said the DOE had not been officially informed but that any energy or fuel project required DOE permits. The DOE said PNOC was pursuing a Philippine strategic reserve, beginning with 1,000,000 barrels, requiring about 8 billion, and potentially taking a year and a half to construct. Tino requested public clarification of US Embassy energy announcements, and the secretary undertook to assess and clarify them as needed. On the West Philippine Sea, the DOE said oil and gas joint activity had to use the service-contract system, while work in the relevant area was under a moratorium because of geopolitical issues.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the DOE's involvement in US-linked energy programs and announcements, the ownership and use of fuel-storage facilities, and the implications for Philippine energy security. It also sought clarification on the status of offshore oil and gas service contracts and any proposed joint development in the West Philippine Sea.

The DOE said most US-linked Energy Secure Philippines activities were technical studies rather than infrastructure or capital-outlay projects, and that all energy and fuel projects would require DOE permits. It supported developing a Philippine strategic reserve through PNOC, while stating that offshore joint activity had to proceed through service contracts and that work in the relevant West Philippine Sea area was subject to a moratorium.

Outcome The DOE undertook to review and clarify the US-linked announcements and said Philippine permits would be required for any energy or fuel project. It presented PNOC's proposed strategic reserve but did not resolve the status of the announced foreign facility or the West Philippine Sea activity, which remained subject to a moratorium and broader geopolitical concerns.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

Offshore-wind development and supporting port and grid infrastructure

Rep. Jan Franz Chan asked whether the cited target of 21 gigawatts by 2040, or about 21% of national electricity, remained the administration's working offshore-wind target. The DOE secretary said offshore wind continued to be promoted but did not confirm the 21% figure, pending a new energy-mix simulation expected at the end of the year. A DOE undersecretary said an offshore-wind auction covering 3,300 megawatts was ongoing. Chan then asked about budget support for port works and grid preparation. The Philippine Ports Authority said offshore-wind ports would require about 30 tons per square meter, compared with six to eight tons for existing ports, and identified projects in Pambuhan and Santa Clara, with stated construction timelines. Curimao Port was described as intended for floating offshore wind and not to be contracted under the current administration because the auction mainly covered fixed-bottom projects. No specific budget amount for grid preparation was committed, but the port project timelines and DOE's year-end energy-mix update were stated.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the administration still supported the Philippine Energy Plan target of 21 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2040, supplying about 21% of national electricity. It also asked what budget and interagency support were needed for port works and grid preparation, including for off-grid islands.

The DOE said it continued to support offshore-wind development but could not yet confirm that the 21% share target remained unchanged. It was conducting a new energy-mix simulation, expected by the end of the year, while offshore wind remained included; the Philippine Ports Authority described port projects and their implementation timelines as the principal enabling infrastructure discussed.

Outcome The committee received confirmation that offshore wind remained part of DOE planning and that a 3,300-megawatt auction was ongoing, but the secretary did not confirm the specific 21% target. Port infrastructure plans and timelines were provided, while specific 2027 budget amounts or grid-preparation funding commitments were not established.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

ERC consumer complaints and regional access to hearings

A committee member questioned the ERC about complaint volumes, informal and formal complaint handling, and case disposition. The discussion cited about 5,380 complaints as of mid-August, 5,329 complaints in 2025, 3,289 in 2024, and 4,000, or 77%, of 2026 complaints concerning service-bureau status. The ERC also cited 3,657 ongoing informal or letter complaints, 620 2026 letter complaints, and a combined figure of 27, although some categories were unclear. The member requested submission of the complaint data, and the ERC agreed. Marlo Bancoro then raised the difficulty of access for complainants facing around 10 hours of land travel and sought regional hearings. The ERC said online hearings were the default but consumers could request in-person proceedings, and committed to prioritizing Cagayan de Oro for Mindanao hearings subject to transportation funding while studying the cost of hearing staff and related expenses.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the volume and disposition of ERC consumer complaints, including the number of informal and formal complaints and who was handling them. It also asked whether consumers could access ERC hearings regionally or online instead of traveling long distances.

The ERC said online video-conference hearings were the default, while consumers could request in-person hearings. It said it had previously held locality-based or satellite-office hearings and committed to prioritizing Cagayan de Oro for in-person Mindanao hearings, subject to transportation funding, while studying how to fund the required hearing staff and related costs.

Outcome The ERC agreed to submit complaint data and committed to prioritizing Cagayan de Oro for qualifying in-person Mindanao hearings, while studying the funding of hearing staff and related costs. The full complaint disposition data and the feasibility and funding of regular regional hearings remained subject to submission or further study.

DOE & ERC · 2026-09-02 · committed

DOE special-fund authority and retained agency income

Rep. Robert Nassal asked whether the proposed 20% authority would ensure DOE access to PD number 910 earmarked funds and what programs would be financed. Secretary Sharon Garin said DOE did not receive the full statutory share because GOCCs were also covered, but identified automation, grid management, regional facilities, green buildings, and energy research as potential uses. She projected that 20% of 2027 Malampaya collections could be about 5.4 billion. DOE officials said more than 2 million households remained without electricity and that about 10 billion a year would be needed for electrification, compared with current annual funding of about 2 billion to 3 billion. Later, DOE requested authority to retain 3% for administrative and engineering costs, but the chair said DBM had previously found no legal basis for similar requests. The committee requested prioritized lists and supporting details by the following day and deferred the legal issue for discussion with DBM before plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed 20% special-fund authority would allow DOE to access legally earmarked PD Number 910 funds, what programs would be financed, and whether the additional fiscal space could accelerate total electrification. It also examined whether DOE-related agencies could retain income for administrative and engineering costs and whether the proposed special provisions had a legal basis.

DOE supported inclusion of the 20% authority so it could obtain greater access to legally earmarked funds, although Secretary Garin said DOE had historically received less than the full amount because other GOCCs were also covered. DOE identified electrification, automation, grid management, regional facilities, green buildings, and energy research as potential uses, while the retained-income request remained subject to DBM's legal position.

Outcome The committee generally supported DOE's access to legally earmarked funds and the need for higher electrification resources, but required program details and prioritized special-provision language. The retained-income request was not resolved during the hearing and was deferred for consultation with DBM before plenary.
