DOTr · 2026-09-02 · unresolved

DOTr FY2027 budget proposal and infrastructure priorities

The chair opened scrutiny of the proposed 300,960,000,000 DOTr FY 2027 budget, emphasizing that only 30 of 179 proposed infrastructure projects were in the NEP. DOTr presented 2025 and July 2026 obligation and disbursement rates, including an overall 2025 obligation rate of about 89.35% and a July 2026 obligation rate of about 74.1%. It said capital outlay accounted for about 81.05% of the proposal and described major railway, road, aviation, maritime, and right-of-way requirements, with only a portion of the proposed projects funded. Representative Romeo Momo questioned the increase from 158,000,000,000 to 300,960,000,000 pesos and raised concerns about absorptive capacity. DOTr answered that foreign-assisted projects, including NSCR and the subway, used cash availment authority that affected the comparison of disbursement rates. The committee's questions on implementation capacity and allocation among regions and sectors remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed DOTr FY 2027 allocation was justified by transport priorities, project coverage in the NEP, and the department's capacity to obligate and disburse funds. It also examined how the large capital-outlay allocation would be distributed among sectors and projects.

DOTr maintained that the FY 2027 proposal was needed for a large capital-outlay program, particularly foreign-assisted rail and other transport infrastructure, while locally funded projects remained equally important. The agency asserted that its obligation and disbursement performance was stronger than the figures cited by Representative Momo and explained that foreign-assisted projects used cash availment authority in addition to regular NCA accounting.

Outcome The agency presented the proposed allocation, infrastructure mix, NEP coverage, and reported obligation and disbursement rates. Representative Momo challenged the department's absorptive capacity and began a further inquiry into regional and sectoral allocations; that inquiry was not completed in the provided transcript.

Service contracting, EDSA Carousel, and fuel subsidy funding

Rep. Percival Cendaña raised the reported zero FY2027 allocation for service contracting and the fuel subsidy program and urged restoration of funding for the EDSA Carousel and PTMP. DOTr Secretary Giovanni Lopez cited an 82.6% obligation rate and an approximately 52% disbursement rate, supported continued assistance, and said the PTMP had been shifted toward a 1,500,000,000 equity subsidy through LTFRB. A DOTr road-sector official reported DBP and Land Bank totals, past-due amounts, private-bank exposure, and 8,766 units receiving equity subsidy, while clarifying that the default figures covered bank loan releases and excluded equity subsidy. Cendaña characterized the defaults as staggering and cited a 176,000,000 FY2027 proposed budget. The agency said subsidies or other incentives were needed, but no formal restoration or detailed funding commitment was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the FY2027 budget showed zero funding for service contracting and the fuel subsidy program, and whether funding should be restored for EDSA Carousel and the Public Transport Modernization Program. It also examined defaults on loans for modernized units and the adequacy of proposed FY2027 support.

DOTr supported restoring or otherwise providing support for service contracting, the EDSA Carousel, and transport modernization. It said the PTMP had been shifted toward an equity subsidy because of the oil crisis and that additional subsidies or other incentives might be needed, while clarifying that the reported default figures covered bank loan releases and excluded equity subsidies.

Outcome DOTr expressed support for continued or restored assistance, but the transcript did not show a formal restoration of the zero allocation or a specific funding commitment. The extent of the loan-default problem and the adequacy of the 176,000,000 proposed budget remained contested.

DOTr · 2026-09-02 · unresolved

Public Transport Modernization Program loan defaults and assistance

Rep. Perci Cendaña raised the absence of service-contracting and fuel-subsidy funding and pressed DOTr on PTMP amortization defaults and assistance. DOTr said it had shifted to an equity-subsidy policy involving 1,500,000,000 through LTFRB and supported restoring modernization-related funding. A road-sector agency official reported DBP loans of about 7.46 billion, with about 4.071 billion past due, and Land Bank loans of about 8.24 billion, with about 1.988 billion past due. The official also reported 6.059 billion in total past due for government financing institutions, 771 million for private banks, and 8,766 units receiving equity subsidies. Centanya described the figures as showing that almost more than half had defaulted and cited the proposed 2027 budget of 176,000,000. DOTr said subsidies or other incentives were needed, but the specific response to the defaults remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the extent of loan defaults among Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP) operators, the assistance available to them, and whether the proposed 2027 budget was adequate to address the problem. Rep. Perci Cendaña also pressed DOTr on restoring funding for service contracting and transport modernization.

DOTr supported restoring service-contracting and modernization funding and said it had pivoted to a PTMP equity subsidy because of the oil crisis. It reported loan exposure and past-due amounts but said the default figures reflected bank-loan releases rather than equity subsidies; it also stated that further assistance could be provided through subsidies or other incentives.

Outcome DOTr provided loan and past-due figures and clarified that the default-rate figures covered bank-loan releases rather than equity subsidies. The agency supported additional subsidy or other incentives, but no specific further assistance, funding restoration, or corrective action was finalized during this exchange.

DOTr · 2026-09-02 · committed

MRT-3 subsidy, operations, and possible privatization

A minority member raised unresolved MRT-3 safety and labor complaints, including alleged train-protection and operating concerns, and pressed DOTr for the status of its investigation. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said three foreign experts had reviewed the safety issue, noted MRT-3's average ridership of about 500,000 passengers daily, and undertook to implement a Civil Service Commission resolution on labor violations and provide the committee a copy. Congressman Antonio then asked about MRT-3's subsidy, direct government operation, and maintenance arrangement with Sumitomo, including a transcript figure of 35,000,000,000 whose context was unclear. The agency described the fare support as a 50% discount, illustrating it with a 12-peso fare reduced to 6 pesos, and characterized the underlying subsidy as a noncash loss of revenue. The agency said the subsidy was included in the 2027 proposal but did not state its exact amount. It also said market sounding for a possible PPP covering MRT-3 operations and maintenance was underway, with affordability still to guide any eventual concession.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status and cost of MRT-3 operations, including the government subsidy and any maintenance-related obligations. It also asked whether the MRT-3 operation might be privatized through a public-private partnership and what safeguards would preserve affordability and safety.

DOTr said MRT-3 remained government-operated and subsidized, with the subsidy described principally as a noncash revenue loss associated with discounted fares. It was conducting market sounding for a possible PPP covering MRT-3 operations and maintenance, but said the concession terms, exact amount, and bidding process were not yet final.

Outcome The committee received the agency's explanation that MRT-3 was government-operated, subsidized, and subject to a possible PPP after market sounding. The exact subsidy amount and final PPP terms were not established during the exchange, while safety and labor matters remained subject to further agency and commission action.

Congresswoman Mula called for continued monitoring of reforms, budget utilization, inspection compliance with international conventions, and maritime-industry oversight. The request remained subject to evaluation and committee consideration, with no final funding decision recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish MARINA’s 2027 plan for addressing gaps in vessel-safety inspection personnel and capacity nationwide. It also sought clarification on the budgetary support requested for additional personnel and continuing technical training.

MARINA stated that its MOOE was so far sufficient, but that additional personnel and continuing technical capacity building were necessary to improve maritime safety. It had submitted a comprehensive manpower proposal under the Government Optimization Plan and appealed for consideration of an additional tier-two proposal for 2027.

Outcome MARINA explained that its MOOE was generally sufficient but that additional personnel and technical capacity building were needed. A manpower proposal had been submitted for DBM evaluation, while the requested tier-two support remained subject to consideration; no final funding action was recorded.

DOTr · 2026-09-02 · committed

DOTr absorptive capacity and regional allocation

DOTr presented 2025 and July 2026 obligation and disbursement rates and said it was confident its performance would improve. Rep. Romeo Momo questioned the proposed increase from about 158 billion to about 301 billion and the agency's ability to absorb a capital-outlay-heavy budget. DOTr answered that its whole-agency 2025 rates were about 89.35% for obligations and 56.94% for disbursements, while July 2026 rates were 74.1% and 56.18%, respectively, and attributed differences to foreign-assisted projects using cash availment authority. Momo also questioned the regional distribution, citing about 0.1% for his region versus Davao's roughly 15.3 billion or 5.1%. The committee pressed for completion of Tandag Airport and improved facilities in Surigao del Sur. DOTr targeted Tandag completion by year-end, said it would reevaluate the project, and committed to prepare a 2027 program for Surigao del Sur.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DOTr could absorb and disburse its substantially increased FY 2027 budget, particularly its capital-outlay allocation. It also questioned whether the proposed allocation adequately covered regions such as Surigao del Sur and whether specific airport and transport projects would be completed.

DOTr maintained that its absorptive capacity was stronger than the member's cited figures suggested, reporting a 2025 whole-agency obligation rate of 89.35% and disbursement rate of 56.94%, and July 2026 rates of 74.1% and 56.18%. It attributed apparent disbursement differences to foreign-assisted projects being funded through cash availment authority rather than regular NCA and committed to evaluate Tandag Airport and prepare a 2027 program for Surigao del Sur.

Outcome DOTr defended its reported absorptive-capacity rates, but the member's concern about the scale and regional equity of the proposed capital-outlay budget remained open. The agency made commitments on Tandag Airport completion and a 2027 Surigao del Sur program.

DOTr · 2026-09-02 · committed

Tandag Airport completion and Surigao del Sur transport facilities

A committee member criticized the area's reported allocation of only about 1% of the DOTr budget and pressed the agency on Tandag Airport's completion. The DOTr said the project was almost substantially complete, identified the seven-story control tower, apron, grade corrections, and perimeter fence, and targeted completion of the vertical structures by year-end. The member pushed for completion within the month and cited 7% disbursement absorptive capacity, while the agency undertook to revisit the accomplishment. The member also sought improvements to Surigao del Sur's port and Kagwa Airport facilities, and the agency committed to immediately prepare a program for 2027.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the DOTr's regional budget allocation and the completion status and operational readiness of Tandag Airport. It also sought action on transport facilities serving Surigao del Sur, including the port and Kagwa Airport.

The DOTr said Tandag Airport's projects were ongoing and almost substantially completed, with the control tower, apron, grade corrections, and perimeter fence among the remaining or recently undertaken works. It targeted completion of the vertical structures by the end of the year, agreed to revisit the project's accomplishment, and committed to immediately program action for 2027 concerning Surigao del Sur's transport needs.

Outcome Tandag Airport was reported as nearly substantially complete, but the committee member rejected the end-of-year pace as too slow and pressed for completion within the month. The agency undertook to revisit the project and prepare a 2027 program for Surigao del Sur, but no definitive turnover date or specific facility-improvement funding was established.

DOTr · 2026-09-02 · committed

NLEX disruption response, toll reimbursement, and traffic management

Rep. Percival Cendaña raised the NLEX disruption, asking about traffic management, toll treatment, and short-, medium-, and long-term mitigation. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said the TRB would examine possible reimbursement within three days, while emphasizing proactive warnings through SMS, RFID-holder notices, variable message signs, and other public-information channels. Cendaña noted that toll-fee collection had continued for more than twenty four hours, and Lopez said toll suspension was governed by the toll-operations agreement and that more reimbursement was needed. Lopez also said the TRB had issued NLEX a notice to explain regarding the toll holiday and liability. Rep. Adore Plato separately questioned the response to severe-weather stranding and the implementation of early-warning protocols. NLEX representative Robin Ignacio said advisories had begun on August 28, but no final reimbursement or protocol determination was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DOTr and the Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) responded to the NLEX disruption, including traffic management, toll collection or reimbursement, and communication with motorists. It also examined whether NLEX and the TRB had adequate early-warning protocols for severe-weather events.

The DOTr said traffic management, infrastructure mitigation, proactive motorist communication, and possible toll reimbursement were the appropriate responses. Giovanni Lopez said the TRB was examining reimbursement within three days and had required NLEX management to explain the toll-holiday and liability issues, while NLEX said it had issued severe-weather advisories through multiple channels.

Outcome The DOTr described ongoing TRB review of possible reimbursement and confirmed that NLEX had been directed to explain the toll-holiday and liability issues. The record did not show a final reimbursement decision, a completed liability determination, or a specific new severe-weather protocol.

DOTr · 2026-09-02 · committed

LTFRB Region 3 hearing-officer requirements and discipline

Eli San Fernando raised an allegation that LTFRB Region 3 hearing officer Attorney Jennifer Rodriguez arbitrarily required additional documents and 40,000 on the same day they were submitted. He also questioned why the hearing officer was operating from a private law office in the LTFRB office and asked who had disciplinary authority, citing possible collusion or conflict of interest and a memorandum dated 02/19/2026. Secretary Giovanni Lopez said it was his first time hearing of the matter and stated that disciplinary authority over appointed officials belonged to the appointing authority. An LTFRB board member identified as Greg said a notice to explain had been issued, a complaint was pending before the LTFRB disciplinary board, and Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office. The board member also said the regional director had begun hearing the complaint and that the LTFRB had filed its comment with the CSC. The immediate allegations and the broader oversight concerns remained open, although the agency reported ongoing disciplinary action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether an LTFRB Region 3 hearing officer had improperly imposed additional requirements and a 40,000 payment on the same day, and whether the regional director or another authority had disciplinary jurisdiction. It also sought the status of the disciplinary case and corrective action, including whether similar conflicts could occur in other regions.

The DOTr Secretary said he had only learned of the matter during the hearing and stated that disciplinary authority over appointed officials rested with the appointing authority. The LTFRB board member said a disciplinary complaint was pending, Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office, the regional director had begun hearing the complaint, and the LTFRB had already filed its comment with the Civil Service Commission.

Outcome The agency reported that disciplinary proceedings were pending, Rodriguez had been transferred to the central office, and the LTFRB had submitted its comment to the CSC. The committee's concerns about the alleged 40,000 requirement, the regional director's disciplinary authority, and possible broader conflicts were not fully resolved during the exchange.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

NIA FY2027 budget restoration and irrigation project flexibility

Sheen Gonzales sought DA intervention and rehabilitation planning for irrigation facilities in Dolores, Eastern Samar, and Secretary Kiko Laurel committed to inspect the area in October for possible 2027 action. Carl Cari asked what rapid funding mechanisms NIA had for typhoon-damaged irrigation facilities; an NIA official cited a request of about 2.8 billion and a proposal of 66,000,000, with repairs requested through OCD. NIA Administrator Ed Gillian said NIA had requested about 233 billion for FY2027, but only 46 billion was included, compared with nearly 64 billion in FY2026. He warned that the reduction could delay ongoing irrigation projects and asked that the budget be restored to a program-based presentation. The chair distinguished that request from the special provision on project modifications and required safeguards, validation, and accountability. NIA agreed to submit proposed special-provision language and a prioritized list of items for the budget amendment subcommittee.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what support was available for irrigation rehabilitation and emergency repairs, and whether NIA’s FY2027 funding was sufficient to complete ongoing projects. It also examined whether NIA should receive greater flexibility to modify project line items while retaining congressional safeguards and accountability.

NIA said its FY2027 allocation was substantially below both its request and the FY2026 budget, creating a risk of delays to ongoing and critical irrigation projects. It sought restoration to a program-based budget presentation and a special provision allowing appropriate project-line modifications for technical, right-of-way, and site-readiness problems, while maintaining strict compliance, safeguards, and congressional oversight.

Outcome The committee expressed support for considering NIA budget restoration and greater implementation flexibility, subject to safeguards and continued oversight. NIA was expected to submit a prioritized list and proposed special-provision language; no final restoration amount or approved modification authority was established during the hearing.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

El Niño, drought, and climate-resilient farmer assistance

Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA how the 2027 budget would help farmers and Palawan fisherfolk withstand climate-related losses and access inputs, insurance, equipment, and markets. The DA cited solar irrigation, solar pumps, solar-powered aerators, drought- and heat-resistant seeds, fertilizer support, crop insurance, recovery loans, and soil laboratories, as well as Palawan port and ice facilities. Carl Cari later asked about direct assistance during a prolonged El Niño and drought, and the DA answered that it would coordinate with DSWD and provide alternative seeds, fertilizer, and land-preparation support. NIA cited a request of about 2.8 billion and a proposal of 66,000,000 for repair-related needs, but did not clearly explain a rapid-release mechanism. The Chair then asked for El Niño contingency funding, and the DA cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and an increase in the fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar aerators and solar pumps. The DA committed to submit detailed, separately prioritized information, while the final adequacy of contingency and emergency-repair funding remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what the 2027 budget would provide for farmers and fisherfolk facing climate-related crop and fisheries losses, especially prolonged El Niño, drought, and water shortages. It also examined whether contingency funds, irrigation repairs, insurance, inputs, equipment, and recovery assistance would be available and quickly released.

The DA said it was responding to climate risks through solar irrigation and pumping, solar-powered aerators, water impounding, drought- and heat-resistant seeds, fertilizer and replanting support, insurance, loans, and soil testing. For El Niño specifically, it cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and an increase in the fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar aerators and solar pumps; NIA identified repair requests but did not clearly establish a rapid-release mechanism.

Outcome The DA presented existing and proposed climate-resilience measures and identified 8,700,000,000 for El Niño fertilizers and a higher BFAR allocation for solar equipment. The Chair requested a separately identified priority list and the DA committed to provide details; the adequacy of the funding and NIA's rapid-release repair mechanism remained unresolved.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

African swine fever response, farmer payouts, and vaccine validation

An Iloilo member questioned the DA's claim that its ASF vaccine was safe and effective, citing the contrary positions of two FDA veterinary experts and the US Department of Agriculture. The DA reported that it had distributed about half a million doses and observed efficacy of about 85% to 90%, then committed to send the supporting clinical-trial documents. Representative Carl Cari asked about 2027 funding for community pig-raising facilities, faster indemnification, and low-cost biosecurity training, citing 4,900,000 in prior indemnification aid in Southern Leyte. The DA mentioned 1,000,000,000 for ASF or AI vaccines in case of an outbreak and described coordination with a state university and ATI under the Inspire 600 program, with a transcript-unclear figure of 12.5 or 13,500,000 per setup. The vaccine documentation and training coordination were committed, but the broader budget and facility-grant questions remained without a complete answer.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the DA had conclusive evidence that its ASF vaccine was safe and effective, and whether the agency would submit that evidence. It also asked what 2027 resources would support ASF vaccine deployment, farmer indemnification, biosecurity training, and community pig-raising or recovery facilities.

The DA maintained that the ASF vaccine had produced an eighty five to ninety percent efficacy result and that vaccinated pigs showed a good response. It defended the Bureau of Animal Industry's assessment, committed to provide supporting documents, and identified 1,000,000,000 for ASF or AI vaccines in case of an outbreak, while agreeing to coordinate on biosecurity training.

Outcome The DA committed to submit conclusive supporting documents for the ASF vaccine and said it could coordinate on biosecurity training. The requested 2027 budget breakdown for community pig-raising facilities, faster farmer payouts, and a Leyte swine recovery facility grant was not fully specified or resolved.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Rice procurement, floor-price implementation, and Rice for All

Rep. Sarah Elago asked how EO 100's rice floor price applied and sought clarification on NFA procurement, Rice for All funding, storage, and EO 101 implementation. The agency said NFA was buying at 21 and cited dry-rice prices of 25 to 27 pesos per kilo, while reporting 9,000,000,000 for NFA and 10,000,000,000 for Rice for All. An agency official said NFA warehouse capacity had risen from 500,000 tons to 800,000 tons, with procurement discussed at 20,000 to eventually 40,000 tons a month. The chair then questioned reports that LGU suppliers were selling imported rice instead of local rice and called for validation and investigation. The agency committed to providing details, and reported that the Sagibsaka desk had about 2,000,000, stated as exactly 1,950,000 for ICT equipment, with an additional 95,000,000 figure that was unclear in context.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how Executive Order 100's rice floor-price policy was being implemented, including whether it applied to private-sector buyers, and how NFA procurement, Rice for All funding, and storage capacity supported the policy. It also sought clarification on supplier validation, the implementation of Executive Orders 100 and 101, and funding for the Sagibsaka desk.

The agency said EO 100's floor-price mechanism was principally a government measure with limited application to the private sector. It maintained that NFA's warehouse capacity and available funding were sufficient for the planned procurement volumes, while stating that supplier arrangements were being validated and the Sagibsaka desk had funding, including 1,950,000 for ICT equipment as described in the transcript.

Outcome The agency said procurement capacity, funding, and storage were substantially improved, but the committee requested further details and validation of supplier practices. The record does not show that the supplier-validation concerns or the unclear Sagibsaka figures were fully resolved.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Rice storage capacity and delayed Iloilo processing facility

The Iloilo member pressed the DA over a rice processing facility that had remained unimplemented despite a commitment made about three years earlier. PhilMech described a warehouse of about 1,200 square meters, a 12-ton dryer, and a processing system with a stated capacity of three tons per hour, while DBM clearance for hauling trucks remained pending. The DA committed the rice processing system for June 2027 and scheduled tractors and combined harvesters for distribution from October through December. Sarah Elago then asked about EO 100, temporary storage, and NFA use of private warehouses. The agency cited Rice-for-All funding of about 10 billion, NFA funding of about 9 billion, and a stated total of 19,000,000,020.26, while reporting NFA internal storage capacity of 800,000 tons and procurement of 20,000 to eventually 40,000 tons a month. The discussion ended with commitments and agency assurances, but unresolved clearance and storage-arrangement details.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the Iloilo rice processing facility had not been implemented despite earlier commitments, what equipment and delivery dates were covered, and whether storage capacity was sufficient for rice procurement and the Rice-for-All program. It also asked how Executive Order No. 100's floor-price policy applied and what funding and warehouse capacity were available.

The DA and PhilMech said the delayed Iloilo facility was moving forward, with the rice processing system committed for June 2027 and agricultural equipment scheduled for distribution from October through December. The agency said storage capacity had substantially increased, with 800,000 tons of NFA internal capacity plus grant warehouses, and that available funding was sufficient for the quantity-buying program, although DBM clearance for hauling trucks remained pending.

Outcome The Iloilo facility was given a revised implementation commitment, but DBM clearance for hauling trucks was still pending. The storage and funding discussion produced agency figures and assurances, but no definitive committee ruling or resolution on temporary and private-warehouse arrangements was recorded.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Fish ports, deepwater ports, and fisheries infrastructure

Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA about fisheries livelihood and production support in Palawan, and the agency cited a 15 hectare Puerto Princesa-area port with ice, cold-storage, and blast-freezer facilities, along with solar-powered ice plants with five to 10 tons per day capacity. Rep. Howard Guintu questioned PFDA’s fish-port funding, which was stated as 3,800,000,003.08 and then 3,800,000,000, while another response cited 8,000,000,000 for old and new ports after an unclear initial figure of 88,000,000,000. He also raised the effect of US restrictions on blue swimming crab, noting that 90% of the market was in the United States; the fisheries undersecretary answered that the issue involved fishing gear and Irrawaddy dolphin interactions and cited a reduction of the gill-net limit to 500 meters. The chair asked about deepwater-port implementation and fisherfolk contingency assistance, and the DA said Mindoro construction would be bid out, cited 8,700,000,000 for El Niño fertilizers, and reported an increase in the BFAR fisherfolk budget from 10 to 12,000,000,000. The chair requested that fisherfolk needs be separately prioritized, and the DA committed to submit the requested details.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much funding was proposed for fish ports and deepwater ports in 2027, how existing and new projects would be financed and implemented, and what support would improve fisheries communities’ access to ice, cold storage, markets, and fishing gear. Members also asked how the agency would protect fisheries market access, particularly for blue swimming crab, and whether contingency support would be available for fisherfolk affected by climate and fuel-related disruptions.

The DA and its fisheries officials presented port, ice-plant, cold-storage, seaweed, and climate-response interventions as support for fisheries communities. The agency said Mindoro deepwater-port construction would be bid out, committed to regulatory and local-government measures addressing the blue swimming crab market-access issue, and agreed to submit details and a prioritized fisheries wish list.

Outcome The agency answered the infrastructure and market-access questions and undertook to bid out the Mindoro deepwater port and submit further fisheries details. The precise allocation between ongoing and new fish-port projects remained unclear, while additional funding for PFDA, fish ports, and the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk program was left for further budget consideration.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Fisherfolk assistance during fishing bans and market restrictions

Franz Vincent Legazpi asked the DA what assistance would be available to Palawan fisherfolk, including fuel, ice, gear, insurance, and market support. The DA cited a port facility near Puerto Princesa, solar-powered ice plants, seaweed and livestock programs, and proposed ice-plant capacities of about five to 10 tons per day. Rep. Howard Guintu questioned PFDA fish-port funding and raised the US restrictions affecting blue swimming crab exports; BFAR explained the Marine Mammal Protection Act issue, the Irrawaddy dolphin risk, the 500-meter gill-net limit, and its assistance and reporting commitments. The committee also sought support for fisherfolk affected by fishing bans and military exercises, but the duration and precise assistance remained unclear. The Chair later pressed the DA on deepwater-port implementation, the depleted Presidential Assistance program, and El Niño contingency funding; the DA cited 8,700,000,000 for fertilizers and a BFAR budget increase from 10 to 12,000,000,000 for solar equipment. The DA agreed to submit detailed, separately identified fisherfolk priorities.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what livelihood, production, market-access, and emergency assistance would be available to fisherfolk affected by fishing restrictions, export-market barriers, and national-security-related fishing bans. It also examined the funding and implementation of fish ports, fisherfolk programs, and contingency support in the FY 2027 budget.

The Department of Agriculture and BFAR stated that assistance would combine fish-port and cold-chain infrastructure, solar-powered ice plants and aerators, seaweed and livelihood programs, regulatory measures, and support for fisherfolk affected by restrictions. The agency committed to BFAR assistance for crab fishers, coordination with local governments and national-security authorities, a report on dolphin-protection compliance, bidding for the Mindoro deepwater port, and submission of detailed 2027 priorities.

Outcome The agency provided program descriptions, infrastructure plans, regulatory measures, and selected funding figures, but several fish-port figures were inconsistent or unclear. The matter landed with commitments to submit detailed priorities, pursue the Mindoro port bidding, report on dolphin-protection compliance, and coordinate on assistance for fisherfolk affected by fishing bans.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

RSSI sugarcane infestation control and the 35,000,000 LGU allocation

Sarah Elago raised concerns about the cost and environmental effects of chemical pesticides and asked whether lower-cost biological controls could reach all RSSI-affected sugarcane farms. The DA reported 134,000 hectares affected and 67,443 hectares verified, while the administrator said chemicals had covered about 35,000 hectares. The DA said it had provided 209,000,000, including 23,000,000 for chemical pesticides, had an additional 10,000,000 for chemicals, and estimated about 120,000,000 more for the initial response. It identified slow fungal production and limited laboratory capacity as the principal constraints, while citing an earmarked 300,000,000 for laboratories. The DA committed 35,000,000 directly to LGUs, based on verified affected areas, for Negros Island, with further quick response funding as needed. Expansion of biocontrol production was committed, but the complete transition away from chemical control was not fully resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the extent of RSSI infestation in sugarcane farms, the cost and coverage of chemical pesticide assistance, and whether lower-cost biological or nature-based controls could replace or complement chemical measures. It also asked what immediate assistance could be provided before the FY 2027 budget, including how the 35,000,000 LGU allocation would be distributed.

The DA said chemical pesticides were being used as the initial response because RSSI infestation was intense and biocontrol production was too slow. It supported expanding fungal biocontrol production through DA, government, university, and proposed LGU laboratories, while releasing immediate chemical assistance to LGUs and additional quick response funds as needed.

Outcome The DA answered the committee's questions with infestation figures, existing pesticide assistance, and estimated funding needs. It committed immediate 35,000,000 LGU assistance for Negros Island and longer-term laboratory expansion, but the broader shift to integrated pest management and the final funding required for all affected areas remained dependent on additional budgets and production capacity.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · unresolved

Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund delivery

Carl Cari asked how the PCA and DA would use the 2027 Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund resources to reduce paperwork and ensure timely delivery of free fertilizer and planting materials. An agency official said the PCA budget was mostly for replanting, with a target of 100,000,000 trees and an expected 40,000,000 trees planted by the end of the year. The official also said coco levy funds needed to be unlocked through the new bill and referred to value-adding facilities, scholarships, and education for coconut farmers. No specific process for reducing paperwork or accelerating input delivery was provided. Cari later supported the DA and NIA budgets, but the Trust Fund delivery question remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the PCA and DA would use the 2027 Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund resources to reduce paperwork and delivery bottlenecks. It specifically asked how free fertilizer and planting materials would reach coconut-farming communities on time.

The agency official presented the PCA's 2027 coconut allocation as focused mainly on replanting, with a target of 100,000,000 trees and an expected 40,000,000 trees planted by the end of the year. The official also emphasized unlocking coco levy funds through the new bill and using facilities, value-adding activities, scholarships, and education to improve coconut farmers' livelihoods, but did not identify specific measures to reduce paperwork or expedite delivery of fertilizer and planting materials.

Outcome The agency described replanting and the proposed unlocking of coco levy funds but did not directly answer how paperwork and delivery bottlenecks would be reduced or how inputs would reach farmers on time. The issue therefore remained open despite the member's support for the overall DA and NIA budgets.

Food logistics chain, mega food hubs, and public markets

A committee member raised consultation with public-market vendors, price monitoring, and local-government responsibilities for public markets. The member then asked for details of the food logistics chain plan. The agency said food hubs were being implemented in 2026 in Clark, Isabella, and an unclear location, citing 22,000,000,000 for Clark, 125,000,000 for Isabella, and other amounts including 500,000,000. For 20.27, it cited 500,000,000, 250,000,000 for San Pablo Lagoon, another 250,000,000, and a stated total of 1,000,000,000 for food hubs. It described a network integrating livestock, laboratories, cold storage, traders, farmers, consumers, LGUs, local cooperatives, and 800 Cadiwa sites, with a target of 10 to 12 mega food hubs. The matter remained informational, with several spoken allocations and references unclear and no further commitment recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how public markets would be coordinated with the Department of Agriculture's price monitoring and logistics functions, and how the proposed mega food hub network would be designed and funded. It also sought details on the food logistics chain, links to local government units, and the planned Cadiwa sites.

The Department of Agriculture supported developing a network of mega food hubs connected to municipal facilities and eventually to a national government distribution network. It said the hubs would integrate livestock, laboratories, cold storage, other storage, traders, farmers, consumers, local cooperatives, LGUs, and Cadiwa sites.

Outcome The agency presented its proposed mega food hub concept, indicative locations and amounts, network components, and links to LGUs and Cadiwa sites. The excerpt ended without a ruling, document submission, or resolution of the unclear allocations and project references.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · informational

Farm-to-market road prioritization and eligibility

A committee member raised the requirements for qualifying and identifying farm-to-market roads. An agency official said the Philippines had 55,000 kilometers of farm-to-market road networks and that 16,000,000,000 would cover only about 1,000 kilometers per year. The official listed poverty incidence, the road influence area, the number of farmer, fish, and fruit beneficiaries, connectivity, road condition, climate-change adaptation, and average daily traffic as prioritization factors. The official added that the roads benefited local communities and the broader local economy, not only agriculture. The exchange ended with the criteria stated and no additional action recorded.

Questions and agency response

What criteria does the Department of Agriculture use to qualify and prioritize farm-to-market road proposals, given the size of the road network and limited annual funding?

The agency official said farm-to-market roads are prioritized under the master plan using factors such as beneficiary coverage, poverty incidence, network connectivity, road condition, climate-change adaptation, and traffic. The official also emphasized that these roads support local economies beyond agriculture, while available funding covers only a limited portion of the 55,000-kilometer network each year.

Outcome The agency provided the stated qualification and prioritization criteria and explained the funding limitation. No further document, funding adjustment, or other action was recorded.

OVP · 2026-09-01 · informational

FY2027 OVP budget overview, program delivery, and utilization

The chair limited the briefing to the OVP budget and then recognized the agency to present its FY 2027 proposal. The OVP presented a proposed budget of about 785 million, with over 70% for operating expenses and about 193.1 million for goods and grants under socioeconomic program delivery. It described delivery through 10 satellite offices and one extension office, with a target of about 1.4 million beneficiaries. The agency reported that it served about 1.396 million individuals and groups in 2025, obligated about 851.8 million, and disbursed about 687.8 million. For the first half of 2026, it reported about 773,858 beneficiaries served, 43% obligation of the available allotment, and a 62% disbursement rate, although the spoken disbursement amount was unclear. The presentation ended without a recorded challenge, request, or commitment.

Questions and agency response

What was the OVP's proposed FY 2027 budget, how would it be distributed across personnel, operating expenses, capital outlay, and direct program delivery, and what did the OVP report about program reach and budget utilization? The committee also sought to establish the implementation structure supporting nationwide delivery.

The OVP presented the proposed FY 2027 budget as a lean, focused allocation centered on direct socioeconomic assistance, satellite-office operations, and nationwide service delivery. It maintained that its historical utilization, beneficiary reach, project completion, partnerships, and satisfaction ratings demonstrated effective implementation.

Outcome The OVP completed its budget and performance presentation, covering the proposed allocation, delivery structure, beneficiary reach, and utilization record. No member question, document request, commitment, or contested issue was recorded in this stretch.

OVP · 2026-09-01 · committed

Libreng Sakay routes, contracting, and passenger capacity

A committee member asked how the 22,000,000 Libreng Sakay allocation related to the reported 1,400,000 beneficiaries, of whom 1,200,000 were attributed to the program. The OVP said the service operated nine buses nationwide, with routes planned in partnership with the LTFRB, MMDA, and another agency rendered as "OTR," and with private operators including Jackliner, Rural Transit Mindanao Incorporated, Oyinco City Tours, and Kudos Trucking Corporation. The agency said two buses had been purchased by the OVP and that each bus had capacity for around 46 passengers. It described peak-hour operations from 5AM to 9AM and 5PM to 9PM, but the passenger examples of 442 and 422 were unclear and did not fully establish the reported reach. The OVP also projected reaching 4,000,000 passengers around mid-November. The committee requested a list of providers, leaving the capacity and allocation calculations partly unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the OVP's Libreng Sakay allocation translated into routes, contracted operators, bus ownership, operating costs, and passenger reach. It also asked how the reported beneficiary figures were calculated and what capacity the program could actually deliver.

The OVP said Libreng Sakay operated nine buses nationwide through partnerships with transport agencies and private bus operators, while two buses had been purchased by the OVP. It said routes were planned by partner transport agencies, operations ran during peak hours, each bus held around 46 passengers, and the program expected to reach 4,000,000 passengers around mid-November.

Outcome The OVP explained the nine-bus operating model, named private transport partners, described peak-hour capacity, and stated that it expected to reach 4,000,000 passengers. The committee requested a provider list, while the discrepancies between the 1,200,000 beneficiary figure, the 22,000,000 allocation, and the unclear 442/422 capacity figures were not fully resolved.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · unresolved

JO/COS absorption, plantilla vacancies, and professionalization funding

Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. led the inquiry into 919,868 JO and COS workers, vacant plantilla positions, and the absence of measurable absorption and vacancy-reduction targets. CSC described preferential rating, qualification requirements, Prime ESG, agency optimization, and a target covering 40 agencies, but said it could not establish a direct correlation between the programs and JO/COS absorption. The agency distinguished regular and necessary functions that should be staffed permanently from temporary or episodic work, and proposed reviews of LGU personnel-service caps and DBM's scrap-and-build policy. Representative Elijah San Fernando and Representative Kaloy Bulilla raised worker precarity, political accommodation, public-sector unionism, and a DSWD worker's case, while CSC discussed joint work with DBM and COA and possible benefits coverage. Representative Democrito Mendoza questioned 224999 vacancies, examination pass rates, and proposed equivalency legislation; CSC said the principal problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete vacancies, staffing constraints, and merit-and-fitness concerns. The issue remained unresolved, with several administrative and legislative follow-ups contemplated.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how CSC would reduce plantilla vacancies and government-wide reliance on job-order (JO) and contract-of-service (COS) workers, including whether qualified long-serving workers could be absorbed into permanent positions. Members also asked what measurable results would come from the proposed professionalization and modernization allocations and whether CSC would support legislative and monitoring mechanisms.

CSC said it could facilitate eligibility, improve HR systems, monitor or analyze JO/COS deployment, and recommend legislative and administrative changes, but could not guarantee absorption into permanent civil service positions. It distinguished workers performing regular and necessary functions, who should be reduced or regularized through proper staffing, from workers performing temporary or episodic functions, for whom JO/COS arrangements remained necessary.

Outcome The committee obtained CSC's explanation of the existing preferential-rating, modernization, optimization, and public-sector unionism measures, but no government-wide numerical targets for vacancy reduction or JO/COS absorption were committed. Legislative equivalency, monitoring, LGU staffing limits, and the precise scope of CSC jurisdiction remained open for further policy or legislative action.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · committed

Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and digital transformation

CSC presented the PCSMP as a central part of its digital transformation, covering Prime ESG, HRMIS plus payroll, a national learning platform, electronic administrative justice, and a civil-service data management system. The agency cited a proposed PCSMP allocation of about 1.34 billion in the budget breakdown, while the opening presentation separately cited 453 million for implementation. Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. pressed for measurable reductions in vacancies, hiring time, and JO/COS dependence, but CSC acknowledged that it had no indicators establishing those correlations and could not guarantee absorption into the civil service. A committee member confirmed that the contact center used written referrals and that CSC's electronic case system could track cases nationwide. Representative Ryan questioned cybersecurity, online oath-taking authentication, SALN rules, and the failed data-center bidding; CSC undertook to submit a cybersecurity cost breakdown and defended the failed bidding as a privacy safeguard. Representative Elijah San Fernando raised delayed administrative cases, and CSC said CLASS would be implemented in 2027 to enable online filing and digital transmission of case records.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Philippine Civil Service Modernization Project and related digital-transformation spending would produce measurable improvements in recruitment, appointment processing, HR records, payroll, case resolution, cybersecurity, and service delivery. Members also asked whether CSC had concrete targets for reducing vacancies and dependence on job-order and contract-of-service workers, and whether safeguards would protect sensitive personnel and SALN data.

CSC said modernization and digitalization were necessary to improve HR governance, appointment processing, learning, payroll, records, administrative justice, and public assistance. It described planned systems and implementation targets, but acknowledged that it did not yet have measurable indicators linking PCSMP spending to vacancy reduction or JO/COS absorption and did not provide a specific cybersecurity or CLASS budget breakdown during the hearing.

Outcome The committee received CSC's explanation of the planned modernization systems and implementation timetable, but the agency did not provide the requested measurable targets linking PCSMP spending to vacancy reduction, hiring time, or JO/COS absorption. Cybersecurity cost disaggregation was requested for later submission, while CLASS and the data-management systems remained implementation commitments rather than completed outcomes.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · committed

Cybersecurity, online oath-taking, and the 212,000,000 data center

Rep. Ryan asked the CSC to identify its cybersecurity allocation, noting a modernization figure of about 1.4 billion, and requested a breakdown because cybersecurity was integrated across digital programs. The CSC said it was drafting a data privacy and cybersecurity manual and committed to submit a disaggregated budget breakdown. Ryan questioned whether online oath-taking relied only on Zoom and warned about AI-enabled impersonation; the CSC said oath administrators had to verify identity, ask questions, and accept liability for inadequate precautions. The CSC said it had a continuing ICT partnership with DICT and would raise the authentication concerns there. On SALN filing, the CSC explained that personal properties could be grouped under "others," while cash and registered properties had separate treatment under rules issued in 2025. Ryan also raised the roughly 212 million pesos data-center project, and the CSC said the sole bidder failed confidentiality requirements, leading to a declared failure of bidding and rebidding. Ryan endorsed that decision, but the cybersecurity breakdown and rebidding outcome were not yet resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much of the CSC's modernization budget was specifically devoted to cybersecurity, how online oath-taking and SALN filing would be authenticated and protected, and why the central-office data-center procurement failed. It also sought assurances that the rebidding would preserve data confidentiality and that the failed bidding would not prejudice the CSC's budget.

The CSC said cybersecurity was integrated across its digital programs and that it was preparing a data privacy and cybersecurity manual, but it could not provide a specific disaggregated cybersecurity amount during the exchange. It maintained that online oath-taking required identity verification and administrator accountability, that SALN rules clarified the treatment of personal and registered properties, and that the data-center bidding was properly declared failed because the sole bidder did not satisfy confidentiality safeguards.

Outcome The CSC's explanations on oath-taking authentication, SALN treatment, and the failed data-center bidding were provided, and Rep. Ryan endorsed the privacy-based failure of bidding. The requested disaggregated cybersecurity budget and the result of the data-center rebidding remained open.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · committed

Civil-service examinations, eligibility, and equivalency pathways

Representative Nassal pressed the CSC for a government-wide plan, measurable targets, and concrete results from proposed programs addressing vacancies and dependence on about 919,868 JO and COS workers. The CSC described preferential rating, including the 70% grade score, 10% avenue, and experience-based treatment, but said it could not guarantee appointments or establish a direct correlation with absorption. Representative Ismula raised possible preferential eligibility for IPMRs, and the CSC said it could work toward extending coverage after consultations and subject to legal requirements. Representative Mendoza later urged support for House Bill 93, which would create an equivalency pathway after at least three years of satisfactory service, but the CSC warned that this could encourage agencies to retain unqualified hires and undermine merit and fitness. The CSC said it was producing more than 160 thousand eligibles annually and that the central problems were vacancies, obsolete positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates rather than a shortage of eligibles. The hearing ended without a clear CSC commitment to support House Bill 93 or deliver numerical vacancy and absorption targets, although the agency undertook related work on IPMR preferential rating, modernization guidance, and JO/COS regulation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the CSC would help qualified JO and COS workers obtain eligibility, fill vacant plantilla positions, and reduce reliance on contractual arrangements. Members also examined preferential-rating and equivalency pathways, civil-service examination standards and pass rates, and the CSC's position on related legislation.

The CSC said preferential rating could help qualified JO, COS, and potentially IPMR workers obtain eligibility, but it did not guarantee appointment because education, training, experience, eligibility, and position-specific qualification standards still applied. The agency maintained that the main problem was not a shortage of eligibles but obsolete or unavailable positions, personnel-service caps, and low examination pass rates; it cautioned that automatic equivalency after three years could undermine merit and fitness.

Outcome The CSC explained its existing preferential-rating pathway and indicated that IPMR coverage could be expanded subject to legal and qualification requirements. The broader issues of measurable vacancy-reduction targets, automatic equivalency under House Bill 93, and the causes of low examination pass rates remained open.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · committed

Public-sector unionism and labor-management representation

Rep. Eli San Fernando asked about the public-sector unionism subprogram's allocation, outputs, and targets and raised the precarious status of job order and contract of service workers. The stated allocation was 30,000 pesos to 88,000 pesos per regional office, and a CSC official said organizations were to be credited and recognized within seven days. The committee did not receive a complete account of the 2026 and 2027 output indicators, and Rep. San Fernando said he would return to the JO/COS issue in the second round. Rep. Democrito Mendoza then questioned the quality of civil-service examinees and sought CSC support for an equivalency or pathway-to-permanency bill based on three years of service. A CSC commissioner said that position was personal and warned that the proposal could undermine merit and fitness. Mendoza also sought support for a labor-representation bill, and a CSC official expressed openness while describing the existing PSLMC selection mechanism. The issues therefore remained partly open, with further consideration implied rather than fully resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the allocation, output indicators, and targets for CSC's public-sector unionism subprogram, including the registration and recognition of public-sector employee organizations. Members also sought CSC's position on the precarious status of job order and contract of service workers and on proposed bills concerning civil-service eligibility and labor-management representation.

CSC described the public-sector unionism subprogram as supporting organization and registration of employee organizations while maintaining noninterference, with recognition targeted within seven days. On equivalency, the responding commissioner personally opposed a three-year route that could weaken merit and fitness, while the agency official was open to labor representation proposals and described the existing PSLMC nomination process.

Outcome CSC provided the stated allocation range and a seven-day recognition target, but the transcript did not establish complete 2026 and 2027 output indicators or targets. The JO/COS worker issue was deferred to a later round, while CSC's support for the bills remained qualified: the responding commissioner personally opposed the equivalency approach, and an agency official expressed openness to labor representation.

Congresswoman Ilago asked whether agencies were complying with the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act and maintaining functional committees on decorum and investigation. It said sexual-harassment and Safe Spaces Act provisions had been integrated into the RACs and related CSC rules, but it did not provide a clear timeline for new Convention 190 guidelines. The CSC cited a special emergency leave policy issued in 2013 that provided five days annually to calamity victims who could show proof. The chair directed the CSC to submit data and a status report, including on wellness leave, leaving those requested materials and the separate wellness-leave issue pending.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether agencies had functional mechanisms for preventing and investigating sexual harassment, how the Civil Service Commission (CSC) enforced compliance, and whether the CSC had issued or planned guidelines implementing ILO Convention 190. It also sought the status of workplace wellness leave and related employee protections.

The CSC said that sexual-harassment compliance mechanisms were required by law and CSC rules, that regional offices conducted regular inspections, and that sexual-harassment and Safe Spaces Act provisions had been integrated into the RACs and related rules. It cited an existing special emergency leave policy for calamity victims but did not state a substantive position or timeline on a separate workplace wellness leave policy or fully answer the requested Convention 190 implementation timeline.

Outcome The CSC described existing compliance rules and inspection practices and undertook to submit inspection data and a status report. The requested timeline for CSC guidelines implementing ILO Convention 190 and the substantive status of a separate wellness leave policy remained open.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · committed

Solo-parent leave and benefits for JO/COS workers

Minority member Roberto Nazal Jr. raised whether qualified JO and COS solo parents were entitled to the seven-day solo-parent leave under Republic 11/1961 and the 2025 joint circular. CSC answered that it interpreted section 11.2 as covering benefits granted under existing laws and said it had recognized seven-day solo-parent leave since 2004. Nassal warned that departments remained hesitant because of audit concerns. CSC undertook to reiterate the provision to departments and said it was coordinating with DSWD, the primary implementing agency, while DBM's position was still needed. Representative Kaloy Bulilla later supported the CSC budget and raised the plight of a DSWD JO worker. CSC official Ryan Alvin Acosta reaffirmed coverage of JO and COS workers and committed to work with DBM and COA on a mechanism for implementation and grievances.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether qualified solo-parent job order (JO) and contract of service (COS) workers were entitled to the seven-day solo-parent leave under Republic Act 11/1961 and the applicable joint memorandum circular. It also sought to determine whether CSC had communicated and would enforce that interpretation across departments despite audit and implementation concerns.

CSC stated that its interpretation of section 11.2 of the JO/COS joint memorandum circular covered qualified JO and COS workers under the Solo Parents Welfare Act and entitled them to seven-day solo-parent leave. CSC said DSWD remained the primary implementing agency for the Act, that DBM's position was still needed, and that CSC would reiterate the relevant provision and work with DBM and COA on implementation and grievance mechanisms.

Outcome CSC affirmed that its interpretation covered qualified JO and COS workers and their entitlement to seven-day solo-parent leave, but said DBM's position and coordination with DSWD remained relevant. CSC committed to reiterating the provision and developing an implementation or grievance mechanism with DBM and COA.

CSC · 2026-09-01 · committed

CSC compliance and enforcement of personnel rules

Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula questioned how the CSC enforced its expanded gambling ban and whether it covered online gambling. The CSC said complaints could be filed anonymously through contact centers and complaints desks in regional and field offices, and Assistant Commissioner Ariel Ronquillo said the prohibition covered both on-site and online gambling. Ismula also asked about preferential civil-service eligibility for IPMRs; the CSC said it would consult Indigenous Peoples communities and could develop a preferential-rating system, potentially crediting one to three years of representative service toward a five-year experience requirement, subject to law. The member raised a 2,000 pesos compensation reform and House Bill Number 3874, and the CSC expressed support for increased benefits and continued discussions with DBM. Rep. Isabel Segabaria then challenged the CSC's authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule. The CSC acknowledged the need for legal basis but defended the rule under the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly, leaving the scope of the agency's authority unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the CSC monitored and enforced its expanded gambling prohibition, whether it could provide preferential civil-service eligibility treatment for indigenous peoples mandatory representatives (IPMRs), and what reforms it supported for government compensation. It also sought to clarify whether the CSC had statutory authority to treat common-law relationships as equivalent to marriage under the nepotism rule.

The CSC said gambling was prohibited both on-site and online and that compliance could be monitored through complaints received by its contact center and complaints desks in regional and field offices. It indicated that preferential eligibility treatment for IPMRs could be developed subject to law, while defending the common-law nepotism rule as an anti-circumvention measure grounded in Supreme Court reasoning, although it acknowledged that an administrative rule must have legal basis.

Outcome The gambling-ban questions were answered with the CSC's position that online gambling was already covered and that complaints systems provided the monitoring mechanism. The IPMR eligibility and compensation matters were left at the level of proposed study, consultation, and continuing dialogue, while the statutory authority for including common-law relationships in the nepotism rule remained contested.

2028 election-preparation funding and proposed COMELEC budget cuts

COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia presented a proposed FY2027 budget of about 29.5 billion, including roughly 23.92 billion for 2028 election preparations, and warned that a reduction of about 9 billion could compromise the election. Rep. Mercy Sindania characterized the NEP level as a recipe for disaster and asked what would happen if the reduction remained; Garcia said COMELEC could sacrifice features such as voter verification but could not compromise core preparation for a presidential and vice-presidential election. Rep. Edgar Erice questioned the 23 billion machine request and suggested that a lower requirement could save about 6 billion, while Garcia defended the need for about 124,000 machines because of voter growth and inflation. Other members supported restoring COMELEC's broader request to about 44 billion. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez moved to approve the budget and sought a special provision allowing about 11 billion in unused Barangay and SK election funds to continue for critical 2028 preparations. Garcia agreed to submit the proposed language, and also committed to provide updates on overseas voting and address vacant positions, but the final funding level and machine allocation remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 funding would give COMELEC sufficient resources to prepare for credible 2028 national and local elections. Members also examined the effect of reduced machine, infrastructure, staffing, overseas-voting, and election-preparation funds, and whether unused Barangay and SK election appropriations could be made available for 2028 preparations.

COMELEC stated that the proposed reductions, particularly the roughly 9,000,000,000 reduction in 2028 preparatory funding, could compromise election preparations and the credibility of the 2028 national and local elections. Garcia maintained that COMELEC needed funding for approximately 124,000 machines, ballot printing, certification, logistics, staffing, and infrastructure, while offering to defer lower-priority features or construction and to submit language for a continuing-appropriation special provision.

Outcome The committee broadly supported restoring COMELEC's election-preparation resources and moved to approve the budget together with a special provision for continuing use of unused Barangay and SK election funds. The precise final budget level, machine funding, and implementation of the proposed restoration were not fully resolved in the transcript, while COMELEC's submission of special-provision language and other updates remained pending.

Automated election-machine procurement, leasing, and readiness

COMELEC Chairman George Irwin M. Garcia warned that the proposed reduction in election-preparation funding could compromise 2028 readiness and said about 74 million voters would require roughly 124,000 machines, including contingency units. He explained that the 2025 lease cost 17,990,000,000 or about 18 billion in the discussion, and covered warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement, while the proposed 2028 lease was discussed at 23,000,000,000. Rep. Edgar Erice challenged that figure and argued that purchase, reuse, or upgrading could reduce the cost to about 17.8 billion and save about 6 billion. A member separately asked about cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting, and COMELEC cited 337,000,000 for ICT equipment, continuous monitoring, enrollment controls, and a projected 55 to 60% overseas turnout. Erice also requested the COMELEC Advisory Council's terms of reference, meeting minutes, and resolution, and Chairman Garcia committed to submit them before plenary debates. The lease-versus-purchase issue remained open, subject to the documents and further congressional budget action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC should lease, purchase, or upgrade automated counting machines for the 2028 elections, and whether the proposed funding would provide enough machines and related readiness measures. Members also asked about machine standards, cybersecurity, overseas Internet voting, and the documents supporting COMELEC's procurement position.

COMELEC maintained that leasing new machines for the 2028 election was necessary because of projected voter growth, the need for additional and contingency machines, and the importance of avoiding questions about reused equipment in a presidential election. It said leasing covered warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement, while cybersecurity and overseas Internet voting would be supported through ICT investment, monitoring, enrollment controls, and related safeguards.

Outcome The committee received COMELEC's justification for leasing new machines, but Rep. Edgar Erice continued to contest the amount and the preference for new leased equipment. COMELEC undertook to provide the procurement and Advisory Council documents, leaving the cost and lease-versus-purchase question open for further budget deliberation.

Barangay and SK election postponement, term fixing, and unused funds

Rep. Renee Co questioned whether the BSKE elections would proceed and asked about COMELEC’s pending procurement and overtime obligations. COMELEC said it had obligated about 8 billion for election materials and reported PHP 1,200,000,000 in six months of overtime, while supporting periodic, regular, and definite elections but deferring the policy decision on postponement or term fixing to Congress and the courts. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported fixing the barangay officials’ terms and sought authority to retain unused BSKE funds, with figures discussed ranging from about 9 billion to 11 billion and an estimated unutilized balance of about 10.9 billion. COMELEC proposed that unused BSKE appropriations become continuing appropriations for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes. DBM raised no objection to the concept or proposed wording, but the committee deferred final action and requested a formal submission for consideration by the budget amendments review subcommittee. The Senior Deputy Speaker also confirmed that COMELEC would implement Congress’s term-fixing decision and remain bound by procurement contracts already covered by notices to proceed.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the barangay and SK elections would proceed as scheduled or be postponed or reset through term fixing, and what that would mean for COMELEC’s procurement, overtime, and election appropriations. Members also sought to determine whether unutilized BSKE funds could remain available for the 2028 national and local elections through a special provision.

COMELEC said it would comply with the law and implement Congress’s decision on whether to hold, reset, postpone, or alter the term of barangay and SK officials. It supported treating unused BSKE appropriations as continuing appropriations for 2028 election preparations and other lawful purposes, subject to audit and the committee’s final special-provision language.

Outcome The committee did not finally approve the special provision during the hearing; the motion was deferred to the budget amendments review subcommittee and the proper time. COMELEC committed to submit formal language, while DBM stated that it had no objection, leaving final inclusion and wording for later committee action.

Machine funding requirement of 23,000,000,000 versus DBM funding

Rep. Edgar Erice raised the gap between COMELEC's 23,000,000,000 machine requirement and DBM's 21,000,000,000 funding, while COMELEC described the shortfall as 1,500,000,000. Chairman Garcia justified the requirement by citing inflation, projected voter growth to about 74 million, and a need for 124,000 machines. Erice argued that the machines could cost about 17.8 billion, potentially producing savings of 6 billion, and another member questioned whether purchasing or upgrading would be cheaper than leasing. COMELEC maintained that a one-time lease was appropriate for the critical 2028 presidential election and cited warehousing, maintenance, and enhancement costs. The agency also described cybersecurity measures and its planned overseas Internet-voting enrollment and authentication process. The chairman undertook to consider the lower-cost proposal, but the final funding and procurement approach remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why COMELEC projected a machine requirement of 23,000,000,000 for the 2028 elections when DBM funding was stated at 21,000,000,000, and whether leasing, purchasing, or upgrading machines would provide the most economical and reliable option. Members also examined machine readiness, cybersecurity, and the implementation of overseas Internet voting.

COMELEC maintained that leasing machines for the 2028 election was justified by the projected increase in voters, technical requirements, and the importance of the presidential and vice-presidential election. The agency also stated that it was addressing cybersecurity and would implement overseas Internet voting through registration, enrollment, identity verification, and a one-time PIN.

Outcome COMELEC defended the 23,000,000,000 machine requirement but agreed to consider the committee member's lower-cost proposal and seek a reasonable plan. The lease-versus-purchase issue, final machine quantity, and funding gap were not conclusively resolved.

ICT, cybersecurity, and election-system security after proposed reductions

Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores questioned COMELEC's ability to protect election data after almost 87.4% of its proposed ICT funding was removed. Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia cited 24-hour monitoring, 32,000,000 Internet attempts before an election, 3,000,000 attempts per month, and 337,000,000 for ICT-related requirements, while saying additional cybersecurity personnel and system improvements were needed. A committee member also questioned the approximately 17,990,000,000 lease for 110,000 ACMs and the readiness and integrity of machines for 2028. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned overseas Internet voting, registration funding, and regulation of social media and artificial intelligence; COMELEC said it supported regulation but acknowledged constitutional and legislative limits. Vice Chair Zia Alonto Adiong asked about security and election-related violence before the BARMM barangay election, and COMELEC reported preparations involving 3,393,000 voters, 5,212 voting centers, and 5,212 machines. COMELEC committed to submit case lists and updates, but the budget restoration and several security and regulatory issues were not finally settled.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC could maintain secure election systems, protect voter and election data, and prepare for the 2028 and BARMM elections despite proposed ICT and other budget reductions. Members also asked how cybersecurity, Internet voting, overseas registration, social-media regulation, and election-related security would be handled.

COMELEC said it could continue operating and disposing of cases despite reductions, but maintained that additional ICT resources were necessary for cybersecurity, system improvement, maintenance, and protection against hacking, data compromise, and foreign interference. It supported secure Internet voting and social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation, while recognizing constitutional and legislative limits on COMELEC's regulatory authority.

Outcome COMELEC defended the need to restore or protect ICT and cybersecurity resources and gave operational assurances on monitoring, Internet voting, and election preparation. It committed to submit case information and updates, but the proposed budget restoration, the precise funding level, the social-media task-force question, and the security determination concerning the BARMM incident remained unresolved.
