Overseas voting, Internet voting, and continuing registration

Committee members, led by Rep. Sarah Elago and a minority member, questioned whether overseas registration and Internet voting would close persistent participation gaps. COMELEC said the DFA supervised overseas voting under the law while COMELEC coordinated, and described registration, identity verification, one-time PINs, and enrollment lasting three to five minutes. Garcia cited 1,200,000 overseas voters, a hoped-for increase to 2,000,000, and turnout targets ranging from at least 50% to 55 to 60%; Elago cited a 67,000,000 proposal for overseas voting and continuing registration. Members also pressed for accessible registration, voter education, and social-media accountability, while Garcia cited 3,000,000 deactivated voters and promised to activate them for 2028. The agency committed to update the committee on reforms and turnout, and a member manifested support for restoring COMELEC's proposed 2027 budget cut, but the funding question remained unsettled.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COMELEC's overseas registration and Internet-voting arrangements would improve participation, accessibility, and security, particularly for overseas voters. Members also asked how continuing registration, funding, social-media regulation, and staffing would support the 2028 elections.

COMELEC supported Internet voting as a means of increasing overseas participation, while emphasizing registration, identity verification, one-time PINs, and security. It said overseas voting was supervised under the law by the DFA in coordination with COMELEC, supported stronger social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation subject to legislative and constitutional limits, and committed to broaden registration and report back on electoral reforms and turnout.

Outcome COMELEC defended Internet voting and described registration, enrollment, and security safeguards, but the committee did not settle the separate overseas-registration funding question or the proposed budget restoration. COMELEC committed to continued registration, activation of deactivated voters, stronger online protections, and a later update to the committee.

Rep. Sarah Elago asked about overseas voting, Internet voting, continuing registration, and a revised proposal of about 67 million, and pressed COMELEC on social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation. Garcia said COMELEC coordinated with the DFA, was preparing for secure Internet voting, had limited authority to punish conduct without a law, and could request takedowns of discriminatory material. The discussion also covered roughly 3 million deactivated voters, Indigenous peoples, elderly voters, and registration in geographically isolated areas. Questions and agency response

It also examined COMELEC's plans for Internet voting, social-media regulation, and inclusive registration.

COMELEC said the printing and registration resources were critical to timely ballot production, machine deployment, voter registration, and the 2028 elections. It maintained that it was coordinating with the DFA on overseas voting, exploring secure Internet voting and technology-enabled registration, and would pursue inclusive registration while respecting legal limits on social-media regulation.

Outcome COMELEC explained the operational risks of the printing and registration reductions and stated that it would pursue expanded registration, reactivation, overseas-voting coordination, and inclusive outreach. The committee received the explanations, but no ruling or restoration of the proposed cut was recorded in the provided transcript.

Election-cycle costs, QRF, and possible longer election intervals

Representative Jobo Yagino asked about the QRF and whether holding elections every five years could produce savings compared with the existing three-year cycle. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said an automated national and local election required about 26 billion for preparation and 20 billion for the election year, or almost 46 billion, while the BSKE figure was stated as 19.57 and 20 billion, with the combined three-year figure rendered unclearly as 6,066,000,000,000. Garcia said changing the election term might be a solution but would require a constitutional amendment or revision because the Constitution provides three-year terms for specified positions. Yagino asked that the issue be placed on the record and potentially referred to House lawyers. He expressed full support for COMELEC's budget, preferred an increase, and moved for approval, but the excerpt contained no ruling on the motion.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much COMELEC's election-related costs could be reduced by lengthening the election interval and whether such a change would affect the proposed budget. It also considered whether the issue required legal or constitutional action and whether COMELEC's budget should be approved.

COMELEC's chairperson presented the recurring costs of national, local, and BSKE elections and indicated that lengthening the election term could offer a solution. He also stated that changing the constitutionally specified three-year terms would require a constitutional amendment or revision; he did not state a final position on a five-year election cycle or receive a recorded ruling on the budget motion.

Outcome COMELEC supplied cost figures and stated that a longer election interval would require constitutional amendment or revision. Yagino moved to approve the COMELEC budget, but no ruling or disposition of the motion was recorded in the provided excerpt.

Election procurement contracts and financial consequences of postponement

Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos and Rep. Renee Co questioned COMELEC about the roughly 19 billion BSK budget, the amounts already spent or obligated, pending deliveries, and overtime costs if the election were postponed. COMELEC cited about 8,000,000,000 in obligations or earmarks, 70,000 ballot boxes, and PHP 1,200,000,000 in six months of overtime, although several obligation figures were unclear in the transcript. Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said notices to proceed could create perfected sales or contracts, leaving COMELEC bound to suppliers and responsible for delivery, warranty, and warehousing. He also said postponement was a policy and political-question issue, while elections should remain periodic, regular, and definite. The Senior Deputy Speaker connected the issue to proposed term fixing and asked whether fiscal autonomy could produce savings if contracts were not yet awarded. COMELEC did not provide a clear savings estimate or definitive treatment of all pending contracts, and the hearing was moved for termination.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much COMELEC had already spent, earmarked, or obligated for the barangay and SK elections; what procurement contracts and deliveries would remain binding if the elections were postponed or canceled; and whether fiscal autonomy could permit savings or budget reallocation. It also examined how term fixing would affect COMELEC’s preparations and liabilities.

COMELEC said it had to comply with the law and continue preparations while the elections remained scheduled, and that notices to proceed could create perfected sales or contracts that remained binding even if the election was postponed. It supported periodic, regular, and definite elections, recognized Congress’s sole authority to fix terms, and said any budget treatment after postponement or cancellation would be subject to committee, DBM, auditing, and other regulatory requirements.

Outcome COMELEC explained that obligations and perfected contracts could continue even if the election were postponed or canceled, but it did not quantify recoverable savings or resolve how each pending contract would be treated. The hearing was moved for termination, while any budget adjustment remained subject to further action by the committees, DBM, and applicable auditing rules.

Social-media, artificial-intelligence, and political-ad regulation

Rep. Sarah Elago asked COMELEC about guidelines for social-media, artificial-intelligence, and Internet technology use in fair, nondiscriminatory campaigning. A COMELEC official said the agency would strengthen measures to protect individual rights and regarded the 2028 election as crucial, with his term ending by 2029. He cautioned that regulation could intrude on freedom of expression and speech and said COMELEC could not punish conduct or define crimes without legal authority. He supported policy addressing foreign intervention and interference but questioned how platforms could be sanctioned. Elago then raised social-media accountability, cited a July 2026 investigative report on rebranded Facebook pages and political ads, and asked about a dedicated task force. COMELEC referred to same-day takedown requests, but the record did not resolve the task-force proposal or the agency's broader enforcement authority.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how COMELEC would regulate social-media political advertising, artificial-intelligence-enabled campaigning, discrimination, and possible foreign intervention while respecting freedom of expression and the limits of its legal authority. It also asked whether COMELEC had a dedicated mechanism to hold platforms and political actors accountable.

COMELEC said it supported strengthening and fully implementing measures to protect individual rights and address social-media and artificial-intelligence risks, especially foreign intervention and interference. It also maintained that its ability to punish or define violations was limited by the absence of a specific law and by constitutional protections for freedom of expression and speech.

Outcome The exchange established COMELEC's support for stronger social-media and artificial-intelligence regulation, but no final agreement or specific dedicated task force was recorded. The scope of COMELEC's enforcement authority, including sanctions against platforms and foreign actors, remained dependent on existing law or possible legislative action.

It also presented staffing figures for unfilled positions and other personnel categories, although the transcript did not clearly identify every category or reconcile the figures.

Outcome COMELEC provided vacancy and personnel figures and committed to filling half of the 800 vacant positions before the end of the year. The transcript did not establish whether the cited figures were reconciled or whether the staffing concern was fully resolved.

Agency unavailable · 2026-09-01 · unresolved

BARMM barangay-election preparation and polling-place security

Rep. Eli San Fernando asked COMELEC to explain the cancellation of a candidate’s candidacy and whether the decision affected the Bangsamoro peace process. COMELEC Chairperson George Irwin M. Garcia said the basis was failure to establish domicile, while the candidate’s name would remain pending the September 14 decision and possible Supreme Court relief. Vice Chair Zia Alonto Adiong then asked for an update on the BARMM barangay election and whether an ambush involving the interim chief minister was politically motivated or likely to threaten the polls. Garcia cited 3,393,000, 5,212, and an unclear reference to “eighteen sixteen” polling places or voting centers, and later said 5,212 machines would undergo final testing and sealing. He also mentioned voter education, September 11 command conferences, proclamation and results transmission, and expressed hope that there would be no failure of election. The security-motive question remained unanswered in the transcript.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how COMELEC was addressing the BARMM barangay election, including the legal and peace-process context of a candidate’s cancellation, election preparations, equipment and polling-place requirements, and security risks. It also asked whether a recent ambush was politically motivated and what measures would support an orderly and peaceful election.

COMELEC said the candidate’s cancellation was based on residency or domicile requirements under the Local Government Code, the Bangsamoro electoral code and Supreme Court jurisprudence, while preserving the candidate’s name pending possible Supreme Court relief. On the election itself, COMELEC presented preparations involving polling centers, machines, voter education, command conferences and results transmission, and expressed hope that the BARMM election would proceed without failure of election.

Outcome The candidacy question was considered answered to San Fernando’s satisfaction, with COMELEC explaining the domicile basis and preserving a path for Supreme Court intervention. The broader security question was not directly resolved: Garcia described operational preparations and expressed hope for a successful election, but the transcript does not show a clear answer on the ambush motive or a specific security undertaking.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

FY 2027 DA budget reduction and available fiscal space

The chair and Undersecretary Nora Olivares presented substantial reductions in the agriculture-sector and DA budgets, including a reported agriculture-sector decrease of about 35.3 billion and a DA decrease of about 17.2 billion, or 8%. The presentation also showed the farm-to-market road allocation falling from 33 billion in 2025 to 16 billion in 2027. A minority representative and the chair questioned whether fiscal space constrained priority programs and whether irrigation projects were being selected transparently. DA and NIA officials cited fiscal ceilings, economic viability, project readiness, statutory requirements, geographic disadvantage, drought, and irrigation-development levels as selection criteria. The chair raised 46,000,000 in fiscal space and concerns about anomalous infrastructure insertions, while NIA described technical validation, costing, procurement, audit, engineering, and reporting controls. The agency committed to submit documentation on irrigation projects under Agrarian Reform Fund guidelines, leaving broader restoration and transparency questions open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the FY 2027 DA and agriculture-sector budgets were reduced, how much fiscal space remained for restoration or priority programs, and how DA and NIA would prioritize projects within that constraint. It also sought the basis for NIA irrigation-project selection and documentation to guard against irregular infrastructure insertions.

The DA and NIA attributed the proposed reductions to limited fiscal space and budget ceilings, while maintaining that priority programs and projects would be selected through economic, technical, readiness, statutory, geographic, climate, and government-priority criteria. The agencies defended project controls based on validation, costing, procurement and audit rules, engineering requirements, monitoring, and congressional reporting, and agreed to submit material concerning irrigation projects under Agrarian Reform Fund guidelines.

Outcome The DA and NIA explained that fiscal-space limits drove the proposed reductions and described their project-prioritization and control procedures. The issue remained open for congressional review, with the agency committed to submit irrigation-project documentation under Agrarian Reform Fund guidelines.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Farm-to-market-road funding, unit costs, releases, and transparency

Members questioned the proposed 16,000,000,000 FY 2027 FMR budget against an estimated 55,000-kilometer network and a reduction from 33,000,000,000 in 2026. DA said project selection considered farmers, production, poverty, connectivity, road condition, climate, traffic, and new production areas, and identified about 60 billion annually as a bare-minimum ideal that could build about 4,000 kilometers. The minority also challenged unit costs ranging from 9,400,000 to 15,900,000 per kilometer, large Benguet projects, and incomplete or questionable project coordinates. DA attributed the higher 15,000,000 cost to fuel and construction-price increases and promised to check the coordinates and present reports. Members further asked about releases, with the transcript citing 10,700,000,000 as the corrected 2025 release and 5.7 as a current release figure whose meaning was unclear. DA's infrastructure official requested an additional 30,000,000,000 for 2,000 kilometers, and Rufus Rodriguez endorsed tripling the allocation, but no final funding decision was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 farm-to-market-road allocation was sufficient, how projects and unit costs were selected, and whether DA could implement the program transparently and within available capacity. Members also asked about releases, road standards, project coordinates, regional allocations, and the effect of budget restrictions on implementation.

DA said FMR priorities were selected using beneficiary, poverty, production, connectivity, road-condition, climate, traffic, and new-production-area criteria. The department maintained that 16,000,000,000 was insufficient against the network gap, identified about 60,000,000,000 annually as a bare-minimum ideal, and supported additional funding while retaining flexibility to adjust standards and routes based on terrain, production needs, and implementation capacity.

Outcome The agency answered the committee's general questions on prioritization, unit costs, releases, and implementation constraints, but concerns over the FY 2027 reduction, Benguet concentration, coordinates, and DA-DPWH standards remained open. DA undertook to provide or present supporting reports, while NIA agreed to submit a written proposal on implementation flexibility; the request to increase or triple FMR funding was not shown as a final appropriation.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

NIA irrigation budget, project prioritization, and district allocations

The chair and NIA administrator presented a FY 2027 irrigation proposal of about 233.85 billion, against an NEP amount of about 47.43 billion, and NIA sought House support for an increase. NIA said the reduced fiscal space required priority for ongoing, validated, high-impact, and implementation-ready projects, while members questioned district allocations, Region 8 funding, Bukidnon support, and the adequacy of maintenance and development funding. The agency described prioritization criteria that included irrigable potential, fiscal and economic viability, project readiness, statutory requirements, geographic disadvantage, and drought exposure. Members Allan Ty and Robert Nazal Jr. pressed NIA on whether program-based appropriations or rigid itemized listings better protected accountability and implementation; NIA preferred program-based appropriations supported by separately submitted project lists. NIA committed to submit allocation and project documents, modification lists, and its request to restore program-based budgeting. The requested budget increase and disputed district allocations remained open for subsequent committee action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether NIA's FY 2027 funding was sufficient to expand, rehabilitate, restore, and climate-proof irrigation systems, and how the agency prioritized projects and district allocations under fiscal constraints. Members also asked whether NIA should retain program-based appropriations or return to rigid, itemized project listings, and what documents and safeguards would preserve congressional oversight.

NIA maintained that the FY 2027 allocation was constrained by fiscal space and therefore had to prioritize tier-one, ongoing, validated, high-impact, and implementation-ready projects. It supported restoring program-based appropriations, with detailed project lists submitted separately for DBM validation, congressional oversight, transparency, and reporting, while seeking greater operational flexibility to respond to changed field conditions.

Outcome The agency's funding request and prioritization framework were presented, but the proposed increase and several district and regional allocation complaints were not finally resolved. NIA committed or was asked to submit project lists, allocation breakdowns, modification requests, and a proposal for program-based flexibility, leaving the budget level and specific allocations for further committee consideration.

Rice production support and fertilizer assistance

Members raised agricultural damage, rice production support, fertilizer procurement, irrigation, mechanization, and high-value-crops funding. The DA cited National Rice Program support of about 26.4 billion, projected 2026 rice production of about 19 million tons, and possible imports of up to 5 million tons because of El Niño. Officials also sought higher funding for farm-to-market roads, post-harvest facilities, and high-value crops, while the committee manifested support for tripling the road request and confirmed a 20% Mindanao share. The DA committed to provide equipment and seed-program details, review the seed proposal for funding, and complete geofencing by year-end.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY 2027 budget would adequately support rice production, fertilizer access, irrigation, mechanization, post-harvest capacity, and high-value crops. Members also pressed the DA on projected rice imports and the measures intended to reduce import dependence.

The DA said rice supply through 2026 was expected to be secure but that El Niño could lower production and require precautionary imports of up to 5,000,000 tons. It supported expanded irrigation, mechanization, seed development, QR-code fertilizer vouchers, post-harvest investment, high-value-crops funding, and geofencing, while agency officials requested additional funding and several officials undertook to provide details or review proposals.

Outcome The DA answered the committee's principal questions on rice targets, projected imports, fertilizer vouchers, and planned production measures, but several funding requests remained proposals rather than final appropriations. The agency committed to submit or review supporting details, including the seed-system breakdown and mechanization concerns, and to pursue geofencing.

Agricultural damage, calamity assistance, and farmer indemnification

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the scale of agricultural damage and the funding available for immediate disaster assistance, replanting, and farmer indemnification in 2027. It also examined whether unresolved hog-raiser claims required supplemental funding and what measures would support affected agricultural sectors.

The agency said disaster assistance would be divided among DSWD, DOLE, and DA, with the DA using its quick response fund for replanting and pursuing indemnification and production-support programs. It reported that hog-raiser indemnification of 391,000,000 was awaiting DBM approval and said it was considering feed support or a supplemental 2027 budget as alternatives or additional funding.

Outcome The agency answered the broad design of disaster assistance and identified a 2027 package of about 10,000,000,000, but the hog-raiser indemnification request remained dependent on DBM approval and possible supplemental funding. Agricultural-land impacts, the detailed production plan, and several garbled production figures were not fully resolved and were referred for submissions or later consultation.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Climate resilience, flood mitigation, and post-harvest loss reduction

Vice Chair Anna York and other members framed flooding, climate risk, food security, and post-harvest losses as central budget concerns. The DA said climate shocks had caused around 114 billion in agricultural damage and losses between 2024 and 2026, while irrigation coverage remained incomplete and post-harvest infrastructure and cold storage had significant gaps. Officials cited 6.7 billion for El Niño-related fuel and transport subsidies, about 10 billion for the 2027 assistance package, and an additional 10 billion being considered for climate-resilient DA facilities. NIA explained that irrigation projects were prioritized using weighted technical, economic, fiscal, regulatory, geographic, and drought-related criteria. Members also sought action on flood mitigation, sedimentation, dam capacity, the Ifugao rice terraces, and rubber-gate replacement. The agencies committed to submit documents and complete geofencing by year-end, but several project-specific issues remained unresolved or unclear.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DA and NIA would use the FY 2027 budget to protect agriculture from flooding, climate shocks, irrigation shortfalls, and post-harvest losses. Members also asked whether the agencies had sufficient fiscal space, how irrigation and flood-control projects were prioritized, and what measures would be taken to preserve vulnerable production areas and facilities.

The DA and NIA said climate resilience required expanded irrigation, resilient facilities, improved storage and processing, post-harvest machinery, cold-chain infrastructure, flood and sedimentation controls, and targeted assistance after calamities. The agencies maintained that projects were prioritized through technical, economic, regulatory, geographic, drought-related, and fiscal-space criteria, but several specific project-status and rubber-gate questions remained unclear.

Outcome The agencies presented climate resilience, irrigation expansion, post-harvest infrastructure, cold storage, disaster assistance, and sedimentation control as budget priorities. The DA committed to submit geofencing-related materials and complete the program by year-end, while NIA committed to submit irrigation-project information; the flood-mitigation status, expropriation concern, heritage-site prioritization, and rubber-gate replacement schedule were not clearly resolved.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Animal-industry competitiveness, ASF, vaccines, and pork imports

Allan Ty asked how the DA would use the animal competitiveness allocation and whether it would comply with RA 12308 and use livestock tariff collections as the revenue source. The DA said full use of 20,000,000,000 would effectively begin in 2028, while a 2027 framework would support herd buildup, repopulation, dairy, and related programs; it undertook to submit an amendment. DA officials cited current livestock tariff collections of about 22 billion annually, including 11,100,000,000 certified collections, and said a tariff classification change could yield 4,000,000,000, peso in additional revenue. Members also sought anti-rabies data, an animal-industry intervention breakdown, and responses to ASF and low hog prices. Secretary Laurel attributed farm-gate pressure to ASF, cited declining pork imports in some categories, opposed continuous importation subject to WTO constraints, and supported ASF vaccine deployment and livestock repopulation. Nicanor Briones requested vaccine funding, border biosecurity facilities, and reference-value import valuation, with the DA undertaking to coordinate with DBM and implement the valuation request.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DA would use the animal competitiveness allocation, finance animal-health and production interventions, address ASF and low hog prices, and manage pork imports and biosecurity. Members also asked whether the DA would provide vaccines, strengthen border inspection, and revise import valuation and tariff practices.

The DA said the ANCEP allocation would support herd buildup, repopulation, dairy, vaccine manufacturing, and related animal-industry interventions, but that full implementation would effectively begin in 2028 because of organizational and administrative requirements. It opposed continuous pork importation, cited WTO constraints, supported ASF and AI vaccine capacity, and undertook to work with DBM and the Tariff Commission on funding, tariffs, classifications, biosecurity, and import valuation.

Outcome The DA answered the principal questions but left several matters dependent on amendments, DBM coordination, Tariff Commission work, and requested data submissions. Support for hog raisers and vaccine funding was expressed, but the implementation details and final funding decisions remained open.

Sugarcane RSSI response, SRA utilization, and biological control

Rep. Raymond Mendoza asked the DA to disclose the RSSI expenditure breakdown and cited 25,000,000 in RSSI spending plus 10,000,000 for application and chemical usage; the Secretary later corrected the next-year pest-intervention figure from 250,000,000 to 300,000,000. Minority member Siberi questioned why the SRA had utilized only about 1,000,000,000 from a 2,000,000,000 budget and was told that procurement rules had delayed utilization and cut CEDA implementation by 50%. The SRA reported industry assistance of 420 something million and almost 100,000,000 in releases, but could not immediately state Bukidnon's share and promised to provide it. The DA Region 10 director described capacity growth from five hectares per day to 30 hectares per day, with a target of 100 hectares per day, and identified a proposed 150,000,000 laboratory quick response plan. Siberi supported increasing both DA and SRA funding, while the SRA committed to address procurement delays and the DA committed to submit requested information.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much had been appropriated and utilized for sugar-sector interventions, including the response to red striped soft scale insect (RSSI), and whether the DA and SRA had sufficient laboratory, biological-control, and procurement capacity. The DA and SRA attributed low utilization primarily to procurement and new procedural requirements, while saying they were working to make up delays. The DA said RSSI response capacity was being expanded through biological control, laboratory improvements, private-sector participation, and a proposed quick response allocation of 150,000,000; the SRA said it planned to reallocate funds to RSSI response.

Outcome The agencies provided figures and described planned RSSI capacity increases, but the DA Region 10 laboratory request and the proposed higher SRA budget were not finally approved during the exchange. The SRA committed to provide the Bukidnon allocation information and make up procurement delays, while the DA committed to provide the RSSI expenditure breakdown.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Mindanao and regional equity in DA and NIA allocations

Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed the DA to raise Mindanao's share to 20%, citing Mindanao's contribution to food production, while DA officials sought additional FMR, post-harvest, fertilizer, and high-value-crops funding. The FMR infrastructure request included about 30 billion for an additional 2,000 kilometers, while post-harvest funding was cited at about 6.5 billion, fertilizer at about 8.73 billion, and the requested high-value-crops increase at about 8 billion over a current 1.7 billion budget. Rep. Reynolds Michael Tan questioned unreleased FMR funds, road standards, and declining Region 8 NIA allocations, and requested province- and project-level breakdowns. Rep. Nelson Legacion challenged FMR reductions and sought proportionate irrigation funding and hatchery support; the DA said its regional director would act on the hatchery concerns. A minority member requested a regional seed-system breakdown, and Secretary Laurel said the DA would review it and commit to funding it. Minority member Soberi linked Bukidnon's output of about 36.09 billion to the need for NIA support, but the apparent district allocation discrepancy remained unresolved while NIA undertook to update the figures.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DA and NIA allocations for Mindanao, regions, provinces, and congressional districts were proportionate to agricultural output, irrigable land, validated projects, and implementation needs. Members also asked whether FMR, irrigation, post-harvest, fertilizer, high-value-crops, seed-system, and hatchery funding should be increased or reallocated.

The DA and NIA said allocations were constrained by available funds, cash flow, priority Tier 1 and ongoing projects, and restrictive special provisions. DA officials nevertheless supported increased or integrated funding for FMRs, post-harvest facilities, fertilizer, high-value crops, and seed-system interventions, while NIA indicated that greater budget flexibility and project-level review were needed.

Outcome The hearing produced support for higher and more flexible regional and program funding, but did not settle the conflicting FMR, Region 8, district irrigation, or Bukidnon figures. The agency undertook to provide or update certain project-level information and to pursue hatchery and seed-system follow-up.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Land-use conversion, geofencing, and agricultural-land protection

Members raised concerns about the PacSilica development, industrial projects, marshland conversion, and solar installations on irrigable or rice land. The DA cited about 1,600 directly affected farmers in the Clark area but said the full agricultural impact had not yet been established. The DA supported geofencing of key crop lands, with 3 million hectares of rice land identified as needed and an 8% slope threshold discussed for land-use decisions. The secretary committed to complete geofencing by the end of this year and to undertake studies on industrial impacts and marshlands, with possible marshland implementation in mid-2027 subject to World Bank support. The DA also said solar-powered pumps could involve 100 megawatts, potential income of 600,000,000, and a proposed rate of 4 pesos per kilowatt hour, but said the agricultural effects of solar use on flat rice land still required research. A minority member additionally requested a breakdown of the 34,000,000 seed system program budget, which the secretary agreed to review.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DA would protect agricultural and irrigable land from conversion, industrial development, and solar projects, including through geofencing and impact studies. Members also asked what studies, implementation timelines, and program-level interventions would be provided for 2027.

The DA supported geofencing to reserve prime agricultural and irrigable areas for food production, using crop, slope, soil, water, and moisture-retention characteristics. It acknowledged that studies on industrial developments, marshlands, and solar use on rice land were incomplete, while undertaking to complete or advance several studies and to finish geofencing by the end of this year.

Outcome The DA undertook to submit geofencing materials, complete geofencing by the end of this year, and produce or advance studies on industrial impacts, marshlands, and solar use on agricultural land. The compatibility of solar projects with flat rice land and the full PacSilica agricultural impact remained unresolved, while implementation of the marshland study was contingent on funding and possible World Bank support.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

National irrigation systems, maintenance, and infrastructure rehabilitation

DA Undersecretary Asis Perez reported that about 2.2 million hectares of an estimated 3.13 million irrigable hectares had been served, while the DA had added about 21,400 hectares and restored about 3,600 hectares through small-scale irrigation and canal works. Representative Juju Cesar Bergara sought action on an irrigation siphon, for which an agency official cited a request for 45,000,000 and a 194.5-meter length. Representative Marlo Bancoro pressed for multi-year irrigation and solar-irrigation implementation; the agency cited a 2027 proposal of about 1.12 billion but only 29,000,000 for the relevant item because of fiscal limits. Members also urged marshland studies, preservation of the Ifugao rice terraces through irrigation, and investigation of stalled solar projects. NIA reported a dam capacity of 54,000,000 cubic meters and discussed rubber-gate lifespans ranging from 15 to 45 years, but the replacement schedule was unclear. Representative Romeo Momo argued that the 5,000,000 NIA maintenance allocation for his district was inadequate, and NIA committed to provide a list of budget modifications or savings.

Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish whether irrigation systems, canals, dams, siphons, gates, and solar-irrigation facilities were adequately funded and maintained for 2027. Members also sought to determine which rehabilitation and expansion projects would be prioritized, and whether the agencies would provide studies, revised allocations, or implementation timelines.

The agencies said irrigation expansion, canal rehabilitation, dam and gate maintenance, and solar-irrigation projects were necessary but constrained by limited fiscal space. NIA stated that ongoing projects were prioritized and indicated that it would provide additional allocation information, while DA officials committed to coordination, studies, and follow-up discussions on delayed or proposed projects.

Outcome The hearing established that irrigation maintenance and expansion needs exceeded available allocations, particularly for siphon repair, solar irrigation, dam and gate maintenance, and NIA upkeep. The agencies gave several follow-up commitments, but the precise rubber-gate timetable, the adequacy and revision of district maintenance allocations, and several project funding decisions remained open.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

Local dairy production and school milk-feeding funding

Krisel Lagman asked the National Dairy Authority and the Philippine Carabao Center about local milk production, import dependence, and the capacity of the school milk-feeding program to create demand for local dairy. The agency reported production of about 29 million liters in 2024 and 43,000,043 liters in 2025, while national milk sufficiency rose from 1% to 2.2% and imported dairy remained at 98 percent. The discussion cited a 2026 target of 44,500,000 and an NDA allocation of about 3 billion for DepEd's program, excluding DSWD's program, while another agency figure was stated as 2,163,000,000,000. Lagman also warned that fermented and flavored milk supplied nine to 21 grams of sugar, or two point two to five teaspoons, per serving. The agency's explanation of its production strategy and future targets was incomplete, and an agency official committed to provide requested sugar and industry data to her office.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the level of local milk production, the extent of reliance on imported dairy, and whether the proposed milk-feeding funding and agricultural support would expand domestic dairy capacity. It also examined the health and sugar implications of serving fermented and flavored milk beverages in schools.

The agency said local milk production had increased but remained insufficient to supply the entire milk-feeding program, leaving the country dependent on imported dairy. It presented the milk-feeding program as a source of demand that could help increase production and referred to feed centers and related support, although its detailed production strategy and targets were not fully stated in the transcript.

Outcome The committee received production, sufficiency, import-dependence, target, and budget figures, but the agency did not provide a clear multi-year production plan or quantified future targets. The sugar-related data request was left for later submission.

Organic agriculture, agricultural credit, and high-value crops

Rep. Marlo Bancoro raised organic agriculture as a national concern and obtained a commitment from DA officials to meet and discuss the program's structure and regional direction. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez pressed the DA on Mindanao's share, citing its contribution to corn, pineapple, banana, and overall food requirements; the Secretary ultimately confirmed a 20% share after an initial unclear response. The high-value-crops official requested an additional 8,000,000,000 over the existing 1,700,000,000 budget, citing targets for annual industry growth, higher farmer income, diversification, value addition, and post-harvest-loss reduction. ACPC requested no additional funding, but asked that credit be integrated into DA programs; it reported annual funding of 2,750,000,000 and lending of 3,250,000,000. The organic-agriculture budget issue was not resolved because the agency said its main concern was program structure and should be handled under another agenda.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DA would support organic agriculture, integrate agricultural credit into commodity programs, and expand assistance for high-value crops. It also examined Mindanao's funding share and the additional resources requested for diversification, value addition, and post-harvest needs.

The DA described high-value crops as a priority requiring a substantial budget increase to address post-harvest losses, diversification, value addition, and climate-related challenges. ACPC did not seek additional funding but wanted credit integrated into commodity programs, while the National Organic Agriculture Program said its main issue was program structure rather than budget.

Outcome The committee received the DA's request for a major high-value-crops budget increase and ACPC's request for credit integration, while the organic-agriculture issue was deferred to a separate discussion on program structure. Mindanao's 20% share was stated as confirmed, but no final budget authorization for the requested increase was recorded.

DA and NIA · 2026-09-01 · committed

NIA appropriation structure and congressional oversight

Allan Ty questioned the NIA administrator on whether irrigation appropriations should be program-based or rigidly itemized, and whether program-based budgeting still subjected projects to DBM validation, procurement laws, auditing, engineering standards, and congressional oversight. NIA answered that it preferred program-based appropriations supported by a separately submitted and validated project list, because itemization in 2026 had limited its ability to respond to cost changes, rights-of-way problems, calamities, and implementation delays. Robert Nazal Jr. separately questioned the DA's farm-to-market road funding, noting a 55,050-kilometer deficit, a reduction from about 33 billion in 2026 to about 16 billion in 2027, and a stated 51.5% cut. Secretary Laurel said roughly 60 billion annually could build about 4,000 kilometers, with the minimum effort taking ten to twelve years, and said DA had allocated 30% of its 33 billion budget based on absorptive capacity and manpower. Nassal also asked whether special provision number eight had constrained NIA utilization and requested a written proposal before plenary. The issue landed with NIA's requested program-based structure still subject to committee consideration, supported by document submissions, while the answer on whether cuts would leave projects functionally incomplete remained unclear.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether NIA's irrigation appropriations should remain program-based or be itemized by project, and whether either structure preserved DBM validation, procurement and audit compliance, implementation flexibility, and congressional oversight. It also examined whether budget restrictions affected NIA's utilization and whether DA had the capacity to implement the proposed farm-to-market road funding.

NIA preferred restoring program-based appropriations under program expenditure classification, with a detailed, validated, and transparent project list submitted separately to DBM and Congress. It maintained that this structure preserved accountability and oversight while allowing adjustments for field conditions, delays, calamities, savings, and implementation readiness.

Outcome NIA's preferred program-based structure was placed on the record, with separate project-list documentation for validation and oversight. The committee requested the Speaker-submitted request and a written implementation proposal; the effect of project cuts on functional completion was not answered clearly.

OP · 2026-08-31 · committed

OP FY2027 budget and proposed budget reduction

The chair presented the Office of the President's proposed FY2027 allocation as 10,156,000,000, while Executive Secretary Ralph Recto stated a proposal of MXN 10,150,000,000. Recto said the proposal was about 0.14% of the proposed national budget and was 64% lower than the previous year's level because of reduced operational requirements and the completion of ASEAN Summit activities. He said the amount would support the Office of the President's 49 delivery units and core presidential operations. The minority and majority moved to extend institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminate the committee deliberations. A minority member objected and raised transparency, flood-control, and confidential and intelligence fund questions, including 550,000,000 in such funds. The motion passed with 37 votes in favor and five against, while the chair recorded that outstanding questions would be answered on or before plenary.

Questions and agency response

What was the Office of the President's proposed FY2027 allocation, and why was it reportedly lower than the previous year's level? The committee also sought to determine whether questions on flood control and confidential and intelligence funds would receive answers despite terminating the committee-level deliberations.

The Office of the President said its proposed FY2027 budget was sufficient to perform its constitutional and administrative functions. Executive Secretary Ralph Recto attributed the reduction to lower operational requirements and the completion of ASEAN Summit-related activities, and said the agency was ready to answer questions.

Outcome The committee granted institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminated the Office of the President's committee-level budget deliberations by a vote of 37-5. Questions on flood control and confidential and intelligence funds remained for answers on or before plenary.

Confidential and intelligence funds and spending transparency

Members objected to ending the Office of the President budget discussion without scrutiny of confidential and intelligence funds and related accountability issues. One member cited 550,000,000 in confidential and intelligence funds, while other members raised transparency, flood-control, and possible political-patronage concerns. The Office of the President did not give a substantive answer in these stretches, although Executive Secretary Ralph Recto stated that the office respected Congress's authority and was ready to answer questions. Rep. Edgar Erice supported the budget and said confidential funds were necessary, while Rep. Iris Marie Montes said her negative vote defended Congress's duty to scrutinize every peso of public funds. The chair carried the motion to terminate deliberations by a vote of 37 to five and committed the outstanding answers to the plenary stage.

Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish whether the Office of the President's confidential and intelligence funds, and related budgetary issues, would receive meaningful congressional scrutiny and transparent accountability before approval. It also sought to determine when the Office of the President would answer the questions deferred by the committee's grant of institutional and interbranch courtesy.

The Office of the President stated that it respected Congress's constitutional authority and was ready to answer questions. It did not provide a substantive answer in the cited stretches on the transparency, accountability, or use of confidential and intelligence funds; the chair recorded that responses would be provided on or before plenary.

Outcome The committee granted institutional and interbranch courtesy and terminated the Office of the President budget deliberations, but members' transparency and confidential-fund questions remained unanswered. The chair recorded the Office of the President's responses as due on or before plenary.

PCO · 2026-08-27 · committed

PCO and attached-agency budget reductions and restoration request

Secretary Dave M. Gomez presented a PCO and attached-agency FY 2027 proposal of about 2.62 billion, 6.6% below the 2026 level, while the net department allocation was about 2.48 billion. Robert Nazal Jr. questioned the reductions and the PIA increase, and Gomez attributed the PCO reduction primarily to the end of ASEAN-hosting requirements while saying the PIA increase would fund retrofitting of its 44-year-old building. Gomez said IBC 13 received no subsidy because it was being prepared for privatization, while IBC officials described arbitration and operating pressures. Representative Zia Alonto Adiong pressed whether PCO could meet rising digital and anti-disinformation demands with a reduced budget; Gomez said it could remain effective but would perform much better with additional resources, including the 128,000,000 pesos requested for Bagong Filipinas Studios. Adiong formally sought restoration of the original PCO and attached-agency requests, and Representative Brian Yamsuan supported increasing and restoring the budget. The committee left restoration for a later review and required PCO to submit its original request, identify the cuts, and justify restoration.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the PCO and most attached agencies received reduced FY 2027 allocations, whether the reductions would impair government communications and digital-information services, and whether the original budget requests should be restored. Members also asked what justified the Philippine Information Agency increase, how IBC 13's privatization affected its funding, and what resources were needed for Bagong Filipinas Studios.

PCO said the reduction was principally expected because the FY 2026 budget included funding associated with ASEAN hosting, but acknowledged that additional resources would allow it to perform much better. It sought restoration of items included in its original NEP submission, including funding for digital communications, Bagong Filipinas Studios, and support for attached agencies, and committed to document the cuts and provide justifications.

Outcome The committee did not finally restore or amend the budget during the hearing. The issue was referred for later budget-amendment review, with PCO committed to submit its original request, a list of cuts, and restoration justifications; members expressed support for pursuing additional funding.

IBC 13 zero budget, privatization, and transitional funding

Representatives Roberto Nazal Jr., Maria Victoria Copilar, Brian Yamsuan, and Antonino Roman III challenged the proposed zero allocation for IBC 13 and questioned the timing and consequences of privatization. The agency said the zero budget was tied to the planned sale, but warned that privatization might not be completed by the end of the year and requested restoration of funding for salaries, station upkeep, programming, and legal obligations. IBC 13 described government-information programming, Congress TV, multiple stations and programs, and employee and arbitration-related needs, including a request cited as 479,000,000 and an arbitration amount generally described as about 50,000,000. Copilar sought a transitional budget, while Secretary Gomez assured the committee that employee welfare would be protected and that Congress TV would move to PTV 4 if needed. DBM said IBC 13's ongoing privatization status explained the zero allocation, but acknowledged that it had not received documentation of the arbitration award. The committee indicated that the matter would be included in a new budget quotation, but the funding amount and final disposition remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why IBC 13 had a zero proposed allocation for FY 2027 despite its continuing operations and government-information programming, and whether transitional funding was needed pending privatization. It also sought clarity on the fate of IBC 13 programs, employees, operating obligations, and the arbitration award.

PCO said the zero allocation resulted from IBC 13's inclusion in the planned privatization program, not from a determination that its operations were unnecessary. PCO and IBC 13 asked for restoration or transitional funding because privatization might not be completed by the end of the year, while DBM said the ongoing privatization status explained the zero budget and said it had not received documentation for the arbitration award.

Outcome The committee did not resolve the amount or mechanism for transitional funding. PCO committed to pursuing privatization, protecting employee welfare, and moving Congress TV to PTV 4 if necessary, while the requested restoration and treatment of the arbitration obligation were left for further budget action and documentation.

DBM said IBC's zero FY 2027 budget resulted from ongoing privatization and that it had received no record or request for the award. Roman pressed whether a budget amendment was required, but DBM said Congress would decide. Secretary Dave asked that IBC 13's funding be restored, and the Chair indicated that a new submission or budget quotation should be made.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the amount and legal status of IBC 13's obligations to former employees, including the arbitration award, and whether FY 2027 funding or a budget amendment was needed. Members also sought to determine why IBC 13 had been given zero funding and how its compensation obligations would be met during the proposed privatization.

The agency and DBM said IBC 13's zero FY 2027 allocation resulted from its ongoing privatization, but acknowledged that legal and compensation obligations still had to be settled. Secretary Dave asked the committee to restore or fund IBC 13's proposed amount, while DBM said it had received no record or request for the arbitration award and that any FY 2027 amendment was for Congress to decide.

Outcome The committee did not resolve the conflicting figures of 58,000,000, 50,000,000, and 15,000,000 or determine whether a FY 2027 amendment would be made. The matter was left for a new submission or budget quotation, with the agency seeking restoration or funding.

PCO · 2026-08-27 · committed

PTV 4 budget, reach, equipment investment, and operating support

Representative Nazzal asked whether PTV 4's budget, reach, equipment, and staffing were adequate for its state-broadcasting mandate. The PTV 4 general manager said the station had about 136,000,000, also referring to 138,000,000, and requested 1,700,000,000; he said a competitive budget could require roughly five to seven billion. He reported current household reach of about 30%, projected reach of about 42% or more after equipment repairs, and reach above 50% with three additional towers. The general manager also said the current budget could not support a network and that international and regional state broadcasters spent billions in pesos. Members Lemanzeras and Yamsuan supported stronger government-media funding, while the PCO secretary said communications resources were inadequate and committed to pushing the request after a formal submission. The issue was not finally resolved in the hearing and was referred for subsequent committee and BARC discussion.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PTV 4's proposed funding, transmission reach, equipment, and staffing were sufficient for it to fulfill its state-broadcasting and developmental-communication mandate. Members also examined the broader adequacy of PCO and government communications funding and whether additional support should be requested.

PTV 4 and PCO said the current funding was inadequate for a competitive state broadcaster and insufficient to carry out the government's developmental-communication mandate. PTV 4 requested 1,700,000,000, stating that equipment repairs could increase household reach from around 30% to around 42% or more, while three additional towers could bring reach above 50%.

Outcome The need for additional PTV 4 and broader PCO communications funding received support from the participating members, but no final appropriation was established in the discussion. PTV 4 was to submit a formal request for later consideration by the BARC and the committees.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why PIA's budget increased, whether the increase would fund rehabilitation of its 44-year-old building, and why the separate request for temporary office rent was omitted. Members also sought support for capital outlay for PIA and attached-agency facilities, including a proposed Region 10 office in El Salvador City.

The PCO said PIA's increased budget was principally for capital outlay to retrofit its severely deteriorated 44-year-old building. Secretary Gomez confirmed that the 20,000,000 rent request had been omitted despite the need for temporary office space during construction, and PIA committed to pursuing the proposed El Salvador City infrastructure project if capital-outlay funding was provided.

Outcome The agency confirmed the need for both PIA building rehabilitation and temporary rent, while members indicated support for restoring the omitted rent appropriation and pursuing capital-outlay funding. PIA's proposed El Salvador City office received an agency commitment contingent on funding, but the transcript does not show a final appropriation, committee ruling, or resolution of the retrofit-versus-new-building question.

PCO · 2026-08-27 · committed

PCO digital information services and misinformation response

Secretary Gomez presented a proposed PCO budget of about 2.62 billion, a 6.6% reduction from the 2026 level, while describing expanded digital, media-literacy, and misinformation-response programs. Representative Adiong questioned whether the reduction would impair the PCO's ability to digitalize information services and provide accurate, timely information amid social-media misinformation. Gomez said the PCO could remain effective through organizational agility and streamlined operations, but acknowledged that it could be much better with additional resources. Adiong then asked about the unfunded continuation of Bagong Filipinas Studios, and Gomez identified a request of 128,000,000 for three to five additional studios. Adiong supported the studios as a means of modernizing state media and rebuilding public trust. Representative Yamsuan also supported increased resources and asked the PCO to submit a formal request for committee consideration; the proposed increase therefore remained subject to later action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed reduction in the PCO budget would impair digital information services, media and information literacy, and the government's response to misinformation and disinformation. It also examined whether funding for Bagong Filipinas Studios would continue and whether additional resources were needed.

The PCO maintained that it could remain effective despite the reduction by improving organizational agility, streamlining operations, and using available resources more efficiently. Secretary Gomez nevertheless acknowledged that the agency could perform much better with additional resources, and said the 128,000,000 Tier 2 request for additional Bagong Filipinas Studios was not included in the proposed budget.

Outcome The committee received the PCO's explanation that it could continue operating under the reduced budget but would deliver better results with additional resources. The 128,000,000 studios request and broader proposed increases were not resolved during the exchange and were left for formal submission and committee discussion.

PCO communications personnel and vacant critical positions

Nazzal and the PTV 4 general manager also discussed PTV 4’s limited budget, with the manager describing the allocation as 136,000,000 and elsewhere 138,000,000, against a request for 1,700,000,000 and an estimated competitive requirement of five to seven billion. The vacancy process was ongoing, while the funding request remained subject to later budget deliberations.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how PCO’s staffing complement and critical vacancies, particularly the Director for Communication Service position, affected its communications and government-media operations. Agency officials maintained that stronger staffing and significantly greater resources were needed for PTV 4 and broader government communications, especially content production and digital operations.

Outcome The vacancy issue was answered procedurally: some appointments were in process, while other positions remained subject to the PCO’s DBM-submitted optimization plan. The requested larger PTV 4 allocation was not resolved during the hearing, although the committee received an undertaking to submit a formal request and members manifested support for pursuing it.

The matter was left with a request for a formal submission and commitments to pursue the issue in the BARC and committee deliberations.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PTV 4, PCO, and other government communication outlets had sufficient resources to carry out developmental communication and compete across broadcast and social-media platforms. Members also sought the agencies' funding needs and any formal request that could support budget deliberations.

The PTV 4 general manager and PCO Secretary Dave Gomez said current funding was insufficient to sustain a national government communications network and developmental communication effort. They argued that the ecosystem required stronger support for PCO, PTV 4, IBC 13, production, personnel, and social-media work.

Outcome The members expressed support for increasing PCO funding and restoring 1,700,000,000 for PTV and IBC, but no budget adjustment was adopted during the excerpt. The agencies were asked to submit a formal request for later discussion in the BARC and committees.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the PCO and several attached agencies faced reductions in the FY 2027 proposed budget while the Philippine Information Agency received an increase. It also questioned the operating needs, subsidy dependence, and planned privatization of IBC 13.

PCO and IBC officials supported continued funding or restoration for operations and modernization while the government completed the required steps for IBC 13's privatization.

Outcome The PCO explained the PIA increase and the PCO proper reduction, but the broader question of reductions for attached agencies and the appropriate funding for IBC 13 remained open. Privatization was ongoing, with PCO undertaking further coordination with GCG, DBP, and other entities; the proposed restoration was not resolved in the excerpt.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

Local Government Support Fund rationale, allocation, and monitoring

Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula and Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DILG's authority, monitoring role, transparency, and treatment of unused LGSF balances. DILG said DBM released and validated the assistance while DILG monitored distribution, implementation, and reports, and Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to submit utilization reports covering 2025 and 2026. The agency defended the proposed LGSF of about 58 billion as supplemental funding because the national tax allotment was spread across many provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays. DILG described engineers, project evaluation officers, local monitoring committees, CSO and NGO participation, and the Subay Bayan portal as safeguards. A civil-society-backed line of questioning sought justification after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, evidence against duplication, open-data disclosure, participatory budgeting, and human-rights safeguards. DILG answered these questions in part, but the broader policy and accountability concerns remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why a separate Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) remained necessary after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling increased LGUs' national tax allotment, what programs and fiscal gaps it addressed, and how funds were allocated, validated, implemented, monitored, and disclosed. Members also asked whether DILG or DBM controlled distribution and whether community participation and human-rights safeguards were adequate.

DILG maintained that DBM controlled LGSF policy, validation, allocation, and release, while DILG monitored, evaluated, and reported on implementation. It defended LGSF as supplemental funding needed because the national tax allotment was divided among many LGUs and said safeguards included engineers, project monitoring officers, three-tier monitoring, local monitoring committees with CSO participation, reporting portals, and referral of confirmed wrongdoing.

Outcome DILG clarified that DBM controlled LGSF validation, policy, and release, while DILG monitored implementation and relied on COA and other monitoring mechanisms for accountability. The committee received commitments for utilization reports, but questions about the fund's discretionary structure, duplication with national tax allotments, unused prior-year balances, measurable outcomes, and independent safeguards were not fully resolved.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

Barangay Development Program and SBDP per-barangay allocations

Jose Teves Jr. pressed for a higher SBDP allocation, arguing that 5,000,000 per barangay was insufficient for classrooms, health centers, water, electrification, and other needs. DILG said it had requested 10,000,000 per barangay and would welcome a congressional increase to 7,000,000 or more. Members then sought delivery rates, audits, beneficiary verification, and third-party monitoring, while DILG reported delivery rates ranging from 29% to 100% across the cited years and said 700 monitoring personnel were deployed. Rep. Caroline Agyao obtained clarifications on EL CAC coverage and annual allocations, including 2,500,000 in 2025, 10,000,000 in 2026, and 5,000,000 proposed for 2027. DILG said municipalities implemented the projects, DILG monitored them, and coordination was intended to prevent duplication. A CSO representative questioned the rationale and accountability of the LGSF and SBDP, and DILG described three-tier monitoring, DBM vetting, grassroots consultations, and the SubayBayan portal. The hearing ended with document requests and commitments, while the adequacy of the 2027 allocation and the broader evidence supporting it remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the appropriate per-barangay allocation for the Barangay Development Program/SBDP, the basis for changes in the proposed budget, and whether projects were properly selected, implemented, audited, monitored, and protected against duplication. Members and CSOs also asked what role DILG played in the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), what safeguards existed, and what documents and performance data would be submitted.

DILG said the SBDP was a targeted program for barangays previously affected by communist armed groups, with projects selected through grassroots consultations and implemented by municipalities. It maintained that DILG's role was monitoring and evaluation, while DBM administered the LGSF and handled proposal vetting; DILG cited local, second-party, and third-party monitoring, the SubayBayan portal, and additional monitoring personnel as safeguards.

Outcome DILG acknowledged that the 2027 SBDP proposal provided only 5,000,000 per barangay despite DILG's request for 10,000,000, and members' calls for a higher amount were left to Congress. DILG committed to submit accomplishment, coverage, and third-party monitoring documents, but the requested independent outcome, audit, duplication, and open-data evidence was not fully supplied during the exchange.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

BFP fire-truck procurement, repair, stations, and emergency capacity

Members repeatedly questioned DILG and the BFP about fire-truck shortages, station gaps, procurement corruption, repair and replacement, and emergency-response capacity. The agency said it was pursuing a government-to-government procurement with South Korea for about 1,500 trucks, with a maintenance contract and a stated cost advantage over prior purchases and Japan. Officials said BFP fire-code collections were remitted to the national treasury, while DBM released only about 1 billion annually, leaving the BFP with limited access to funds despite collections and earmarks totaling several billion pesos. Members cited municipalities without stations or trucks and shortages in protective equipment, while the BFP requested search-and-rescue trucks, ambulances, Unified 911 operating funds, and additional recruitment. The committee noted or supported possible trust-fund and appropriations action, and Rodriguez manifested an intent to seek approval of the requested increases. The Korea procurement remained under negotiation, with technical specifications and a written status update requested, so the issue landed as a supported but not fully resolved commitment.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the BFP would finance, procure, maintain, and distribute fire trucks, rescue vehicles, ambulances, stations, and related equipment; how much it collected and actually received from fire-code fees; and whether the proposed government-to-government procurement with Korea would address national shortages. Members also asked about procurement safeguards, repair and replacement needs, station gaps, and emergency-response capacity.

DILG and the BFP said procurement reforms and government-to-government purchasing, particularly with South Korea, would reduce corruption and lower unit costs while expanding the number of trucks acquired. They maintained that BFP fire-code collections were remitted to the national treasury but that DBM released only a limited portion, and asked Congress to support fuller use of the trust fund for trucks, stations, ambulances, rescue equipment, maintenance, and recruitment.

Outcome The committee generally supported the proposed Korea government-to-government procurement and the BFP's requests for additional trucks, stations, ambulances, rescue equipment, operating funds, and manpower. However, fuller access to fire-code collections, final procurement terms, supplier selection, and the requested budget increases remained dependent on congressional action, DBM releases, and further agency submissions.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

PNP additional funding, mobility, staffing, and regional equipment

The chair presented the DILG's proposed budget of about 32.5 billion, including about 142.5 billion for the PNP, and linked public-safety funding to school security and law-enforcement capability. Mark Huanko supported the DILG budget but pressed for implementation of the Lingayen road project, recovery of disputed PNP property, and replacement of aging vehicles; the PNP committed to act, investigate, coordinate, and report back. The agency said 95% of the Mahindra vehicles acquired in 2010 and 2011 were beyond economic repair, and Huanko requested 231 vehicles for the district's 231 barangays. Mica Gonzales asked about recruitment into violence and permanent police presence near schools, and the agency said sensitive details could be discussed in executive session while school police presence was already policy. Rufus Rodriguez cited Region 10 mobility deliveries and supported additional PNP funding; the PNP chief confirmed an additional request of 2,025,000,000 after initially stating conflicting figures. A majority member also raised DILG field-office staffing shortages, and the agency said a government optimization plan was being prepared.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the DILG and PNP had sufficient funding, vehicles, personnel, and regional equipment to meet public-safety needs. Members also asked about the implementation of a Lingayen police-road project, recovery of disputed PNP property, school-area police deployment, and proposed staffing increases for DILG field offices.

The DILG and PNP supported additional operational capacity through vehicles, capital outlays, recruitment, school-area police presence, and field-office staffing. The PNP committed to pursuing the Lingayen road and property matters, accounting for vehicle needs, updating the member, augmenting police forces in the next recruitment or fiscal-year cycle, and seeking an additional request identified as 2,025,000,000.

Outcome The hearing produced agency commitments on the Lingayen road and property matters, vehicle accounting, police augmentation, school-area deployment, and a field-office optimization plan. The PNP additional request was identified as 2,025,000,000, but final congressional action on that request and the vehicle allocations remained subject to the budget process.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

School-violence prevention, active-shooter drills, and school police presence

The Chair and several members raised concerns about school violence, online recruitment into violence, firearms used by minors, and the need for faster police response. DILG and PNP officials said police were already present during school entry and dismissal and that barangay tanods would be allowed inside schools under a joint memorandum circular. Officials reported 50 school-related incidents involving minors, a 97% five-minute 911 response compliance rate, and a PNP operations increase of about 15 billion. The agencies proposed nationwide active-attack drills with DepEd, a youth ambassadors program, coordination with DICT and NTC on malicious online sites, and expanded Unified 911 vehicles. The Secretary also proposed stricter firearm-safekeeping inspections and penalties, while members questioned the emphasis on video games and stressed broader social and mental-health factors. The agencies committed to refine and submit drill guidelines, but the hearing left the definite schedule, dedicated budget line, and firearm-enforcement data unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what DILG, the PNP, DepEd, LGUs, and attached agencies were budgeting and implementing to prevent school violence, monitor online recruitment into violence, secure firearms, conduct active-attack drills, and ensure rapid police response. Members also asked whether police presence near schools could be made permanent or assigned to individual schools.

DILG and the PNP stated that school security required layered measures: police presence during student entry and dismissal, barangay tanod augmentation inside schools, coordination with DepEd, online-threat monitoring with DICT and NTC, active-attack drills, Unified 911 response, and stricter firearm-safekeeping rules. The PNP reported 97% compliance with a five-minute response target for 911 calls, but officials did not identify a dedicated school-drill budget line or provide all requested firearm-enforcement data.

Outcome The hearing established a package of planned or ongoing measures—school police presence, barangay tanod augmentation, DepEd coordination, active-attack drills, online-site coordination, firearm-safekeeping reforms, and expanded emergency response. The committee did not receive a separate school-drill budget line, a definite drill date, or the requested firearm-license enforcement counts, leaving implementation and funding details open.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

Firearms control, safekeeping, and police use of firearms

Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula, Rep. Rolando Valeriano, Rep. Edgar Erice, Renee Co, Rep. Robert Raymond Estrella, and Anna York Bondoc questioned the DILG and PNP about firearm safekeeping, loose firearms, mobilization protocols, and school safety. The agency said 800,000 uniformed personnel were covered by firearm-responsibility rules, but acknowledged that firearms in the Tacloban and Zamboanga incidents had not been properly secured. Officials proposed advance-notice PNP inspections of lawful firearm owners' homes, stronger penalties for irresponsible safekeeping, and repeal of the Robin Padilla law; they repeatedly cited 98% as the share of firearm violence or firearm-related cases involving loose or unlicensed firearms. The PNP said it had only 2,000 body cameras for 320,000 personnel and was procuring another 10 or 20,000, while acknowledging that firearms carried during mobilizations may have reflected a mistake. For school security, officials cited barangay tanods, police coordination, active-attack drills, online-platform coordination, and community participation, but said assigning police to each of about 56,000 schools was impractical. The committee requested reports on the mobilizations, the Zamboanga mistaken-identity case, and the DILG's firearm-regulation recommendations; data on license suspensions and related cases was not supplied.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DILG and PNP were preventing firearms from being misused, particularly firearms issued to uniformed personnel or legally owned by civilians. Members also asked about controls during police mobilizations, penalties for irresponsible safekeeping, school security, and whether additional enforcement, inspection, identification, and accountability measures were needed.

The DILG and PNP said firearm owners and custodians were responsible for secure safekeeping, but acknowledged that the two school-shooting incidents reflected failures in that responsibility. They supported revising the IRR to permit advance-notice inspections of firearm storage, imposing stronger penalties for irresponsible or illegal possession, and repealing the Robin Padilla law to make loose-firearm offenses non-bailable. They also maintained that school security required coordinated police, barangay, education, and community measures rather than a dedicated police officer for every school.

Outcome The agency's proposals for IRR amendments, home inspections, stronger penalties, and repeal of the Robin Padilla law were presented but were not enacted during the hearing. The committee requested investigative and policy documents, while the requested statistics on firearm-related license suspensions and cases remained unanswered.
