DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

PCW budget cut and gender-based violence services

Rep. Sarah Elago questioned the PCW and ECCD Council budget reductions, regionalization plans, gender-and-development compliance, and the adequacy of local gender-based violence services. The PCW said the cut would mainly affect expansion to Mindanao, sought another 30,000,000 for that purpose, and reported 488 agencies in its gender mainstream system with about 77.46% compliance. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said DBM had cut the submitted budget and that restoration could make it more effective, while the ECCD Council reported a gap affecting 3,743 centers. DILG and PNP officials said local governments should address many frontline services within their budgets and committed to corrective or enforcement action on personnel-related violence and insensitive materials. The NCMF later reported inadequate Hajj medical funding, citing 95 pesos per pilgrim from a spoken allocation of 600 16,000 pesos, and requested support for three priority programs. The committee directed the NCMF to submit its request, and members expressed support, but the funding issues were not finally resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the reduced PCW and ECCD Council allocations would affect regionalization, gender-and-development compliance, child development centers, and frontline services for survivors of gender-based violence. It also examined whether NCMF's reduced medical allocation for Hajj and its priority programs required additional funding.

The PCW said the proposed cut would chiefly constrain regionalization, particularly expansion to Mindanao, while it could live with the rest of the allocation. The DILG and PNP said local governments should fund local protection and training needs, while the PNP stated that it took personnel-related violence seriously and would file appropriate charges. The NCMF said its Hajj medical allocation was inadequate and requested additional funding for medical needs and three priority programs.

Outcome The PCW and ECCD Council funding gaps were identified, with possible PCW restoration and a proposed child development center line item, but no restoration was approved during the exchange. The NCMF was directed to submit its written funding request and received an expression of committee support; the requested amounts remained subject to subsequent budget action.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

ECCD Council budget cut and child development centers

A committee member raised the scale of the child development center and day-care network and asked how the early childhood system would be supported. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said day-care centers were primarily funded through barangays and other LGUs, with additional infrastructure potentially involving DPWH and the provinces, because 96% of the DILG budget covered operating expenses or salaries. He cited an allocation of about 124 million for early-childhood feeding and capacity building. Representative Sarah Elago then questioned the 2027 ECCD Council figure of 232,000,000 pesos and asked how the cut would affect the council's mandate. The secretary said DBM had reduced DILG's submitted budget and that restoration could be requested, while the ECCD Council warned that the cut would limit center rehabilitation and the procurement of learning materials, furniture, fixtures, and other contents. Elago said she would propose a special line item for child development centers, but no restoration or final funding action was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the ECCD Council's reduced 2027 allocation would affect its mandate, regional services, and child development center infrastructure. It also examined which government level or agency was responsible for funding additional day-care centers and their contents.

DILG said additional day-care center funding was principally a barangay, provincial, DPWH, and other LGU responsibility because most of the DILG budget covered operating expenses and salaries. Secretary Remulla said DILG's submitted budget had been reduced by DBM and could be restored, while the ECCD Council said the cut would significantly limit rehabilitation and the provision of learning materials, furniture, fixtures, and other center contents.

Outcome The committee received the agency's explanation that the cut resulted from DBM's reduction of the submitted budget and that the cut would affect center rehabilitation and contents. Restoration was raised but not finalized, while a special child development center line item was proposed for later consideration.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

BFP recruitment integrity, manpower, and personnel needs

Perci Cendaña raised alleged BFP recruitment slot-selling and sought clarification on the agency's controls. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said prior slot prices ranged from 200,000 to 800,000 per slot and referred the matter to the BFP chief, who described the online e-hiring system and confirmed a recent Region Three entrapment operation involving recruitment anomalies. The BFP said future recruitment would be fair, transparent, and based on merit and fitness. The chief reported that DBM provided about 2,000 recruits annually against a stated ideal manpower requirement of about 78,000; the transcript also gave an authorized strength of 43, with the unit unclear. He said the current rate would require twenty years and sought an additional 2,000 recruits per year. The Chair welcomed the agency action, but no approval of the additional recruitment request was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether BFP recruitment slots had been sold, whether the agency had detected and acted on recruitment-related corruption, and what controls were in place to prevent a recurrence. It also examined whether BFP's manpower level was adequate and whether additional annual recruitment authority was needed.

The BFP said it had detected and acted on a recruitment anomaly through an entrapment operation involving personnel in Region Three, and that e-hiring, online applications, system-generated examinations, and immediate results would reduce opportunities for slot-selling. It committed to fair, transparent, merit- and fitness-based recruitment, while stating that the agency needed more than the 2,000 recruits currently provided annually to address its manpower shortfall.

Outcome The BFP confirmed that a recruitment anomaly had been exposed and acted on, and the Chair accepted the explanation that the matter had reached the bureau. The broader request for additional annual recruitment remained an agency appeal rather than a recorded committee approval.

A committee member questioned the NYC's proposed budget reduction of about 19,000,000 and the omission of requests for Muslim and creative youth summits and ICT modernization. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula and Jambaranda pressed the NYC on programs, data, and curriculum for out-of-school youth; the NYC cited a 2,500,000 youth entrepreneurship allocation, support for a Magna Carta, and interagency coordination, but said available data was incomplete. Jambaronda also sought broader SK training and compliance, leading DILG to commit to revisiting modules and issuing further guidance. Members additionally requested active-shooter-drill guidelines and information on political-dynasty recommendations, with agencies undertaking to submit or obtain the requested materials. The budget increase itself remained unapproved in the transcript.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the National Youth Commission's reduced 2027 budget could support its expanding youth mandate, including Muslim and creative youth summits, ICT modernization, youth mental-health and entrepreneurship programs, SK training, and services for out-of-school youth. Members also sought specific agency commitments, data, and interagency coordination on youth safety and political-dynasty concerns.

The NYC said its youth mandate was primarily advocacy, policy, coordination, and capacity building, while acknowledging that its budget and staffing constrained implementation and absorptive capacity. It supported additional funding and personnel services, particularly for ICT modernization, youth entrepreneurship, SK training, research, and expanded youth programs, but said it lacked police power and certain data, which required coordination with DILG, DepEd, COMELEC, and other agencies.

Outcome The NYC budget issue was not finally resolved: the committee chair expressed support for restoration or increases, while the NYC acknowledged both unmet program requests and staffing-related absorptive-capacity limits. The committee obtained commitments for additional documents, revised SK guidance, active-shooter-drill guidelines, and follow-up with COMELEC.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

SK training, compliance, elections, and local youth governance

Rep. Jambaranda raised concerns about SK training, annual development plans, fiscal compliance, regular federation meetings, and the possible postponement of SK elections. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla committed to an immediate memorandum circular on annual development plans and said noncompliant local governments could be excluded from the SGLG; he also took note of the request to regulate barangay travel. Rep. Bambi Mano asked whether DILG could hear and correct an appeal from an SK chair's dismissal, and the DILG undersecretary answered that it could under section 67 of the Local Government Code and the SK-related laws, subject to a written follow-up. The NYC described continuing SK training, auditing guidance, trainer-of-trainers arrangements, and an MOU with local government accountants, while DILG committed to revisit the one-day orientation modules. The NYC reported a training estimate of roughly 70 plus million, with the transcript also recording 72,000,000,000, and said a survey of 120 federation presidents was examining support for an extension or special elections. The agencies agreed to issue further guidance and submit information, but election timing, removal data, and out-of-school youth data remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether SK and barangay officials were receiving adequate training, complying with planning and fiscal requirements, and subject to effective oversight and removal procedures. It also sought clarification on DILG's appellate authority over SK dismissals, the timing of SK elections or special elections, and the reliability of out-of-school youth data.

DILG maintained that it had appellate authority to resolve an appeal from an SK chair's dismissal under section 67 of the Local Government Code and that dismissal propriety could also be considered under Republic Act 10742 and the SK Reform Law of 2015. The NYC and DILG supported expanded training, auditing guidance, and compliance monitoring, but the NYC said it could encourage SK compliance rather than mandate it and deferred removal questions to DILG.

Outcome The hearing produced commitments for memorandum circulars, enhanced SK orientation and training, additional compliance guidance, submission of SK membership figures, and possible NYC research funding. DILG answered the appellate-authority question affirmatively, but the dismissal case remained subject to the submission and review of Rep. Mano's documents; the election timing and reliable out-of-school youth figures were not resolved.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

Disaster preparedness, LGU capacity, and flood rescue

The chair and members linked disaster resilience and LGU capacity to the DILG budget, citing 50,441 evacuation centers and more than 126,000 deployed uniformed personnel. Teves questioned BFP capital outlay and rescue capacity, while Remulla attributed the earlier reduction to procurement reforms and pointed to planned acquisitions, including 1,500 trucks through a government-to-government transaction. Erice pressed for an integrated Metro Manila flood-control and garbage-management structure, and Remulla said aging drainage systems and fragmented LGU responsibilities required structural reform. Rodriguez sought additional BFP resources from collected fire-code fees, and the chair noted the proposal. York asked about institutional disaster preparation, class-suspension deadlines, and water rescue in flood-prone Pampanga; DILG described operational protocols, Pagasa coordination, monitoring, and continued LGU training. BFP said watercraft and life vests would be distributed geographically and committed to capacity building and future equipment acquisition, while the broader funding and governance issues remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DILG and LGUs were being capacitated for recurring disasters, flooding, and emergency rescue, including the availability and deployment of fire stations, fire trucks, boats, ambulances, personnel, and operating protocols. Members also sought clearer timelines and guidelines for disaster response and class suspensions, and asked whether funding and institutional responsibilities were sufficient.

DILG said disaster preparedness depended on coordinated national-agency information, operational protocols, trained LGUs, and monitoring by local officials. It said BFP's response capacity was being improved through procurement reforms, planned government-to-government truck purchases, geographically distributed water-rescue equipment, ambulances, and additional support, but access to trust-fund resources remained dependent on budget action.

Outcome The agency provided its existing disaster-preparedness protocols and described planned improvements in fire-truck procurement, water rescue, ambulances, LGU training, and information sharing. Additional trust-fund support and clearer class-suspension rules were supported or under consideration, but the committee did not finally resolve the funding release, integrated Metro Manila flood governance, or the revised suspension guidelines.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

Seal of Good Local Governance validation and compliance

Rep. Edgar Erice challenged whether the SGLG measured actual governance outcomes or merely documentary compliance. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the DILG had moved to a whole-of-term assessment, reducing the former 10 indicators and as many as 14 categories to resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation; he cited 5,000,000 man hours previously spent annually and an estimated 5,000,000,000 cost for full third-party validation. Erice proposed using an appropriations provision to fund third-party validation, which the secretary welcomed. Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked that electric-bill compliance be added to fiscal-management criteria, and the secretary committed to include it in the next evaluation. In response to Rep. Jambaranda, the secretary committed to an immediate memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and excluding noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG. The request to regulate barangay travel orders was noted but not resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) measured actual improvements in local services and governance, rather than merely documentary compliance. Members also asked whether third-party validation and additional fiscal-management criteria could be incorporated into the SGLG.

The DILG said the SGLG had been redesigned as a whole-of-term assessment rather than an annual checklist, with three principal indicators: resiliency, fiscal management, and innovation. The agency supported third-party validation if Congress provided funding and committed to include an electric-bill criterion in the next evaluation and to issue a memorandum circular linking annual development-plan submission to SGLG eligibility.

Outcome The agency answered that the SGLG had been shifted to a whole-of-term, three-area assessment and accepted the possibility of third-party validation if Congress funded it. It also undertook specific follow-up measures on electric-bill compliance and annual development plans, while travel regulation and broader SK concerns remained open.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

LGU revenue sharing and local fiscal management

Rep. Sergio Dagooc asked DILG to enforce the local-tax exemption for the 121 electric cooperatives and to include electric-bill compliance in fiscal-management awards. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla assured him of support, and committed to include the criterion in the next evaluation round. Rep. Jambaranda raised SK, barangay development-plan, social-protection, and travel-regulation concerns; the Secretary said DILG could issue a memorandum circular requiring annual development plans and exclude noncompliant LGUs from the SGLG, while taking note of the travel request. Rep. Antonino Roman III asked for the status and timetable of Local Government Code amendments. DILG said consultations were under way, committed to submit available materials by next week, and supported reviewing the LGU share of national tax allocation from 40% to a higher level. The agency also discussed replacing the 25% equal-sharing component with equity sharing, but the allocation changes remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DILG would enforce local-tax exemptions for electric cooperatives, strengthen local planning and fiscal-management requirements, and regulate barangay travel. It also examined the status of proposed Local Government Code amendments, including possible changes to national tax allocation and equalization criteria.

DILG and the Secretary committed to support enforcement of electric-cooperative local-tax exemptions and to include electric-bill performance in the next fiscal-management-award evaluation. DILG supported reviewing and potentially increasing LGUs' national tax allocation share, while also considering an equity-based formula that would direct more resources to LGUs with greater geographic, disaster, conflict, or socioeconomic needs.

Outcome The electric-cooperative exemption and fiscal-award issue received affirmative commitments, while the annual development-plan issue also resulted in a proposed immediate memorandum circular. National tax allocation and Local Government Code changes remained under consultation, with DILG committed to provide materials but no final formula or amendment submitted during the hearing.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · unresolved

Solid-waste management and LGU contract oversight

Jose Teves Jr. asked who was responsible for overseeing LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003. Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla said the Local Government Code assigned waste disposal to municipalities and cities, producing fragmented and potentially inefficient systems, and proposed a regional approach. Rep. Edgar Erice later tied the issue to Metro Manila's 14,000,000 residents and 12,000 metric tons of daily garbage, asking whether DILG could use its general-supervision authority to review LGU contracts. Remulla said DILG had no supervisory power over those contracts and identified COWA as the responsible body as rendered in the transcript. He maintained that the Local Government Code should be revisited because regionalized collection would be more effective than detailed supervision of 40,000 LGUs. The issue remained unresolved, with no specific legal change or oversight mechanism adopted.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which level or agency was responsible for ensuring LGU compliance with solid-waste obligations under Republic Act 9003 and whether DILG could exercise supervisory authority over LGU garbage-collection contracts. Members also examined whether the current LGU-by-LGU system was adequate for the scale of waste and flooding problems, particularly in Metro Manila.

DILG said it did not have supervisory power over LGU contracts, identifying COWA as the office with that authority as rendered in the transcript. Secretary Remulla argued that the central problem was the LGU-by-LGU structure required by the Local Government Code and supported revisiting the law to establish a more integrated, regional system with clearer accountability and oversight.

Outcome The agency answered that DILG could not oversee LGU contracts under its current authority and proposed structural and legal reform toward regional garbage management. The committee did not adopt a specific amendment, assign a new oversight agency, or resolve the contract-supervision issue during the hearing.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

PNP accountability, body cameras, and public-assembly operations

Jose Teves Jr. raised PNP oversight and anti-hazing accountability, while DILG Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla reported that NAPOCOM had cleared a backlog of about 15,000 cases and had no remaining backlog. Renee Co questioned arrests during mobilizations, police firearms, and the reported more than 700,000 Safer Cities apprehensions. The secretary defended the arrests and initiative but acknowledged that the PNP had only 2,000 body-worn cameras for 320,000 personnel, with another 10 or 20,000 being procured, and said crime reductions ranged from about 30% to 60% depending on the category. The member also challenged the agency’s explanation of school violence and raised arbitrary barangay-level drug-watch listings; officials cited intelligence procedures, supply-and-demand reduction, and operational safeguards. The agency agreed to provide operation reports, incident logs, updated statistics, and a disciplinary report, with the latter committed for submission on Tuesday. The broader questions about firearms, arrests, and enforcement safeguards remained contested.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PNP arrests and public-assembly operations complied with human-rights and public-assembly rules, including restrictions on firearms and requirements for body-worn cameras. Members also sought the factual basis and safeguards for the Safer Cities Initiative, the agency’s approach to school violence and drug-watch listings, and the status of police-accountability cases and reports.

The DILG and its police-accountability officials maintained that arrests were based on vandalism or aggression, that firearms were not drawn or used against rally participants, and that the Safer Cities Initiative did not violate constitutional rights. The agency acknowledged obsolete and insufficient body-worn-camera equipment, defended its intelligence and drug-enforcement procedures, reported zero NAPOCOM backlog, and undertook to submit operation, incident, statistical, and disciplinary documents.

Outcome The agency defended its arrest and enforcement practices but acknowledged deficient body-camera coverage and left the legality and proportionality concerns contested. It committed to investigate and submit operational, statistical, and disciplinary records, with the disciplinary report specifically set for Tuesday; the broader accountability questions were not fully resolved during the hearing.

DILG · 2026-08-27 · committed

LGSF and local-project implementation safeguards

Rep. Miro Quimbo raised recurring building-permit delays that had stranded local projects, especially schools and health facilities, and DILG agreed to examine specific cases after receiving data. A member then asked DILG and the PNP to distinguish excavation from quarrying and clarify heavy-equipment impoundment; DILG said local governments generally lacked that authority, while the PNP said it enforced violations in coordination with the DENR and LGUs. A CSO representative questioned the rationale for retaining LGSF despite an estimated national tax allocation of about 1.32 to 1.4 billion trillion pesos, and DILG defended the roughly 58 billion fund as additional support for local basic services. DILG said DBM handled proposal vetting while DILG monitored implementation through technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. Members also sought safeguards against duplicate projects, weak participation, red-tagging, and ineffective implementation, while DILG and NAPOLCOM described existing monitoring and complaint mechanisms. DILG said the proposed SBDP allocation of about 9.74 billion actually reduced the per-barangay amount to 5,000,000 because coverage expanded to 1,904 barangays, leaving several requests for supporting evidence and public accountability information unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DILG would use its supervisory and monitoring powers to address delayed building permits, stranded local projects, and questionable local enforcement actions. It also examined the policy rationale, safeguards, monitoring responsibilities, and proposed funding levels for the Local Government Support Fund and related programs.

DILG maintained that compliant building-permit applications should not be delayed and undertook to examine specific cases. It said local governments identified and procured LGSF projects, DBM handled proposal vetting and validation, and DILG monitored implementation through deployed technical personnel, three-tier monitoring, and the SubayBayan portal. DILG also defended LGSF and SBDP as additional resources for local basic services, while the PNP and NAPOLCOM described enforcement and red-tagging safeguards.

Outcome DILG answered the committee's questions in general terms and undertook to examine the building-permit and local-enforcement cases after receiving supporting details. The LGSF and SBDP safeguards and allocations were explained, but questions about independent validation, public reporting, outcome evidence, and the adequacy of funding remained open.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Free higher education deficiency payments to SUCs

Members questioned CHED about unpaid free-higher-education deficiencies, SUC budget reductions, and whether continuing and incoming scholarship beneficiaries would be funded. CHED said 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing deficiency, while 667,000,000 remained associated with unpaid 2025 free higher education for 137,000 beneficiaries. The agency attributed future deficiencies partly to SUCs enrolling beyond capacity and to the unrealistic one-is-to-25 faculty-student assumption, and said it was developing a one-is-to-40 formula. Members also highlighted an 11,000,000,000 scholarship funding gap affecting roughly 1,000,000 students and a reported 29,200,000,000 deficit under UACTE alone. The chair required CHED to submit updated enrollment simulations, a prioritized funding request, and aligned beneficiary figures with DSWD before plenary. CHED committed to settle the existing deficiency by the third week of September, but the full 2027 funding requirement remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether free higher education deficiency payments to SUCs had been released, what deficiencies remained for 2025–2027, and whether proposed scholarship and SUC funding would cover continuing and incoming beneficiaries. Members also examined the enrollment-capacity and faculty-ratio assumptions behind the deficiency calculations and requested measures to prevent future shortfalls.

CHED said the principal source of free-higher-education deficiencies was the mismatch between SUC enrollment beyond absorptive capacity and the funding assumptions used by DBM, particularly the faculty-student ratio. CHED maintained that 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing deficiency, committed to process remaining requirements by the third week of September, and said it was developing a one-is-to-40 enrollment-capacity formula and coordinating with DBM, PASUC, SUCs, and DSWD.

Outcome CHED stated that 9,700,000,000 had been released for the existing SUC deficiency and committed to settle the remaining requirements by the third week of September. However, the broader 2027 scholarship and UACTE deficiencies, including the reported 29,200,000,000 UACTE deficit and possible beneficiary double-counting, remained subject to further CHED-DBM-DSWD review and committee budget action.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Tertiary scholarships, TES and TDP funding gaps

CHED presented a proposed 70,200,000,000 budget against a 35,430,000,000 NEP amount and identified a gap of roughly 34.8 billion, including scholarship, TES, TDP, and free-higher-education deficiencies. It said the TES proposal of about 35.5 billion was reduced to about 17.1 billion, potentially affecting roughly 833,780 beneficiaries, while TDP faced a shortfall that could affect 93,000 students. Members questioned delayed releases, unused funds, access for 4Ps and solo-parent beneficiaries, and the accuracy of CHED's overlapping beneficiary categories. CHED attributed prior delays to liquidation and validation requirements, reported that about 721,000 to 722,000 students had LandBank accounts, and committed to faster direct releases and reconciliation with DSWD. Members also challenged the scholarship reduction of 697,000,000 and requested detailed allocation and program breakdowns. The committee accepted CHED's explanations provisionally but left the funding and beneficiary totals for further reconciliation and plenary consideration.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether CHED's proposed funding for tertiary scholarships, TES, TDP, free higher education, and related student assistance would cover continuing and incoming beneficiaries. Members also examined delayed or unused funds, the accuracy of beneficiary counts, distribution mechanisms, and what CHED would submit or do to address funding gaps and possible reductions.

CHED maintained that the proposed scholarship, TES, TDP, and free-higher-education amounts were data-driven and reflected continuing and incoming beneficiaries rather than speculative requests. It said funding reductions could leave substantial numbers of students and faculty scholars unfunded, but asserted that LandBank distribution, validated DSWD lists, digital systems, and revised enrollment-capacity formulas had improved delivery and would help prevent future deficiencies.

Outcome The committee recognized CHED's improved disbursement performance but did not resolve the proposed scholarship, TES, TDP, and free-higher-education funding gaps. CHED was directed or expected to submit allocation, beneficiary, deficiency, and prioritization data and to reconcile the figures with DSWD, DBM, PASUC, and SUCs before plenary and budget-amendment deliberations.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

CHED FY 2027 funding gap and restoration request

CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis presented a proposed budget of about 70.2 billion against an NEP allocation of about 35.43 billion, leaving a gap of roughly 34.8 billion. She identified major unfunded priorities including scholarships, free higher education, digital transformation, and monitoring and evaluation, and said the full request was data-driven. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez supported restoring the entire gap, while Brian Poe focused on the scholarship reduction and asked about AI funding; CHED reported 5,000,000 for AI initiatives. Chair Mikaswan Singh questioned the release of about 9.7 billion in SUC deficiency payments and sought assurance that remaining deficiencies would be settled by the third week of September. Singh also required CHED to reconcile scholarship and 4Ps beneficiary counts with DSWD and submit enrollment-capacity data and a prioritized formal request. The issue remained subject to validation and budget amendments review rather than being resolved at the hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the size and composition of CHED's FY 2027 funding gap, which priorities were unfunded, and whether the agency's beneficiary and deficiency estimates were accurate. Members also sought commitments for detailed breakdowns, coordination with DSWD and DBM, and settlement of SUC deficiencies.

CHED maintained that its requests were data-driven and that the FY 2027 NEP left a 34,800,000,000 gap involving scholarships, free higher education, digital transformation, monitoring and evaluation, and other commitments. CHED sought restoration of the full gap, while acknowledging that beneficiary data, 4Ps-related categories, SUC deficiencies, and priority rankings still had to be reconciled with the committee, DSWD, DBM, and SUCs.

Outcome CHED's full 34,800,000,000 restoration request was not approved during the hearing. The committee requested detailed and prioritized submissions, further validation with DSWD, DBM, and SUCs, and indicated that any amendments would undergo review before plenary.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Scholarship and education-assistance utilization and validation

Rep. Chel Diokno and Rep. Robert Nassal questioned unobligated CHED allotments, access to TES, solo-parent scholarship implementation, and billions in unused or lapsed education-assistance funds. CHED attributed the delays to school-year timing, reliance on DSWD lists, validation requirements, and processing constraints, while reporting improved utilization and committing to submit beneficiary lists and address rejected cases. Rep. Mauricio Domogan challenged the centralized processing system and the 7,500 assistance amount, while CHED explained that regional offices validated applications before central processing and agreed to verify Baguio's submissions. Rep. Brian Poe highlighted the LandBank system, through which CHED reported about 722,000 students had received accounts, and reviewed the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship's 20,000 slots and more than 39,000 applicants. Chair Mikaswan Singh focused on SUC deficiencies, citing a 12,000,000,000 initial requirement, a 9,700,000,000 release or processing amount, and a possible 29,200,000,000 UACTE deficit. CHED committed to settle deficiencies by the third week of September, reconcile 4Ps beneficiary categories with DSWD, update its enrollment-capacity simulations, and submit a prioritized funding request.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why CHED had unobligated or delayed scholarship and education-assistance funds, how beneficiaries were identified and validated, and whether the reported beneficiary gaps reflected funding, processing, or data problems. Members also sought assurances on the settlement of SUC deficiencies and requested beneficiary and utilization data before budget deliberations.

CHED maintained that delayed obligations and utilization were primarily caused by school-year timing, validation and listing requirements, regional processing, liquidation rules, and SUC over-enrollment rather than an inability to deliver assistance. It said utilization had substantially improved, while committing to submit lists, reconcile beneficiary data with DSWD, settle SUC deficiencies by the third week of September, and provide updated capacity and funding information.

Outcome CHED provided explanations for the low or delayed utilization and reported substantial catch-up, but the committee required further beneficiary-list reconciliation, SUC-deficiency data, and regional validation information. Settlement of SUC deficiencies was committed for the third week of September, while the broader funding gaps and possible double counting remained subject to further discussions and budget review.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

4Ps beneficiary alignment and access to student assistance

Rep. Chel Diokno raised the low participation of poor and 4Ps-linked students in TES and cited a 5.54% rate against a 40% government target. CHED said it was using DSWD data, targeting 50% of 423,000 identified 4Ps beneficiaries, and validating a larger applicant pool. Rep. Mauricio Domogan argued that the 7,500 assistance amount was inadequate against tuition of about 50,000 and suggested 15,500, while CHED said the amount was set by the UniFAST Board to broaden coverage and could be reviewed. Rep. Edgar Erice requested CHED's 2026 allocation data and 2027 plan before plenary. Chair Mikaswan Singh later questioned an 11,370,000,000 4Ps deficiency, possible double-counting, and a 29,200,000,000 UACTE deficit. CHED and the House undertook to reconcile the categories with DSWD and submit prioritized and updated data, leaving the final funding decision unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether TES and other student-assistance programs were reaching the poorest students, particularly 4Ps beneficiaries, and whether CHED's beneficiary counts and allocations were aligned with DSWD data. Members also sought to determine whether assistance amounts and program categories were sufficient, accurately counted, and free from duplication.

CHED said it was using DSWD data and regional validation to improve 4Ps targeting, while distinguishing 4Ps TES beneficiaries from broader TDP coverage. CHED acknowledged that beneficiary categories and funding requirements still required reconciliation with DSWD and committed to provide data, review guidelines, and submit prioritized funding requests.

Outcome The issue was not finally resolved. CHED undertook to review the assistance amount, submit allocation and prioritization data, and reconcile 4Ps beneficiary counts with DSWD before plenary, while the committee left the amount of any additional funding and the final beneficiary totals open.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

SUC enrollment capacity, faculty plantilla items and staffing

Jude Acidre, Antonio Tinio, Cheeno Almario, and Chair Mikaswan Singh raised concerns about enrollment growth, overcrowded SUCs, faculty shortages, free higher education deficiencies, and regular plantilla positions. CHED reported that 68% of surveyed SUCs exceeded estimated capacity and supported a one-is-to-40 faculty-student ratio, with additional classrooms, faculty items, and nonteaching positions needed. Tinio cited 20,964 faculty plantilla items and asked CHED to address job-order staffing and the salary grade 12 entry level for instructors requiring a master's degree. CHED undertook to provide validated staffing data, consult the Civil Service Commission, and submit a position paper. On deficiencies, CHED reported a release of about 9.7 billion against a prior total of about 12 billion, while Singh cited a broader UACTE deficit of about 29.2 billion and requested reconciliation of the figures. The committee and CHED set a third-week-of-September target for deficiency settlement and requested updated capacity simulations and a prioritized funding letter, but the final staffing and funding requirements remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether SUCs had sufficient enrollment capacity, classrooms, regular faculty plantilla items, and nonteaching staff to support free higher education. It also examined the faculty-student ratio used for funding and enrollment projections, the treatment of job-order and contract-of-service faculty, and the salary grade and qualification of entry-level instructors.

CHED said enrollment growth had outpaced the absorptive capacity of many SUCs and that additional classrooms, regular faculty plantilla positions, and nonteaching staff were necessary to maintain education quality. CHED supported using a more realistic one-is-to-40 faculty-student ratio, was developing an enrollment-capacity formula with DBM and PASUC, and undertook to submit validated staffing and capacity data and a prioritized funding request.

Outcome The hearing established that many SUCs exceeded capacity and that staffing and classroom shortages were linked to recurring free higher education deficiencies. CHED committed to submit validated plantilla and enrollment-capacity data, coordinate with DBM and DSWD, prepare a position paper on salary grades, and work toward settling deficiencies by the third week of September; the final number of new plantilla items and the long-term funding requirement remained open.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Student housing and PPP dormitory facilities

Rep. Chel Diokno and Ian Amatong raised student housing as an infrastructure need affecting disadvantaged students' access and graduation. CHED said more than 100 SUCs could avail of Pag-IBIG financing and proposed one dormitory per SUC, with a possible government-funded second unit through a multiyear allocation. The agency cited financing at 3% rather than 8% per annum, a 10-year period, and an initial indicative cost of about 100 to 120 million per unit. CHED said small facilities would have 20 to 30 rooms, medium facilities 50 to 80 rooms, and large facilities would be three to five stories, depending on the SUC's land and capacity. Rep. Amatong requested the design and costing, and CHED agreed to provide them and arrange further consultations. Final design, capacity, and funding commitments remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how CHED proposed to address student housing shortages affecting access and graduation, including the scale, financing, design, cost, and capacity of dormitory facilities. Members also asked whether CHED could provide the dormitory design and costing and consult more regularly with legislators and universities.

CHED stated that student accommodation was a major infrastructure bottleneck and that it was pursuing a Pag-IBIG financing arrangement, potentially through a PPP structure, to support dormitory construction. The agency proposed one dormitory per SUC, with a possible government-funded complement, but said final capacity and design would depend on each SUC's land and absorptive and payment capacity.

Outcome CHED presented a proposed Pag-IBIG PPP-based dormitory approach, an initial per-unit allocation, and indicative room categories. The design, final costing, facility capacity, and broader multiyear government allocation remained subject to ongoing work and were not finally resolved during the hearing.

Questions and agency response

CHED said its overall unfunded requirement was 34,800,000,000 and that the detailed requirements would be submitted to the appropriations committee. The LEB representative said CLEP, LEAP, and LEADS received 0 pesos in the proposed budget, while the agency presented a multi-item request for restoration and augmentation.

Outcome The committee did not finally approve or restore the LEB funding during the hearing. CHED was expected to submit detailed requirements, while members manifested support for restoration and the chair deferred consideration to the proper time.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · unresolved

Inclusive education and equity-group funding

Rep. Percy raised inclusive education priorities, including resource centers, health professionals, and learners with disabilities, and called for restoration of the budget during a learning crisis. CHED Chairperson Shirley A. Agrupis said CHED had completed research identifying equity groups and had incorporated them into policy and scholarship priorities. She cited programs in special needs education, speech pathology, occupational therapy, clinical psychology, and certification. CHED had proposed 418,000,000, or about 418 million, under the equity-group proposal. The exchange ended with Rep. Percy describing the funding situation as depriving programs of resources, without a recorded commitment to restore the budget.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how CHED was funding inclusive education, inclusive learning resource centers, and health-professional programs for learners with disabilities and other equity groups. The member also pressed whether the proposed budget cuts should be restored in light of the learning crisis.

CHED said it had identified equity groups through completed research and incorporated them into policy and scholarship priorities. It stated that its 2027 proposal included priority programs for special needs education and related health professions, with 418,000,000 proposed under the equity-group proposal.

Outcome CHED explained its equity-group policy work and identified 418,000,000 in its 2027 proposal for related programs. Rep. Percy continued to seek restoration of the budget, but no restoration or other committee action was recorded.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Higher-education research, development and artificial intelligence

CHED Chairperson Shirley Agropis presented a proposed budget of about 70.2 billion against an NEP allocation of about 35 billion, identifying a roughly 34.8 billion gap that included scholarship, digital-system, and monitoring shortfalls. Rep. Brian Poe asked which items had been reduced, clarified the 697,000,000 scholarship gap, and requested its breakdown. He also asked about CHED's AI road map and research-and-development funding. CHED said it had adopted a national AI in higher education policy, allocated 5,000,000 for several AI applications, and was building faculty capacity. For research, CHED said faculty-researcher capacity building was in its proposal while project funding was placed under HEDF, including about 1.4 billion for pillar-funded projects. CHED undertook to submit the scholarship breakdown, research initiatives, and scholar-distribution data, while Rep. Poe expressed support for additional or restored CHED funding.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which higher-education priorities were reduced or excluded from CHED's FY 2027 budget, particularly digital transformation, artificial intelligence, research and development, and scholarships. It also asked how CHED was funding AI and research initiatives and which scholars would be affected by the reported reductions.

CHED maintained that digital transformation, artificial intelligence, faculty capacity building, and research were central to its modernization and Achieve Agenda. It said the ISSP request was not funded in 2027, AI initiatives had a 5,000,000 allocation, faculty-researcher capacity building was included in the proposal, and research projects were to be funded through HEDF, including 1,400,000,000 for pillar-funded projects.

Outcome CHED explained that AI and research activities were being funded through limited allocations and HEDF rather than through a clearly identified standalone research-and-development line. The scholarship breakdown and scholar-distribution data were to be submitted, but the adequacy of the AI, digital-transformation, research, and scholarship funding remained open.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Higher-education safety, Safe Spaces compliance and mental health

Rep. Chel Diokno raised reports of restrictions on speech and assembly, red-tagging, online harassment, and potentially harmful active-attack drills, and CHED committed to policy review, student dialogue, and mental-health and campus-safety measures. Minority member Sara Elago focused on Safe Spaces Law enforcement, routine inspection, and CODI functionality. CHED said it was surveying about 2,347 higher-education institutions, including 561 SUCs and campuses, and reported that 66% had functional CODIs for informal anti-sexual-harassment investigations. CHED cited 697,000,000 for scholarship and faculty development and 258,000,000 for monitoring and evaluation, including Safe Spaces monitoring, but promised to submit the precise allocation for Safe Spaces compliance monitoring. Jay Vergara received CHED's account of a student safety portal covering about 5.8 million students and identifying online threats, bullying, violence, and dormitory safety among reported concerns. The agency's commitments were recorded, but the full compliance picture and exact Safe Spaces funding remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether CHED was monitoring and enforcing Safe Spaces compliance and whether its policies and programs adequately protected academic freedom, student dialogue, campus safety, and mental health. Members also asked whether CHED had sufficient monitoring, complaint, and intervention mechanisms for violence, online threats, and psychological risks.

CHED said it was actively reviewing higher-education policies, monitoring Safe Spaces compliance through regional offices and institutional programs, and responding to complaints through CODIs and board processes. It also said it was expanding mental-health, campus-safety, anti-terrorism, and student-dialogue initiatives, while acknowledging that compliance data and the exact Safe Spaces monitoring budget still had to be submitted.

Outcome CHED stated that it was undertaking policy review, institutional monitoring, complaint handling, mental-health programming, and campus-safety initiatives. However, the exact Safe Spaces monitoring budget and complete institutional compliance data were not provided during the hearing and were left for submission.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Private higher-education regulation and tuition-fee sharing

Eli San Fernando questioned CHED's delayed labor-education rules and enforcement of the 70% tuition-fee-sharing requirement in private HEIs. CHED said labor education would be integrated into NSTP and other courses, and it undertook to investigate faculty and staff complaints, coordinate with DOLE, and revise the private-higher-education regulatory manual. Rep. Solomon Chungalao asked about open universities, diploma mills, student complaints, and a campus building; CHED said about 31 of 113 universities were authorized for limited open-university programs, that violations could lead to closure, and that it would receive his documents. Rep. Renee Co raised unresolved free-higher-education deficiencies and student-welfare protections, while CHED acknowledged continuing deficiencies and said it was moving toward a one-to-forty faculty-student ratio and ongoing guideline deployment. Rep. Cheeno Almario cited severe faculty shortages and requested higher TDP funding and possible private-institution partnerships, with the chair taking the budget manifestation into consideration. Rep. Antonio Tinio raised constitutional concerns over legislative intervention in scholarship implementation, and Rep. Jude Acidre urged stronger attention to private HEIs because more than half of college students were enrolled there.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether CHED was enforcing labor-education and tuition-fee-sharing requirements in private higher-education institutions, regulating open universities and diploma mills, and protecting faculty, staff, and student rights. Members also asked how CHED was addressing free-higher-education deficiencies, overcrowding and faculty shortages, the role of private institutions, and regulatory gaps affecting local and private institutions.

CHED said it was strengthening regulation of private HEIs, open universities, diploma mills, tuition-fee compliance, and student welfare through guidelines, monitoring, consultations, and coordination with DOLE and DBM. It acknowledged unresolved deficiencies, uneven faculty-student ratios, and the difficulty of monitoring all institutions, while maintaining that violations could result in closure and that private institutions could participate in tuition-subsidy programs.

Outcome CHED undertook to investigate the tuition-fee-sharing complaint, coordinate with DOLE, revise private-HEI regulations, receive documents on complaints, and continue student-welfare consultations. The open-university and enforcement questions received general answers, but the free-higher-education deficiencies, faculty shortages, private-sector partnership model, and constitutional concerns remained subject to further documentation, budget action, or policy work.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · unresolved

HEDF portfolio management and travel-tax funding

CHED chairperson Shirley Agropis reported that HEDF had released about 7.8 billion to address free higher-education deficiencies, with Congress adding about 4 billion plus and bringing the cited total to about 12 billion. She also reported remittances of about 12.54 billion and said CHED had submitted about 11.3 billion, while describing the average HEDF release rate as 54%. Nassal asked which government financial institution was the HEDF portfolio manager under Republic Act 7722, and Agropis said the Bureau of the Treasury was involved while CHED had approached Land Bank and other institutions. Nassal challenged that arrangement as a violation of the law and demanded transfer to a qualified government financial institution or an amendatory law. The chair said the issue would be taken up with partner agencies. Brian Yamsoo An later raised the 40% travel-tax collection, and CHED said it did not object provided its HEDF utilization was presented, while warning that it lacked capacity to finance existing programs without another funding source.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) was being managed, whether CHED had appointed the government financial institution required by Section 11 of Republic Act 7722, and how much of requested HEDF funding was actually released. It also asked about the proposed 40% travel-tax collection and whether CHED could finance its existing higher-education programs without that funding window.

CHED said it had used and was disbursing HEDF resources for existing higher-education deficiencies and programs, but received only about 54% of its cumulative requests. It did not object to the proposed 40% travel-tax collection, provided HEDF uses were documented, and said another funding source was necessary because CHED lacked the capacity to finance its existing programs.

Outcome CHED's position on the 40% travel-tax collection was recorded as non-objection, subject to showing HEDF utilization and identifying another funding window. The portfolio-manager issue remained contested: CHED identified the Bureau of the Treasury's involvement and discussions with Land Bank, while the member demanded compliance with Section 11 or an amendatory law; the chair referred the matter to CHED and partner agencies.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

Scholarship program administration and constitutional authority

Rep. Brian Poe examined CHED's LandBank partnership and sought assurance that the agency could manage a larger scholarship budget. CHED said the system expedited direct distribution, and reported that about 80% of the backlog had been addressed, including 722,000 students with bank accounts. Poe also questioned the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship, for which CHED described eligibility based on grades, household income, first-generation status, priority programs, and regional allocation; the program had 20,000 slots and more than 39,000 applicants, with support figures including 80,000, 90,000, and 45,000 as spoken. Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez then challenged the reduction from roughly 35.5 billion to roughly 17.1 billion, identifying an 11,000,000,000 gap and warning that about 1,000,000 students could be affected. He urged restoration and coordination of barangay scholarship funds with CHED. Rep. Antonio Tinio separately argued that legislative intervention in implementation could violate the PDAF ruling and executive authority, but the chair only noted the manifestation. CHED committed to provide regional distribution data and more accurate figures, leaving the funding and constitutional issues open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether CHED could efficiently administer an expanded scholarship budget, how the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship selected beneficiaries, and why tertiary scholarship funding was being reduced. Members also questioned whether legislative involvement in scholarship implementation raised constitutional concerns under the PDAF ruling.

CHED presented the LandBank arrangement as a reform that accelerated scholarship disbursement, reduced school control over funds, and enabled direct student banking. It said the Barangay Pilipinas Merit Scholarship used a formula combining grades, household income, first-generation status, and regional graduate counts, while the agency officials did not provide a substantive response to the constitutional objection or the requested explanation of the DBM reductions in the excerpt.

Outcome The committee received CHED's explanation of the LandBank mechanism and scholarship-selection formula, but the proposed tertiary scholarship reduction remained contested. The constitutional objection to legislative intervention was noted without a substantive agency or committee resolution, while CHED undertook to submit supporting distribution and more accurate budget figures.

CHED · 2026-08-27 · committed

CHED regional access, monitoring and administrative capacity

CHED Chairperson Shirley Agropis said the commission lacked sufficient personnel, regional-office support, monitoring resources, and digital infrastructure to oversee about 39,000 academic programs across 2,365 higher education institutions. She cited 258,252,500 for monitoring and evaluation, regional-office requirements of 35,600,000 for CAR, 16,640,000 for Caraga, and 12,860,000 for Region 2, as well as an unfunded 331,300,000 ISSP request. Ian Amatong asked for assurances that TES would be released within the semester, requested dormitory design and costing, and sought better access to consultations. CHED said it was targeting full direct delivery by the end of September, agreed to provide the dormitory documents, and accepted a consultation arrangement. Rep. Rommel T. Angara proposed a CHED annex or sub-office in Aurora because travel to Pampanga took about four to six hours; the chair accepted the proposal, committed to interim outreach there, and directed preparation of complete staff work. The issue therefore landed with agency commitments, while the funding and final institutional approval remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee was seeking to establish whether CHED had sufficient personnel, regional offices, monitoring resources, digital systems, and consultation capacity to oversee higher education programs nationwide. Members also asked whether CHED could improve access for geographically distant areas, including Aurora, and provide timely assistance and requested documents.

CHED said its regional and monitoring capacity was constrained by insufficient personnel, training, IT support, infrastructure, and funding. It maintained that digital systems, stronger monitoring and evaluation, direct payment arrangements, regional outreach, and additional offices or sub-offices were necessary to improve oversight and access.

Outcome The agency's general capacity concerns were presented but the additional regional, monitoring, and digital-system funding remained part of CHED's broader budget request. Specific operational matters produced commitments on TES timeliness, dormitory documents, consultations, and staff work for an Aurora sub-office, but no final appropriation or approval was recorded.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

OWA's additional 2,000,000,000 request and Emergency Repatriation Fund

Minority member Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether OWA's additional 2,000,000,000 request was the minimum needed for life-and-safety and crisis-response obligations. OWA cited emergency repatriation expenses and geopolitical uncertainty, while Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac expressly endorsed the full request and said utilization alone was not a safe basis for reducing the ERF. Nazal raised the need for contingency planning for nearly 200,000 Filipinos potentially affected by a Taiwan Strait conflict and asked for information on OFWs in China and Hong Kong; DMW said it lacked data on overstayers and secondary employment but had crisis manuals and interagency preparations. DMW reported extensive Action Fund assistance, including 44,445 financial-assistance beneficiaries and 606,921 total assistance and beneficiaries over the longer period reported. Majority member Johanne Monich Bautista supported an additional 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund and restoration of the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000. The chair later sought DBM clarification because the apparent NEP gap depended on how programs and net levels were presented, leaving the final funding decision open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether OWA's requested additional 2,000,000,000 was the irreducible minimum for statutory life-and-safety services, emergency repatriation, and other crisis-response needs. It also examined the adequacy of the Emergency Repatriation Fund (ERF), the basis for its proposed reduction, and whether contingency plans for Taiwan, China, and Hong Kong were costed and funded.

DMW and OWA endorsed the full additional 2,000,000,000 request and rejected reliance on historical utilization alone to set a life-and-safety contingency fund. They said at least 1,200,000,000 should be restored for the ERF, while crisis-response planning and additional resources would be coordinated across agencies as conditions developed.

Outcome DMW and OWA secured an express agency-level endorsement of the additional 2,000,000,000 request, while members supported additional Action Fund resources and restoration of the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000. The precise funding level, the costed Taiwan evacuation plan, and the reconciliation of the NEP figures remained subject to further budget clarification and submissions.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

Restoration of 2,000,000,000 in DMW funding

Rep. Rufus Rodriguez questioned the reduction of DMW's proposed budget and asked for a documented restoration request. Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said DMW was seeking about 2 billion, including about 1 billion for the Action Fund, 60 million for Servicio caravans, 60 million for international labor affairs, 180 million for general administration, and amounts for NMP, the OFW Hospital, migrant protection, and migrant workers' offices. OWWA separately defended an additional 2 billion for MOOE, operations, emergency repatriation, capital outlay, facilities, upskilling, and scholarships. Rodriguez moved to approve both increases, but the chair deferred action because the proceeding was only a budget briefing. Rep. Niko Raul Daza also supported the increases and established that NMP's free maritime training could continue under the proposed budget, while NMP sought 92 million for additional facilities and information systems. The issue therefore remained subject to later committee consideration, with document submissions and facility assessments still expected.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why DMW's proposed budget had been reduced, whether DMW and OWWA needed additional funding, and how the requested amounts would be itemized and justified. Members also examined whether the proposed funding would sustain expanded OFW services, including the Action Fund, free maritime training, facilities, and anti-illegal-recruitment programs.

DMW said it accepted the NEP as part of the government's fiscal framework but requested a reasonable restoration of 2,000,000,000 to sustain urgent OFW services and programs. OWWA likewise defended an additional 2,000,000,000 for MOOE, operations, emergency repatriation, capital outlay, facilities, upskilling, and scholarships; NMP said its existing personnel and operating budgets could sustain free training but sought 92,000,000 for additional facilities and information systems.

Outcome DMW and OWWA presented and defended separate additional requests of 2,000,000,000 each, and Rep. Rodriguez moved for their approval. The chair did not approve the increases during the briefing, instead deferring the ruling; DMW was asked to submit its itemized request and OWWA committed to present facility assessments.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

Action Fund disbursement, assistance, and crisis-response funding

Members questioned how the Action Fund had been used for financial, legal, medical, welfare, and repatriation assistance, particularly during the Middle East crisis. DMW reported 80,000 financial-assistance cases, 14,000 legal cases, around 5,000 medical cases, and January-to-July 2026 assistance figures including 44,445 financial beneficiaries, 2,610 legal beneficiaries, 7,329 repatriation beneficiaries, and 9,891 welfare-case beneficiaries. The agency cited general rates of 50,000 for distressed cases, seventy five thousand for medical situations, and one hundred thousand for an OFW, with quick-action assistance ranging from 5,000 to 30,000 and a 30,000 pesos rate for certain trafficking and scam-hub victims. It said the Action Fund covered documented and undocumented OFWs, had no ceiling for certain hospital bills, and could assist in medical disputes and abused dependents. DMW undertook to review and amend the disbursement guidelines, while Johanne Monich Bautista manifested support for an additional 1,000,000,000 for the fund. The funding request and some garbled utilization figures were not finally resolved in the excerpt.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the Action Fund was being disbursed, what standards governed legal, medical, financial, and repatriation assistance, and whether its funding was sufficient for ordinary cases and geopolitical crises. Members also asked whether the fund covered medical disputes and abused dependents, and requested utilization and beneficiary records.

The DMW said the Action Fund covered legal, medical, financial, welfare, airport, and repatriation assistance for both documented and undocumented OFWs, including abused dependents. It said current resources could cover pending claims and medical-assistance needs, but acknowledged that disbursement rates were under review and requested additional funding for continuing geopolitical and welfare demands.

Outcome The committee received the agency's utilization figures, disbursement rates, coverage assurances, and crisis-response explanation. The agency committed to revise the disbursement guidelines and pursue broader support systems, while the requested additional funding remained a committee-supported request rather than a final appropriation.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

Emergency repatriation and evacuation preparedness amid global conflicts

Members questioned whether DMW and OWWA could sustain OFW repatriation, financial assistance, and evacuation during the Middle East conflict and future geopolitical crises. DMW described activated crisis manuals, DFA coordination, prepositioned personnel, and the repatriation of about 12,000 people, while reporting Action Fund amounts of about 2 billion and a presidential supplemental allocation of 3 billion peso. Members, particularly Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. and Rep. Johanne Monich Bautista, argued that emergency funding should not be reduced solely because of historical utilization and supported restoring the ERF to at least 1.2 billion and increasing the Action Fund by about 1 billion. OWWA reported that the ERF had served 139,688 clients by July 31 and forecast serving roughly 240,000 to 250,000 clients. The agency also addressed Cambodia scam-hub victims, Strait of Hormuz seafarer evacuations, and medical-repatriation procedures. The issue landed with agency commitments to endorse and justify the requested increases and submit supporting records, but final congressional funding levels remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DMW and OWWA had sufficient funds, personnel, systems, and contingency plans to protect and repatriate OFWs during the Middle East conflict and other geopolitical emergencies. Members also asked how Action Fund and emergency repatriation resources were being disbursed, whether proposed increases were justified, and whether specific evacuation and medical-repatriation procedures were ready.

DMW and OWWA maintained that they had activated crisis manuals, coordinated through a one-country-team and whole-of-government approach, and were improving personnel, financial systems, overseas posts, and prepositioned response capacity. They argued that utilization rates alone were an unsafe basis for reducing contingency funds and endorsed additional funding, including restoration of the emergency repatriation fund to at least 1,200,000,000 and additional Action Fund support.

Outcome The committee did not finally resolve the level of DMW and OWWA emergency funding, but the agency endorsed the additional 2,000,000,000 OWWA request, sought an additional 1,000,000,000 for the Action Fund, and supported restoring the ERF to at least 1,200,000,000. The agency also undertook to submit supporting documents, crisis manuals or confidential operational details, release records, and Strait of Hormuz data.

Questions and agency response

NMP budget reduction and free seafarer training

Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac and NMP Executive Director Vic Del Rosario presented NMP's modernization projects and explained that the apparent reduction in its budget was mainly due to lower capital outlay after a large current-year infrastructure allocation. Representative Niko Raul Daza asked whether free maritime training, begun on August 3 under DMW Memorandum Order 360, could be sustained despite the cited 210,000,000 or 52% reduction between the 2026 GAA and 2027 NEP. Del Rosario said operating funds were sufficient, with NMP expecting to serve about 30,000 seafarers in 2027 after training about 28,000 in the current year. He said NMP needed restoration of 92,000,000, including 67,000,000 for a training building and 16,000,000 for information systems, to add 15 training rooms and address increased enrollment. Daza manifested support for the requested increase, while NMP said feasibility studies for separate Cavite and Davao centers could support a budget proposal for fiscal year 2028. No final restoration or committee action was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the National Maritime Polytechnic could sustain its free maritime training program despite the reported reduction in its 2027 budget. Members also asked what funding and facilities were needed to accommodate increased enrollment and whether requested infrastructure funds would be restored.

NMP maintained that the apparent budget reduction was chiefly a capital-outlay reduction following the current year's 271,000,000 infrastructure allocation, while personnel services and operating funds remained sufficient to sustain free training in 2027. It said the program could serve approximately 30,000 seafarers in 2027, but requested restoration of 92,000,000 for additional training capacity and information systems.

Outcome The agency answered that the free training program could be sustained under the proposed 2027 operating budget, but acknowledged that expanded facilities depended on restoration of the requested 92,000,000. Daza supported the restoration and broader DMW increase, but the transcript did not show a committee ruling or final funding action.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

OFW reintegration, livelihood assistance, and outcome measurement

Rep. Mica Gonzales asked how Middle East returnees were being reintegrated and whether they could return to overseas employment or pursue local options. DMW reported that about 12,000 people had returned, including roughly 9,000 OFWs and 3,000 dependents, and said it was profiling skills and matching job orders while offering livelihood and training assistance. DMW and OWWA later reported about 6,000 welfare interventions, nearly 5,000 training interventions, projected beneficiaries of about 51,000, and funding figures including 300,000,000 and 321,000,000. Rep. Johanne Monich Bautista said she supported the requested 300,000,000 increase for reintegration and additional funding for the action plan and ERF. Rep. Jude Acidre pressed for impact data rather than beneficiary counts and urged proactive pathways before OFWs returned. OWWA reported that over 60% had an employment or livelihood pathway after twelve months and supplied pathway percentages from interviews, but acknowledged continuing needs for monitoring, digitalization, and resources for a broader rollout.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how returning OFWs, particularly those affected by Middle East conflicts, were being profiled and assisted toward overseas reemployment, local employment, livelihood, or skills training. It also sought the funding, beneficiary basis, and measurable outcomes of the reintegration programs, including whether beneficiaries had obtained jobs or sustained businesses.

DMW and OWWA stated that reintegration required a whole-of-government approach combining profiling, psychosocial assistance, livelihood and capital support, reemployment, and skills training. They reported substantial intervention and pathway figures, acknowledged the need for more systematic impact monitoring and proactive pre-return planning, and supported digital tools and a virtual one-stop shop to improve referrals and data collection.

Outcome The committee received the agencies' program, funding, beneficiary, and preliminary pathway data and expressed support for increased reintegration resources. However, the requested outcome data on sustained employment and businesses was only partly answered; monitoring and improved digital profiling were still ongoing.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

OFW medical, mental-health, and dependent-support services

Rep. Bryan Revilla raised OFW health-care coverage and urged the government to provide extra assistance to OFWs. DMW said PhilHealth coverage was mandatory, most OFWs had host-country insurance, and the Action Fund could assist with hospital bills without a set ceiling, citing a case costing more than 1,000,000. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned regional cooperation, medical retainerships, mental-health care, gender-sensitive services, and the use of verification fees; DMW identified 130,000,000 for medical and legal retainers and said each verified contract carried a 10 US dollar fee. DMW reported verification-fee collections of about 5.85 billion and earmarks ranging from about 163 million to about 700 million across the cited years. Vice Chair Bella Suansing asked whether abused OFW dependents were covered, and DMW answered yes while proposing an interagency aftercare system for children left behind. The OFW Hospital reported having a psychologist but needing a psychiatrist, leaving expansion of regional mental-health capacity as an ongoing commitment.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DMW and partner agencies covered OFWs' medical and mental-health needs, including insurance, hospital assistance, medical retainership, and gender-responsive care. It also examined whether assistance extended to abused OFW dependents and children left behind, and how contract-verification fees supported these services.

DMW stated that the Action Fund could provide uncapped hospital assistance, cover abused OFW dependents, and support medical retainerships and mental-health care. It said gender-responsive training and interagency programs for children left behind were being pursued, while acknowledging that the OFW Hospital still needed to strengthen psychiatric capacity.

Outcome The agency answered that the Action Fund covered medical assistance and abused OFW dependents, while medical retainership and mental-health services were being expanded. The committee received commitments on PhilHealth coordination, medical retainerships, gender-responsive care, interagency support, and psychiatric capacity, but specific regional mental-health coverage remained subject to further strengthening.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

US500 minimum wage for migrant domestic workers

Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula asked how DMW would enforce the increase in the minimum wage for migrant domestic workers from 400 US dollar to 500 US dollar. DMW said the policy, issued through Department Order 25 in August 2025, was initially voluntary because of its effect on existing contracts, and reported 17,375 processed job orders at the 500 US dollar salary. The agency cited video interviews, employer screening, skills training, and livelihood options as safeguards and said it would continue implementation until the rate became acceptable enough for mandatory imposition. The exchange also covered Action Fund disbursement, including a 2,000,000,000 fund, a 3,000,000,000 peso allocation, and assistance rates ranging from 2,000 to 100,000. DMW committed to provide release documentation, cover pending claims by the early fourth quarter, and review and amend the disbursement guidelines. The wage issue was therefore committed for continued implementation but was not shown to have been fully enforced across all destination countries and agencies.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DMW would ensure implementation and compliance with the increased minimum wage for migrant domestic workers, including whether the standard would eventually become mandatory. The member also asked about Action Fund disbursement and the adequacy and timing of assistance for distressed workers.

DMW said the 500 US dollar wage was being implemented initially on a voluntary basis because of its effect on existing contracts, with 17,375 job orders already processed at that salary. The agency said it would continue promoting the standard through employer screening, video interviews, skills training, livelihood options, and eventual mandatory imposition once the rate achieved broad acceptability.

Outcome DMW answered that the 500 US dollar wage remained under voluntary implementation, with 17,375 job orders processed, and committed to continued implementation and eventual mandatory imposition. The committee received the assurance, but the transcript did not establish that compliance across all destination countries and recruitment agencies had been achieved.

Outcome The DMW answered that the verification fee had not increased and remained 10 US dollars per verified contract. It reported total collections deposited in the Bureau of Treasury and stated the annual GAA earmarks, but no separate documentation request or further action was recorded.
