DMW · 2026-08-26 · committed

Illegal recruitment and human-trafficking enforcement outside Metro Manila

Rep. Jude Acidre raised the case of 23 families of 23 OFWs imprisoned in Cambodia and asked about DMW's broader response to scam-hub trafficking. DMW said it was providing welfare assistance, repatriation, financial assistance, legal support, and coordination with the DFA and DOJ, while expanding migrant workers offices in Cambodia and Thailand and working toward a presence in Myanmar. The secretary also described bilateral and ASEAN efforts on fair and ethical recruitment, while a medical arrangement in Dubai served about 700,000 Filipino workers. Rep. Niko Raul Daza questioned whether NMP could sustain free maritime training after a 52% budget reduction; NMP said its national-government subsidy could support training about 30,000 seafarers in 2027 but requested 92,000,000 for facilities and information systems. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez then asked how DMW would make anti-illegal-recruitment and anti-trafficking services accessible outside Metro Manila after applicants were reportedly charged 350,000 by an unauthorized recruiter. DMW answered that it had expanded regional staffing, operated 16 regional offices, and used surveillance, verification, closure operations, and LGU and law-enforcement partnerships. The funding restoration and broader budget increases were not resolved in the excerpt.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DMW was responding to Filipinos trapped in overseas scam hubs and how it was coordinating with other countries to prevent trafficking and illegal recruitment. It also examined whether DMW and NMP had sufficient regional personnel, facilities, medical arrangements, and funding to provide protection and services outside Metro Manila.

DMW said it was addressing trafficking and illegal recruitment through welfare assistance, repatriation, financial assistance, legal support, law-enforcement coordination, migrant workers offices, regional surveillance, and closure operations. It also maintained that NMP's operating requirements could sustain free training under the proposed budget, while acknowledging that NMP hoped Congress would restore 92,000,000 for additional facilities and information systems.

Outcome DMW's operational responses were presented without a recorded objection, but several funding and capacity matters remained requests rather than approved appropriations. The agency committed to continuing regional enforcement, international coordination, and NMP capacity expansion, while the restoration of NMP's 92,000,000 and other DMW funding increases were left for budget deliberation.

DMW · 2026-08-26 · parked

Saudi residence permits and OFW legal assistance

Rep. Rufus Rodriguez raised a constituent's case involving the non-issuance of a Saudi residence permit and asked why the permit was not being issued and who was responsible for assisting affected OFWs. An agency official answered that residence-permit problems could involve overstaying or perceived violations and said legal assistance was available through the action fund, the Tebian Law Office, retained counsel, and in-house lawyers. The official said the Saudi law firm had 30 lawyers and that the agency shouldered hospital or immigration-related penalties. Rodriguez then moved to increase the DMW and OA budgets by 2,000,000,000 each. The chair said the motion would be considered at the proper time because the proceeding was only a budget briefing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why some OFWs in Saudi Arabia were not receiving residence permits and which office or mechanism was responsible for addressing their cases. It also sought clarification on whether legal assistance and related penalties were covered.

The agency stated that Saudi residence-permit problems generally stemmed from legal issues such as overstaying or perceived violations. It said legal assistance was available through the action fund, retained and in-house lawyers, and the Tebian Law Office, and that it shouldered hospital or immigration-related penalties.

Outcome The agency provided a general explanation and described its legal-assistance mechanisms, but no case-specific resolution or responsible office for the constituent's permit problem was identified. Rep. Rodriguez's budget motion was deferred for consideration at the proper time.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

DENR FY2027 budget reduction and institutional amendments

The DENR presented a requested FY 2027 budget of about 28.04 billion and later disclosed that it had proposed about 55.04 billion to the DBM, including tier two. Members questioned the substantial reduction and identified priority augmentations for land management, patent registration, foreshore mapping, the Land Management Bureau building, and water-resource programs. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez moved an additional 556,617,000 pesos, and the committee approved it subject to consolidation and available fiscal space. The DENR also committed to follow up on Nagat Island monitoring, Eastern Samar mining rehabilitation, and stewardship-approval thresholds. Rep. Rodriguez separately sought 400,000,000 for rehabilitation of previously planted areas, but the chair required a new written request. The Appropriations chair directed the DENR to submit a formal and prioritized list for budget amendments review before plenary deliberations.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the DENR's FY 2027 request, the extent and reasons for the reduction from the amount proposed to the DBM, and which additional programs or institutional amendments should receive funding. It also examined whether the proposed augmentation was approved or remained subject to available fiscal space and further review.

The DENR said its proposed budget was needed to carry out its broad environmental and natural-resources mandate, but it acknowledged that priority augmentation requests were necessary after the reduction from the amount proposed to the DBM. The department agreed to submit a formal, prioritized request and undertook specific follow-up actions on monitoring, mining rehabilitation, and approval thresholds.

Outcome The committee approved an additional 556,617,000 pesos in principle, but the presiding officer qualified the action as subject to executive fiscal space and final apportionment across agencies. Further DENR institutional amendments, including the proposed 400,000,000 rehabilitation funding, were left for formal submission, prioritization, and review by the budget amendments review subcommittee.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Mining monitoring, enforcement, and illegal-mining operations

Members questioned whether the roughly 53.6 million national MGB monitoring budget and the 12.829 million Caraga regional budget were adequate for illegal-mining enforcement, particularly in Dinagat Island. DENR committed to visit Dinagat, review mining claims, issue a proper public statement, and consider closure where warranted, but no final closure decision was recorded. Rep. Alexander Pimentel pressed DENR to release 10 seized conveyances in a Surigao del Sur case, and the secretary assured him that release would occur the following day. Members also sought action on Chinese nationals in illegal mining, small-scale mining applications, white-clay extraction and stockpiles, and quarry permits; the agency committed to reports, inspections, operator lists, and coordination. The agency stated that small-scale mining was capped at 50,000 metric tons per annum and cited 3.1 billion pesos for EMB and 1.89 billion for MGB. The hearing ended with several actions committed but with the Dinagat closure, white-clay seizure order, and mangrove earth-balling suspension unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DENR and the Mines and Geosciences Bureau had sufficient budget, personnel, and authority to monitor mining and quarrying, stop illegal operations, and act on confiscation, closure, and permit-compliance issues. Members also sought specific follow-through on Dinagat Island, small-scale mining, white-clay stockpiles, quarry permits, and mining claims.

DENR maintained that monitoring, enforcement, seizure, confiscation, and environmental-compliance functions were being carried out under the Mining Act and related regulations, while acknowledging regional staffing and monitoring limitations. The agency repeatedly committed to site visits, claims and permit reviews, reports, equipment release, operator lists, and coordination with regional offices, but several requested actions remained subject to evaluation or verification.

Outcome The agency provided budget and regulatory explanations and made multiple commitments, including a Dinagat visit and claims review, equipment release, reports and operator lists, permit inspections, and an assessment before plenary. Closure of Dinagat mining, issuance of a white-clay seizure order, suspension of mangrove earth-balling, and several enforcement questions remained subject to further verification or agency action.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Mining permits, FTAAs, MPSAs, and small-scale mining regulation

Members questioned DENR on illegal mining involving Chinese nationals, FTAA renewals, dredging permits, MPSA assignments and operating agreements, small-scale mining applications, and contested exploration permits in Nueva Vizcaya. DENR reported six approved FTAAs, said renewal extensions could apply in force-majeure cases, and described public consultation at the project-feasibility and ECC stages. It said small-scale mining was limited to 50,000 metric tons per annum and committed to a one-stop shop in Davao de Oro, inspections, and submission of operator lists. MGB said one operator per MPSA had been prohibited by policy in 2021 or 2022 and committed to investigate the Mount Sinai and Eastern Samar arrangements. On critical minerals, DENR cited about 9,000,000 hectares of potentially mineralized land, current exploration funding of 157,000,000, a proposed MGB budget of 1,577,000,000, and only 2% of the potential area explored. The discussion landed on multiple agency commitments, while the allocation of mining proceeds for exploration and the suspension of mangrove earth-balling remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status and regulatory basis of mining permits, FTAAs, MPSAs, operating agreements, and small-scale mining applications. It also examined whether DENR had adequate guidelines, enforcement capacity, consultation procedures, rehabilitation requirements, and funding for mineral exploration and critical-mineral development.

DENR said mining regulation should proceed under existing environmental, permitting, progressive-rehabilitation, consultation, and small-scale-mining rules while new Executive Order 122 guidelines and a critical-minerals list were developed. The agency supported regulated mineral development and value addition but acknowledged the need for additional investigation, inspections, reports, policy review, and exploration funding.

Outcome The hearing produced agency answers on FTAA status, small-scale mining limits, MPSA operating arrangements, exploration permits, and critical-mineral policy, but several matters remained under investigation. DENR and MGB undertook to submit reports and lists, conduct inspections and assessments, organize a Davao de Oro one-stop shop, and report on the Mount Sinai case before plenary; the proposed use of mining proceeds and the requested suspension of mangrove earth-balling were left for further action.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Land management, surveys, patents, foreshore tenure, and reversion

DENR presented land titling as a priority, with a target of up to 43,000 patents, while its Land Management Bureau acknowledged that survey-dispute funding was insufficient and that regional offices handled the work. Rep. Rodriguez secured committee approval of an additional 556,617,000 pesos for land management, foreshore mapping, patent issuance, the Land Management Bureau building, and water resources, subject to fiscal space. A member raised the 1,014.92-hectare Wanderlust Corporation claim in Siroma, and the Secretary said DENR was completing a survey and targeting a reversion filing in the second week of October limited to forest lands. Members also sought funding and action for Cordillera forest reserves, solid-waste disposal sites, a proposed marine protected area, and development options for built-up forest land. MGB committed to investigate contested Nueva Vizcaya exploration activities, while the Secretary committed to a biophysical assessment for possible reclassification. The chair required DENR to submit a formal, prioritized request for additional funding before further budget deliberation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DENR would fund and administer land surveys, dispute resolution, patents, foreshore tenure, land classification, and reversion proceedings. Members also asked whether specific forest, protected-area, and land-management concerns would receive funding or agency action.

DENR said land surveys, dispute resolution, patent issuance, foreshore delineation, and land-management activities were being implemented through regional offices and bureau programs but were constrained by limited funding. The department maintained that timberland and bodies of water could not lawfully be included in private titles, committed to pursue the Siroma reversion case after completing the survey, and offered further assessments, coordination, and tenure or reclassification options for other land concerns.

Outcome The committee approved an additional 556,617,000 pesos for DENR, but the addition remained subject to available fiscal space and final allocation. Several land matters were answered or assigned follow-up action, while the Siroma reversion filing, survey-record search, Nueva Vizcaya assessment, and formal funding submission remained commitments rather than completed outcomes.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Solid-waste management, LGU compliance, and waste-facility funding

Members questioned DENR's role in LGU waste-contract oversight, RA 9003 enforcement, source segregation, flooding, and the availability of waste facilities. DENR said LGUs were primarily responsible, while DENR provided technical assistance for MRFs and solid-waste plans, conducted education campaigns, and monitored sanitary landfills for ECC compliance. Rep. Teves cited 92% LGU compliance, a 95% 2027 target, and only six of 17 Metro Manila LGUs compliant with source segregation; he also cited 2,230,000,000 in 2025 annual DENR appropriations as a possible source of assistance. The commission representative disclosed a very limited budget, described the status of ten-year LGU plans, and reported a resolution recommending activation of barangay solid-waste committees. Rep. Rise linked roughly 12,000 tons a day of Metro Manila garbage and an estimated 30% left in waterways to flooding, while proposing a regional-government approach. Rep. Domogan requested identification or reservation of suitable disposal sites, and DENR committed to coordinate regionally; other requests and enforcement concerns remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DENR, the National Solid Waste Management Commission, and LGUs had adequate authority, funding, facilities, and enforcement mechanisms to comply with RA 9003 and address flooding caused by improper waste disposal. Members also sought commitments on technical assistance, environmental education, waste-facility siting, and requests for additional funding.

DENR maintained that LGUs bear primary responsibility for waste management under RA 9003, while DENR provides technical assistance, education, MRF and planning support, and monitors sanitary-landfill compliance with ECC conditions. The agency acknowledged enforcement and facility-use deficiencies, supported stronger coordination with DILG and DepEd, and undertook to coordinate on regional disposal-site and Metro Manila waste-management concerns.

Outcome The hearing clarified that LGUs retain primary responsibility for waste management and private waste-contract renewals, while DENR monitors environmental compliance and provides technical and educational assistance. Several enforcement, funding, and disposal-site concerns remained open, with agency coordination and document or area submissions undertaken rather than a final funding or compliance resolution.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Flood management, watershed rehabilitation, and nature-based mitigation

Members asked DENR to define its responsibility for waterways, flood prevention, watershed rehabilitation, and coordination with DPWH. DENR said its mandate included environmental impact assessment, wastewater regulation, water-quality management, watershed and river-basin programs, and nature-based solutions complementary to DPWH infrastructure. It cited about 28 million for nature-based solutions, 78 million for integrated water-resource management, 21 million for river-basin operations, and 33 billion for forest development, protection, soil conservation, and related rehabilitation, although the watershed-by-watershed allocation was not provided. DENR said the national and Central Luzon flood frameworks and a unified water database were still being finalized or developed, while the Pampanga initiative remained at the risk-assessment stage. Members pressed for greater mangrove and greening support, and the chair said an additional 30 million would be pursued. DENR also committed to examine the Bulacan Airport’s environmental effects, submit Manila Bay enforcement and rehabilitation information, and continue work on ECC thresholds for flood-control projects.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish DENR’s responsibility for flood prevention, watershed and waterway management, and nature-based mitigation; its coordination with DPWH; and the funding, monitoring, and environmental-clearance requirements for related projects. Members also asked what specific programs and databases would support flood-risk reduction in Central Luzon and Manila Bay.

DENR said its flood-related mandate covered environmental assessment and enforcement, watershed and river-basin management, water-quality regulation, ecosystem restoration, and coordination with DPWH. It presented nature-based solutions as complementary to DPWH’s gray infrastructure, but acknowledged that funding and implementation remained limited and that the national and Central Luzon frameworks and unified database were still being finalized or developed.

Outcome DENR clarified its existing responsibilities and identified funding for watershed management, river-basin operations, nature-based solutions, and Manila Bay enforcement. The flood management framework, Central Luzon nature-based interventions, unified database, Bulacan Airport assessment, and several requested documents remained subject to further review, consultation, or submission.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Protected-area funding, staffing, and forest protection

DENR presented protected-area management and forest landscape restoration as strategic priorities within its proposed budget of about 28 billion, covering 121 legislated protected areas and 15.8 million hectares of classified forest lands. Members questioned the 1,300,000,000 protected-area management budget and learned that allocations generally arose from regional fiscal space, equity considerations, and protected-area management-board proposals rather than a single needs-based formula. Rep. Mario cited Mount Hamiguitan's 16,923 hectares of protected land and 9,000-plus hectare buffer zone and requested a more concrete funding formula, while also criticizing ranger coverage ratios involving as much as 3,000 hectares per ranger. DENR reported National Greening Program targets of 18,000 hectares for planting, 30,375 hectares for enhancement, and 30,000 hectares with a stated budget of 408,000,000, while Rep. Rufus Rodriguez sought an additional 400,000,000 for rehabilitation. Members also raised Cordillera forest-reserve funding, Catanduanes' lack of permanent plantilla positions, and a proposed marine protected area, and DENR described requests to DBM ranging from 1,000 to 1,706 positions. The issues remained dependent on written submissions, DBM approvals, and possible budget augmentation, with DENR undertaking follow-up coordination and documents.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DENR's proposed funding and staffing were sufficient to manage protected areas, protect forests, support National Greening Program priorities, and respond to local conservation and rehabilitation needs. Members also sought a needs-based protected-area funding formula, permanent plantilla positions for rangers, and clearer options for managing forest lands and reserves.

DENR stated that protected-area funding was developed through regional fiscal space, regional proposals, equity considerations, standard administrative costs, and protected-area management-board approvals rather than a single area- or needs-based formula. The agency acknowledged staffing gaps, said it had requested additional permanent positions from DBM, and committed to submit priority-area information and coordinate on local forest and protected-area concerns.

Outcome DENR answered the committee's questions but did not provide a needs-based protected-area funding formula or resolve the forest-ranger and protected-area plantilla shortfalls. The agency committed to submit priority-area information, pursue staffing requests with DBM, coordinate on local protected-area and forest concerns, and support further consideration of budget augmentation.

Environmental impact assessments and ECCs for major projects

Members raised concerns about mining-related tree cutting, quarry and exploration permits, tree-cutting requirements for ADB bridges, New Clark City data centers, the Bulacan Airport ECC, and ECC coverage for flood-control and pumping-station projects. DENR said specific projects required clear descriptions and, where applicable, EIA, ECC processing, consultation, public hearings, and cumulative-impact assessment; it also said the New Clark City master-plan ECC covered about 9,400 hectares while projects within a 1,600-hectare area would require project-specific review. The committee cited an EIA budget of about 251 million, DENR budget figures including a 2027 request of about 28.05 billion, mangrove allocations of 13,900,000 for 2026 and 15,000,015 million for 2027, and a proposed additional 30,000,000 for water-related work. DENR returned the ADB bridge application covering 17 trees, reduced from 21, pending consultation and other requirements, and stated replacement ratios of 100 for naturally growing trees and 50 for planted trees. For Bulacan Airport, DENR undertook to develop terms of reference for an environmental review addressing Pampanga impacts. The hearing ended with commitments for reports, investigations, interagency coordination, and an administrative order clarifying which flood-control projects require ECCs.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DENR evaluates environmental impacts, processes ECC applications, conducts consultations, and enforces mitigation requirements for major infrastructure, energy, industrial, airport, mining, quarrying, and flood-control projects. Members also asked what funding, reviews, and interagency mechanisms were available to support those functions.

DENR said specific projects must be evaluated on the basis of a clear project description and, where applicable, must undergo EIA, public consultation, and ECC processing. The agency said it was coordinating with DPWH, BCDA, regional offices, and other agencies on project reviews, tree-cutting requirements, flood-control classifications, mitigation, and environmental monitoring, but several assessments and reports remained to be completed.

Outcome DENR answered the committee's questions on the general EIA, ECC, consultation, mitigation, and tree-replacement framework, but several project-specific matters were left for reports, written information, investigations, or terms of reference. The Bulacan Airport review, quarry-permit report, New Clark City information, and flood-control classification remained subject to follow-up.

Water resources governance, river basins, and water-district support

DENR presented direct assistance of PHP 124,000,000 for local water districts and described funding for aquifer recharge and digital water governance. Rep. Rodriguez secured approval of an additional 556,617,000 pesos for the DENR budget, including water-resource priorities. Members raised delays involving the Butuan City Water District, insufficient LWUA funding, and the need for a technical review of La Mesa Dam; officials undertook follow-up actions, but the transcript did not show final resolution of those matters. DENR said its flood-management framework remained subject to final review and interagency consultation, while its 2027 water-related allocations included about 78,000,000 for integrated water-resource management, PHP21 million for river-basin organizations, and 28,000,000 for nature-based solutions. Members also pressed for a unified water database and stronger watershed rehabilitation, with DENR identifying 131 critical watersheds and 16 priority landscapes. The hearing left the framework, database, water-district financing needs, and dam review as committed or continuing actions rather than fully resolved outcomes.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DENR and its attached agencies would finance and coordinate water-resource management, river-basin planning, watershed rehabilitation, flood mitigation, and support for water districts. Members also asked whether agencies had adequate authority, data systems, and technical capacity to address water-district delays, dam safety, and disputes involving joint-venture operators.

DENR said its water mandate covered water-resource regulation, managed aquifer recharge, digital and regionalized water governance, river-basin operations, watershed management, and nature-based flood mitigation. It acknowledged that available funding and monitoring capacity were insufficient, and said the flood-management framework and unified database still required further review, consultation, approval, and funding.

Outcome The DENR budget was approved with an additional 556,617,000 pesos, while the committee also recorded requests for more LWUA funding and follow-up on La Mesa Dam, Butuan water-district documents, the flood-management framework, and a unified database. Several technical and institutional matters remained dependent on DBM approval, interagency consultation, or future review.

Members also sought needs-based protected-area funding, more forest rangers, and detailed watershed funding; DENR committed to several submissions, but the allocation formulas and some figures remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DENR would fund and implement forest restoration, the National Greening Program, watershed rehabilitation, protected-area management, and mine rehabilitation. Members also asked whether DENR had adequate enforcement, staffing, allocation formulas, and safeguards against abusive mining and deforestation.

DENR said it was shifting the National Greening Program toward landscape restoration and applying progressive rehabilitation to mining operations, requiring disturbed areas to be rehabilitated before operators moved to new areas. It said watershed and protected-area funding was largely structured through regional fiscal space and approved activities, while it undertook to investigate mining allegations, revisit approval thresholds, and submit requested priority-area information.

Outcome The hearing produced commitments to investigate mining-related tree cutting and rehabilitation, meet with Eastern Samar stakeholders, submit mining-policy and NGP information, and revisit stewardship-approval thresholds. The proposed additional rehabilitation funding, protected-area allocation formula, complete watershed allocation data, and consistent forest-ranger ratio remained open.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Mangrove rehabilitation and earth-balling policy

Leila de Lima questioned whether DENR had a mangrove rehabilitation budget and challenged the October 2025 memorandum allowing mangrove earth-balling for infrastructure projects. DENR said cutting mangroves was prohibited, earth-balling was allowed under a mitigation hierarchy, and a survival-rate study involving its research and biodiversity bureaus and civil-society groups was still underway. The agency projected completion of the study by December and a new policy in early 2027, but Delima and the Chair questioned the memorandum's scientific basis and the claimed survival results. Delima requested suspension of earth-balling, and the Secretary said DENR would evaluate the suggestion. A separate congresswoman pressed for mangrove planting as natural flood control; DENR cited 13,900,000 for 2026, a 200-hectare target, and a stated 2027 allocation of 15,000,015 million, while the Chair undertook to seek an additional 30,000,000.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DENR had adequate funding for mangrove rehabilitation and planting, and what natural flood-control measures it was implementing. It also sought to determine the scientific, legal, and consultative basis for allowing mangrove earth-balling and whether the interim memorandum had effectively become a permanent policy.

DENR maintained that mangrove cutting was prohibited by law and that earth-balling was the permitted alternative when projects could not avoid or minimize impacts. The agency said the interim memorandum had been issued in response to project requests, that earth-balling was subject to mitigation and offsetting requirements, and that a survival-rate study and consultative policy process were still underway.

Outcome The scientific basis and survival rate of mangrove earth-balling remained contested, and the Chair's request for suspension was not granted during the hearing; DENR undertook only to evaluate it. On funding, DENR stated its 2026 and 2027 allocations, while the Chair undertook to seek additional funding.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · unresolved

Critical-mineral exploration and mineral-reservation program

Rep. Brian asked DENR to clarify the guidelines and safeguards required under EO 122, and DENR cited progressive rehabilitation and a planned critical-minerals list. Rep. Reniko then asked DENR and MGB to implement a national exploration and mineral-reservation program and requested the United States-Philippines MOU. MGB said exploration was continuing for minerals including gold, copper, and nickel, while DENR said domestic processing and value-adding were policy objectives. The secretary cited current exploration funding of about 157 million, and MGB cited a proposal of about 1.577 billion while saying more resources were needed. Members proposed using a percentage of mineral-related proceeds for exploration and development, and MGB identified only 2% of the prospective area as explored and 17 highly prospective areas for prioritization. The matter remained unresolved pending policy documents, the MOU, and possible legislative action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DENR and MGB would implement EO 122, identify and reserve critical-mineral deposits, and determine whether the Philippines had sufficient reserves for feasible domestic processing. Members also asked what exploration funding was needed and whether mineral-related proceeds could be reused for exploration and resource development.

DENR and MGB supported EO 122 as a framework for identifying critical minerals, strengthening exploration, improving environmental safeguards, and developing domestic processing and value-adding. The agencies said exploration was continuing but required substantially more resources; they also identified mineral-reservation royalties as a possible source of funding, subject to further legislative work.

Outcome The agencies described ongoing implementation of EO 122, exploration, critical-mineral identification, and mineral-reservation work, but did not establish whether reserves were sufficient or processing was feasible at scale. A policy submission, the MOU, and possible legislation on reusing proceeds were left for follow-up.

Geohazard, liquefaction, and elevation mapping for land-use decisions

A member asked DENR and MGB to integrate liquefaction data into geohazard maps used for building permits, zoning, CLUPs, and infrastructure decisions, citing a magnitude 7.8 event and a reported 38% liquefaction figure. MGB said Administrative Order 2000-28 already required engineering geological and geohazard assessments before infrastructure projects and that hazard maps could be integrated for local land-use planning. Jay Vergara raised additional concerns involving elevation references, permitting, agency coordination, and gravel-tax collections of about 400,935 in 2022 and 1,034,880 in 2,023. The Secretary and MGB Central committed to establish a technical working group with DPWH and other agencies and to study and report on the matter. Congressman Clayton separately sought review of exploration permits in Nueva Vizcaya, citing protests, alleged lack of consultation, and possible overlap with forest reserves, ancestral domains, and watersheds. MGB said operations were suspended and an investigation would be conducted, while DENR committed to a biophysical assessment supporting possible land reclassification.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether liquefaction and other geohazard data were being integrated into maps used for building permits, zoning, CLUPs, and infrastructure planning. It also sought clarification on elevation references, interagency coordination, mining-permit reviews in Nueva Vizcaya, and the classification of occupied forest or public land.

DENR-MGB stated that geohazard assessment is already required for infrastructure projects under Administrative Order 2000-28, with private geologists preparing assessments and DENR-MGB reviewing them. The agency said hazard layers can be integrated for CLUPs and committed to coordinate on a technical working group, investigate the Nueva Vizcaya exploration allegations, and conduct a biophysical assessment for possible land reclassification.

Outcome The geohazard issue led to agency confirmation that hazard layers could be integrated and to commitments for interagency coordination and CLUP review. The Nueva Vizcaya permit and land-classification concerns remained subject to investigation, assessment, and possible subsequent legislation.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

Manila Bay rehabilitation, pollution enforcement, and relocation

Congresswoman York asked what the DENR was doing on natural flood control in the Manila Bay area and pressed for more mangrove funding. The DENR cited mangrove planting, Estero Rangers, a 200-hectare 2026 target, 13,900,000 for 2026, and a 2027 figure transcribed as 15,000,015 million. The chair committed to fighting for an additional 30,000,000, while the member advocated 30,000,000 a year for ten years. York also sought Pampanga's inclusion in the Bulacan Airport environmental assessment and ECC mitigation measures; the DENR committed to coordinate with the region and formulate terms of reference. Sarah Elago asked about the Manila Bay strategy through 2031, relocation and resettlement, funding, enforcement collections, and a status report. The DENR described five key result areas and reported inspections of 67,535 establishments, 16,722 notices of violation, 350 cease-and-desist orders, and 191 ex parte orders, while committing to submit collection and rehabilitation-status data.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what natural flood-control and mangrove measures the DENR was implementing in the Manila Bay area, and whether funding was adequate. It also asked about the Bulacan Airport's environmental impacts on Pampanga, Manila Bay rehabilitation planning and funding through 2031, pollution-enforcement results, collections, and relocation requirements.

The DENR said Manila Bay rehabilitation was being implemented through five key result areas covering liquid waste, solid waste, informal settlers, ecosystem rehabilitation, and enforcement. It said mangrove planting and ranger deployments were continuing, enforcement actions were being taken against wastewater dischargers, and it would examine the Bulacan Airport's possible environmental impact on Pampanga and formulate terms of reference for an assessment.

Outcome The DENR answered the questions on its natural flood-control program, Manila Bay rehabilitation framework, and enforcement results. Funding expansion, Pampanga's inclusion in the Bulacan Airport assessment and ECC mitigation, and the requested collection and status reports remained subject to the stated commitments.

DENR · 2026-08-26 · committed

E-waste, solar-panel, and lithium-battery waste management

A member questioned whether DENR was ready to manage end-of-life rooftop solar panels and lithium batteries, noting that batteries could be discarded after about 10 years and that disposal could become imminent within two or three years. DENR and the EMB said TSD facilities existed and were being accredited and registered, but the EMB acknowledged the scale concern; no specific nationwide personnel or capacity plan was given. Rep. Remeco then raised 234 e-waste shipments through March 2026, plus additional intercepted shipments, and asked whether they could be returned to their countries of origin. The EMB said it was monitoring recyclers, coordinating with Customs, retaining subsequent shipments onboard, and generally pursuing return of shipments or segregated materials. Rep. Remeco also sought an update on Basel Ban Amendment ratification; DENR said PEZA and DTI had not yet issued certificates of concurrence. The matter therefore landed with agency monitoring and return-related commitments, while ratification and long-term waste capacity remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DENR had the facilities, personnel, and nationwide enforcement capacity to manage end-of-life solar panels and lithium batteries. It also sought clarification on DENR's handling of imported e-waste shipments and the status of the Basel Ban Amendment ratification.

DENR said it had TSD facilities for electronic waste and was accrediting and registering facilities, but the EMB acknowledged that the scale of future solar-panel and lithium-battery waste was a valid concern. On imported e-waste, DENR said it was monitoring recyclers, coordinating with Customs, retaining subsequent shipments onboard where possible, and pursuing segregation and return of materials; Basel Ban Amendment ratification remained dependent on outstanding certificates of concurrence from PEZA and DTI.

Outcome DENR described existing facilities, monitoring, and Customs coordination, but did not provide a concrete nationwide capacity or personnel plan for future solar-panel and lithium-battery waste. The e-waste shipment issue received a qualified answer favoring retention and return, while Basel Ban Amendment ratification remained open because PEZA and DTI had not issued certificates of concurrence.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Flood-control master plans and integrated Metro Manila drainage planning

Rep. Chel Diokno established that DPWH did not have a consolidated national flood-control and drainage plan, although the agency maintained master plans for all 18 major river basins and was updating 14 of them. DPWH said the updates were targeted for the first half of 2027 and supported a national legislative framework while favoring river-basin and locality-level implementation. Rep. Edgar Erice pressed for an integrated Metro Manila plan, and DPWH said an NCR-wide master-plan update would be completed by the end of the year or early the following year, with coordination among local-government plans. Rep. Renee Co cited the 2016 audit concerns and asked about delayed planning and projects that might worsen flooding; DPWH said audits and investigations were ongoing. An Iloilo member sought priority for floodway and drainage studies, and DPWH confirmed 102,000,000 for the feasibility-study update, although the stated combined total of 150,000,000 or 152,000,000 was not resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had a national flood-control and drainage plan, how river-basin and urban plans were being coordinated, and when outdated plans would be completed. Members also asked whether Metro Manila had an integrated, NCR-wide plan and whether specific local studies and floodway projects would be funded and prioritized.

DPWH said a single nationwide flood-control plan was not the preferred operational model; experts had recommended master plans by major river basin and locality, supported by common national principles. The agency nevertheless supported a national framework and committed to updating the 18 major river-basin plans and completing or finalizing an NCR-wide flood-mitigation plan, while coordinating with local governments.

Outcome DPWH gave planning and timing assurances, including updates to the 18 major river-basin plans and an NCR-wide master plan, and confirmed 102,000,000 for the Iloilo feasibility-study update. However, the national-versus-river-basin planning question, the final Metro Manila governance and coordination mechanism, the alleged project-selection problems, and the discrepancy between 150,000,000 and 152,000,000 remained open.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Ghost, substandard, and ineffective flood-control projects

Rep. Chel Diokno questioned the absence of a consolidated national flood-control plan, and Secretary Vince Dizon defended the river-basin and urban-center approach while committing to update the plans by 2027. Members also pressed DPWH on lifestyle checks, contractor disclosures, convergence-program reforms, and nature-based solutions; the agency cited a one-strike policy, 12 blacklisted contractors, and proposed stronger disclosure rules. Rep. Antonio Tinio examined project vetting and central-office allocations, including the 50,000,000 threshold for central implementation, while DPWH cited certificates of implementability, geotagged photographs, and other documentation. Rep. Renee Co raised delayed master plans and projects that may have worsened flooding, and DPWH said audits with investigative agencies were ongoing. Rep. Stephen James Tan asked for the number of ghost projects; DPWH identified two areas, while the member characterized the situation as roughly 10 projects across two districts and about 183 engineering districts. DPWH reported 76% of contracts advertised, 32% awarded, and an 80% target by the end of September, but the ghost-project inventory and the status of flood-aggravating projects remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate nationwide or river-basin flood-control plans, and whether its systems could prevent ghost, double-funded, substandard, or ineffective projects. Members also asked how projects were vetted and audited, how contractors and personnel were disciplined, how appropriations were distributed and implemented, and what reforms or reports DPWH would provide.

DPWH said it was pursuing river-basin and urban-center master plans rather than a single consolidated national plan, while applying common flood-mitigation principles nationwide. It said it had instituted stricter project documentation, certificates of implementability, geotagging, contractor disclosures, blacklisting, audits, and convergence-program reforms, but acknowledged that the systems were not foolproof and that ghost, substandard, planning, and implementation problems remained under assessment.

Outcome DPWH presented reforms and gave commitments to update plans, submit a ghost-project report, strengthen contractor disclosures, and continue audits. The existence and extent of ghost and flood-aggravating projects remained under investigation, and the committee did not receive a final nationwide inventory or definitive resolution.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Distribution of DPWH projects between districts, regions, and central office

Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales raised concerns about weak engineering studies, consultant accountability, district project implementation, and earthquake rehabilitation. Secretary Vince Dizon said proper studies ideally required 5% to 6% of capital outlay—roughly about 30 billion based on 460,000,000,000—but only 6,000,000,000 was budgeted for those activities, and he committed to report on project and rehabilitation concerns. Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned project traceability, leadership and district allocables, and the concentration of funds in the central office; Dizon cited certificates of implementability, geotagging, LGU coordination, and the 50,000,000 implementation threshold. A minority member questioned unusually uniform evacuation-center and social-facility allocations and wide district disparities, but the agency's explanation of five-year planning and interagency site identification did not fully resolve the basis for all allocations. Tinio also questioned why projects were distributed among only some of the 1,099 district engineering offices and warned that amendments and insertions could contribute to delays. Dizon committed to submit reports, justify changes, and move toward stricter, more consolidated and multiyear flood-control programming.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH projects were properly vetted, traceable, and allocated on a needs-based basis among district engineering offices, regional offices, and the central office. Members also questioned whether fragmented project allocations and congressional changes contributed to duplication, weak accountability, and delays, particularly in flood control and post-earthquake rehabilitation.

DPWH said project distribution was governed by certifications of implementability, LGU and RDC coordination, geotagged documentation, and DBM thresholds, with projects above 50,000,000 generally implemented centrally and projects below 50,000,000 generally assigned to district engineering offices. The agency acknowledged that central management and fragmented flood-control implementation were not yet ideal, said it was moving toward stricter and more coordinated programming, and supported multiyear appropriations.

Outcome The agency provided explanations for its vetting controls and central-versus-district implementation rules, but several allocation questions remained open. DPWH undertook to submit reports, verify project and accountability information, address earthquake rehabilitation, justify later changes, and pursue more coherent multiyear flood-control programming.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Fragmented flood-control projects versus concentrated flagship investments

Minority members questioned the basis for district and regional allocations and argued that flood-control funding should respond to need, hazard exposure, and project readiness rather than political or district distribution. They cited annual district allocations ranging from about 36,000,000 to 18 billion, as well as a 2022–2025 allocation of about 8.1 billion for Quezon City's 4th District. A member also criticized flood-control projects below 50,000,000 as fragmented and proposed concentrating resources in a flagship program for priority areas. Secretary Vince Dizon said centralized management was ideal, acknowledged that the current arrangement was not yet ideal, and pointed to stricter controls. He committed DPWH to environmental-impact studies for flood-mitigation projects affecting waterways and agreed that multiyear appropriations were the best solution, leaving the specific allocation formula unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether flood-control funding should be allocated through fragmented district-level projects or concentrated in priority areas under a flagship, needs-based program. It also examined whether environmental-impact and project-preparation requirements should govern flood-control allocations.

DPWH acknowledged that centrally managed and concentrated flood-mitigation programming was ideal and said it was moving toward stricter, more coordinated programming. Secretary Vince Dizon supported multiyear appropriations and committed to environmental-impact studies for flood-mitigation projects affecting waterways, but did not provide a complete resolution of district-level allocation disparities or fragmented projects.

Outcome The agency agreed in principle with more centralized, needs-based, environmentally screened, and multiyear flood-control programming, but the hearing did not settle the specific allocation formula or eliminate fragmented district-level projects. DPWH made a commitment on environmental-impact studies and endorsed multiyear appropriations.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Flood-control facilities, pumping stations, detention basins, and water diversion

Rep. Chel Diokno established that DPWH did not have a single consolidated national flood-control plan, although all 18 major river basins had plans and 14 were being updated, with completion targeted for 2027. Secretary Vince Dizon defended a river-basin and locality-based approach, while supporting detention basins, nature-based measures such as gabions, and upstream interventions. Rep. Roy Gonzales sought a Silang-Santa Rosa diversion or spillway solution, and DPWH cited 82,000,000 for a related feasibility study and undertook to pursue the study next year. Members raised Metro Manila detention sites, Pampanga pumping stations and bridges, Iloilo floodway studies, and dredging; DPWH committed to maintain or complete facilities, confirmed 102,000,000 for the Iloilo study update, and described dredging as a regular maintenance need. The hearing produced several agency commitments, but detention-facility performance targets and the final funding and sequencing of some projects remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had a coherent national and river-basin flood-control plan, how proposed detention, diversion, pumping, dredging, and nature-based facilities would be prioritized and maintained, and whether specific local projects would receive funding or completion commitments. Members also asked for technical studies, measurable flood-mitigation targets, and updates on unfinished facilities and bridges.

DPWH said its flood-control strategy was based on major river-basin and urban-center master plans rather than a single technically uniform national plan, while applying common principles such as upstream interventions, detention basins, needs-based protection, and nature-based measures. The department presented detention facilities, diversion studies, pumping stations, dredging and desilting, and completion of unfinished structures as active or intended priorities, but several site-specific projects remained subject to feasibility studies, technical review, funding, or approval.

Outcome The agency answered the principal planning and technical questions and made commitments on plan updates, the Silang-Santa Rosa study, pumping stations, unfinished bridges, Iloilo studies, and regular dredging. However, the measurable targets for detention facilities, final project sequencing, and funding or approval of several local facilities remained open.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Right-of-way acquisition and landowner compensation funding

Rep. Sarah Elago sought updates and records concerning right-of-way payments and compensation for affected households and small businesses in the ADB Metro Manila Bridges Project. DPWH cited right-of-way obligations close to 90,000,000,009.00 and later described an accumulated obligation of 90,000,000,000. Rep. Mark Cojuangco urged stronger nationwide right-of-way acquisition funding, while Secretary Vince Dizon expressed support. Rep. Howard asked how funds were allocated and was told that payments were prioritized by project, voucher readiness, court order, or negotiated settlement; expropriation cases required a 15% deposit. The Secretary stated an FY 2027 allocation of 15,000,000,020.27, while the exchange also referred to 5,000,000,000 and 5,000,000,020.26 for the current year. Howard requested additional funding because right-of-way payment delays were delaying projects, and Dizon said additional funding would be welcome but made no specific appropriation commitment.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DPWH allocated and prioritized funds for right-of-way acquisition and landowner compensation, including the FY 2027 amount. Members also asked whether additional funding was needed to prevent project delays and requested records on affected households, businesses, and major projects.

DPWH stated that right-of-way payments were prioritized on a project basis, particularly when vouchers were ready and when payments were supported by court orders or negotiated settlements. The agency identified a cumulative obligation of 90,000,000,000 and said additional right-of-way funding would be welcome, but it did not undertake a specific additional appropriation.

Outcome DPWH explained its project-based prioritization process and stated an FY 2027 right-of-way figure of 15,000,000,020.27, against an accumulated obligation cited as 90,000,000,000. Members' requests for records were accepted, but the request for additional right-of-way funding received only a general expression of welcome and no specific commitment.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

FY2025 SAROs, discontinued projects, savings, and fund realignment

Rep. Robert Massal asked Secretary Vince Dizon about FY 2025 projects whose SAROs had been issued but whose SARs were not, including the disposition of their allotments. Dizon cited a total of 90,000,000,000, alternatively stated as 90,300,000,000, with more than 30,000,000,000 attributed to flood control projects, and said projects with incomplete documents were returned to DBM after additional vetting. He agreed to provide the committee with the relevant letters and a list of discontinued projects. Dizon said the funds were effectively declared savings and that much of the budget cover was used for the uplift program, relying on the GAA general provisions and describing the projects as unimplementable or abandoned. Erice then cited DBM records dated 11/27/2025 showing augmentation sourced from declared DPWH savings and sought clarification on whether the affected projects were included. DPWH did not resolve that specific question during the hearing and committed to comply with documentary requirements.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what happened to FY 2025 projects whose SAROs had been issued but whose corresponding SARs were not issued, including the status of their allotments. It also questioned whether the funds were declared savings, how they were used or realigned, and what legal authority supported those actions.

DPWH said projects with missing or incomplete documents were subjected to additional vetting and returned to DBM when they were considered unimplementable or abandoned. It stated that the GAA general provisions provided the legal basis for treating the resulting funds as savings and realigning them, while indicating that DBM would be better positioned to clarify the specific authority and augmentation transactions.

Outcome DPWH explained that the projects were subjected to additional vetting and that funds for projects deemed unimplementable or abandoned were treated as savings under the GAA general provisions. The specific project list, documentary trail, and whether the questioned funds were used for augmentation remained for written submission and further clarification, including from DBM.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

MVUC and the discontinued stand-alone Special Road Fund

Rep. Sidhu Ongwam questioned why the stand-alone Special Road Fund had disappeared from the FY 2027 PAP schedule and been placed under Asset Preservation. He cited the prior amount of 14,833,952,000 and the FY 2027 amount of 15,000,000,000, arguing that the new presentation made the earmarked fund less visible and could narrow its use because bridges were in a separate PAP. DPWH Undersecretary Nick Conti answered that Republic Act 11239 limited MVUC to roads, bridges, and road drainage and that qualifying projects under Asset Preservation Organizational Outcome No. 1 were attributed to MVUC. The agency said the 15,000,000,000 amount had been specified by DBM and offered to submit the detailed project list. Ongwam also raised constitutional, Supreme Court, and prior veto-message concerns, but those issues were not directly resolved. The immediate result was an agency commitment to provide supporting project documentation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the FY 2027 presentation of MVUC collections under the DPWH Asset Preservation Program improperly obscured or narrowed the statutory Special Road Fund. Rep. Sidhu Ongwam also asked whether DPWH requested this treatment or whether it was imposed by DBM.

DPWH stated that the MVUC collections were attributed to qualifying Asset Preservation projects under Organizational Outcome No. 1, consistent with the statutory scope under Republic Act 11239, and that the amount identified by DBM for 2027 was 15,000,000,000. The agency offered to furnish the committee with the detailed list of projects, but did not directly resolve whether DPWH requested the presentation or whether DBM imposed it, nor did it directly answer the constitutional and statutory concerns raised by Ongwam.

Outcome DPWH explained that the 2027 MVUC amount was attributed to qualifying Asset Preservation projects and undertook to provide the project list. The committee's concerns about the loss of a stand-alone line, the treatment of bridges, and the constitutional and statutory implications remained open.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Project vetting, feasibility studies, and detailed engineering capacity

Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales questioned DPWH's allocation for detailed engineering and geotechnical studies, consultant accountability, and the basis for earthquake rehabilitation projects. Secretary Vince Dizon said the ideal allocation was about 5% to 6% of capital outlay—roughly about 30 billion based on the cited 2026 capital outlay—but only 6 billion was budgeted for the studies. He also acknowledged that DPWH lacked the personnel and specialized equipment needed to conduct studies for all 11,000 proposed 2027 projects. Rep. Antonio Tinio examined project traceability, certificates of implementability, geotagged documentation, and the central-office implementation of projects above the 50 million threshold. A congresswoman secured commitments for lists of feasibility-study and tourism-road projects and was told that projects costing 1 billion and above required a feasibility study. DPWH said tourism-road identification would be led by the concerned department, with joint technical validation with DPWH, while foreign-assisted and convergence projects would continue under documented implementation arrangements.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had sufficient funding, personnel, systems, and accountability mechanisms for feasibility studies, detailed engineering, geotechnical investigations, and project validation. Members also asked how projects were assigned, technically validated, and implemented, including convergence and foreign-assisted projects.

DPWH said proper feasibility studies, detailed engineering, geotechnical work, certificates of implementability, geotagged documentation, and local-government coordination were necessary safeguards, but acknowledged that funding, personnel, and specialized equipment were insufficient for the full project workload. The agency maintained that implementation generally followed DBM thresholds and program-specific rules, with joint validation for convergence projects and commitments to submit requested lists and reports.

Outcome DPWH acknowledged substantial gaps in study funding and internal technical capacity, while defending its project-vetting and implementation controls. The department undertook to provide lists, reports, and follow-up on consultant accountability and earthquake rehabilitation, but the adequacy of funding, the final responsibility for some projects, and the accountability record remained open.

Rufus Rodriguez sought support for Cagayan de Oro bypass roads and bridges, citing about 34 billion for the Coastal Bypass Road, about 7 billion for the Eastern Interior Road, and additional funding for local bridges and walkways. Earthquake rehabilitation, bridge safety, and seismic retrofitting

Rep. Cherilyn Banias Lugrales questioned DPWH's allocation and capacity for geotechnical and detailed engineering studies, citing earthquake-related structural damage and soil-liquefaction risks. Secretary Vince Dizon said the department ideally needed 5% to 6% of capital outlay for such work—roughly about 30 billion based on 460 billion—but had only 6 billion in 2026. He acknowledged that DPWH lacked the personnel and equipment to conduct studies for all 11,000 proposed 2027 projects and committed to seek additional funds and report on consultant accountability and procurement requirements. Lugrales also raised her district's reduction from about 1.7 billion to more or less 500 million after a 7.8 earthquake, and Dizon committed to having regional and district officials address rehabilitation of yellow- and red-tagged facilities. Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores raised a dangerous critical bridge whose delays cost around 147 million per day, and Dizon cited retrofit and replacement amounts, including 150,000,000 and unclear figures spoken as 150.20 26 and 600,000,020.27. Rep. Salvador Pleyto requested plans for retrofitting critical infrastructure and inspecting buildings for the West Valley Fault risk, and Dizon committed to submit the ongoing World Bank-funded NCR assessment.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate resources, technical capacity, and accountability mechanisms for geotechnical studies and the rehabilitation or retrofitting of earthquake-damaged and critical bridges. It also sought commitments on completing bridge projects, assessing critical infrastructure, and reporting measurable resilience and rehabilitation plans.

DPWH acknowledged that funding and capacity for feasibility studies, detailed engineering, and geotechnical investigations were inadequate, and that the department was not yet equipped to perform all studies internally. It stated that it would address earthquake-damaged facilities, pursue retrofit or replacement of critical bridges through a nationwide strategy, use multiyear appropriations for major projects, and submit the ongoing World Bank-funded NCR assessment.

Outcome DPWH gave assurances on district rehabilitation, critical-bridge retrofit or replacement, and a nationwide bridge strategy, but several requested details remained subject to verification, reports, or ongoing assessments. The World Bank-funded NCR assessment and specific rehabilitation and accountability information had not yet been submitted during the hearing.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

National-road maintenance and post-construction asset preservation

Rep. Sidhu Ongwam questioned why the MVUC special road fund was no longer displayed as a standalone FY 2027 program and argued that embedding it in Asset Preservation reduced legislative visibility. DPWH Undersecretary Nick Conti and Secretary Vince Dizon said the amount was attributed to itemized Asset Preservation projects pursuant to the statutory limits on MVUC use and identified the 2027 amount as about 15 billion. DPWH undertook to furnish the committee with the relevant project lists, but the record did not resolve Ongwam's concerns about bridges, post-enactment disaggregation, or the legality of the presentation. Rep. Michael Pan raised right-of-way and routine and post-construction maintenance problems affecting national highways, particularly in Samar. The secretary committed to address post-construction maintenance and said national roads remained DPWH's primary mandate, while local-road concerns involving remote and island municipalities were left for continuing coordination with regional and district offices.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the motor vehicle users charge (MVUC) collections were properly and visibly appropriated for their statutory purposes, including roads, bridges, and drainage. Members also sought assurance that DPWH would adequately fund routine and post-construction maintenance of national highways while addressing right-of-way and local-road concerns in remote areas.

DPWH stated that the 2027 MVUC amount was attributed to itemized projects under Asset Preservation Organizational Outcome No. 1 and remained limited to the statutory purposes of construction, upgrading, repair, and rehabilitation of roads, bridges, and road drainage. The department said it could furnish the committee with the project list and undertook to address post-construction maintenance, while maintaining that national roads were its primary mandate and local roads would be considered through regional and district offices.

Outcome DPWH explained that the 15,000,000,000 MVUC amount was attributed to itemized Asset Preservation projects and undertook to provide supporting project information, but the committee's concerns about visibility, the treatment of bridges, and possible statutory or constitutional issues were not definitively resolved. DPWH separately committed to address post-construction maintenance, while the broader Samar local-road and right-of-way concerns remained subject to further agency action.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Transparency, contractor accountability, and anti-corruption controls

Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked Secretary Vince Dizon to make DPWH project information, procurement records, financial data, monitoring results, contractor ratings, and complaints publicly accessible. Dizon said the Transparency Portal already covered completed and ongoing projects, bidding livestreams, satellite-based monitoring, and supporting documents for PLN 11,000 plus projects, and committed to quarterly reports. Rep. Chel Diokno pressed DPWH on the absence of a consolidated national flood-control plan, lifestyle checks, contractor disclosures, convergence-program reforms, and nature-based solutions; Dizon cited plans for all 18 major river basins, with 14 being updated, and a target of 2027 for completion. Rep. Renee Co asked about blacklisting, delayed master plans, and audits, and DPWH reported 12 blacklisted contractors and ongoing investigations. Eli San Fernando questioned Redicon and R2 Builders, including figures of 9,000,000,000 and 2,700,000,000 pesos, and raised an alleged worker-wage shortfall involving 60 pesos over an 85 pesos rate. The agency's response on that allegation was garbled, leaving that issue unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had effective transparency, disclosure, monitoring, auditing, and contractor-accountability mechanisms to protect public funds. Members also asked what information would be published, how anti-corruption controls were being implemented, and whether DPWH would act on questionable contracts, project quality, and worker-wage compliance.

DPWH said it was institutionalizing transparency through a public portal containing project, bidding, monitoring, and supporting documentation, while developing quarterly reporting, enhanced disclosures, and closer coordination with the Ombudsman, SEC, and investigative agencies. It also defended river-basin-based planning and program reforms, reported that 12 contractors had been blacklisted, and said audits and master-plan updates were ongoing; however, the response on R2 Builders' wage compliance was unclear.

Outcome The agency made commitments on quarterly portal reporting, enhanced contractor disclosures, nature-based-solution reporting, master-plan updates, and submission of contractor information. Blacklisting and audits were reported as ongoing, but the wage-compliance allegation involving R2 Builders and several details concerning contractor accountability remained unresolved.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Classroom construction, evacuation centers, and social-facility appropriations

A minority member questioned the specificity and allocation basis of regional appropriations for evacuation centers, PWD facilities, and senior-citizen facilities, citing 180,000,000, 5,000,000, and 20,000,000. The agency said evacuation-center sites and amounts were governed by a five-year plan and required coordination, validation, and implementability checks, while the Chair requested a district-by-district breakdown. Congressman Joseph Tan discussed project convergence, foreign-assisted projects, and a total DPWH amount of about 200 plus billion pesos, but the exchange did not produce a detailed accounting. Another member said only 30% of the FY2026 budget had been awarded and warned that the delay threatened the 6,000-classroom target. Secretary Vince Dizon corrected the reported classroom data and cited a 20,000,000,000 DPWH budget for 6,000 classrooms, while explaining that construction commonly began in the third quarter after validation and bidding. The Chair agreed to bring forward a proposal for clearer GAA line items and closer coordination or grouping of classroom funds with DepEd, leaving the broader accountability questions unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether FY2027 appropriations for evacuation centers, facilities for persons with disabilities and senior citizens, and classrooms were sufficiently specific, needs-based, and implementable. Members also questioned whether project-award delays and broad GAA line items were undermining accountability and the target to complete 6,000 classrooms.

DPWH said project allocations were subject to implementability, site, coordination, and validation requirements, and that evacuation-center sites and amounts were determined under a five-year plan with other disaster-management agencies. On classrooms, DPWH said third-quarter starts and October-November bidding were longstanding consequences of coordination and validation, while supporting closer grouping of the budget with DepEd and clearer planning.

Outcome The Chair undertook to raise the proposal for clearer GAA line items, but the record did not resolve the disputed allocation basis, the district figures, or the classroom-award delay. The issue therefore remained open subject to the requested breakdown and further committee consideration.

DPWH · 2026-08-26 · committed

Pedestrian, bicycle, sidewalk, and PWD infrastructure

Rep. Renee Co pressed DPWH to prioritize pedestrians and cyclists, separate pedestrian projects from general rehabilitation, and provide wider sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and improved PWD facilities. DPWH cited a pedestrian-walkway expansion cost of about 6 billion, an original EDSA project cost of about 17 billion, EDSA pedestrian widths ranging from a minimum of 2.8 meters to as much as five meters, and a minimum bike-lane width of 1.5 meters. Co also cited a total DPWH budget of roughly 644 billion and a 510 million allocation for PWD, elderly, senior, and gender-responsive facilities, while the secretary said the PWD budget would increase three times from 170 million. Rep. Timothy Titan then asked for stronger anti-overloading enforcement, additional weighing facilities, multiyear bridge funding, and two more pedestrian overpasses along the Maharlika Highway. Secretary Vince Dizon committed to doing his best to enforce anti-overloading rules and suggested multiyear bridge appropriations from 2027 onward, but no definitive action on the overpass request was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's FY2027 program adequately funded pedestrianization, protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and facilities for persons with disabilities, and whether the agency would address unsafe bridges, overloaded trucks, and requested pedestrian overpasses. Members also pressed DPWH on applicable standards, enforcement, and multiyear infrastructure planning.

DPWH said pedestrian widths and bike-lane standards were being considered, but pedestrian facilities remained part of broader rehabilitation projects and were constrained by available space. The agency also supported stronger anti-overloading enforcement, indicated that multiyear bridge appropriations could be pursued from 2027 onward, and did not record a clear disposition on the requested pedestrian overpasses.

Outcome DPWH acknowledged the need for pedestrian, bicycle, and PWD facilities and indicated that the PWD allocation would increase, but pedestrian projects were still embedded in broader rehabilitation work. The secretary committed to anti-overloading enforcement and discussed multiyear bridge funding, while the pedestrian-overpass request remained without a recorded agency disposition.

Foreign-assisted, convergence, tourism-road, and special infrastructure projects

Rep. Chel Diokno and another congresswoman pressed DPWH on convergence-program reforms, feasibility-study funding, and responsibility for tourism roads. DPWH said sector departments would identify and prioritize their own projects, while DPWH would participate in joint technical validation and implementation; it also said projects costing 1,000,000,000 and above required a feasibility study. The agency cited 130,000,000 in counterpart funding and 350,000,000 for the Southern Gate to Surigao feasibility study, while Rep. Tan referred to a total DPWH amount of 200 plus billion pesos. Rep. Tan also raised approval documents, foreign-assisted projects, project clustering, and figures that were partly garbled in the transcript. A Pampanga member separately urged progress on the Korea-assisted flood-control project's second part, while DPWH described dredging as a critical and regular maintenance activity. DPWH undertook to submit lists of major feasibility-study projects and ongoing Trip C projects, but the status of several foreign-assisted and Korea-assisted items remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DPWH was restructuring convergence and special infrastructure programs, including which agencies would identify, validate, and implement sector-specific projects. Members also asked about feasibility-study requirements, foreign-assisted projects, project clustering, the total DPWH allocation, and the status of a Korea-assisted flood-control project.

DPWH said it was removing or tightening convergence-program components and assigning sector-specific project identification to the departments with primary responsibility, while retaining joint technical validation and implementation with DPWH where appropriate. It supported feasibility studies before major projects proceeded, continued foreign-assisted and critical projects, and viewed dredging as a necessary regular flood-mitigation maintenance activity.

Outcome DPWH explained the intended restructuring of convergence programs and accepted requests to submit project lists, but several questions on ongoing Trip C appropriations, foreign-assisted projects, clustering figures, and the Korea-assisted project's approval status remained unclear. The Korea-assisted project was flagged for follow-up rather than resolved during the exchange.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Flood mitigation, drainage, and river-basin master-plan alignment

Bivensio Dizon presented flood mitigation as a 2027 priority and said DPWH would shift toward basin-wide flood management, using major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans. He cited 83.84 billion in locally funded 2027 flood-mitigation projects and described ongoing dredging and desilting needs after more than twelve years without dredging major rivers. Representative Tobit Janko pressed for full publication of projects and allocations by legislative district, while Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula requested complete master-plan data and tables showing whether 2025–2027 projects aligned with those plans. DPWH's flood-mitigation director said the agency was updating plans for all 18 major river basins with catchment areas of 1,400 square kilometer and up, with climate-change updating every three years. Bivensio Dizon undertook to provide the requested alignment information and said a dredging and desilting plan was being prepared. A majority member also identified nationwide lump-sum items of 369,000,000 for dredging and waterway cleaning and 500,000,000 for drainage and flood-mitigation repairs, which DPWH said would be implemented based on need.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's flood-mitigation, drainage, dredging, and desilting projects were guided by current river-basin and local drainage master plans. It also sought the plans' status, the projects aligned with them, and how nationwide flood-mitigation lump-sum items would be allocated.

DPWH said flood mitigation should be guided by major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans, with projects coordinated across national, regional, district, and local levels. The department said it was updating plans for all 18 major river basins, incorporating climate-change considerations, and allocating dredging, drainage, and other flood-mitigation works based on need, while relying in some cases on augmentation and savings.

Outcome DPWH answered the committee's questions in principle and undertook to submit master-plan data, project-alignment tables, district-level project information, and a dredging and desilting plan. The record did not show that the requested alignment tables or plan had been submitted during the hearing.
