DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Project rationalization and DPWH absorptive capacity

Bivensio Dizon said DPWH had reduced project numbers by eliminating duplicate and overlapping projects, removing projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program, and focusing on larger projects that implementing offices could absorb. He said DPWH had previously reached about 25,000 projects, compared with a typical average of 20,000, and that some offices had carried two to four times their ideal workload. The agency also reported that its 2026 capital outlay involved about 460 billion, with 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded as of 08/23/2026, and targeted 80% awards by the end of September. Representative Mike Tan asked whether DPWH had conservatively estimated implementing-office capacity and requested rough capacity figures. Yusick Ador answered that the ideal was seven projects per PE and requested congressional support for additional engineers. Tan also sought support for ongoing convergence projects, but Dizon deferred the matter to Congress while citing executive policies.

Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish whether DPWH had rationalized its project portfolio to match the capacity of its implementing offices and whether the 2027 budget should prioritize projects that could realistically be delivered. It also examined the effect of delayed releases, early procurement, ongoing-project funding, and convergence-program reforms on DPWH’s implementation capacity.

DPWH said it was rationalizing projects to eliminate duplication, reduce small-ticket projects, focus on larger priorities, and bring project volume closer to the capacity of district and regional implementing offices. It acknowledged implementation constraints from late release of the 2026 capital outlay, sought additional engineers, committed to help identify priority and unfinished projects, and deferred the treatment and funding of ongoing convergence projects to Congress while complying with executive policies.

Outcome The committee received DPWH’s explanation of project rationalization and the stated implementing-office capacity benchmark, including seven projects per PE and the district-office example. The question of whether ongoing convergence projects would be funded, and the final allocation of projects among implementing offices, was left for congressional consideration and was not resolved in the exchange.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

District-level project and congressional-allocation transparency

Rep. Tobit Janko raised the need for full, nonselective transparency in DPWH infrastructure allocations and requested publication by region, legislative district, party-list representative, and line item. DPWH said its portal already carried roughly ten years of project records and supporting documents, but acknowledged that its existing summary followed district engineering offices rather than legislative districts. Bivensio Dizon committed to submit and publish the legislative-district NEP and supporting information, initially requested before the end of the meeting and later set by the chair for before 01:00. Rep. Janko also cited a flood-control example involving 900 million, 1 billion, and 100 million to show why phased project amounts should be disclosed. Dizon described multiyear appropriations as the policy direction for ongoing projects and agreed to follow the process for identifying congressional amendments or insertions. The chair clarified that the submission had to cover all legislative districts nationwide, but the transcript did not establish that delivery or publication had already occurred.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's proposed 2027 projects and allocations could be published by region and by legislative district, including party-list districts and project-level amounts. It also examined whether multiyear treatment and disclosure of congressional amendments would improve transparency and manage expectations for phased projects.

DPWH stated that its transparency portal already contained project information, including ongoing projects and supporting documents, but acknowledged that its summary was organized by district engineering office rather than legislative district. Bivensio Dizon committed to provide and publish the NEP and supporting information by legislative district and line item, and supported multiyear appropriations as a policy direction for ongoing and phased projects.

Outcome The issue landed with DPWH commitments to submit and publish the NEP and project information by legislative district and line item, and to cover all legislative districts rather than only Rep. Janko's district. The transcript does not confirm that the documents were actually submitted or published during the hearing.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Unfinished, ongoing, and delayed DPWH projects

The DPWH presenter attributed slow 2026 procurement to the late release of roughly 460 billion in capital-outlay projects and reported 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded out of 17,764 projects. DPWH targeted 80% awards by the end of September 2026. Ian Amatong pressed for stronger project-engineer oversight, rapid completion of a hospital, and a policy prioritizing unfinished roads and other ongoing works; Bivensio Dizon agreed but said staffing and DBM rules constrained DPWH. Dizon said the department would seek additional engineer items and a possible exemption for continuing projects, and would provide an update on the Quezon Bridge. Dadah Kiram Ismula requested data on 50 ODA projects, commitment fees, and possible penalties, citing around 3,400,000,000 pesos in fees; DPWH undertook to submit the information. Mike Tan then questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH reiterated the need for additional engineers and agreed to help identify unfinished projects. The issue landed with commitments for follow-up, while key policy and funding questions remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why DPWH projects remained unfinished, delayed, or slow to be awarded and whether the department had sufficient implementation and supervisory capacity. Members also asked DPWH to prioritize ongoing works, complete hospitals and other unfinished projects, and account for delay-related commitment fees and other charges.

DPWH attributed delays primarily to the late release of roughly 460,000,000,000 in 2026 capital-outlay projects and to limited project-engineer capacity. The department agreed that unfinished and ongoing projects should be prioritized, sought congressional help with DBM for additional engineers and possible exemptions for continuing projects, and undertook to submit project, bridge, ODA, and fee data.

Outcome DPWH acknowledged the delays and capacity constraints and agreed in principle that ongoing and unfinished projects should be prioritized. Several requested datasets and project updates were promised, but the DBM exemption, additional staffing, hospital completion schedule, and broader funding prioritization remained subject to further action.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Road widening and national road-system priorities

Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan raised the proposed national road system, and Bivensio Dizon said DPWH was rationalizing widening toward the most dilapidated and priority sections. Libanan then pressed for a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, for which Dizon cited allocations of 120,000,000 and later 130,000,000, although the year-by-year breakdown was unclear. Dizon described the bridge as roughly 20 kilometers long, cited economic returns of 33% and 42%, and estimated six years for construction; he also committed to consider tourism in the evaluation. Representative Ian Amatong raised inadequate project-engineer coverage, citing an actual workload of one engineer for 30 projects against an ideal one-to-seven or one-to-10 ratio, and Dizon sought committee help for more DBM items. Amatong also sought faster hospital completion and prioritization of unfinished approach works, while Dizon agreed in principle and said DPWH would pursue a DBM exemption and prioritize ongoing projects. The chair additionally called for stronger preconstruction coordination, and Dizon agreed that such activities were critical.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DPWH was prioritizing road widening within the proposed national road system and whether major inter-island links, particularly the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, were feasible and adequately funded. It also examined whether project oversight, hospital construction, unfinished works, and preconstruction coordination were sufficient to ensure that district infrastructure priorities were delivered.

DPWH said road widening should be rationalized and directed to the most dilapidated or otherwise priority sections rather than pursued indiscriminately. It supported a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, sought more project-engineer positions, agreed that unfinished works should be prioritized, and was willing to pursue a DBM exemption for continuing hospital projects, although funding and policy decisions remained partly outside DPWH's control.

Outcome DPWH committed to funding and advancing the Sorsogon–Northern Samar feasibility study, subject to subsequent funding and approval, and agreed to examine tourism considerations. Road-widening priorities were not contested after DPWH's explanation, but the hospital exemption, additional project-engineer items, and Quezon Bridge estimates remained dependent on DBM or later agency follow-up.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Sorsogon–Northern Samar and other major bridge projects

Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan asked DPWH to establish the feasibility of the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, including its economic return, timetable, and financing. Bivensio Dizon said the project was a critical Luzon–Visayas link and cited 120,000,000, later correcting or supplementing the figure with 130,000,000 for the feasibility study. He described the link as roughly 20 kilometers, cited a 42% economic rate of return, identified ADB, Korea, JICA, and AIIB as possible funders, and estimated six years for construction after feasibility and approvals. The Chair required tourism benefits to be considered in the evaluation, and the Secretary agreed. Rep. Ian Amatong and Rep. Mike Tan separately raised concerns about project-engineer workloads, technical assignment, absorptive capacity, and unfinished or ongoing projects; DPWH acknowledged the constraints and sought additional engineer items and continued coordination with Congress and DBM. The bridge feasibility commitment advanced, but financing, final approvals, and implementation remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the feasibility, economic return, financing, timetable, and technical implementation arrangements for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge and other major bridge projects. Members also examined whether DPWH had enough project engineers and absorptive capacity to deliver technically demanding and ongoing bridge works.

DPWH supported proceeding with the Sorsogon–Northern Samar feasibility study and considered the bridge a high-value Luzon–Visayas link with strong economic-return potential and possible external financing. The agency acknowledged serious project-engineer capacity constraints, sought additional DBM items, and said it would coordinate with Congress and other agencies on technically complex and ongoing projects.

Outcome The feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge was supported by DPWH, with funding figures stated and possible external financiers identified, but final financing, approvals, and construction remained prospective. The broader issues of engineer capacity, project assignment, and funding for ongoing bridge-related works were acknowledged and referred for further coordination with DBM and Congress.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · unresolved

School-building and basic-education facility allocations

A majority member asked DPWH to provide the 2025 and 2026 school-building allocations for Regions 3, 4A, and 5 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund. The member cited 595,000,000 and 261 classrooms for Region 3, 523,000,000 pesos I 48 and 297 classrooms for Region 4A, and 5 hundred seventy eight million and 280 completed classrooms for Region 5, with some accompanying figures unclear. Bivensio Dizon responded that DPWH had a 5,000-classroom catch-up target for 2026 using the 13,000,000,000 Basic Education Fund for 2025. He attributed the 2025 timing problem to an August 2025 DepEd-DPWH agreement and said classroom bidding could begin in October or November, while the 2026 process had started earlier in April and proceeded to procurement in August. He expected construction to start by September and occur in November or December. The transcript did not record a complete regional 2025-2026 breakdown or a formal follow-up submission, so the matter remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the budget intended for school-building construction in Regions 3, 4A, and 5 for 2025 and 2026 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund, which had been assigned to DPWH as implementing agency. It also sought clarification on DPWH's classroom catch-up target and the timing of the DepEd-DPWH procurement and construction process.

DPWH stated that it was implementing a 5,000-classroom catch-up plan for 2026 using the Basic Education Fund for 2025. It attributed delays in 2025 to the later completion of the DepEd-DPWH memorandum of agreement and said the 2026 process began earlier, with construction expected to begin by September and proceed in November or December.

Outcome DPWH provided a general catch-up target and implementation timetable, but the transcript did not show a complete regional breakdown for both 2025 and 2026 or a formal document submission. The issue therefore remained only partially clarified.

Questions and agency response

Members also sought to establish whether project-engineer workloads, preconstruction coordination, and budget policies were contributing to delays or quality risks.

DPWH said asset preservation, bridge rehabilitation, drainage, flood mitigation, replacement of makeshift bridges, and completion of unfinished buildings required additional and more predictable funding rather than repeated reliance on savings. The agency also maintained that project-engineer shortages and budget-policy constraints limited implementation, and it sought congressional assistance with DBM for additional personnel and possible exemptions for continuing projects.

Outcome The committee received DPWH's explanation of asset-preservation needs and implementation constraints, but no final funding adjustment or policy resolution was made. DPWH undertook to seek DBM assistance, provide project information, and help identify unfinished works.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · informational

Project evaluation, geotagging, and right-of-way controls

Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's stricter project-evaluation and documentation system. He said projects would require supporting documents, validated on-site geotagged photographs, and certificates covering implementability, right-of-way availability, duplicate-project checks, and specific locations. He also said DPWH would require BP two zero two compliance forms, although the transcript's wording was unclear. Dizon reported that many master plans were about ten or fifteen years old and cited rainfall assumptions associated with 2010, 2013, and 2015. He said DPWH would update outdated plans and seek development-council coordination or certificates of no objection from local government units. The segment ended with the reforms presented as transparency and project-readiness controls, without a recorded committee ruling or unresolved challenge.

Questions and agency response

The committee was seeking to establish how DPWH would evaluate projects before inclusion in the budget, verify project locations and readiness, prevent duplicate funding, and address right-of-way and outdated master-plan risks. The presentation also set out what certifications and supporting documents implementing offices would be required to provide.

DPWH stated that it had tightened project evaluation through mandatory technical vetting, supporting documents, geotagged on-site photographs, certificates of implementability, right-of-way certifications, and duplicate-project checks. It also maintained that outdated river-basin, drainage, and related master plans needed updating because climate change and changed rainfall conditions affected infrastructure design.

Outcome The agency presented the reforms and the certifications it said would be required for project inclusion and implementation. No member challenge, separate document request, or committee ruling was recorded in the provided segment.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Road, construction-site, and accessibility compliance

Rep. Percy Sindania questioned DPWH about blacklisted contractors, labor and occupational-safety violations, BP 344 compliance, PWD facilities, and road-crash prevention. Bivensio Dizon estimated that between 10 to 15 contractors or suppliers were blacklisted and committed to submit the complete list, as well as projects awarded to Reddycon in the last three years. Dizon candidly described historical accessibility compliance as poor, but said rehabilitation projects would widen sidewalks and meet accessibility standards, supported by about 100 million previously, 170 million last year, and 500 million this year. He and a DPWH safety official described stricter construction-site enforcement, project-engineer training, and an updated safety handbook. Sindania cited 13,125 road-crash deaths in 2023 and said 94% of commuters were at risk daily, while the agency undertook corrective and reporting measures. The chair was told that PWD structures had a separate funding line item, leaving implementation of the standards as the principal open issue.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH was funding and enforcing standards for road rehabilitation, bridge and construction-site safety, and accessibility under BP 344. Members also asked how many contractors had been blacklisted, whether labor violations could support blacklisting, and whether PWD facilities had dedicated funding.

DPWH acknowledged that past compliance with BP 344 had been poor but said rehabilitation projects were being redesigned to provide sufficiently wide sidewalks and meet accessibility standards. The department said it was separately funding PWD infrastructure, enforcing construction-site safety standards, training project engineers, updating its handbook, and would submit the requested contractor and project lists.

Outcome DPWH acknowledged serious historical accessibility-compliance deficiencies and described ongoing corrective measures, dedicated PWD funding, and tighter road and construction-site safety enforcement. Contractor lists and the updated safety handbook were committed for submission, while the broader questions of actual BP 344 compliance and road-crash reduction remained subject to implementation.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Regional allocation equity and convergence priorities

Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's effort to shift regional allocations toward a more needs-based distribution, reducing Luzon's historical share from about 56% to roughly 52%, while raising the Visayas share to 20% and placing Mindanao at about 28%. He acknowledged that the distribution was not yet fully equitable and invited Congress to consider further reallocations, particularly for high-poverty regions. Dizon also said DPWH had reduced projects from a typical average of about 20,000 and the 2024–2025 level of about 25,000 by removing duplicates, emphasizing larger projects, and eliminating projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program. Representative Mike Tan questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH answered that 80% of the 2026 program was expected to be awarded by the end of September; Yusick Ador gave an ideal capacity of seven projects per project engineer and requested help securing additional engineers. Tan later asked about ongoing convergence projects, including hospital and tourism-road works, and Dizon said their funding would be submitted to Congress subject to executive policies. The issue therefore produced agency commitments and explanations but left final reallocations and ongoing-project funding for congressional action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's regional allocations and convergence projects were distributed according to need and whether implementing offices had sufficient absorptive capacity. It also asked whether ongoing hospital, tourism-road, and related convergence projects would continue to receive funding despite the rationalization of responsibilities.

DPWH said it was rationalizing convergence projects to eliminate duplication, assign department-specific priorities to the responsible agencies, and reduce project loads that exceeded implementing-office capacity. It said the 2027 regional distribution was more needs-based but acknowledged that further reallocations might still be warranted, while the continuation of ongoing convergence projects would be submitted to Congress subject to executive policies.

Outcome The committee received DPWH's explanation of the more needs-based regional allocation and its rationale for reducing and transferring convergence projects. The continuation of ongoing convergence projects and any further regional reallocations remained subject to Congress's subsequent judgment.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Hospital construction and interagency project coordination

Rep. Ian Amatong raised concerns about absent project engineers, a delayed hospital in his district, and the need to finish unfinished works before starting new projects. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged that engineers were handling workloads as high as one to thirty projects against an ideal one-to-seven ratio and sought additional DBM items. Dizon said hospitals often fell under DOH budgets and that DPWH would seek flexibility for continuing hospital projects, while the chair called for stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangays. Rep. Mike Tan then questioned DPWH's absorptive capacity, and Dizon projected 80% award of the 2026 program by the end of September. DPWH official Yusick Ador reiterated the ideal seven-project workload and requested more engineers. The agency agreed to help identify unfinished projects and said funding for ongoing convergence projects would be submitted to Congress, leaving DBM approvals and several project-specific matters open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DPWH had adequate project-engineer and implementing-office capacity to supervise hospital, road, bridge, and other convergence projects. It also examined whether DPWH coordinated sufficiently with local governments and partner agencies before construction, and whether unfinished or ongoing projects should be prioritized and funded.

DPWH said project supervision was being strained by workloads far above the ideal one-to-seven engineer-to-project ratio and that additional project-engineer positions were needed from DBM. The department supported coordinating with local governments before construction, prioritizing unfinished and ongoing projects, matching projects to capable implementing offices, and seeking flexibility for continuing hospital and convergence projects, but said DBM and executive policies limited what DPWH could do directly.

Outcome The agency agreed in principle with the members' calls for stronger preconstruction coordination, additional engineering capacity, and prioritization of unfinished and ongoing projects. Specific DBM approvals, additional staffing, the hospital completion timetable, and the status information on the Quezon Bridge remained subject to later action or submission.

DPWH · 2026-08-25 · committed

Project-engineer oversight and implementation accountability

Ian Amatong raised concerns about project engineers being absent during implementation and asked for stronger transparency, coordination, and accountability before project turnover. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged a structural staffing problem: about 75,000 employees supported a workload that could reach one engineer for thirty projects or more, compared with an ideal ratio of one to seven or one to ten. Amatong also pressed for completion of a hospital in his district within one year rather than four or five years; the transcript gave the hospital amount as "607,100,000,000,000 million," which was unclear. Vince said hospital funding arrangements involved DOH and DBM and offered to seek an exemption for continuing projects, while asking the committee to help persuade DBM. Amatong urged DPWH to prioritize unfinished works and requested exact information on the Quezon Bridge, with Vince undertaking to report back. The chair and secretary also supported stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials, barangay captains, and communities.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DPWH would ensure that project engineers were present and accountable during implementation, and whether the department could improve coordination with local communities before construction. Members also pressed for faster completion and prioritization of unfinished and continuing projects.

DPWH acknowledged that project-engineer staffing was inadequate, with actual assignments reaching one engineer for thirty projects or more instead of the ideal one to seven or one to ten. The department supported stronger community and preconstruction coordination, agreed to prioritize unfinished and ongoing projects, and said it would seek DBM assistance or an exemption for continuing projects, but stated that the hospital funding and policy issue was not entirely within DPWH's control.

Outcome DPWH agreed in principle to improve project-engineer oversight, prioritize unfinished and ongoing projects, and strengthen preconstruction coordination. Additional engineer staffing, the hospital's funding and completion schedule, and the requested DBM policy relief remained dependent on DBM or further information, while DPWH undertook to provide an update on the Quezon Bridge.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

AFP modernization funding, loans, and Horizon Three acquisitions

Secretary Teodoro said AFP modernization required an integrated package of equipment, infrastructure, logistics, secure networks, and support systems. Deputy Majority Leader Panaligan asked for the items charged to the 2026 modernization allocation of about 40 billion and the proposed 2027 allocation of about 50 billion, as well as the appropriate loan-ceiling policy; the Secretary favored retaining a cap controlled by DBM and DOF. The DND confirmed an intent to acquire additional frigates and said multirole fighters remained under consideration, but only as part of a broader force package. Members Poe and Patalbano pressed for a clearer drone-program update, and the DND said drones were funded through modernization but that detailed systems were classified and that control, connectivity, and integration were the immediate priorities. The DND cited about 40 billion for a complete Tagoloan dry dock and said U.S. support for Lumbia was still being scoped. The chair requested a prioritized formal letter identifying omitted capital-outlay and other institutional needs, and the DND committed to submit it within the week.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the AFP modernization program would be financed and implemented, including the items charged to the 2026 and 2027 modernization appropriations, the treatment of unprogrammed appropriations and loans, and the status of Horizon Three acquisitions. Members also asked how modernization funding would support drones, fighters, frigates, infrastructure, EDCA sites, and a proposed naval dry dock.

The DND said modernization must be treated as an integrated force package requiring core systems, secure networks, domain awareness, logistics, infrastructure, trained personnel, and sustainment, rather than as isolated platform purchases. It supported retaining a loan cap subject to DBM and DOF control, confirmed that frigate and drone acquisitions were being pursued or studied, but withheld detailed acquisition and agreement information where classified or operationally sensitive.

Outcome The hearing established the DND's broad modernization priorities and elicited commitments for itemized funding and prioritized capital-outlay requests, but the detailed 2026-2027 Horizon Three line items were not supplied on the record. Classified drone systems, modernization agreements, and some exercise-related amounts remained undisclosed, while the loan-ceiling legislation, unprogrammed funding, Lumbia support, and Tagoloan dry dock remained subject to further action or funding.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

AFP modernization’s proposed 50,000,000,000 and prior 40,000,000,000

Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan asked DND to identify the items covered by about 40 billion for 2026 and the proposed 50 billion for 2027, and urged access to 50 billion in unprogrammed appropriations. The secretary's recorded response to the itemization request was unclear, and no detailed list was supplied in the exchange. Panaligan then raised his bill to revise or remove the PD 415 loan ceiling, while Secretary Gilbert Teodoro favored retaining a cap controlled by DBM and DOF. Teodoro said enacted US legislation could provide about 100 million in the following year, with a maximum of US500 million dollars per year subject to availability, and that Japan's assistance would also help. He confirmed an intent to acquire two more missile frigates but said the acquisition trigger had not been pulled, and said multirole fighters remained dependent on financing and supporting systems. The loan-ceiling question was committed to a technical working group, while the requested allocation documents and unprogrammed-funding access remained unanswered in the transcript.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which AFP modernization items would be charged against the proposed 2027 allocation and the prior-year allocation, including whether unprogrammed appropriations could be accessed. It also examined whether the statutory ceiling on modernization loans should be retained, increased, or removed, and how external financing could support the program.

DND supported retaining a loan cap administered by DBM and DOF, rather than removing the ceiling, because those agencies could set borrowing limits according to fiscal capacity and debt-service considerations. Teodoro said foreign military financing and Japan's security assistance would help modernization, but that the domestic allocation reflected broader fiscal constraints and that major acquisitions depended on financing and supporting infrastructure.

Outcome The secretary answered the loan-policy and external-financing questions, but the transcript did not provide a clear itemization of the 2026 and 2027 modernization allocations or confirm access to the unprogrammed funds. The loan-ceiling issue was left for further consideration by the National Defense committee's technical working group.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

Modernization-loan ceiling and foreign defense assistance

Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan asked which items would be financed from the proposed PHP 50,000,000,000 2027 modernization allocation and requested the corresponding 2026 and 2027 itemization. He also proposed increasing or removing the USD 300,000,000 loan ceiling, while Secretary Gilbert Teodoro favored retaining a cap set by DBM and DOF according to fiscal capacity. Teodoro confirmed that a U.S. defense-capabilities measure had been enacted, with about 100,000,000 expected for the following year and a US500 million dollars annual maximum subject to Treasury availability. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez then asked about Lumbia, where DND reported 115,000,000 remaining for the current year, no U.S. counterpart funding yet, and no agreed U.S.-built structure because assistance was still being scoped. Teodoro estimated the proposed Tagoloan dry dock at about 40,000,000,000 including equipment, but said titling had to be completed before construction could proceed. The loan issue and modernization documents required further action, while Lumbia assistance and the construction timetable remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which AFP modernization items would be funded under the proposed 2027 allocation and whether DND preferred retaining, increasing, or removing the statutory modernization-loan ceiling. It also examined how foreign military financing and U.S. assistance would support modernization-related facilities, including Lumbia and the proposed Tagoloan dry dock.

DND favored retaining a modernization-loan cap because DBM and DOF would determine the ceiling according to fiscal capacity and loan terms. It said U.S. assistance would support modernization but that no Lumbia counterpart funding or agreed U.S.-built structure existed yet; Lumbia assistance was still being scoped. DND supported the proposed Tagoloan dry dock in principle, subject to titling, at an estimated cost of 40,000,000,000.

Outcome The loan-ceiling issue was left for further deliberation in the technical working group, while the requested modernization itemization was to be furnished. U.S. support for Lumbia remained unagreed and under scoping, and the Tagoloan dry dock remained contingent on titling, with no construction timetable given.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

AFP earmarked revenues, BCDA shares, and DND off-budget balances

Roberto Nazal Jr. raised whether about 10.285 billion in accumulated BCDA earmarked revenues and about 4.029 billion in DND off-budget balances were available before Congress provided additional funding. He asked whether the balances reflected insufficient AFP requests, DBM non-approval, deliberate conservation, or legal and regulatory restrictions. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro answered that the BCDA funds were matched to existing programs and contracts and were pledged for payments, while the off-budget funds were held in the BTR and were not earning interest. He identified ongoing projects, including the Lumbia Airbase runway, and said trust-receipt items had to be remitted to DBM before disbursement. He also stated that the resources and interest receipts were considered in the AFP submissions used to prepare the FY 2027 request. The committee requested lists of the pledged and ongoing projects, with the Chair directing the department to provide the information.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether AFP earmarked revenues and DND off-budget balances were genuinely available for additional programs or were already committed, legally restricted, or unused because of agency or DBM action. It also asked whether these resources had been considered in preparing the FY 2027 budget request.

The DND stated that the accumulated BCDA earmarked revenues were already matched to ongoing projects and existing contracts and were pledged for payments, rather than being freely available for new projects. It also stated that the off-budget accounts were held in the BTR, were not earning interest, were associated with implementable projects or trust-receipt items, and that interest receipts and these resources were considered in the AFP submissions underlying the FY 2027 request.

Outcome The Secretary answered that the balances were committed to existing contracts or ongoing projects, were subject to DBM remittance procedures, and were considered in the budget submission. The committee requested project lists, and the Chair undertook to direct the department to submit them; the underlying off-budget balance figures and project-level documentation remained subject to submission.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

Defense self-reliance, Government Arsenal cuts, and ammunition production

Eli San Fernando asked Secretary Gilbert Teodoro to define self-reliance and explain the Government Arsenal's roughly 21.8% budget reduction. The Secretary defined self-reliance as securing supply chains quickly and cost-effectively, rather than achieving complete domestic production. He said the Arsenal had produced 60 million rounds but was being redirected toward more advanced capabilities, while the member highlighted a 2026 target of 60 million rounds against actual output of 500,000. The Secretary attributed the shortfall to a worldwide shortage of nitrocellulose precursors and said the materials could come from a small number of foreign sources. San Fernando argued that industrial policy was essential for defense resilience, and the Secretary agreed. Representative Jay Vernego separately asked about reducing imported-arms dependence, local manufacturing, LBIT Systems procurement, and drone guidelines; the Secretary said there were no new LBIT contracts, local industry remained focused on small arms, and drone guidelines could be shared in non-sensitive form. The issue remained substantively unresolved on restoring Arsenal funding or closing the production gap, although the agency committed to support industrial policy and provide or report additional information.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what the Department of National Defense meant by a self-reliant defense force, whether the Government Arsenal's reduced budget and low ammunition output undermined that goal, and what role local industry and industrial policy should play. Members also asked how foreign procurement, technology transfer, local arms and drone production, and operational guidelines fit within that policy.

The DND defined self-reliance as resilient, secure, cost-effective, and timely supply chains rather than complete domestic production. It supported industrial policy and domestic capability development, but said the Government Arsenal should move beyond small arms toward more advanced systems, while local industry should pursue forward-looking capabilities that could scale and provide value.

Outcome The Secretary agreed in principle that industrial policy was necessary, but maintained that self-reliance did not require complete indigenous production and that current local industry was not yet suited to the DND's priority capabilities. The Government Arsenal's budget reduction and ammunition-production shortfall were attributed to capital-outlay reprioritization and precursor shortages; no funding restoration or production remedy was committed during the exchange.

Local defense-industry procurement and technology transfer

Johanne Monich Bautista asked DND about uniform and fabric allocations and compliance with the Philippine Tropical Fabrics Law, including the cited 5% Philippine-fabric requirement. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro identified 162,000 for uniformed personnel but said the aggregated clothing figure and projected compliant-fabric spending were not yet available, citing safety, fireproofing, and supply-chain constraints. Bautista then asked about 2027 spending under the Self-Reliant Defense Posture Law, and Teodoro said there would be none because the law lacked equity, risk capital, research and development, and meaningful intellectual-property rights. Rep. Elijah San Fernando questioned the meaning of self-reliance, the 21.8% Government Arsenal budget reduction, and the gap between a 60,000,000 ammunition target and 500,000 actual output; DND attributed the output gap to a worldwide precursor shortage and endorsed industrial policy in principle. Rep. Vernego asked about Elbit Systems procurement, local arms production, drones, and written operational guidelines; Teodoro said only missile replenishment was planned, local industry was not yet suited to DND's priority capabilities, and drone guidelines could be disclosed subject to protecting sensitive system details. The discussion ended with information and document-related commitments, while several policy and implementation issues remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DND's uniform and defense procurement would comply with Philippine-made fabric requirements and strengthen local suppliers, manufacturing, maintenance, and technology transfer. Members also examined the meaning of self-reliance, the Government Arsenal's reduced budget and output, local arms production, and guidelines for drone procurement and use.

DND said self-reliance meant resilient, secure, cost-effective, and timely supply chains rather than complete indigenous production. It said the Self-Reliant Defense Posture Law was unworkable without equity, risk capital, research and development, and shared intellectual property rights; local industry should be developed where it could provide forward-looking, scalable capabilities, while sensitive operational details and technology constraints limited immediate local production and drone-guideline disclosure.

Outcome The committee received DND's explanations but did not resolve the missing uniform and fabric figures, the law's implementation gap, or the precise status of local-industry support. DND undertook to provide information and consider or support further work on fabric sourcing, statutory amendments, Ombudsman-related documentation, and disclosable drone guidelines.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

West Philippine Sea operations and maritime-security capability

Secretary Gilbert Teodoro framed the West Philippine Sea as the immediate focus of a broader maritime domain of about 2.4 million square kilometers and described the need for naval, Coast Guard, infrastructure, logistics, and technically trained personnel. A minority member asked about hazard pay for civilian personnel deployed in the West Philippine Sea, and Teodoro supported it while acknowledging unresolved issues concerning implementation and other benefits. The minority member also questioned alleged Chinese recruitment and influence operations; the Secretary said there were grounds for suspicion but that evidentiary determinations belonged largely to law-enforcement and financial authorities. The member manifested support for an increased West Philippine Sea budget, but no specific increase was recorded. Representative Egay Risa obtained the DND's position that EDCA and Philippine territory could be used only consistently with Philippine law, the Constitution, presidential guidance, and defensive treaty circumstances. Representative Rufus Rodriguez raised evacuation-center criteria and Eastern Seaboard surveillance and naval-basing needs; the agency undertook to provide an update on the proposed base, while the site criteria and funding questions remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the DND was funding and strengthening operations in the West Philippine Sea and other maritime domains, including surveillance, patrols, Pag-asa Island services, and personnel capability. It also examined the legal and operational limits of the Mutual Defense Treaty, EDCA sites, and DND-supervised facilities in relation to China-related security concerns.

The DND said West Philippine Sea operations required sustained regular operating funds, naval and Coast Guard coordination, services and habitation support for Pag-asa Island, strategic infrastructure, surveillance, logistics, training, and technically qualified personnel. It maintained that Philippine law, the Constitution, presidential guidance, and the Mutual Defense Treaty limited EDCA and foreign military use of Philippine territory to defensive circumstances, while specific Eastern Seaboard basing and Ligtas Pinoy site questions remained subject to further work.

Outcome The DND answered the legal and policy questions and stated that Pag-asa services would be fast-tracked, while a minority member supported increased West Philippine Sea funding. Specific funding for the maritime-security increase, the Ligtas Pinoy site list and criteria, and the proposed Eastern Seaboard naval base were not finally resolved.

DND · 2026-08-25 · unresolved

EDCA, U.S. facilities, and defense-cooperation infrastructure

Representative Egay Risa questioned Secretary Gilbert Teodoro on what would trigger the Mutual Defense Treaty and whether EDCA sites could be used in a Taiwan conflict or for offensive missile operations. Teodoro answered that treaty activation required a government call after an attack and that EDCA sites could not be used offensively unless the Philippines was under attack or threat, subject to the Constitution and Philippine law. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez asked about Lumbia's budget and U.S. counterpart funding; DND cited about 115 million for the current-year remaining amount, while the reference to 450 million for the following year was unclear, and it said no U.S. counterpart contribution had yet been agreed. DND said Lumbia development was delayed by right-of-way and informal-settlement issues and that U.S. officials were still scoping a possible warehouse. The proposed Tagoloan dry dock was estimated at about 40 billion including equipment, but titling and a construction timetable remained pending. Congressman Antonio Tinio warned that dual-use U.S. facilities and critical infrastructure could become targets and expose the Philippines to supply-chain risks, while Teodoro defended broader partnerships and resilient domestic supply chains as necessary for deterrence.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the legal and operational limits of the Mutual Defense Treaty and EDCA, including whether U.S. forces could use Philippine territory for offensive operations. It also examined the Philippine and U.S. contributions to EDCA-related infrastructure, the status and cost of planned facilities, and the security and supply-chain risks associated with expanded defense cooperation.

DND said EDCA and other security-cooperation arrangements strengthened deterrence, interoperability, training, technology access, and defense resilience. It maintained that the Mutual Defense Treaty and EDCA did not authorize offensive use of Philippine territory absent an attack or threat to the Philippines, while acknowledging that U.S. contributions to Lumbia had not yet been agreed and that key infrastructure projects remained subject to land, titling, and scoping issues.

Outcome The legal limits on offensive use of EDCA sites were stated by DND, but U.S. counterpart funding and specific Lumbia construction commitments remained unsettled. The Tagoloan dry dock remained dependent on land titling, with no construction timetable given, while broader concerns about dual-use facilities and regional supply-chain vulnerability remained matters for continuing policy and budget consideration.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

Drones and unmanned systems for the AFP

Brian Poe asked whether the Philippine Air Force and Navy budgets contained specific drone-procurement line items and whether modernization planning was preparing for rapidly changing drone technology. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro answered that drones were covered by the modernization fund, while specific systems were classified, and emphasized integration, secure connectivity, and operational control rather than hardware alone. Poe cited an approximate 70 million cost for one F-16 and compared it with about 2,000 Shahed-class drones. Rep. Vernego then asked about local drone production and written operational guidelines; Teodoro said drone production was relatively easy, but payload technology and AI-related systems were the critical elements, and that current use was for surveillance. Vernego requested guideline and program updates, with Teodoro indicating that disclosable material could be provided without compromising sensitive details. Tony Patalbano separately requested a status report on the drone program, and Teodoro said the DND was building its framework and backbone and developing control systems.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether drone procurement was specifically funded in the FY 2027 DND or service budgets, how drones were treated under the AFP modernization program, and whether the AFP had the personnel, network, control systems, and guidelines needed to use them responsibly. Members also sought an update on the drone program and related reporting to the committee.

The DND said drone procurement was covered by the AFP modernization fund, although specific systems and budget details were classified. It maintained that the priority was integrating drones into operations, building secure connectivity and control systems, and developing responsible-use guidelines; current drone use was for surveillance rather than offensive operations.

Outcome The DND assured the committee that drones were covered under modernization and that the AFP was developing the necessary integration, backbone, and control systems, but it withheld specific procurement details as classified. The committee requested guideline and program updates; the extent and timing of those submissions were not specified.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

Veterans’ pensions, health care, and retirement support

Representative Erline Ayon raised concerns about whether the budget adequately protected veterans’ pensions, benefits, health care, and retirement support, especially for elderly and medically vulnerable veterans. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said pension increases should be decoupled from active-duty salaries and reported a compromise providing 5% increases for three years, or 15% by 2028. He also cited 71,000,000,000 for AFP retirees and JPY 11,000,000,000 for veterans ameliorations in the special-purpose-fund breakdown. The Department described valor clinics, preventive care, mental-health and geriatric programs, and Veterans Memorial Medical Center improvements; it said the center had treated 11,100 inpatients but could accommodate only about nine percent of veterans. Teodoro committed to pursuing a first hospice by the end of the year and assured the committee that the Department would fight for veterans’ benefits. Pension reform, including separate treatment for AFP retirees, was not settled and remained subject to further study.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget adequately protected veterans’ pensions, health care, retirement support, and related welfare programs. It also asked how Congress and the Department of National Defense could ensure that elderly and medically vulnerable veterans would not be left without benefits or care.

The Department stated that veterans’ welfare required continued pension support, preventive and specialized health care, socialization, transition assistance, outpatient access through valor clinics, and improved facilities at the Veterans Memorial Medical Center. Secretary Teodoro supported studying pension reform and decoupling veterans’ pensions from active-duty salaries, but opposed treating AFP retirees identically with retirees from other uniformed services and favored preserving retirement security while a sustainable system was developed.

Outcome The Secretary gave assurances on continued advocacy for veterans’ benefits and described ongoing and planned health-care and retirement-support programs, including a hospice targeted for launch by year-end. Pension reform and the legal decoupling of pensions from active-duty salaries remained matters for further study and legislative action.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

MUP pension reform and contribution-based financing

Antonio Tinio raised the increase in the MUP pension budget from about 68.6 billion in 2015 to about 154 billion in the proposed 2027 budget and asked about a contribution-based reform. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said the reform required decisions on when it would begin and who would be covered, with the armed forces separated from civilian agencies. He said LGUs might fairly share the pension burden for locally oriented services such as the police, but that the fiscal and actuarial effects needed study. The secretary said the department was open to requiring greater contributions and to proposals easing the national government's burden. He also said a system could be designed to mature gradually before pension drawdown. The issue landed with further study and no definitive contribution or LGU-sharing arrangement.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the proposed MUP pension reform would shift from government-subsidized pensions toward contributions, including when the system would begin and who would be covered. It also asked whether LGUs would share responsibility for the pension burden of civilian uniformed personnel, particularly the police.

The DND supported studying a contribution-based MUP pension reform and was open to proposals that would ease the national government's fiscal burden. Secretary Teodoro said the armed forces should be treated separately from civilian agencies, while LGU burden sharing for locally oriented uniformed services should be evaluated through actuarial and fiscal analysis; no definitive plan or contribution level had yet been adopted.

Outcome The department agreed to consider contribution-based reform and possible LGU burden sharing, but left the timing, coverage, contribution level, and allocation of liability for further study. No final reform plan or LGU share was presented.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

Disaster-response assets, OCD capacity, and evacuation centers

DND said disaster response required larger airlift platforms, distributed logistics centers, prepositioned supplies, and stronger OCD coordination; it cited about 46 Black Hawk helicopters but said that capacity was insufficient. Representative Poe questioned OCD's 0.96% capital-outlay reduction from a budget of 2,500,000,000, and Secretary Teodoro said the reduction affected capital outlay and that OCD needed relocation from crowded Camp Aguinaldo. Representative Rufus Rodriguez asked for 2027 Ligtas Pinoy sites and selection criteria; the response referred to DNR hazard mapping but did not clearly identify the sites, while the transcript gave inconsistent figures of 60,000,000, 34 centers, and 90,000,000 per center. Members raised delays in rescue and relief processing, the need for Navy dredgers, insufficiently detailed Negros rehabilitation plans, and climate-flooded roads in Central Luzon. Secretary Teodoro committed to national-level coordination, an OCD anticipation deliverable, a revised earthquake-impact study process, and infrastructure referrals, while Representative Salvador cited delivery of 1,200 family packs and supported the FY 2027 DND budget.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DND and OCD had sufficient assets, logistics, evacuation facilities, communications, and coordination systems for disaster response, including prepositioning and response to flooding and a major earthquake. Members also asked how the 2027 evacuation-center program would select sites and whether OCD's reduced capital outlay would impair operations.

DND said OCD should concentrate on coordinated awareness, prediction, preemptive response, and logistics rather than directly undertaking rehabilitation or major infrastructure works. The agency identified joint logistics centers, prepositioned supplies and water, improved rescue and airlift capacity, evacuation-site planning, and stronger communications and infrastructure resilience as necessary, while acknowledging that OCD's rehabilitation plans and response procedures still needed improvement.

Outcome The committee received assurances that DND was prioritizing OCD coordination, prepositioned logistics, evacuation planning, and earthquake and flood resilience, but several matters remained dependent on future studies, site identification, interagency action, or additional appropriations. The record included commitments to submit project information, pursue relocation and infrastructure coordination, and elevate national flood and earthquake-resilience measures.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

DND-DPWH military infrastructure and unfinished projects

Representative Sara Hirado questioned Secretary Gilbert Teodoro about the DND-DPWH infrastructure program and projects that remained unfinished or unusable. Teodoro said DND had received 100% of released amounts but that funding was insufficient, citing 27 non-implementable and 51 implementable projects out of 78. Hirado cited an earlier report of 648 completed out of 944 projects and a figure of 15,000,000,000 pesos for uncompleted, idle, and unusable infrastructure, but the discrepancy was not clearly resolved. Teodoro also said reduced capital outlays threatened modernization support and delayed rehabilitation of the 70-year-old DND and Legacy buildings. The chair requested a formal prioritized list of omitted or reduced projects, and Teodoro committed to submit it within the week. The committee indicated that restoration would be considered during the budget amendment process.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status of the DND-DPWH military infrastructure program, particularly projects that remained unfinished or unusable, the accountability measures taken, and the funding needed to complete or rehabilitate them. It also sought to determine whether reduced capital outlays had omitted critical infrastructure support for modernization projects.

DND said military modernization could not be sustained without corresponding capital outlays for bases, logistics, maintenance, and other support infrastructure. It said the DND-DPWH project record included 27 non-implementable and 51 implementable projects out of 78, but did not clearly reconcile that figure with the earlier 218-project reference or provide a definitive update on inspections, completion, or possible charges.

Outcome The committee received a partial project-status explanation but the conflicting project counts, completion status, inspection results, and potential filing of charges were not resolved. DND committed to submit a prioritized list of omitted or reduced capital-outlay needs within the week, leaving possible restoration for the budget amendment process.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

Naval bases, dry docks, and strategic military facilities

Members examined AFP modernization allocations, naval frigate plans, base logistics, and the development of Lumbia and Tagoloan facilities. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro said the proposed 2027 modernization allocation was tied to fiscal capacity, confirmed an intent to acquire additional frigates, and emphasized that infrastructure was necessary to make advanced equipment useful. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez was told that Lumbia had about 115 million remaining for the current year and a 450 million amount cited for the next year, while no U.S. EDCA counterpart had yet been agreed. DND estimated the proposed complete Tagoloan dry dock at about 40 billion, including equipment, but said titling had to be completed and Sangley was becoming unusable for naval maneuvering. Anna York Bondoc requested Navy dredgers for silted ports, and the secretary agreed that dredging was needed and said one dredger was in the pipeline. Antonio Tinio's security questions about the Sangley-area Chinese-linked company were answered with references to environmental and enforcement actions, but the Navy's need for a dedicated dry dock remained.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DND and the AFP would prioritize modernization, naval-base and dry-dock development, and related logistics facilities within fiscal constraints. Members also asked whether proposed sites were legally, operationally, and securely ready, and what documents or follow-up actions the agency would provide.

DND said naval and AFP infrastructure was essential to logistics, readiness, external defense, and disaster response. It supported developing dedicated dry-dock and port capacity, including the proposed Tagoloan facility, but said titling, right-of-way, environmental, and security matters remained prerequisites; it also supported dredging and said a dredger was already in the pipeline.

Outcome The committee received DND's explanations and endorsements for Lumbia, Tagoloan, dredging, and dedicated naval infrastructure, but the Tagoloan project remained dependent on titling and the Lumbia U.S. contribution remained unagreed. Requested modernization and earmarked-fund documents were to be furnished, while the Payao camp and Sangley-area development required further coordination.

DND · 2026-08-25 · committed

FY 2027 DND budget restorations and institutional amendments

DND presented a proposed budget of about 324.6 billion and identified reduced capital outlay as the principal immediate restoration concern. The agency said the capital-outlay proposal was 239,000,000 and that reductions could delay infrastructure supporting modernization equipment and the restoration of the DND's 70-year-old legacy building. The agency also cited a 50,000,000,000 modernization fund, a 98 or 99% troop-strength fill-up rate, and 10 modernization projects, but no restoration amount was approved. The committee chair asked for a formal and prioritized list of critical programs omitted from the NEP for consideration in the H-GAP. Secretary Gilbert Teodoro committed to submit the list within the week, while the chair committed to have the requests reviewed line by line by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee. Representatives Isidro Ungab and Salvador expressed support for the DND and AFP budgets, with Ungab separately requesting a brief district-related meeting.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which DND and AFP programs or projects had been reduced or omitted from the NEP and should be restored through institutional amendments. It also sought a prioritized, formal list from the agency so the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee could evaluate the requests line by line.

DND said the most urgent restoration need was capital outlay, because reductions would leave modernization equipment without the infrastructure needed to house, support, and maintain it. The agency said it would submit a prioritized list of its other institutional amendment needs through the undersecretary and provide a formal letter within the week.

Outcome The committee did not approve specific restoration amounts during the hearing. DND was asked to submit a formal, prioritized list of omitted or reduced programs and institutional amendment requests within the week, after which the subcommittee would conduct line-by-line deliberations.

COA · 2026-08-25 · committed

COA FY2027 budget and omitted priority requests

COA presented a FY2027 NEP budget of about 16.46 billion, with no capital outlay, while identifying substantial omitted requests for technology, citizen participatory audit, furniture, vehicles, and pre-audit staffing. Members questioned whether the allocation matched the government’s anti-corruption priority, citing the proposed 107 billion flood-control budget and COA’s reported PHP158 billion in DPWH notices. COA said it had proposed 146 additional pre-audit teams at an estimated 2.5 billion and explained that DBM had excluded several Tier 2 and capital-outlay items. Members also pressed COA on using its existing authority for pre-audit, expanding citizen participatory audit, and supporting a draft bill. Rep. Dumogan moved to seek an augmentation, and the committee requested detailed capital-outlay, omitted-item, and audit-report submissions. The issue landed with possible budget amendments still pending, but with COA commitments to submit the requested documents and add pre-audit personnel funding to its wish list.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish COA’s FY2027 funding level, including which Tier 2, capital outlay, staffing, pre-audit, technology, and citizen-participatory-audit requests were omitted. It also examined whether COA could expand pre-audit and anti-corruption work under its existing authority and what documents COA would submit to support possible budget amendments.

COA maintained that its FY2027 NEP allocation excluded important Tier 2 and capital-outlay requests, limiting its ability to expand technology, citizen participatory audit, staffing, and pre-audit capabilities. It supported additional resources and agreed to include pre-audit personnel funding in its wish list, submit detailed capital-outlay information, resubmit audit reports, and provide a position paper supporting the draft bill.

Outcome The committee did not finally resolve COA’s FY2027 augmentation or restore capital outlay during the hearing. It moved toward possible institutional amendments and requested detailed wish-list, capital-outlay, and audit-report submissions; COA committed to provide the materials and include pre-audit personnel funding.

COA · 2026-08-25 · committed

COA capital outlay zeroed out in the FY2027 NEP

COA reported that its FY2027 capital outlay proposal had been excluded from the NEP, leaving the agency with no capital outlay despite requests for ICT, facilities, equipment, vehicles, and related investments. Members argued that the omission was inconsistent with the government's anti-corruption priority and pressed COA on pre-audit capacity, including 146 additional teams and an unclear estimate of around 2,500,000,000. COA explained that DBM set the relevant ceiling, that the omitted items were submitted as Tier Two requests, and that the ISSP had been reviewed by DICT and endorsed to DBM. COA identified a capital outlay request of R656.528 million, including PHP525.405 million for ICT and PHP125.523 million for furniture and fixtures, while other wish-list figures were also cited. Rep. Dumogan moved to seek augmentation, including for pre-audit personnel. The Committee on Operations requested detailed capital outlay and institutional-amendment documents, and COA agreed to submit them, leaving funding itself unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why COA's capital outlay request was omitted from the FY2027 NEP, what investments and capabilities were affected, and whether COA had alternative authority or budget mechanisms to implement pre-audit and other anti-corruption functions. It also sought to determine what additional funding, personnel, and supporting documents should be considered through institutional amendments.

COA said its capital outlay proposal was submitted as a Tier Two request but was not included in the FY2027 NEP, and it received no explanation from DBM for the zeroing out. COA maintained that the omitted ICT, facilities, equipment, vehicles, citizen participatory audit, and pre-audit personnel requirements were necessary to improve audit capacity, and agreed to add pre-audit personnel costs to its wish list and submit detailed supporting documents.

Outcome The zeroing out of capital outlay was not explained by DBM and was not resolved during the hearing. COA undertook to submit detailed capital outlay, institutional-amendment, and pre-audit personnel requests for possible committee consideration and augmentation.

COA · 2026-08-25 · committed

Funding 146 pre-audit teams with personnel and geotagging

Rep. Percival Sindania and Rep. Mauricio Domogan raised the need for personnel, technology, geotagging, and funding to expand COA's pre-audit capacity. COA said it needed 146 additional pre-audit teams and gave estimates ranging from more or less around 2,500,000,000 to around 2,200,000,000, while citing DPWH notices totaling 158,000,000,000. Rep. Iris Marie Montes pressed COA on its existing constitutional and statutory authority to conduct pre-audit without waiting for legislation, and COA agreed that it could do so but said the bill would strengthen the mandate. Rep. Salvador Pleyto called for continued congressional support for COA's technical manpower and systems. Rep. Mauricio Domogan later noted that COA's listed augmentation did not include pre-audit personnel, after which COA undertook to add the requirement to its wish list and Dumogan moved for budget augmentation. The transcript recorded no final ruling or approved augmentation amount.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COA had sufficient personnel, technology, and budget authority to create and operate 146 additional pre-audit teams, including geotagging or geomapping of infrastructure projects. Members also asked whether COA could use its existing authority and budget mechanisms to begin pre-audit and whether additional funding and personnel would be requested.

COA said it could conduct pre-audit under its existing constitutional and statutory authority, but it lacked the personnel and resources to implement it at the desired scale. It supported the proposed legislation, estimated the requirement for 146 additional pre-audit teams at around 2,200,000,000, and undertook to resubmit or include the requirement in its budget wish list.

Outcome COA acknowledged that existing authority allowed it to conduct pre-audit but said implementation at scale required additional personnel and funding. It undertook to resubmit and include the pre-audit requirement in its wish list, while Dumogan moved for budget augmentation; no final committee ruling or approved amount was recorded.

COA staffing losses and restored plantilla positions

Rep. Percival Sindania raised COA’s staffing losses and asked about the agency’s capacity to audit potentially anomalous infrastructure projects. Mauricio Domogan supported mandatory pre-audit with geotagging and said members would support a budget motion for additional personnel. COA undertook to resubmit its estimate, but the final funding decision and requested progress report were not shown.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the extent and causes of COA’s staffing losses, how many plantilla positions had been restored, and whether COA had sufficient personnel and funding for expanded pre-audit and geotagging work. COA said it needed 146 additional pre-audit teams, estimated the requirement at 2,200,000,000 pesos, and supported geotagging, while also undertaking to resubmit its budget estimate.

Outcome The committee received COA’s explanation of the restored and remaining plantilla positions, attrition causes, and the estimated requirement for 146 additional pre-audit teams. COA committed to resubmit its estimate, while member support for funding and legislative action was expressed; final budget action and the requested progress report were not resolved in the excerpt.

COA · 2026-08-25 · committed

Safeguards against manufactured savings and withheld SAROs

Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned COA on whether earmarked funds remained traceable after Treasury used cash under the one-fund concept. COA said it monitored the funds, followed the money trail after release, and would flag expenditures outside the authorized purpose; DBM had also committed to place information on its portal. Nazal then raised DPWH projects that had SAROs, bidding, and validation under NDC five ninety five but allegedly lacked SAAs, asking why they were withheld and could later become manufactured savings. COA cited missing supporting documents and prior reversions caused by implementing-office unreadiness, agreed to submit a project list, and undertook to coordinate with DPWH. Nazal warned that withholding Congress-approved projects and augmenting other items with the resulting savings could let the executive rewrite the GAA. In the second round, COA agreed with the concern and promised to confirm reportedly ready projects with the DPWH central office, but no concrete safeguard was finalized.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COA tracked earmarked funds after Treasury received them and whether cash fungibility could obscure their use. It also sought to determine why DPWH withheld or reverted Congress-approved projects, and what safeguards prevented implementable projects from being converted into manufactured savings and used for augmentation.

COA said it tracked earmarked and special funds, followed the money trail after release, and would flag use outside the authorized purpose. On DPWH projects, COA attributed some withheld SAAs to missing supporting documents and cited prior reversions caused by implementing-office unreadiness; it agreed to coordinate with DPWH, submit a project list, and confirm the status of reportedly ready projects.

Outcome COA agreed in principle with the committee's concern and undertook coordination, reporting, and confirmation actions, but the record did not establish a completed safeguard or resolve whether projects had been improperly converted into manufactured savings. The second-round request for a concrete prevention mechanism remained unanswered in the transcript.

COA · 2026-08-25 · committed

Tracking earmarked and off-budget funds under cash fungibility

Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether COA could track earmarked and off-budget funds while Treasury treated cash as fungible. COA said it monitored earmarked funds, had a latest report as of May 2026, and would flag use outside the authorized purpose, but described Treasury and DBM cash management as executive functions. The member cited DICT’s reported budget of about 25 billion or 26 billion and questioned why government systems lacked cloud capacity. The discussion also examined DPWH projects whose funds or SAAs were withheld or reverted; DPWH’s COA representative attributed some delays to missing supporting documents and unready regional or district offices. Nazal further asked whether such delays could manufacture savings and allow the Executive to rewrite the GAA, and COA agreed with his observations. On off-budget accounts, COA said deposits in authorized government depository banks were controlled by the collecting agency, earned interest for the agency in principle, and could not legally be used for another purpose without complications. COA committed to develop a protocol for monitoring balances and movements and to coordinate with DBM and the Bureau of the Treasury.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COA tracked earmarked and off-budget fund balances and the movement of related cash even when Treasury treated the cash as fungible. It also examined whether agencies could delay congressionally appropriated projects, generate savings, or use off-budget funds for purposes other than those authorized by law.

COA said it monitored earmarked and off-budget funds and audited their use once funds were released or disbursed by agencies. It treated Treasury and DBM management of cash and restrictions on releases as executive functions, but said it would flag charges or uses outside the authorized purpose and committed to develop a protocol for monitoring balances, use, and movements.

Outcome COA maintained that it would flag improper charges or uses outside an earmarked or off-budget fund’s authorized purpose, but its direct audit role generally began when agencies received or disbursed the funds. COA undertook further coordination and a monitoring protocol, while the question of tracing Treasury-held cash and preventing manufactured savings remained dependent in part on executive fund-management and release processes.

Citizen Participatory Audit funding and implementation

Rep. Iris Marie Montes argued that COA could conduct pre-audits under its existing authority and should budget for that function, while COA said most of its budget was already devoted to personal services and that some Tier 2 requests had been omitted. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how COA could use its existing authority and budget mechanisms to conduct or expand pre-audits and Citizen Participatory Audits. COA said expansion depended on available funding and manpower, and undertook to add the recommended pre-audit amount to its wish list.

Outcome COA explained the existing complaint-routing and formal Citizen Participatory Audit mechanisms, but the adequacy of its manpower and funding remained a concern. Digital audit systems, records management, and technical capacity

Rep. Iris Marie Montes pressed COA to use its existing authority for pre-audit and to seek appropriate budget mechanisms, while COA explained that DBM controlled the budget ceiling and that almost 92% of its budget was for personal services. The chair requested detailed capital-outlay and omitted-item lists and previous audit reports, and COA committed to submit or resend them, but no higher budget was promised.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COA was using its existing authority and budget mechanisms to strengthen pre-audit, digitize and securely retain records, and obtain the ICT, capital outlay, and technical manpower needed for modern auditing. It also sought details on COA's capital outlay proposal and audit-report submissions so Congress could assess possible budget amendments.

COA said its ability to expand pre-audit, the Citizen Participatory Audit, digital operations, and technical capacity was constrained by the budget process and available resources. It said its ICT and capital proposals formed part of a DICT-reviewed roadmap, while records retention requirements still imposed physical-storage burdens and its zeroed-out capital-outlay proposal had received no explanation from DBM.

Outcome COA answered the questions and described its digital, records, participatory-audit, and capital needs, but the zero capital-outlay issue was not resolved during the hearing. COA committed to submit detailed capital-outlay and omitted-item requests and to resend audit reports for the committee's later budget-amendment review.
