COA · 2026-08-25 · committed

Annual audit-report delays, publication, and congressional use

Members Iris Marie Montes and other committee officials focused on whether COA's annual audit reports were available in time for congressional oversight. COA said reports were transmitted by June 30, agencies had sixty days to submit management actions, and publication on the website was due by October 31. COA maintained that it was on time and said it provided reports to Congress and other oversight bodies, while incomplete financial statements and publication protocols could create bottlenecks. Montes questioned whether the process was substantive transparency or merely ARTA compliance and urged earlier, more useful reports. The Committee on Operations also questioned why COA's capital-outlay proposal of 1.171180000000, including an ICT request of 1,180,000,000, had been zeroed out and requested detailed capital and audit-report submissions. COA committed to resend the requested reports and materials, including the following morning.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether COA's annual audit reports were being completed, transmitted, and published within the applicable deadlines, and whether Congress received them in time and in a usable form for budget oversight. Members also asked what caused publication bottlenecks and requested reports and budget details to strengthen congressional review.

COA maintained that it was meeting the legal reporting schedule: annual audit reports were transmitted by June 30, management actions were incorporated afterward, and website publication was due by October 31. It said reports were also furnished to Congress and other oversight bodies, while acknowledging that incomplete financial statements and publication protocols could affect the process.

Outcome COA stated that its reports were timely under the GAA schedule and that Congress received copies before website publication. The committee nevertheless requested detailed capital-outlay and audit-report submissions, leaving the broader concern over whether publication and congressional access were sufficiently timely subject to follow-up.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

FY2027 DHSUD budget, funding gaps, and proposed increases

The committee examined a FY2027 DHSUD-and-attached-agency allocation of about 5.5 billion against an aggregate agency proposal of about 60 billion. DHSUD said the funding gap would constrain its planning, housing production, emergency assistance, and community mortgage programs, and requested additional amounts including about 280 million for DHSUD, about 47.5 million for HSAC, and substantial increases for NHA and SHFC. Members generally supported higher housing appropriations, with motions and manifestations from Representatives Co-Pilar, Gonzales, Roman Romulo, Catulpos, and Vice Chair Rodriguez. The committee also raised the use of NHA unobligated funds, submerged Bacolor settlement sites, permitting delays, and whether calamity assistance could continue under the proposed allocation. DHSUD and its agencies provided answers and undertook to submit documents or proposals, including a prioritized list of additional requests. No final budget increase was approved in the recorded proceedings; consideration was left for the budget amendments process and plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to determine whether DHSUD and its attached agencies had sufficient FY2027 funding to address housing needs, continue ongoing programs, and respond to calamities. It also examined which proposed increases should be prioritized and what administrative or interagency actions were needed to accelerate housing delivery.

DHSUD maintained that the proposed FY2027 allocation was insufficient for its mandate and the programs of its attached agencies. It sought additional funding, especially for DHSUD planning and regulatory functions, HSAC staffing, NHA housing and emergency assistance, and SHFC's enhanced community mortgage program, while reporting reforms intended to improve utilization and speed housing delivery.

Outcome Members broadly supported increasing DHSUD and attached-agency funding, but the transcript did not record final approval of the proposed increases. DHSUD was required to submit a prioritized written request for consideration in the budget amendments review process, while the motions were deferred to the proper time and plenary.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

4PH housing delivery, production targets, and interest subsidies

Chair Julian Jambaronda and Representative Sarah Elago pressed DHSUD and its shelter agencies on expanded 4PH eligibility, modalities, amortization, construction, takeouts, developer participation, and interest-subsidy validation. DHSUD cited 588,757 completed direct and indirect units or assistance, 544,000 still to be undertaken, and a 1,133,000 administration target, while stating that private-sector production was needed to address the 3,700,000 backlog. Officials described rental amounts below 1,500 pesos, a 3% socialized-housing interest rate, approximately 100,000 units of inventory, 30,000 approved-loan takeouts, and almost 130,000 expanded 4PH inventory units. Ilago also cited 66,700,000 pesos in 2025 interest and non-interest subsidy payments and sought independent validation. DHSUD said it was still waiting for DBM SAROs for IDSAP and EHAP, prompting a written-explanation request and a separate request for NHA's bank and developer lists. Howard Guintu later established that NHA had requested 1,000,000,000 for EHAP and 500,000,000 million million for the quick-response fund, while Pag-IBIG expected 15,000 takeouts against coverage of 33,000 units. The issues were not fully resolved, but follow-up submissions and committee consideration of additional funding were undertaken.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the expanded 4PH program was delivering eligible, affordable, and completed housing units at the required scale, and whether its financing and interest-subsidy mechanisms were adequate. It also examined delayed shelter funds, NHA production and facilities funding, developer performance, and the documents needed to validate implementation.

DHSUD said expanded 4PH offered multiple housing modalities and relied on private developers, Pag-IBIG financing, and other shelter agencies to supplement government production. It expressed confidence in meeting the 1,130,000-unit administration target, while acknowledging that the larger backlog required private-sector production; DHSUD and NHA also cited pending or insufficient funds and delayed SAROs.

Outcome The committee received DHSUD's explanations but continued to question the gap between inventory, takeouts, construction, and the administration target. Document submissions on DBM's delayed SAROs and NHA's banks and developer performance were requested, while additional shelter and facilities funding remained for committee consideration.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

Emergency and disaster shelter assistance, including IDSAP, EHAP, and quick-response funds

Sarah Elago raised delays in IDSAP and EHAP, and NHA said it was still waiting for DBM SAROs. Howard Guintu established that NHA had requested about 1 billion for EHAP and 500 million for the quick-response fund for FY2027. Vice Chair Rufus Rodriguez supported 1.6 billion for NHA integrated housing and an additional 1 billion for EHAP, while citing NHA fire assistance of 20,000 for total damage and 10,000 for partial damage. Maria Isabel Gavaria asked how indigent families with fire-damaged homes could receive assistance, and DHSUD identified IDSAP, EHAP, construction materials, repair kits, and LGU modular houses. The committee requested written and supporting documents, supported budget increases, and left the delayed releases and final funding outcome for further action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why emergency and disaster shelter assistance, including IDSAP and EHAP, had been delayed; whether NHA had requested FY2027 EHAP and quick-response funds; and whether the proposed resources were sufficient to assist disaster- and fire-damaged homes. Members also asked what procedures, funding, and interagency measures would prevent delays and sustain housing projects during calamities.

DHSUD and NHA stated that emergency shelter assistance had been affected by the delayed release of DBM SAROs and the availability of funds. They said NHA had requested 1,000,000,000 for EHAP and 500,000,000 for the quick-response fund, while DHSUD identified IDSAP, EHAP, construction materials, repair kits, and LGU modular houses as available assistance mechanisms.

Outcome The committee supported additional emergency shelter funding, including the NHA request for EHAP and the quick-response fund, but the record did not show final approval or the release of the delayed SAROs. Written explanations and agency lists were requested, and one local housing intervention was left for DHSUD review.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

NHA funding, production targets, and proposed budget cut

Undersecretary Henry Eliap presented a FY2027 NEP allocation of about 5.5 billion against attached-agency requests of approximately 60 billion, including an NHA request of about 44.7 billion versus an allocation of about 2.27 billion. Sarah Elago questioned emergency-shelter delays and NHA production, prompting a DBM explanation request and requests for lists of banks and developers. Victoria Co-Pilar and Lani Mercado argued that the funding was inadequate and moved or supported an increase, while the chair deferred the motion to plenary. Mercado specifically questioned whether 370,000,000 could address Manila Bay relocation needs; NHA said a building cost around 70 to 90,000,000 pesos and that the amount could cover around four buildings. NHA also stated that it had requested 1,000,000,000 for EHAP and 500,000,000 million million for the quick-response fund, with the latter wording unclear in the transcript. Members raised submerged Bacolor sites, old resettlement amenities, and vacant Rizal units, leading to commitments for agency follow-up and documents rather than a final funding decision.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed FY2027 funding would allow NHA and other attached agencies to meet resettlement, Manila Bay relocation, emergency shelter, and old-site amenity obligations. Members also asked whether requested funds had been sought from DBM and what additional actions or budget increases were needed.

DHSUD and NHA stated that the FY2027 proposal was insufficient for the agencies' full requests and would constrain new resettlement and housing projects, while existing projects and housing-unit production would be prioritized. NHA and related agencies committed or indicated that they would pursue DBM authority, submit requested information, study local project needs, and seek releases or support for emergency and amenity funding.

Outcome The committee did not resolve the adequacy of the proposed NHA and attached-agency budgets. It deferred the proposed budget increase to plenary, while recording commitments for DBM explanations, NHA submissions and funding-authority requests, an SHFC project review, and an NHA-LGU meeting on Bacolor.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

Attached-agency budgets, unobligated funds, and SHFC self-financing

Undersecretary Henry Eliap presented a 2027 NEP allocation of about 5.5 billion against agency requests totaling roughly 60 billion, including NHA's request of about 44.7 billion and SHFC's request of about 4.7 billion. Representative Victoria Co-Pilar questioned whether SHFC and the other corporate attached agencies could rely on their own income and highlighted 64 SHFC priority projects. DBM cited projected income of about 1.745 billion and said subsidies could be provided when necessary, but SHFC said its operating costs and limited net receipts prevented it from funding all programs. DBM also identified about 2.896 billion in NHA unobligated obligations from 2011 through 2024 and said NHA needed authority to use them. Co-Pilar moved to increase the budgets of SHFC and the other attached agencies, but the chair deferred action to plenary, while NHA committed to submit the requested letter to DBM. Representative Miro Quimbo separately raised concerns about housing underspending and supported the Community Mortgage Program.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the attached agencies' corporate income, operating resources, and unobligated balances justified their proposed appropriations, particularly for SHFC priority projects and NHA resettlement programs. It also sought to determine whether the requested budget increases should be acted on immediately or referred to plenary.

DHSUD and its attached agencies stated that the proposed allocations were substantially below their program requirements. DBM maintained that the corporate agencies' projected income and existing resources should be considered, while SHFC said its income was consumed by operating costs and could not fund all programs; NHA said it would seek authority to use unobligated balances.

Outcome The committee did not finally approve the proposed budget increase during the exchange; the motion was left for consideration at plenary. NHA committed to request DBM authority to use its unobligated funds, while the sufficiency of SHFC's income and the extent of housing underspending remained contested.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

Continuing-fund utilization and 52% disbursement rate

The chair questioned DHSUD's 52% disbursement rate for total continuing funds and asked how the backlog would be addressed before expiration. DHSUD attributed the low utilization to the expansion of the 4PH program from a single vertical modality to multiple modalities, including horizontal, rental, transitory, proclamation, and CMP projects. The agency also cited delays while developers awaited a revised price ceiling and said ISSP had not been implemented in the previous year. DHSUD reported a current budget of about 1.455 billion, a continuing budget spoken as 1.497, and a total disbursement rate of 74%, while its comparative 2021–2025 figures showed a 95.37 overall disbursement rate. A DHSUD official assured the committee that the remaining interest-subsidy and ISSP funds would be utilized before the end of the year.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the utilization of DHSUD's current and continuing funds, particularly the reported 52% disbursement rate for continuing appropriations. It also asked what caused the backlog and whether the remaining funds would be fully utilized before expiration.

DHSUD stated that the lower utilization of continuing funds resulted mainly from the expansion of the 4PH program from a single vertical modality to multiple housing modalities, as well as delays caused by developers' requests for a revised price ceiling. The agency assured the committee that the remaining interest-subsidy and ISSP funds would be utilized before the end of the year.

Outcome DHSUD explained the causes of the continuing-fund backlog and committed that the remaining interest-subsidy and ISSP funds would be utilized before year-end. The committee received the explanation and assurance, but no separate documentary submission or detailed catch-up schedule was stated.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

Community Mortgage Program financing and coastal or informal-settler communities

Secretary Aliling presented CMP as a major housing-needs solution, citing 1,100,000 projected CMP-related needs. Rep. Sarah Elago questioned project coverage, beneficiary amortization, interest subsidies, and the shortfall between planned production and actual takeouts; SHFC officials cited 47 projects, 60 applications, 37 projects, about 1,600,000,000, and amortization figures including 4,000 and 4,900 per month. Rep. Leila de Lima asked how many approved CMP projects served coastal fisherfolk communities, after citing 36 projects and 6,000 potential beneficiaries. SHFC answered that 47 projects had benefited almost 9,000 families and undertook to check its records for the coastal breakdown; it also reported 60 pending pipeline applications subject to funding. Rep. Miro Quimbo endorsed CMP as a social-housing and regularization mechanism. DHSUD later identified the SHFC mortgage program as a top additional-budget priority, with the chair stating figures of 4,600,000,000 and 4,660,000,000, and Secretary Aliling committed to submit a prioritized request.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the Community Mortgage Program (CMP) was being financed and implemented, including its coverage of informal-settler and fisherfolk communities. It also examined CMP production, beneficiary costs, pending applications, and DHSUD's priorities for additional funding.

DHSUD and SHFC presented CMP as a central housing solution and a priority for additional resources. The agencies reported expedited processing, approved projects and beneficiaries, and a pipeline constrained by funding, but they had not yet produced the requested breakdown of coastal projects serving fisherfolk communities.

Outcome CMP was recognized by DHSUD and the committee as a priority program, with an additional SHFC mortgage-program request identified for possible funding. The specific number of CMP projects serving coastal or fisherfolk communities remained pending the agency's records check, while DHSUD's prioritized funding letter was committed but not yet submitted in the hearing.

Presidential proclamations, land allocation, surveys, and legal assistance

Leila de Lima raised recurring delays in presidential proclamations, land titles, certificates of land allocation, basic services, and land-acquisition funding, and requested project-level status reports and 2027 budget coverage. The secretary undertook to submit the requested information, while the agency said it had received only 3,000,000 against a request for 151,000,000 for survey-related work. DHSUD officials said they were working with the Office of the Executive Secretary and the Office of the Cabinet Secretary on a consolidated interagency proclamation process, but the hearing did not establish a legal-assistance mechanism for private land claims. Mica Gonzales sought an agency-LGU response to submerged Bacolor settlement sites; NHA said three to four sites were fully submerged, was exploring financial assistance, and agreed to coordinate. Rep. Miro Quimbo criticized housing underspending and endorsed the CMP, but no resolution of the funding and implementation concerns was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status, funding, and completion timelines of delayed presidential proclamations and socialized housing projects, including surveys, titles, land allocation, estate management, and legal assistance. It also asked what agencies would do for submerged housing sites in Bacolor and how the Community Mortgage Program (CMP) and available housing funds were being implemented.

The agency said it would submit project-by-project status information once Rep. Delima's list was provided, while acknowledging that the survey allocation was 3,000,000 against a requested 151,000,000. It supported consolidated, interagency handling of presidential proclamations, said it was exploring assistance for submerged Bacolor housing sites, and said SHFC would verify coastal CMP projects and pending applications.

Outcome The agency undertook to submit project status information, follow up a consolidated proclamation process, verify coastal CMP data, and coordinate on Bacolor with the LGU and Rep. Gonzales. The legal-assistance mechanism for private land claims, the adequacy of survey funding, and concrete rehabilitation or relocation measures for submerged sites remained open.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · committed

Manila Bay resettlement and the 370,000,000 NHA allocation

Rep. Lanny Mercado questioned whether the NHA's allocation of about 370 million was sufficient for Manila Bay resettlement, citing a backlog of more than 2,000 units in her district. Mercado also raised a shortage involving 117 families due 30,000 pesos each, and an agency official said EHAP funds were expected to be released within two weeks. Mercado seconded a motion for additional housing funding, which the chair said would be acted on at the proper time.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the NHA's 370,000,000 allocation was sufficient to relocate informal settler families affected by the Supreme Court Mandamus on Manila Bay, including the reported backlog in the member's district. It also asked whether EHAP funds and SHFC assistance for parking facilities could address related shortfalls.

The agency indicated that the 370,000,000 allocation was constrained because projects were multiyear and current funding did not allow it to accommodate new projects, while an agency official estimated that the amount could cover about four buildings. The agency also said EHAP funds were expected to be released within two weeks and committed to revisit and study SHFC assistance for the parking request.

Outcome The agency acknowledged funding constraints, while EHAP fund release and SHFC review were identified as prospective responses. The request for additional housing funding was seconded but deferred for committee action at the proper time.

Former President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo asked DHSUD about the escrow fund balance, its allocation, beneficiaries, and the construction status of about 23,000 units. DHSUD stated that the balance was "12.7 around 12,700,000,000," that around 80% of 12,000,000,000 was ongoing, and that disbursements were progressive, although other allocation figures were unclear. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the balance and utilization of the escrow housing-for-balanced-development fund, the status of projects and beneficiaries, and DHSUD's treatment of balanced-housing compliance in light of DOJ guidance and a COA audit observation. Members also sought clarification on the proposed 2027 budget and support for low-income housing.

DHSUD stated that the escrow fund was being allocated almost fully to direct housing production and related programs, with disbursement proceeding progressively as projects advanced. On balanced-housing compliance, the agency said it was processing and validating the applicable amounts, had sought additional time, was operating under a moratorium through February 2027, and intended to implement the DOJ opinion prospectively while addressing the COA AOM.

Outcome DHSUD provided partial answers on the escrow balance, allocation, project status, and balanced-housing guidance. It undertook to submit project information and continue reviewing the homeowners' association rules and the DOJ-COA issue, but several financial computations and the detailed status of compliance remained unclear.

Socialized-housing permit streamlining and developer payment delays

Representative Elmer Catulpos raised concerns that socialized-housing permitting was insufficiently attractive to developers and cited a permitting example involving 86 documents, 35 documents, and sixteen days, although the comparison was unclear. DHSUD answered that an interagency memorandum had reduced subdivision requirements from 223 to 62 and condominium requirements from 162 to 71, corresponding to reductions of 72% and 56%. The agency also reported stage-level processing-time reductions of as much as 76% for subdivisions and 75% for condominiums, with a 50% target for total processing time. Catulpos asked whether socialized housing would receive comparable streamlining, and DHSUD said socialized and non-socialized projects would have more or less the same streamlined requirements, with BP 220 serving as a technical reference. He also raised reports that developer payments took six months or more and could result in penalties. DHSUD cited digitalization and coordination with the Land Bank as the response, while Catulpos manifested support for increasing DHSUD's 2027 budget.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DHSUD had reduced permitting requirements and processing times for socialized-housing projects, and whether delays in processing payments to developers were being addressed. It also sought clarification on whether streamlining applied equally to socialized and open-market housing.

DHSUD stated that it had no pending or overdue regulatory applications for ten consecutive weeks and acted on applications within fifteen days, while allowing ninety days to comply with deficiencies and permitting temporary licenses in appropriate cases. It said the 2026 interagency streamlining initiative would substantially reduce documentary requirements and target a 50% reduction in total processing time for subdivision and condominium projects, while digitalization and coordination with the Land Bank were intended to address delayed developer payments.

Outcome DHSUD answered that permitting requirements and processing times were being streamlined for both socialized and open-market projects, with implementation targeting a 50% reduction in total processing time. The developer-payment concern was acknowledged through a stated digitalization and Land Bank coordination approach, but no specific deadline, payment target, or further document submission was provided.

DHSUD · 2026-08-25 · unresolved

Resettlement units, vacant housing, and Supreme Court Mandamus obligations

Rep. Sarah Elago raised the status of 26,041 resettlement units and questioned a report listing 8,477 vacant units. The NHA said most Mandamus-related units were occupied, while about 8,000 vacant units in Rizal were affected by the provincial government's preference for Rizal beneficiaries and opposition to relocations from other areas. Elago also asked about community interventions, the proposed 2027 budget, balanced housing compliance, and DOJ-COA guidance. The agency cited training, utility coordination, financial assistance, off-site CMP, and SHFC community programs, and stated that the proposed 2027 budget was about 44 billion in readable magnitude. It said a one-year moratorium ran through February 2027 and that the DOJ-related requirement would be implemented prospectively, but the computation and the additional requested budget figure remained unclear. The matter ended without a recorded resolution or final ruling.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how many resettlement units remained vacant, why vacancies persisted, and how the units related to Supreme Court Mandamus obligations. It also examined DHSUD's proposed 2027 budget, balanced housing compliance, applicable DOJ-COA guidance, and whether resettlement and community interventions were adequately funded.

The agency said most resettlement units connected with the Mandamus were occupied, but a large group of vacant units in Rizal could not readily be filled because the provincial government preferred beneficiaries from Rizal and opposed relocation from other areas. It said it was pursuing training, utility coordination, community and CMP interventions, and prospective implementation of the DOJ opinion after the moratorium, while seeking time to comply with related COA guidance.

Outcome The agency explained the principal reason given for the vacant units in Rizal and described its planned compliance and housing interventions, but the committee did not resolve the vacancy issue, the disputed computation, or the unclear budget figure. The exchange ended after the agency's statements, with no recorded request for a specific follow-up document or final ruling.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DHSUD, the NHA, and partner agencies would assist communities whose settlement sites or homes were submerged, damaged by fire, or otherwise affected by calamities. The NHA and DHSUD said they were assessing financial and emergency assistance for submerged settlement sites, fire-damaged homes, and other calamity-affected households. They maintained that additional funds were needed to continue housing programs and emergency assistance, while identifying construction materials, shelter repair kits, IDSAP and EHAB, and LGU modular houses as available forms of support.

Outcome The agency undertook to coordinate with the Bacolor LGU, assess possible financial support, and review the landmaster-LGU request. DHSUD also stated that additional funding was necessary for continued housing and emergency programs, and the vice chair expressed support; no final budget increase or specific additional amount was approved in the exchange.

Rufus Rodriguez raised delayed emergency shelter assistance of 68 to 343 days and a proposed student dormitory; the agency attributed delays to fund availability and cited an existing Pag-IBIG joint-venture program. Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether NHA and SHFC had sufficient funding for relocation housing and essential facilities at existing resettlement sites, including parking buildings, daycare centers, and covered courts. Members also asked about emergency shelter assistance funding and the feasibility of student dormitories through existing housing programs.

NHA said limited funding required it to prioritize housing units over amenities at older resettlement sites, while seeking assistance from DepEd and LGUs for daycare centers, covered courts, and related facilities. The agency said EHAP and quick-response funds had been requested, that emergency-assistance delays were linked to fund availability, and that SHFC and Pag-IBIG-related facility requests would be studied through existing programs.

Outcome The committee recorded agency explanations and requests for additional support, but no additional appropriation was approved during these exchanges. Follow-up remained pending on the NHA facilities list, the release of emergency funds, SHFC’s parking-facility study, and the student-dormitory discussions.

Secretary Cristina Aldeguer identified 5,000,000,000 for SB Corporation, 150,000,000 each for fair trade and foreign trade, and restoration of trade-show funding from 80,000,000 toward the requested 250,000,000. Members also sought additional support for CDA, Cagayan de Oro projects, cooperative officers, RAISE, and APECO, while DTI and attached agencies gave several commitments to submit information or check with DBM. Brian Poe separately requested documents on PAXILICA's technology transfer, worker protections, and economic effects, and DTI said the agreement had a tentative November signing target. The chair concluded that restoration priorities would be reviewed through the committee and Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee, leaving the final amount unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why DTI's proposed budget was reduced from the prior year's appropriation, which programs and attached agencies were affected, and which items should be restored. Members also asked whether DTI's funding was adequate for industrial development, MSME support, cooperative development, trade promotion, halal exports, and related projects.

DTI said the DBM allocation was insufficient for its mandates and for programs supporting investment promotion, consumer protection and fair trade, MSMEs, industry development, exports, trade shows, creative industries, halal certification, and skills development. It requested restoration or additional funding, including 5,000,000,000 for SB Corporation, 150,000,000 for fair trade, 150,000,000 for foreign trade, and restoration of other reduced programs, while acknowledging that any increase would have to compete within the available fiscal space.

Outcome The budget reduction was not finally resolved during the hearing. The committee undertook further review, including consideration by the Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee, while DTI was asked to submit its prioritized restoration requests and supporting projections.

Agency unavailable · 2026-08-24 · committed

PAXILICA investment, economic-security zone, and data-center safeguards

Rep. Perci Cendaña asked DTI to disclose the Paxilica agreement's scope, prospective sites, and community-consultation status. DTI said the partnership was nonbinding, involved 23 other countries and economies, and that New Clark City was a 1,620-hectare advanced-manufacturing project rather than a data-center site. Members Antonio Tinio and Brian Poe pressed officials on data centers, Israel and defense-related supply chains, knowledge transfer, wages, mineral extraction, and resource requirements. Officials said locators would provide their own roads, power, and water; possible water and energy solutions included Subic facilities and piping across the 75-kilometer distance to Clark. They also said Philippine laws, environmental rules, ECC requirements, and DOE and ERC regulations would apply, while a tentative signing target was November. The committee sought additional documents and briefings, and the chair indicated that further discussion was necessary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what the Paxilica partnership and its Philippine projects would entail, including the scope of New Clark City activities, possible data centers, resource and ownership arrangements, labor and technology-transfer terms, mineral processing, and the role of Philippine law. Members also sought documents, community-consultation updates, and safeguards before implementation or signing.

DTI and BCDA officials stated that Paxilica was a nonbinding supply-chain partnership, while New Clark City was only one project and was intended primarily for advanced manufacturing rather than AI data centers. They said locators would provide their own roads, power, and water, and that Philippine laws, environmental requirements, ECCs, labor rules, DOE and ERC regulations, and BCDA law would govern implementation.

Outcome Officials clarified that the partnership was nonbinding and that New Clark City was intended for advanced manufacturing, while data-center locations and several resource, mineral-processing, and commercial terms remained under discussion. The committee requested documents, consultation updates, and further briefings; Philippine-law, environmental, and permitting safeguards were stated but the broader project terms and tax-relief questions remained open.

Agency unavailable · 2026-08-24 · committed

CARS and RACE automotive incentives and funding

Representatives Perci Cendaña and Renee Luizco questioned DTI on the restoration and design of RACE, the completed CARS program, and the treatment of local automotive manufacturers. DTI said CARS had awarded two slots to Toyota and Mitsubishi, while RACE was still being finalized and would be opened to more participants. DTI also described EV incentives and said the policy was to shift the sector toward electric vehicles, but Luizco questioned whether the PHP5 billion capitalization requirement and other standards would exclude local manufacturers. Secretary Cristina Roque undertook to contact Francisco Motors and submit or provide requested program and policy information. Antonio Tinio then asked how CARS would be funded; DTI initially stated 5,100,000,000 and linked the funding to DPWH savings, but an agency official later corrected the savings figure to 4,081,000,000, with other figures in the exchange unclear. The issue therefore led to agency commitments and a funding clarification, but the requested documentation and final RACE budget were not yet presented.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the CARS and RACE automotive incentive programs would be restored or expanded, how they would be funded, and whether the programs would benefit local manufacturers and require actual local production. It also asked which companies had received or could receive incentives, including under the electric-vehicle incentive scheme.

DTI said CARS had been completed for Toyota and Mitsubishi, while RACE was still being finalized and would be opened to more participants. It supported a transition toward electric vehicles and stated that incentives were intended to attract Philippine manufacturing, with local-purchasing and capitalization requirements; it also said CARS funding came from DPWH savings, although the figures were corrected and partly unclear in the exchange.

Outcome DTI clarified that CARS had been completed for Toyota and Mitsubishi, while RACE remained under finalization and was intended to accommodate more participants. The committee received a funding explanation pointing to DPWH savings, but the discussion contained conflicting figures, with 4,081,000,000 identified as the corrected savings amount; requested program and industry documents remained to be submitted.

Electric-vehicle policy and local automotive manufacturing

Rep. Perci Cendaña asked DTI to explain its EV programs and submit an industrial roadmap; DTI said it was shifting the automotive sector toward electric vehicles and would provide the requested information. Secretary Maria Cristina Roque reported that the SB Corporation e-transport loan had approved 18 applications and released 47,000,000 pesos, while the chair promoted electric transport as cheaper to operate than conventional vehicles. Rep. Renee Luizco challenged whether the CARS, RACE, and EV programs would support genuine local manufacturing rather than foreign companies and flagged the PHP5 billion capitalization requirement. DTI said local suppliers and partnerships were included, but acknowledged that Filipino companies supplying foreign participants were not necessarily vehicle manufacturers. DTI undertook to contact Francisco Motors and other local manufacturers and to submit requested data. Rep. Tina Pancho later sought priority for Filipino jeepney manufacturers, and DTI assured her that it would assist them and provide an update after consultations.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DTI's electric-vehicle incentive policies would overcome capitalization barriers, require meaningful local manufacturing and local-content participation, and prioritize Filipino jeepney and vehicle manufacturers. Members also asked how electric transport operators could access financing and whether DTI would provide policy, program, and consultation documents.

DTI stated that its automotive policy was transitioning toward electric vehicles and that its incentive schemes were intended to attract both hybrid and fully electric vehicle manufacturing in the Philippines. It maintained that local participation would be supported through SME purchasing requirements, local partnerships, supply-chain participation, industry consultations, and direct coordination with Francisco Motors and other local manufacturers.

Outcome DTI answered the policy and financing questions and made several commitments to submit information, coordinate with manufacturers, and assist local firms. The capitalization barrier, the distinction between local parts supply and local vehicle manufacturing, and the eventual prioritization of Filipino manufacturers remained open for follow-up.

SB Corporation P3 loans and consolidated fund accountability

Rep. Iris Marie Montes first asked DTI for SB Corporation loan-release, repayment, rate, and MSME-reach data, while Secretary Cristina Roque described collateral-free loans of up to 5,000,000 and a one-year payment grace period. DTI also reported 274 Women Enterprise Fund approvals and 56,000,000 disbursed, and 18 approved e-transport applications with 47,000,000 released. Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. then questioned the proposed 140,170,000 P3 allocation and requested consolidated accounting of all SB Corporation government funds. SB Corporation President Bobby reported around PHP 10,000,000,000 received since 2017, more than 500,000 P3 beneficiaries, and a portfolio figure transcribed as R10 billion dollars, while the transcript also recorded 30,000,000 yen in releases with unclear currency wording. Nazal highlighted the gap between 19,373 beneficiaries and the 40,000 target despite 1,000,000,000 being reported as fully disbursed, and asked for a detailed status and rate breakdown. The agency committed to provide the records and consult the SB Corporation board, leaving the accounting and effective-rate issues pending.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how SB Corporation had used and managed P3 and other government funds, including the borrowers reached, amounts released, repayments, loan portfolio status, and the meaning of reported disbursements. It also questioned whether P3 borrowers were being charged rates consistent with the program's purpose and whether the proposed 140,170,000 allocation should be released before consolidated accounting was provided.

DTI maintained that SB Corporation financing was a key MSME intervention and that demand exceeded available funds. It defended simplified, collateral-free loans and one-year payment relief, but did not provide during the hearing the requested consolidated accounting, portfolio-status breakdown, or effective-rate analysis; those matters were referred for submission and discussion with the SB Corporation board.

Outcome The agency committed to submit borrower-level and consolidated portfolio information and to return with the SB Corporation board's assessment of P3 rates and charges. The proposed allocation, accounting status, and rate concerns were not resolved during the hearing.

MSME market access, financing, and bottom-up priorities

DTI presented market access, trade-fair, MSME financing, and provincial-support programs, including about 100,000,000 pesos in proposed additional international-marketing funding, 33 trade fairs in 2025, and 38 planned local fairs in 2026. Secretary Roque said SB Corp. offered collateral-free loans of up to 5,000,000 with a one-year payment holiday, but available funds were insufficient. Rep. Montes sought trade-deficit measures and details on the Women Enterprise Fund, which had approved 274 applicants and disbursed 56,000,000 pesos. Rep. Garcia requested restoration of bottom-up priorities and documentation of investment gains, while Rep. Sagarbarria sought more than 66,000,000 for the Negros Island Region. Rep. Nazal questioned retail access, P3 fund accounting, beneficiary counts, and loan rates, prompting commitments for detailed records and possible policy changes. A minority member supported more Halal funding after DTI reported 277 certified MSMEs and a proposed 81,000,000 pesos allocation, although the transcript contained unclear Halal budget figures.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DTI would expand MSME financing, market access, trade promotion, and provincial support within the proposed budget. Members also asked whether DTI would restore locally identified priorities, protect MSMEs from restrictive retail practices, account for SB Corp. funds, and strengthen the Halal industry.

DTI maintained that MSME development required simultaneous market access, affordable financing, skills and technology support, and stronger provincial implementation. It said demand for SB Corp. loans and Halal certification exceeded available funds, while committing to provide requested SB Corp. and investment documents and to consider further budget or policy changes.

Outcome DTI defended its strategy and stated that it needed additional funding, but several matters remained open. The agency committed to submit investment and SB Corp. records, consult on retail practices and P3 pricing, and seek more support for the Negros Island Region and Halal programs.

Halal industry assistance and certification

Former President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo questioned DTI about why Philippine Halal exports lagged despite trade missions and said multiple certifying bodies and logos confused Muslim-country buyers. DTI acknowledged the certification problem, said exporters were being directed to bodies accredited in destination markets, and undertook to provide a list of companies that had engaged with those bodies. DTI reported 277 certified MSMEs and assistance to 140 MSMEs for 2026, with a Halal allocation stated inconsistently as PHP 90,000,000 and 90,000,000,000 and a target of 81,000,000 pesos for the following year. The secretary said more funding was needed for certification, trade shows, slaughterhouses, and market expansion, citing 13,000,000 Muslims in the Philippines and a global market estimated at 2 to 3,000,000,000,000 US dollars. A minority member and Rep. Brian Poe supported increased Halal funding, while DTI said domestic violations were not recorded but export-market partners had raised certification concerns. The issue landed with continued DTI coordination and funding requests, but without resolution of the single-certifying-body proposal, export-growth evidence, or the conflicting budget figures.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed Halal budget was sufficient, how widely DTI's assistance reached provincial MSMEs, and whether Philippine Halal certification was credible and recognized in export markets. Members also asked what institutional and whole-of-government measures were being taken to address fragmented certification and expand Halal exports.

DTI acknowledged that fragmented and sometimes unreliable certification was limiting Philippine Halal exports. It said it was working with certifying bodies recognized by destination markets, assisting MSMEs across regions, coordinating through the Halal board, and seeking more funding for certification, promotion, trade shows, and related facilities.

Outcome DTI acknowledged certification credibility and market recognition problems, but said it was aligning exporters with certifying bodies recognized by destination markets and supporting MSMEs across eight regions. The committee expressed support for increased Halal funding, while export-growth results, the exact budget figures, and the future single-certification framework remained open.

Creative-industries funding and Center for Excellence

Rep. Sarah Elago requested a detailed breakdown of the Film Academy of the Philippines' proposed appropriation; its director general said the original proposal was 267,000,000 and had been reduced to 104,000,000. Rep. Javi Benitez then pressed DTI on creative-industries funding, citing the sector's 7.8% GDP contribution, an estimated 30% budget decline, a previous high of 300,000,000, and a reported zero in the FY2027 national expenditure program. DTI said the current regular creative-industry budget was 50,000,000, acknowledged the reduction, and said it would seek more funding because the sector could drive trade, tourism, jobs, and ASEAN engagement. DTI also confirmed that creative industries were a priority for ASEAN activities and that they would be featured in meetings, trade shows, and dedicated areas, including a potential Center for Excellence. The committee chair identified creative-industries development as a restoration priority and requested DTI's priority programs for submission to the budget review process. The issue remained open pending those submissions and committee deliberation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the proposed funding for creative industries, including whether a previously higher allocation had fallen to zero or to a lower regular line-item amount. Members also asked whether creative industries and a proposed Center for Excellence were priorities for DTI and ASEAN-related activities, and what funding restoration or documents the agency would seek.

DTI said creative industries were a priority and could drive trade, tourism, employment, ASEAN engagement, and global market access. It acknowledged that funding had fallen substantially, citing a 50,000,000 regular budget and confirming that the FY2027 proposal was at zero, and said it would seek a larger allocation.

Outcome The committee recognized creative industries as a priority and indicated that funding reductions, including the reported zero FY2027 proposal, would be considered for restoration. DTI was expected to submit its priority restoration items, but no restoration amount or final appropriation was decided during the hearing.

Trade deficit, export diversification, and tariff effects

Representative Iris Marie Montes asked which DTI budget measures would address the trade deficit through export diversification, import substitution, and industry modernization. Secretary Cristina Roque pointed to export promotion, trade shows, foreign trade attaches, domestic market access, free-trade agreements, and interagency industry training, citing an 8,000,000 investment that generated 150,000,000 in sales. Representative Antonio Tinio separately questioned the source and amount of CARS funding, and the agency ultimately cited DPWH savings of 4,081,000,000, after other figures were stated or corrected. Tinio also asked about United States tariffs and forced-labor compliance; DTI said the 12.5% tariff covered 30% of exports to the United States, with several sectors affected and specified products exempted. DTI said the Philippines had a legal framework addressing forced labor but that United States evaluation and negotiations remained ongoing. The committee requested supporting documents and asked DTI to submit budget-restoration priorities for further deliberation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which 2027 DTI budget allocations would reduce the trade deficit through export diversification, import substitution, and industry modernization. It also examined the effect of United States tariffs and forced-labor compliance requirements on Philippine exports, and clarified the funding source and amount for the CARS program.

DTI said the trade deficit should be addressed by expanding exports, diversifying products and markets, strengthening domestic market access and local industrial capacity, and using free-trade agreements to secure preferential tariffs. On United States tariffs, DTI said the Philippines had a legal and administrative framework addressing forced labor, but the United States evaluation and negotiations were still ongoing; DTI also said it would help affected exporters find alternative markets.

Outcome The trade-deficit and tariff issues were not finally resolved during the hearing. DTI was to submit tariff documentation and identify budget items for possible restoration, while the committee reserved the matters for further budget deliberation.

Investment promotion authorities and foreign direct investment

DTI presented BOI and PEZA investment approvals as evidence that investment-promotion authorities were attracting projects and generating employment. It reported BOI approvals of about 1.56 trillion in 2025 linked to 40,175 projected jobs, and PEZA approvals of roughly 216.46 billion in the first eight months of 2026 linked to 27,000 projected direct jobs. Rep. Albert Garcia questioned whether the Create More framework, investment-promotion authorities, and free ports had actually increased FDI and requested documents showing the investment gains and sunk investment in the country. Secretary Cristina Roque cited a 94.4% PEZA increase from January to June and committed to provide the requested documents. Rep. Jay Vergara separately raised a Korean agricultural-machinery project in Cabanatuan, and Undersecretary Perry committed to examine and support it. A DTI official also cited an investment pipeline of about 18 billion for renewable energy, but the hearing did not resolve the documentation or project follow-through.

Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish whether investment-promotion authorities, free-port structures, and related agreements were producing actual foreign direct investment, employment, industrial activity, and regional gains. Members also sought documentation supporting the agency's reported investment results and clarification on a Korean agricultural-machinery project in Cabanatuan.

DTI maintained that BOI, PEZA, the Create More Act, the SIPP, Green Lanes, economic zones, and free-trade or digital agreements were attracting investment, encouraging expansions, and generating jobs. It presented BOI and PEZA approvals, projected employment, an investment pipeline, and examples of investor activity as evidence, while acknowledging that additional budget and documentation could support further gains.

Outcome DTI defended the investment-promotion framework with reported approvals, projected jobs, expansion activity, and an investment pipeline. The committee required supporting investment documentation, and DTI committed to provide it; the Korean project was also left for agency review and assistance.

DTI industry-development strategy and job quality

Secretary Cristina Roque presented DTI's strategy of investment and export promotion, MSME market access and finance, consumer protection, and skills development, citing about 1.56 trillion in BOI-approved investments and 40,175 projected jobs, as well as 216.46 billion in PEZA investments and 27,000 projected direct jobs. Representative Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned the reduced DTI budget, MSME programs, retailer charges, and the accountability of P3 funds; DTI and SB Corp. cited about 10 billion in GAA allocations since 2017, more than 500,000 beneficiaries, and a loan portfolio described unclearly in the transcript as R10 billion dollars. Nazal also challenged the reported 100% disbursement of 1 billion against 19,373 beneficiaries and questioned rates of up to 2.5% monthly or around 30% annually. Representative Eli San Fernando challenged DTI's claim that industry development was producing high-paying, quality jobs, citing 225,000 jobs and a separate unclear figure of 177,000. DTI said employment ranged from high-end technical work to mass factory and BPO jobs, acknowledged the need for higher-paying employment, and pointed to skills programs and industrial-policy coordination. The agency undertook to provide documents, obtain data, consult the SB Corp. board, and seek more industrial-development resources, leaving the quality-of-jobs issue contested.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DTI's 2027 industry-development strategy would generate high-paying, quality jobs rather than mainly low-wage or retail employment. Members also tested how DTI would coordinate industrial policy, develop skills, support priority industries, expand MSME market access, and account for SB Corp. funds.

DTI said its strategy combined investment and export promotion, consumer protection, MSME market access and finance, skills development, and sector-specific industrial programs. It maintained that industrial development could generate both high-end and mass employment, acknowledged that not all current jobs were high-paying, and committed to seek more resources and provide requested SB Corp. data.

Outcome DTI's broad strategy was presented, but the committee did not resolve whether its employment outcomes were genuinely high-paying and high-quality. SB Corp. accounting and rate information, retail employment data, and possible industrial-policy and budget adjustments remained subject to agency submissions or further discussion.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the Bureau of Philippine Standards had sufficient funding, personnel, and regional reach to inspect products and enforce standards, particularly for materials used in infrastructure. It also examined the value of substandard steel products, the cases against violators, and whether penalties under Republic Act 7394 were adequate.

DTI said its product standards enforcement was constrained by insufficient personnel and funding despite having 18 regional offices and nationwide inspection responsibilities. It requested 150,000,000 for the current year, committed to submit annual case details, and said it was recommending legislation to expand visitorial powers and allow higher penalties.

Outcome The committee received DTI's explanation that enforcement needed additional personnel and funding and that 150,000,000 was requested for the current year. DTI undertook to submit case details and the budget basis, while the adequacy of Republic Act 7394 penalties remained unresolved pending possible legislation.

Price monitoring and the PHP78 food benchmark

Representative Sarah Elago asked DTI about enforcement of prices for basic necessities and prime commodities and whether its monitoring reached public markets. Secretary Maria Cristina Lopez said DTI monitored supermarkets and groceries daily through 18 regional offices, while the Department of Agriculture handled wet and public markets. Asek Malayari reported very good compliance and said DTI issued letters of inquiry when prices exceeded suggested retail prices. Elago then questioned whether PHP78 per person per day, derived from the PHP111 per-person poverty threshold and a 70% food threshold, realistically covered basic nutritional needs. Lopez said she was not aware of the basis for PHP78 and committed to coordinate with SECRC and Balisakan, leaving the benchmark's adequacy unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DTI monitored and enforced prices for basic necessities and prime commodities, including the limits of its jurisdiction over public markets. It also asked whether the PHP78 per-person food benchmark realistically covered basic nutritional needs.

DTI stated that it monitored basic necessities and prime commodities daily through 18 regional offices, primarily in supermarkets and groceries, where it reported generally good compliance. It did not take a position on whether PHP78 was nutritionally adequate, saying it needed to coordinate with SECRC and Balisakan and that public-market and food-logistics matters belonged principally to the Department of Agriculture.

Outcome DTI explained its price-monitoring jurisdiction and reported generally good compliance in supermarkets and groceries, while public markets and food logistics were left to the Department of Agriculture. The adequacy of the PHP78 food benchmark remained unanswered, subject to DTI's promised coordination with SECRC and Balisakan.

Abaca industry decline and integrated value-chain support

Rufus Rodriguez raised the sharp decline in national and Catanduanes abaca production and asked about its effects on the entire value chain, including employment, income, and markets. DTI said it provided MSME assistance, market access, product development, shared service facilities, and cluster coordination through 18 regional offices and 1,400 Negotio centers. The regional DTI official acknowledged that industry-wide resources were lacking and identified both reduced raw-material supply and shrinking markets as concerns. The DTI Secretary said abaca production was under the Department of Agriculture but reported that abaca fiber exports rose by 25% in 2025 to 21,700,000. Rodriguez then asked for an integrated FY2027 plan, citing 4,300,000 in shared service facilities for Catanduanes producers. DTI committed to coordinate with the province and offered a report, but did not present specific FY2027 programs or investments.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the causes and effects of declining abaca production across the value chain, including producers, traders, processors, handicraft and furniture makers, employment, income, and markets. It also asked whether DTI had an integrated industry-development plan and what specific FY2027 programs and investments would support higher-value abaca products and expanded markets.

DTI stated that it supported abaca enterprises mainly at the MSME level through market access, product development, shared service facilities, cluster coordination, and regional and Negotio Center services. It acknowledged that industry-wide resources were lacking, while pointing to increased abaca fiber exports and committing to coordinate with the province and help producers access domestic and global markets.

Outcome DTI answered that it had existing MSME and market-access mechanisms but lacked resources for additional industry-wide programs. It offered coordination and a report on possible interventions, but the requested integrated FY2027 abaca industry plan and specific investments were not clearly provided.

Bamboo development transfer and interagency coordination

Gloria Macapagal Arroyo raised the pending proposal to transfer bamboo development from DTI to DA and asked whether DTI had already ceded the function. DTI said its role concerned finished bamboo products and market access, but it did not clarify the transfer status or confirm compliance with the DepEd bamboo procurement requirement. Arroyo also questioned DTI's whole-of-government coordination and argued that multiple halal certifiers and logos confused importing countries. DTI acknowledged the certification problem, said exporters were directed to destination-country-accredited certifiers, and said some companies had engaged with them. Arroyo requested evidence of actual purchases and export growth in Malaysia and Pakistan, but DTI did not provide figures. DTI committed to provide a list of companies and speak with Seksani again, while the broader coordination and legislative questions remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DTI was aware of pending legislation to transfer bamboo development to the Department of Agriculture and whether DTI had voluntarily ceded that function. It also examined whether DTI's whole-of-government approach was producing concrete coordination on bamboo procurement and halal certification, including the proposed move toward a single certifying body.

DTI said its bamboo role focused on finished bamboo products and market access, while bamboo development was described as being with DA. It acknowledged problems with halal certification, said exporters could use certifiers accredited in destination countries, and stated that some companies had already engaged with those bodies. DTI did not provide the requested export figures or resolve whether the bamboo procurement requirement was being implemented.

Outcome DTI acknowledged coordination and certification problems but did not establish that it had voluntarily transferred bamboo development to DA, provide the requested halal export results, or confirm compliance with the bamboo procurement requirement. It undertook to submit a company list and follow up with Seksani, leaving the substantive issues open.

DOJ FY2027 budget reductions and restoration requests

The DOJ presented a FY2027 recommended budget with major reductions affecting OSEC programs, BI, NBI, OADR, corrections, OSAIC, IACAT, and cybercrime-related work. Members Pajernos, Ann Matibag, Adelima, and Rodriguez expressed support for the DOJ budget and for restoring or increasing priority allocations. DOJ officials requested restoration to FY2026 levels, including OSEC MOOE and priority enforcement programs, while the NBI sought restoration of about 882 million and hazard pay of PHP15000 monthly. PAO sought additional lawyers and staff costing about 700 million, BI requested capital outlay for its new building and IT systems, and OSG identified about 123 million for digitalization. The committee said it would work on these requests, but no final restoration was adopted during the exchange.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the scale and operational effects of the reductions in the DOJ's FY2027 recommended budget, and which DOJ offices and programs required restoration. It also sought specific restoration amounts, staffing and capital-outlay needs, and agency commitments to improve budget utilization.

The DOJ stated that the FY2027 recommended budget could sustain its performance targets but acknowledged that reductions in OSEC, NBI, BI, OSAIC, IACAT, cybercrime, ICT, OADR, PAO, and other programs would constrain operations. DOJ officials requested restoration to FY2026 levels for priority programs and identified specific needs for NBI hazard pay, PAO staffing, BI capital outlay, OSG digitalization, and PPA computerization.

Outcome The committee broadly supported restoring reductions to FY2026 levels but did not adopt a final department-wide restoration figure. Specific agency requests were identified for further committee action, while the BI fee and some capital-outlay amounts remained under review or unclear.

Anti-trafficking, cybercrime, and OSAEC budget cuts

Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores, a Gabriela member, and Rep. Percy Sandania questioned the proposed reductions affecting anti-trafficking, cybercrime enforcement, OSAEC, and the NCC. DOJ officials said the cuts would weaken capacity-building, local task forces, rescue operations, IT infrastructure, international data sharing, and the response to AI-enabled exploitation. The figures cited included reductions of 71%, 58%, 41%, 58.93%, and 14%, while the DOJ requested restoration of the relevant budgets to 2026 levels and identified additional NCC plantilla positions as a need. The DOJ later provided budget figures for the NCC, anti-trafficking secretariat, and Office of Cybercrime, including an unclear transcribed 2027 cybercrime figure. Members Ann Matibag and Laila Adelima manifested support for restoring or increasing the affected funding and asked to work with the DOJ on specific priority items. No final committee restoration was recorded, but the issue was committed for further work before plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why the proposed budgets for anti-trafficking, cybercrime enforcement, and OSAEC-related programs were sharply reduced, whether the reductions reflected absorptive-capacity problems, and how they would affect enforcement, rescue operations, staffing, and responses to AI-enabled crimes. Members also sought the DOJ's requested funding levels and whether the cuts should be restored to 2026 levels.

The DOJ said the reductions would undermine national and local responses to trafficking, OSAEC, cybercrime, and AI-enabled exploitation, delay capacity-building, weaken rescue operations, and threaten the Philippines' Tier One status in the U.S. TIP report. It requested restoration of the relevant budgets to 2026 levels, additional NCC plantilla positions, stronger IT and investigative capacity, and continued international information-sharing mechanisms.

Outcome DOJ officials consistently requested restoration of the affected programs to 2026 levels, and several members expressed support for that position. The transcript did not record a committee ruling or final restoration, although members indicated that the issue would be pursued before plenary.

Questions and agency response

Bureau of Immigration modernization, e-gates, and BMIS funding

Rep. Pachernos asked about e-gate operations and modernization procurement, and the Bureau reported 78 e-gates at Terminals 1 and 3 and described Phase one, Phase two, and Phase three funding. Allan Ty then questioned BMIS's purpose, total cost, government share, and relationship to the government-funded e-gates project. The Bureau said the private proponent would shoulder about 10.7 billion for the first five years and described additional twenty-year costs, although the stated government-share figures were unclear. Members identified substantial unobligated allotments, including 4.071 for 2025 and 3,558,000,000 for 2026, which the Bureau attributed to failed bidding, rebidding, and revisions after donated e-gates required changes to the procurement plan. Commissioner Beado and Commissioner Viejo committed to complete procurement and fully obligate the affected funds by November, while some release and disbursement figures were to be verified later. Mr. Erviato clarified that the broader CAES-integrated border-control system was under a PPP arrangement and was distinct from the appropriated e-gates project.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the operational status, procurement progress, costs, funding sources, obligations, and implementation schedule of the Bureau of Immigration's e-gates, modernization, and border-management information system projects. Members also examined why substantial allotments remained unobligated and how the government-funded e-gates project differed from the proposed PPP-based border-control system.

The Bureau stated that the government-funded e-gates modernization effort was separate from the larger PPP-based BMIS or enhanced border-control system, although the e-gates would be integrated with the CAES platform. It attributed unobligated allotments and delays to failed bidding, rebidding, and revisions required after donated e-gates created a risk of duplicative procurement, while committing to complete the affected obligations and modernization activities.

Outcome The Bureau attributed the unobligated allotments to failed bidding, rebidding, and procurement revisions and committed to full obligation by November and to completing the modernization program. The committee also established that the government-funded e-gates project was distinct from the proposed PPP-based BMIS or enhanced border-control system, but exact release and disbursement figures remained subject to confirmation.

Rennyko specifically cited the reported transfer of 15,730 inmates and asked how transportation, security, infrastructure, medical services, and staffing were funded and provided. Questions and agency response

BuCor said it was gradually reducing congestion through yearly transfers, regionalization, and construction or expansion of dormitory and other prison capacity, with 2028 as the target period for decongestion and NBP closure. It said transfers were funded from BuCor's existing MOE budget, NBP congestion had fallen from 300% to almost 200%, and additional capacity for 11,000 plus PDL was expected by 2028.

Outcome BuCor maintained that it was progressing toward the 2028 decongestion and NBP-closure objective, but the hearing did not establish a fully documented transfer schedule, complete receiving-facility capacity assessment, or definitive resolution of the conflicting congestion figures. The requested budget-utilization data and facility-by-facility transfer list remained commitments for subsequent submission.

DOJ petition-for-review backlog and case-disposition performance

DOJ officials presented high NPS case-disposition and prosecution-success rates, including 395,780 disposed cases out of a 428,779 caseload in 2025 and a 90.84% prosecution success rate. Members then distinguished those field-office indicators from the separate petition-for-review backlog before the Secretary, reported at about 16,000 cases from 2020 to November 11, 2025, plus approximately 10,000 cases filed earlier. Secretary Vida said his office had resolved almost 500, or roughly 2.5% of the 16,000-case group, and had delegated work to eight undersecretaries with a target of 800 cases per month. Members questioned whether the PSR overstated actual conviction performance and requested separate graft, corruption, drug, filing, disposition, and conviction data. Rep. Luizco also sought review and status data for terrorism-related cases under the DOJ's stricter evidentiary standard. The DOJ committed to submit the requested disaggregated data and backlog breakdowns, leaving the underlying backlog unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the size and age of the DOJ's petition-for-review backlog, the rate at which the Office of the Secretary was disposing of those petitions, and whether the DOJ's broader prosecution and conviction indicators accurately reflected case outcomes. Members also asked whether the DOJ's stricter evidentiary standard would improve case quality and requested disaggregated data on prosecution, conviction, dismissal, filing, and terrorism-related cases.

The DOJ stated that its NPS performance remained high, but acknowledged that the separate petition-for-review backlog was substantial and was not captured by the field-office disposition indicators. The DOJ said it had delegated new petitions to eight undersecretaries, established a target of 800 monthly dispositions, was reviewing older cases through task forces and publication, and would submit disaggregated backlog, filing, disposition, conviction, and case-type data.

Outcome The DOJ answered that the NPS performance indicators did not include petitions for review pending before the Secretary's office. The petition backlog remained largely unresolved: the DOJ reported about 16,000 cases from 2020 to November 11, 2025, approximately 10,000 older cases, and only around 400 to almost 500 resolved cases; the DOJ committed to submit detailed breakdowns and related prosecution data.

DOJ evidentiary threshold and terrorism-financing case review

Rep. Renee Luizco questioned DOJ's 2024 move from a probable-cause threshold to reasonable certainty of conviction and asked whether it had reduced filings or changed conviction rates. DOJ acknowledged fewer filings but characterized them as quality cases, while the Chair cited about 395,000 preliminary investigations and promised disaggregated data. Luizco then raised dismissed terrorism-financing and counterterrorism cases, including cases involving jurisdictional defects, and asked whether older or pending cases would be withdrawn or reviewed. DOJ said older cases would be scrutinized before elevation, while pending cases could not simply be withdrawn and could be challenged through certiorari where appropriate. Luizco requested an update on 106 task-force cases and described coordination questions involving the Anti-Terror Council, military, intelligence community, and Bureau of Immigration. The Chair undertook to submit the requested material, but the disposition of the cited cases and the broader review remained open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DOJ's 2024 shift from a probable-cause evidentiary threshold to a reasonable-certainty-of-conviction standard affected filing, disposition, and conviction rates. It also sought DOJ's position on reviewing terrorism-financing and counterterrorism cases filed under the former standard, including pending cases and coordination with other agencies.

DOJ said the stricter standard resulted in fewer filings but was intended to produce quality cases. It said pre-filing review would test older cases against the department's required quantum, while pending court cases could not automatically be withdrawn; DOJ would consider available legal options, including certiorari, and coordinate with the Anti-Terror Council, military, and intelligence community.

Outcome DOJ answered that older cases would be scrutinized before elevation and that pending cases would be assessed within the limits of ongoing court proceedings, with possible recourse through certiorari. The committee requested case-level and disposition data and additional material on interagency operations; submission of the requested information was committed, while the effect on the cited pending cases remained unresolved.

Flood-control corruption cases and interagency anti-corruption coordination

Rep. Kjell Jokno raised DOJ's reported flood-control cases and asked whether investigators had coordinated with AMLA, secured bank-secrecy waivers, and independently checked witness accounts. He questioned DOJ's 2025 prosecutorial success rate of 90.8% and sought separate conviction data for graft and corruption cases, contrasting it with a cited 2022 conviction rate of 25%. The DOJ secretary said the data had to be disaggregated and committed to submit it, including clarification on whether drug cases were included. Jokno also warned that witness intimidation or purchase could distort the prosecutorial success rate, and the secretary agreed that DOJ should monitor it. On coordination, DOJ cited its memorandum of agreement with the Ombudsman, with the Ombudsman handling salary grade 27 and above and DOJ handling cases below that level, and described technical work on an anti-corruption code. The secretary agreed that a legal framework and consolidated conviction-tracking effort were needed, but the database issue remained uncompleted.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether DOJ's flood-control investigations were supported by financial-intelligence checks and interagency coordination, rather than relying only on witness accounts. It also asked whether DOJ tracked final convictions separately from its prosecutorial success rate and whether government agencies maintained a consolidated anti-corruption database.

DOJ said its available prosecutorial data needed to be disaggregated, particularly to identify graft, corruption, and drug-case results, and committed to submit the requested information. The department agreed that witness intimidation should be monitored and that a government-wide legal framework or consolidated system for tracking convictions was needed, while citing its memorandum of agreement with the Ombudsman and ongoing technical work on an anti-corruption code.

Outcome The secretary agreed with the need for disaggregated conviction data, witness monitoring, and a consolidated framework for tracking corruption convictions. DOJ undertook to submit data and continue internal and interagency work, but no centralized database or final conviction-tracking system was established during the exchange.
