LRA special account, lost titles, and Friar Lands reconstitution

Rep. Allan Ty asked the LRA administrator about the proposed special-account allocation of roughly 1.78 billion for 2027 and the destination of the agency's collections. The administrator said the LRA retained 20% while 80% went to the National Treasury, and indicated that about 1.7 billion could potentially support registration of unregistered DENR free patents, subject to DBM approval. The administrator said registries of deeds were repositories of titles and had to conduct annual inventories, but owners generally bore responsibility for judicial reconstitution when records were lost. Administrative reconstitution could be pursued when at least 10% of titles, and not fewer than 500, were lost. On Friar Lands, the LRA said it would explore administrative remedies and the possible use of derivative titles, but the legal basis and procedure remained to be checked. The administrator committed to attend the DENR budget hearing and bring or invite the relevant registries of deeds.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much the LRA would receive through its special account, how those collections could support the registration of DENR-issued free patents, and where responsibility lay for safeguarding and reconstituting lost titles. It also examined whether lost Friar Lands records could be addressed through administrative remedies and derivative-title documentation.

The LRA said its special account could potentially fund registration of DENR-issued free patents, subject to DBM approval and the limits of the account. It said owners generally bear responsibility for judicial reconstitution of lost titles, while the LRA can undertake administrative reconstitution when the statutory threshold is met and can otherwise provide documents and explore administrative remedies for Friar Lands cases.

Outcome The committee obtained the LRA's explanation of the special account, the disposition of collections, and the legal framework for lost-title reconstitution. The Friar Lands remedy remained under discussion with the LMB and was carried forward to the DENR budget hearing, with the LRA administrator and relevant registries of deeds expected to participate.

Outcome PCGG's recoveries, remittances, and need for a larger budget were presented but not subjected to a final budget resolution in the quoted exchange. The mandate-expansion issue moved toward legislation, with the chair committing to coauthor the bill.

The committee sought to establish which NBI general administration and support services items had been cut and which restoration requests should be prioritized. It also sought the NBI's operational justification for additional funding, particularly for personnel support, investigations, vehicles, and cybercrime capabilities.

The NBI said its 42% cut to general administration and support services affected resources needed for higher agent hazard pay, frequent operations, operational expenses, administrative capability, vehicles, and cybercrime tools and facilities. Director Melvin maintained that additional funding was necessary to sustain the bureau's investigations and build regional cybercrime laboratory capacity, while acknowledging prior-year budget-utilization issues.

Outcome The NBI identified its principal restoration needs, but no specific restoration amount was approved or restored during the discussion. The issue was committed to the DOJ's submission of a prioritized list for subsequent committee review.

PCSO sales, taxes, dividends, and special-law remittances

PCSO presented rising sales and net-receipt estimates, from about 61.46 billion in 2023 to about 68.55 billion in projected 2027 retail receipts. It reported UHC remittances, including about 570 million in 2025 and 651.47 million and 690.67 million in the first two quarters of 2026, and said amounts due and remitted matched. The agency also reported total contributions rising from 14.56 billion in 2021 to 21.85 billion in 2025, with an additional 11.06 billion remitted by June 2026 and a table total of 112.35 billion. Chair Mika Swan Singh questioned why taxes, dividends, and other remittances appeared to decline or remain flat despite rising sales. PCSO's accounting and budget official attributed the pattern to corporate income, final income, and winnings-related taxes, income-based dividends, sales-related UHC and DST computations, and contingent special-law obligations. The chair accepted the explanation, commended PCSO's contributions, and left the matter informational.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why PCSO sales and projected revenues were rising while taxes, dividends, and other statutory remittances appeared flat or declining. It also asked whether the decline in remittances under Republic Acts and executive orders reflected specific laws or factors outside PCSO's control.

PCSO stated that taxes and dividends were driven principally by corporate income, final income, and winnings-related taxes, while some special-law contributions depended on sales and other contingent factors. It maintained that UHC remittances were fully remitted for the periods reflected and emphasized its significant overall contribution to government revenues and national programs.

Outcome PCSO explained that the differing trajectories reflected the separate statutory and financial bases of taxes, dividends, UHC, and special-law contributions. The chair acknowledged the explanation and commended PCSO; no document request or further undertaking was recorded.

OMB · 2026-08-24 · committed

Fact-finding capacity and corruption-case processing delays

Mauricio Domogan questioned the Ombudsman about pending complaints, conflict-of-interest investigations, pre-audit, and processing times. The Ombudsman said fact-finding generally took thirty to sixty days and preliminary investigation another thirty to sixty days, and reported hiring 60 lawyers with 40 more planned. Rep. Chel Diokno raised the absence of a centralized system for tracking final convictions, and the Ombudsman proposed an Ombudsman Marshal office for conviction tracking, process service, and related functions. The Ombudsman also reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks and agreed that a government-wide conviction-rate measure would be useful. Rep. Kjell Jochno cited a report involving 2,051 fact-finding investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases, then requested detailed filing and flood-control data. The hearing ended with commitments on staffing and marshals, but the requested case data and broader solutions to judicial delays remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how the Ombudsman conducts fact-finding and preliminary investigations, how staffing and resources affect case-processing timelines, and how many corruption cases—particularly flood-control cases—advance to prosecution and conviction. Members also asked how the government tracks final convictions, conducts lifestyle checks, and addresses delays in the justice system.

The Ombudsman said fact-finding should take thirty days for non-complex cases and sixty days for complex cases, followed by a preliminary investigation of another thirty to sixty days, and said additional lawyers were being hired to meet those deadlines. It supported centralized conviction tracking, proposed an Ombudsman Marshal office for tracking and process-serving functions, reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks, and favored stronger coordination, digital-forensics capacity, and measures to reduce judicial delay.

Outcome The Ombudsman answered the basic fact-finding timelines and described staffing increases, but several requested datasets—including the annual filing figures and flood-control breakdown—were not clearly provided. The Ombudsman Marshal proposal and additional staffing were commitments, while the constitutional, legislative, and judicial mechanisms for conviction tracking and reducing case delays remained open.

Representative Antonio Tinio raised allegations involving flood-control corruption, a 2025 budget insertion of 100,000,000,000, an allegedly related 51,000,000,000, and alleged kickbacks totaling 8,000,000,000, including 2,000,000,000 allegedly delivered through armored cars. Chel Diokno questioned the Ombudsman's fact-finding performance, citing 2,051 investigations, roughly 55% completion, and 17 resulting cases, and asked for personnel, digital-forensics, and flood-control case data. Conviction rates and tracking of graft cases

Representative Iris Marie Montes asked about the Ombudsman’s conviction rates, comparisons with prior years, high-ranking-official cases, and Moto Propio investigations. The agency reported a Sandigan Bayan conviction rate of sixty five point five two percent, compared with forty two percent previously, and lower-court rates of seventy seven point six percent in 2025 and sixty four point nine one percent as of June 30 of the current year. It could not immediately distinguish Moto Propio cases but committed to provide the data. Representative Chel Diokno raised a decades-old recommendation for a centralized system to track convictions and asked whether the Ombudsman had acted on it. Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said the proposed Ombudsman Marshall office, for which funding was requested, would track case and sentence statuses and perform related functions; the chair supported the proposal, although disagreement over imprisonment before final judgment remained. The agency also agreed that a government-wide conviction-rate statistic would be beneficial and reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman’s conviction performance, including comparisons with prior years and between courts, and whether the agency could track cases through final judgment and service of sentence. Members also asked whether the Ombudsman had safeguards against political influence, a centralized conviction-tracking system, a government-wide conviction metric, and active lifestyle-check and marshal programs.

The Ombudsman reported improved conviction rates and attributed the gains to procedural changes that accelerated investigations. It supported creating an Ombudsman Marshall office to track convictions and related case statuses, perform process-serving and witness-protection functions, and improve enforcement, and it agreed that a government-wide conviction statistic would be useful.

Outcome The Ombudsman committed to providing missing Moto Propio data and said its budget request included funding for a marshal office that would track convictions and support enforcement-related functions. The need for a government-wide conviction metric was acknowledged, but the centralized system, constitutional issues concerning imprisonment pending appeal, and implementation details remained unresolved.

The Ombudsman also reported 107 ongoing lifestyle checks, and the chair manifested support for creating Ombudsman marshals.

The committee sought to establish the Ombudsman's conviction performance, safeguards against political influence, capacity for proactive and moto proprio investigations, regional accessibility, and the status of lifestyle checks. It supported improved conviction tracking and proposed an Ombudsman Marshall office to track convictions, serve subpoenas, and perform related enforcement and witness-protection functions.

OMB · 2026-08-24 · unresolved

Pre-audit and geo-mapping support for government projects

Rep. Mauricio Domogan asked whether mandatory pre-audit of government-project payments, combined with geo-mapping, should be pursued to address ghost projects and corruption. He said the pre-audit requirement had been removed in 2011 and that COA supported the proposal with one additional personnel. Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla said the measure would be a big help but belonged to COA, which might need more staff. Domogan also asked about investigation timelines; Remulla cited fact-finding periods of about 30 to 60 days and preliminary-investigation periods of about 30 to 60 days. Remulla reported that 60 lawyers had been hired, 40 more were planned, and the total would reach 100 lawyers. The issue ended with member support but without a recorded ruling or final action on the bill.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether mandatory pre-audit of government-project payments, coupled with geo-mapping, should be pursued to detect ghost projects and corruption. It also asked how the Ombudsman handled conflict-of-interest complaints and how long investigations took.

The Ombudsman said mandatory pre-audit and geo-mapping would be a major help, but identified COA—not the Ombudsman—as the office with responsibility for pre-audit. Remulla said staffing constraints affected COA's ability to perform the function and reported tighter investigative deadlines and additional Ombudsman lawyers.

Outcome The Ombudsman expressed support in principle for mandatory pre-audit with geo-mapping, while stating that implementation belonged to COA and might require additional personnel. Domogan supported passage of the bill, but no committee ruling or final legislative action on the proposal was recorded.

DOST and attached-agency budget reduction, including 12.5% cut

Rep. Antonio Tinio raised the DOST and attached-agency reductions, including the 12.5% cut, and was told that the main reductions were in capital outlay for completed or already funded projects. DOST said the major agency reductions were primarily capital-outlay reductions caused by projects whose funding or phases had already been completed. The grants issue was not finally resolved in the hearing: DBM deferred to Congress, while the chair proposed possible re-centralization with safeguards and requested further DBM-DOST consultations. DOST grants allocation, GIA reallocation, and implementation flexibility

Rep. Antonio Tinio asked about DOST's GIA-supported AI infrastructure, the planned 26-fold expansion of high-performance computing, and data-sovereignty plans; DOST said initial seed funding was 100,000,000 and requested capacity and strategy documents were to be submitted. The committee chair then questioned DBM's transfer of about 1.25 billion in grants from the OSEC to agency-specific budgets. DBM said the transfer was a new policy intended to streamline implementation, while DOST said grants were proposal-driven, had achieved 98% utilization, and required flexibility for cross-agency and emergency needs. The chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards and requested post-hearing consultations between DBM and DOST. DOST also identified 800,000,000 for the virology institute and 309,000,000 for graduate grants covering 5,000 recipients, with updated monthly grant levels, and was asked to submit supporting tables and prioritized amendment requests. The issue was left for consultations and further congressional action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how DOST grants were allocated under the proposed budget, why the GIA funding was transferred to agency-specific budgets, and whether that arrangement would reduce DOST's ability to respond to proposal-driven and emergency research needs. It also asked what additional funding and documentation DOST needed for national AI infrastructure, virology facilities, graduate grants, and other priority amendments.

DOST supported retaining centralized, flexible grant authority because grants were proposal-driven and needed to respond to qualified proposals, cross-agency needs, and emergencies. DOST also stated that it had already raised concerns about the transfer of some grants to agencies that could not implement or distribute them as intended, while supporting additional funding for AI compute capacity, the virology institute, and graduate grants.

Outcome The chair indicated that the GIA issue would undergo post-hearing DBM-DOST consultations, with possible re-centralization in the OSEC and special safeguards. DOST was asked to submit AI, construction, graduate-grant, and prioritized amendment documents; the final treatment of the grant allocation remained open.

National AI infrastructure, high-performance computing, and data sovereignty

Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned DOST about the proposed national AI center, the target of increasing high-performance computing capacity by 26 fold by 2028, and whether the expansion was funded in the budget. ASTI said the existing service had evolved from a shared supercomputer into GPU-based infrastructure, with H200 processors, five major compute servers, commercial data-center space, and planned regional expansion. It identified 100,000,000 in initial DOST grant-in-aid seed funding but did not state the total cost of the expansion. The DOST Secretary said DOST would lead research and development infrastructure, talent management, and language models, while DICT would handle connectivity and related private-sector infrastructure. DOST also described a Philippine data-sovereignty platform and a planned government-managed AI hub, while acknowledging insufficient compute power and scale. Tinio supported AI and data sovereignty and requested documents on the National AI Strategy, existing compute capacity, and expansion plans.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish what national high-performance computing and data infrastructure the government was building for artificial intelligence, how large and capable it was, how much expansion would cost, and whether it was reflected in the proposed budget. It also sought to clarify which agency would lead the effort and how the government would protect Philippine data and AI sovereignty.

DOST said it should lead research-and-development infrastructure, talent development, and Philippine language-model development, while DICT would lead connectivity and related infrastructure involving the private sector. The agency supported building nationally controlled compute and data capabilities, including regional expansion and a data-sovereignty platform, but acknowledged that compute power and scale remained insufficient.

Outcome DOST explained the institutional division of responsibilities and described existing and planned compute and data-sovereignty initiatives. The committee requested supporting documents and expansion information; the total cost, precise scale, power requirements, and full budget treatment of the 26-fold expansion remained unprovided.

DOST said it was shifting from pilots toward regional implementation with agriculture agencies, local governments, cooperatives, and farmers, and cited a mobile solar irrigation trailer developed in Region 3. It also asked how DOST-developed platforms and technologies could be accelerated in response to El Niño and climate change.

DOST stated that Project SARAI and related smart-agriculture technologies were being moved from pilot and use-case applications toward regional implementation with the Department of Agriculture, local governments, cooperatives, and farmer partners. DOST also maintained that its irrigation, information, monitoring, and disaster-response platforms could be customized and adopted locally to address El Niño, climate resilience, and disaster preparedness.

Outcome The committee received an explanation of SARAI's functions, deployment model, interagency links, and related climate and disaster technologies. Wider regional and local adoption was encouraged, but no specific funding, implementation schedule, or additional submission was resolved during the exchange.

PAGASA and PNRI capital-outlay-related budget decreases

The committee chair asked why PAGASA and PNRI had lower capital-outlay allocations, and the agency-side response attributed the decreases to completed projects, including about 345 million for PNRI. The chair then questioned the transfer of roughly 1.25 billion in DOST grants from the Office of the Secretary to attached agencies. DBM said the distribution reflected a new policy intended to fund ongoing R&D projects directly and streamline implementation, while DOST said the proposal-driven nature of grants required flexibility and that some funds had been transferred to agencies unable to implement the relevant programs. DOST reported 98% utilization under the previous centralized arrangement. The chair favored possible re-centralization with safeguards, and DBM deferred to Congress. The chair requested post-hearing DBM-DOST consultations and the drafting of any necessary special provisions.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why PAGASA and PNRI had lower capital-outlay allocations and whether the transfer of DOST grants from the Office of the Secretary to attached agencies should be reversed. It also examined whether the new grant structure would reduce flexibility and utilization, and whether safeguards or special provisions were needed.

DBM said the distributed grant structure resulted from a new internal policy intended to place funding for ongoing R&D projects directly with attached agencies, speed implementation, and leave GIA for externally proposed projects. DOST said the transfer had included grants that agencies could not themselves implement and would reduce the flexibility of the proposal-driven system, which had achieved 98% utilization.

Outcome The capital-outlay decreases were explained as resulting from completed projects, including the 345,000,000 PNRI decrease. The grant issue was not finally resolved; DBM deferred to Congress, while the chair sought post-hearing consultations and possible special provisions to preserve flexibility.

PAGCOR FY 2026 income decline and FY 2027 revenue outlook

Chair Mika Suansing asked PAGCOR to explain the decline from its 2025 income and to clarify the 2027 outlook. PAGCOR attributed the decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, weaker land-based casino and licensee revenues, and economic conditions affecting its CDE customer market; it projected 2027 total revenues of about 88.33 billion. PAGCOR said first-semester 2026 income was about 43.32 billion, with about 30.16 billion going to nation-building programs, and reported 2026 gaming-operations income of about 80 billion divided roughly equally between land-based and online gaming. Members also questioned the retroactive 37,000,000,000 pesos PSC obligation and online-gaming regulation, including the policing of illegal operators, advertising, influencers, and minors. PAGCOR said it was updating its regulatory framework and disclosed projected 2026 revenues of between 9 and 10 billion for Casino Filipino, about 31.5 billion for licensed casinos, and 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038 for digital e-games. The issue landed with requests for PSC remittance records and detailed revenue data, while stronger online-gaming regulation remained an ongoing commitment rather than a resolved matter.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's 2026 income and net income had declined from the assumptions underlying its approved budget, what the 2027 revenue outlook was, and how the decline would affect government remittances and social-responsibility programs. Members also sought to determine whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory capacity to manage the growth of online gaming and illegal operators.

PAGCOR attributed the 2026 income decline mainly to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, weaker land-based casino and licensee revenues, and economic conditions affecting its CDE customer market. It maintained that online gaming remained a significant revenue opportunity but acknowledged regulatory risks and said it was regularly updating its rules and strengthening its structures. PAGCOR also said it was implementing the Supreme Court's retroactive PSC remittance ruling while continuing discussions concerning payment.

Outcome PAGCOR explained the principal causes of the 2026 decline and presented a 2027 revenue projection, but the committee did not resolve the longer-term regulatory and social risks of online gaming. The committee required PAGCOR's PSC remittance records and detailed revenue breakdown for further budget scrutiny.

Casino Filipino privatization, proceeds, and PAGCOR’s future role

Members asked PAGCOR about the status of privatizing roughly 30 to 40 Casino Filipino properties, its expected proceeds, and the agency's future regulatory role. PAGCOR said the transaction remained pending the GCG recommendation and Office of the President's approval, with estimated proceeds ranging from about 20 billion to 30 billion, and later about 25 billion to 30 billion. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised safeguards for approximately 10,000 employees, while PAGCOR cited retirement and special incentive packages, buyer absorption, and extensive retraining. Rep. Iris Marie Montes and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned how privatization would affect PhilHealth's UHC earmark; PAGCOR said it remitted to the National Treasury, which was responsible for the subsequent 50% UHC remittance. PAGCOR cited about 50 billion pesos remitted in 2025, implying 25 billion for the UHC fund under the statutory formula, and estimated retirement needs of about 28 billion to 30 billion against 12 billion in current retirement funding. PAGCOR agreed to submit remittance and privatization computations within forty eight hours and to study whether any proceeds remaining after retirement costs could support a UHC stabilization fund.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the status, scope, valuation, and proceeds of the proposed Casino Filipino privatization, including PAGCOR's transition from operator-regulator to primarily regulator. Members also asked how privatization would affect employees, PhilHealth's Universal Health Care remittances, PAGCOR's future revenues, and the use of sale proceeds.

PAGCOR said the privatization remained subject to the GCG recommendation and approval by the Office of the President. It estimated proceeds in the range of 20,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000, or about 25,000,000,000 to 30,000,000,000 under a later estimate, with employee retirement obligations taking priority; it maintained that PAGCOR would continue remitting its share to the National Treasury and that the national government would remain responsible for the 50% UHC remittance.

Outcome The privatization was not yet approved; PAGCOR was still awaiting the GCG recommendation and presidential approval. PAGCOR committed to submit remittance and privatization-related computations within forty eight hours and said a UHC stabilization fund could be studied after employee retirement obligations, but the final proceeds, post-privatization UHC base, and legislative guarantees remained unresolved.

Universal Health Care and PhilHealth remittances after privatization

Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked whether PAGCOR had complied with the UHC Act and requested a complete remittance history. PAGCOR chairman Alejandro Tengco said PAGCOR had remitted regularly to the National Treasury, while the national government was responsible for transferring 50% to PhilHealth or the UHC Fund; he cited about 50 billion remitted in 2025, implying 25 billion should have gone to the UHC Fund. Montes and Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked how privatization of Casino Filipino would affect the PhilHealth earmark and sought projections for 2026, 2027, 2028, and the first full year after privatization. Tengco said privatization proceeds would first cover roughly 28 billion to 30 billion in retirement obligations, against an existing retirement fund of about 12 billion, and that any balance could potentially support a stabilization fund. The requested projections and confirmation of onward remittances were not supplied during the hearing, but PAGCOR committed to provide documents within forty eight hours and to study the stabilization-fund proposal. Rep. Jean Baronda separately sought a contingency plan for UHC and support for hospitals and children with special needs, which PAGCOR said it would consider.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR had complied with the Universal Health Care Act's remittance requirement, how much had been remitted to the National Treasury and ultimately to the Universal Health Care Fund, and how privatizing Casino Filipino would affect the PhilHealth earmark. Members also asked whether a transitional UHC stabilization fund would be needed and whether PAGCOR had a contingency plan to sustain support for Universal Health Care.

PAGCOR stated that it had been current and compliant in remitting its required share to the National Treasury, while the national government—not PAGCOR—was responsible for transferring 50% to PhilHealth or the Universal Health Care Fund. PAGCOR said privatization proceeds would first be used for employee retirement and incentive obligations, but any balance could potentially support a transitional UHC stabilization fund; it also agreed to provide records and internal projections.

Outcome PAGCOR's compliance with its own remittance obligation was affirmed, but the committee did not receive during the hearing the requested full remittance history, projected post-privatization UHC contributions, or confirmation of the national government's onward transfers. PAGCOR agreed to submit documents and study a stabilization fund, leaving the fund and the post-privatization revenue treatment unresolved.

PSC retroactive 5% remittance ruling and PAGCOR’s PSC budget

Chair Mika Suansing asked PAGCOR to explain the decline in 2026 income and the effect of the Supreme Court's final PSC remittance ruling. PAGCOR attributed the income decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, and weak casino revenues, while saying gaming activity had begun to recover. PAGCOR said the ruling required 5% of gross income rather than gaming revenue alone, applied retroactively to 1993, and created an obligation of 37,000,000,000 pesos. The agency said its prior average PSC contribution was about 190,000,000 pesos per month and identified a payment of 3,300,000,000 every year for the next ten years. The chair said the PSC's proposed 2027 budget was not yet commensurate with the higher remittances and undertook to scrutinize it. PAGCOR was asked to provide its 2025 and 2026 PSC remittance records, while the payment arrangement remained under discussion.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's 2026 income was projected to decline and how the Supreme Court's final ruling changed PAGCOR's remittances to the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). It also sought to determine the ruling's retroactive fiscal impact and whether the PSC's proposed budget adequately reflected the higher remittances.

PAGCOR said it was implementing the Supreme Court's final ruling effective 01/01/2026, applying the 5% PSC share to gross income rather than gaming revenue alone. It acknowledged a retroactive obligation of 37,000,000,000 pesos dating to 1993, said discussions on payment were ongoing, and indicated that it was close to an agreement.

Outcome The committee accepted PAGCOR's explanation of the ruling and its effect on remittances but left the adequacy of the PSC budget open for later deliberation. PAGCOR's payment arrangement for the retroactive obligation remained subject to ongoing discussions, and the committee requested remittance records.

Nation-building contributions and PAGCOR social-responsibility spending

PAGCOR reported that it had contributed about 67 billion to nation building in 2025 and projected about 61 billion in 2026 and 63 billion in 2027, while social-civic projects rose to about 13.99 billion in 2026. It also presented a PHP 7,500,000,000 school-building commitment, PHP 300,000,000 in recent calamity-relief spending, patient transport vehicle donations, and hospital-equipment support. The chair commended PAGCOR for preserving these commitments despite lower income, while the agency explained that the Supreme Court's retroactive PSC ruling created a 37,000,000,000 pesos obligation and could substantially affect its finances. Members pressed for stronger control of illegal online gambling, protection of vulnerable gamblers, and funding for responsible-gaming and mental-health programs; PAGCOR cited KYC requirements, a licensing moratorium, enforcement coordination, and a responsible-gaming partner. Members also sought relief and classroom assistance for General Santos and hospital support for Western Visayas and Pangasinan. The hearing ended with PAGCOR agreeing to provide documents, review requests, and explore equipment assistance, but several allocations and enforcement measures remained for follow-up.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR's nation-building and social-responsibility contributions were being maintained despite lower revenues, including its relief, hospital, school-building, and social-civic programs. Members also examined whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory and responsible-gaming measures to address illegal online gambling and protect vulnerable gamblers.

PAGCOR stated that it continued to protect nation-building and social-civic commitments despite lower revenues, including school construction, relief operations, patient transport vehicles, hospital equipment, and universal-health-care support. It said responsible-gaming safeguards, licensing controls, enforcement coordination, and regular rule updates were being used, but acknowledged that illegal operators and rapidly changing technology remained difficult to control.

Outcome The committee received PAGCOR's account of its nation-building and social-responsibility allocations and generally commended its continued spending despite revenue weakness. Several matters remained subject to submissions or follow-up, including PSC remittance records, responsible-gaming data, illegal-site enforcement equipment, classroom requests, and possible hospital-equipment assistance.

PAGCOR said it had earmarked close to about 3.5 billion for the 50% down payment, with later payments tied to construction progress. Rep. Sarah Elago requested a breakdown of fund utilization, but no such breakdown was submitted during the hearing. Members also questioned whether the program displaced community wellness centers, e-libraries, and evacuation centers, and PAGCOR said it could consider balancing those priorities. PAGCOR undertook to review assistance for earthquake-damaged classrooms and a district request, while conflicting transcript figures for classroom totals remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the scope, funding, implementation period, and allocation of PAGCOR's nationwide school-building program. Members also asked how much had been earmarked or utilized, how schools and local government units were selected, and whether other proposed infrastructure projects would be displaced.

PAGCOR stated that its nationwide school-building program, undertaken with the Department of Education, would fund 125 three-storey, 12-classroom buildings and approximately 1,500 classrooms from 2026 through 2027. It said the program had a total funding commitment of PHP 7,500,000,000, with close to about 3,500,000,000 earmarked for the 50% down payment, and that site selection and project recommendations would be handled by the Department of Education while LGUs would conduct procurement and construction.

Outcome PAGCOR explained the program's total commitment, implementation period, down-payment plan, and allocation process, but the requested utilization breakdown was not presented during the hearing. PAGCOR also left open the possibility of balancing the school-building allocation with other infrastructure priorities and undertook to review a district-level request.

Online-gaming revenues, e-games decline, and regulatory strategy

The chair and several members questioned PAGCOR about declining gaming income, especially the effects of e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, illegal operators, and weaker land-based casino activity. PAGCOR attributed the decline to a roughly 40% fall in activity after payment-app delinking, while reporting a later increase of about 10% in July and August. Members also challenged PAGCOR on advertising approvals, influencer liability, foreign operators, KYC enforcement, minors' access, and the adequacy of responsible-gaming programs. PAGCOR cited fines, coordination with BSP, DICT, NTC, CICC, and police authorities, regular rule updates, a 1% gross-gaming-revenue allocation for responsible gaming, and a possible PAGCOR application for identifying legitimate operators. Revenue figures discussed included projected 2026 gaming operations of 80,000,000,000 pesos, digital e-games revenue of 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038, Casino Filipino revenue of between 9 and 10,000,000,000, and licensed-casino revenue of about 31 and a half billion. The committee requested remittance and revenue documents and left further regulatory strengthening and several enforcement concerns for follow-up.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why PAGCOR's projected and reported gaming revenues were declining, particularly in online and e-games operations, and how payment restrictions, illegal operators, advertising, and market conditions affected collections. It also examined whether PAGCOR had sufficient regulatory, responsible-gaming, and monitoring measures to protect players and sustain revenues and remittances.

PAGCOR attributed the revenue decline to e-wallet delinking, the Middle East crisis, weaker economic conditions, and reduced land-based and online gaming activity. It maintained that it was updating its rules, monitoring operators, coordinating with BSP and other enforcement agencies, pursuing illegal operators, supporting responsible-gaming programs, and exploring new revenue sources, while acknowledging that illegal operations and regulatory capacity remained significant challenges.

Outcome PAGCOR explained the revenue decline and described regulatory, payment, enforcement, and responsible-gaming measures, but the committee remained concerned about illegal operators, e-wallet restrictions, minors' access, and the agency's capacity to police online platforms. The agency undertook to provide remittance and revenue documents, continue the helpline, consider a player-verification application, and further strengthen its regulatory framework.

Illegal online-gaming operators, enforcement, and monitoring capacity

Rep. Sarah Elago asked how foreign illegal operators were being addressed and how the 24/7 problem-gambling helpline and related counseling programs were funded. PAGCOR said it lacked police powers, depended on DICT, CICC, NTC, and other partners, and would continue responsible-gaming initiatives supported by 1% of online gross gaming revenue, estimated at about a billion pesos per annum. Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos questioned e-wallet restrictions, unauthorized payment channels, mule accounts, and KYC enforcement; PAGCOR cited coordination with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, monitoring, fines, and suspensions. Vice Chair Brian Poe reported that 44 of 52 illegal websites had initially been taken down but that some had returned, and PAGCOR said the sites had not been licensed because of a moratorium lasting two years. PAGCOR projected 2026 gross gaming revenue at about 370 billion and estimated total wagers at about 3 trillion, while acknowledging that only legal operators were tracked. The committee requested website lists, responsible-gaming data, and equipment-procurement and revenue projections, with further enforcement discussion assigned to the DICT budget hearing.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR and other enforcement agencies were addressing illegal online-gaming operators, reopened websites, unauthorized payment channels, mule accounts, and gaps in KYC monitoring. Members also asked what resources, programs, and interagency equipment were needed to protect consumers and recover revenue that might otherwise be lost to illegal wagering.

PAGCOR said illegal online operators and payment channels required continuing coordination with DICT, CICC, NTC, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and other entities because PAGCOR lacked police powers and tracked only licensed operators. It maintained that responsible-gaming programs, the planned PAGCOR application, KYC enforcement, site takedowns, and additional VPN-tracking equipment were the principal responses, but acknowledged that illegal sites could reopen and that more enforcement tools were needed.

Outcome The committee received PAGCOR's explanations but did not resolve the scale of illegal wagering, the revenue lost from reopened sites, or the funding and equipment needed for stronger enforcement. The matter was carried forward through documentary requests, PAGCOR commitments, and a planned discussion during the DICT budget hearing.

Gambling advertising, influencers, and penalties

Rep. Elijah San Fernando raised concerns about advertising controls and influencer promotion in light of approximately 30 million registered and 10 million active online-gaming players. PAGCOR said gambling advertisements required Ad Standards Council clearance and that a licensed operator had been fined 1,000,000 pesos, with suspension and license cancellation available for repeated violations. The agency said 50% of current online-gaming operators were illegal and that it relied on DICT, NTC, CICC, and social-media platforms for enforcement against operators and endorsers outside its jurisdiction. Rep. Sarah Elago pressed for action against foreign operators and asked about support for the 24/7 helpline; PAGCOR committed to continuing the initiative and cited 1% of online gross gaming revenue, or about a billion pesos per annum, for responsible-gaming and social civic projects. Rep. Presley de Jesus challenged whether the first-offense 1,000,000 penalty was sufficient, and PAGCOR said it had been increased from 50,000 and was not the maximum sanction. The chair committed to consolidating documentary requests and following up, leaving interagency enforcement and supporting documents pending.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR's controls over gambling advertisements, content creators, influencers, and foreign operators were sufficient to protect vulnerable players and deter violations. Members also examined the adequacy of the first-offense penalty, the responsible-gaming helpline and programs, and the enforcement authority available against illegal operators and endorsers.

PAGCOR stated that advertisements required Ad Standards Council clearance and that it could penalize licensed operators, suspend them for a second offense, and cancel their licenses for a third offense. It also said enforcement against illegal foreign operators and some influencers depended on DICT, NTC, CICC, and social-media platforms, while responsible-gaming programs and the 24/7 helpline would continue through PAGCOR funding and partnerships.

Outcome PAGCOR answered that 1,000,000 was only the first-offense penalty, with suspension and cancellation available for subsequent offenses, and committed to continue responsible-gaming initiatives. Enforcement against foreign operators and some influencers remained dependent on other agencies and platforms, with documentary follow-up still pending.

Responsible-gaming, addiction treatment, and player safeguards

Members questioned PAGCOR about advertising clearance, influencer regulation, illegal foreign operators, and protections for vulnerable online gamblers. PAGCOR described a 24/7 helpline and responsible-gaming programs with the Seagulls Flock Foundation, supported in part by 1% of online gross gaming revenue, or about a billion pesos per annum. The agency said it used KYC and secondary screening to exclude government employees and maintained a restricted-persons list of 15,000 names, while online deposit and activity caps had not yet been set. Vice Chair Brian Poe raised the reopening of illegal sites, cited about 3,000,000,000,000 pesos in estimated annual wagers, and sought enforcement and program-funding documents. PAGCOR committed to continue the helpline and submit responsible-gaming information, while the chair directed that equipment and enforcement questions also be taken up during the ICT budget deliberation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR regulated online gambling and advertising, protected vulnerable players, and funded or operated responsible-gaming, counseling, rehabilitation, and player-exclusion programs. Members also examined enforcement against illegal operators and the safeguards available to minors, government employees, and low-income earners.

PAGCOR said it operated responsible-gaming programs through a 24/7 helpline, the Seagulls Flock Foundation, counseling and rehabilitation referrals, prevention and awareness activities, and self- or family-exclusion mechanisms. It said KYC and secondary screening were used to exclude government employees and other restricted players, while enforcement against illegal operators depended substantially on DICT, CICC, NTC, and other agencies with police powers. PAGCOR had not yet established online betting or deposit caps but expected proposed legislation to provide them.

Outcome PAGCOR answered the committee's questions on existing safeguards and responsible-gaming services, but online caps and the adequacy of funding and technical enforcement remained dependent on proposed legislation, interagency action, and requested submissions. PAGCOR committed to continue the helpline and responsible-gaming programs and to provide program information; the committee deferred broader enforcement and equipment-funding questions to the ICT budget deliberation.

Casino Filipino employee transition, retirement, and incentive packages

Bong Thebes Jinger and Jan Attorney Jan Rurik Padiernos raised the status of Casino Filipino privatization and the safeguards for approximately 10,000 employees across about 40 properties. PAGCOR said affected employees would receive regular retirement benefits plus a special incentive package, while acquiring entities would absorb employees where feasible. PAGCOR reported 5,000 completed training initiatives, initial Civil Service-related training for about 80 to 100 people, and a target of about 10,000 training initiatives by year-end. Roberto Nazal Jr. asked whether the 50% UHC earmark would continue after PAGCOR ceased operating casinos and requested projected contributions and a possible stabilization fund. PAGCOR said it had remitted 50,000,000,000 pesos to the national treasury in 2025, implying 25,000,000,000 should have gone to the UHC Fund, but it did not control the national government's onward remittance. The chairman estimated retirement needs at about 28 billion to 30 billion, an existing retirement fund of about 12 billion, and privatization proceeds of about 25 billion to 30 billion, while prioritizing employee retirement before any UHC fund. PAGCOR committed to provide the requested computations and documents within forty eight hours, leaving absorption rules and the UHC stabilization mechanism open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how Casino Filipino privatization would protect approximately 10,000 employees through absorption, training, retirement, and special incentive packages. It also sought to determine how privatization would affect the Universal Health Care earmark and whether PAGCOR or the Executive would provide transition funding or projected remittance figures.

PAGCOR said employee protection would rely on regular retirement benefits, a separate special incentive package, absorption by acquiring entities where feasible, and training and Civil Service Commission transition programs. It said retirement costs would take priority over any UHC stabilization fund, but that PAGCOR would provide internal projections and study whether residual privatization proceeds could support such a fund.

Outcome PAGCOR answered the employee-protection questions by identifying retirement, special incentive, training, and CSC-transition measures, but the final absorption requirement and privatization decision remained pending. The UHC impact and possible stabilization fund were not resolved; PAGCOR undertook to submit computations and documents within forty eight hours and to study the use of residual proceeds.

Agency unavailable · 2026-08-24 · unresolved

Integrated resorts, gaming service administrators, and PAGCOR’s mandate

Rep. Presley de Jesus asked PAGCOR to define integrated resorts and explain the consequences for other casinos as the sector developed. PAGCOR cited a minimum investment of at least 1,000,000,000 US dollars for an integrated resort, a lowest category of 100,000,000 US dollars, and a license-fee range of 25 to 30 percent; the member described the billion-dollar threshold as around 60 billion in local currency. The member also questioned whether privatization would separate PAGCOR’s operator and regulator roles, but the agency’s response was unclear. On penalties, PAGCOR said the cited first-offense penalty was not the maximum: repeat violations could lead to suspension and then cancellation, with the prior 50,000 penalty calibrated to 1 million. PAGCOR said GSAs had fallen from 74 at their peak to 48, largely because operators surrendered after losing money, and it cited a 9,000,000 pesos minimum guarantee fee effective July 1, 2026. The agency confirmed that casino and online gaming were within PAGCOR’s mandate, while horse racing was under the Philippine Racing Commission; the operator-regulator transition and some financial figures remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to clarify what qualifies as an integrated resort, how casino privatization would affect PAGCOR’s operator-regulator role, and how penalties and gaming service administrator rules would work. It also asked how many gaming service administrators remained, why some surrendered their licenses, and which games fell within PAGCOR’s mandate.

PAGCOR stated that integrated resorts were investment-based classifications, with the highest category requiring at least 1,000,000,000 US dollars and the lowest cited at 100,000,000 US dollars. It said GSAs were licensed online gaming operators, that their number had declined because of suspensions and business losses, and that a minimum guarantee fee was intended to stabilize the online gaming industry. PAGCOR also maintained that its mandate covered casino and online gaming but not horse racing, which was assigned to the Philippine Racing Commission.

Outcome The agency answered the definitional, penalty, GSA-count, fee, and mandate questions, but did not provide a clear answer on the operator-regulator transition or assure the committee about the remaining operators. The discussion ended without a recorded document request or further resolution of the privatization issue.

Online-gambling limits, KYC, and government-employee screening

Rep. Jan Rurik Padiernos raised concerns about e-wallet restrictions, illegal payment aggregators, declining e-games revenues, and KYC bypasses involving mule accounts and minors. PAGCOR said it was coordinating with the central bank, enforcing KYC and sanctions, and considering a PAGCOR app, while citing more than 106 billion in revenues and other public-purpose allocations. Rep. Michael Gonzalez asked about daily or weekly online-gambling caps, government-employee screening, and permanent player bans; PAGCOR said caps had not yet been set but were expected in proposed legislation, while KYC and screening had prevented close to 5 billion in winnings and covered a restricted list of 15,000 names. Rep. Sherlyn Banas-Nograles asked for stronger safeguards for minors, government employees, low-income earners, and vulnerable sectors, including people affected by micro-bets. PAGCOR identified KYC as its safeguard and said it had provided more than 100,000 relief packs and was constructing 125 school buildings equivalent to about 200 classrooms. The committee left specific General Santos classroom assistance to a written request, while the broader cap issue remained dependent on proposed legislation.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how PAGCOR was controlling online-gambling access and risks, including e-wallet use, illegal operators, KYC compliance, wager or deposit limits, government-employee participation, and exclusion of vulnerable or prohibited players. Members also asked what safeguards and assistance programs PAGCOR maintained for affected communities.

PAGCOR said it was enforcing KYC, secondary screening, fines, suspensions, payment-provider controls, and exclusion lists to prevent prohibited or vulnerable persons from accessing gambling. It acknowledged that player caps had not yet been set but said proposed online-gaming legislation was expected to include deposit and gaming-activity caps.

Outcome PAGCOR answered that KYC, screening, exclusion lists, and sanctions were in place, but acknowledged that online deposit and gaming-activity caps had not yet been established. Further assistance for General Santos classroom reconstruction was left to a written request and was not specifically confirmed.

Infrastructure, hospital, cancer-center, and special-needs-school assistance

Rep. Iris Marie Montes questioned PAGCOR's UHC remittances, privatization proceeds, and infrastructure priorities, and PAGCOR undertook to submit a remittance listing within 48 hours. PAGCOR said it was current with National Treasury remittances and estimated possible privatization proceeds at about 20 billion to 30 billion, while the detailed PhilHealth treatment of those proceeds remained partly unclear. Rep. Jean Baronda sought support for cancer-center equipment and schools serving children with special needs, and PAGCOR said it would seriously consider those requests. Rep. Shirlyn Bañas-Nograles asked about General Santos relief and roughly 1,400 damaged classrooms; PAGCOR cited more than 100,000 relief packs and a program for 125 new school buildings. Rep. Marco Wangkol sought help for a Pangasinan hospital project estimated at about 1 billion, but PAGCOR advised that equipment for a completed building was more feasible than partial construction funding. The requests landed as conditional commitments requiring follow-up letters, coordination, and project completion.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether PAGCOR was complying with its Universal Health Care remittance obligations and whether its social funds, infrastructure programs, and affiliated foundations could support hospitals, cancer-center equipment, damaged classrooms, and schools serving children with special needs. Members also sought to identify the process and conditions for obtaining such assistance, including for a Pangasinan hospital project.

PAGCOR said it was current on its National Treasury remittances, while the national government—not PAGCOR directly—remitted the applicable share to PhilHealth. It said hospital construction was generally handled by licensee foundations, but PAGCOR could provide equipment or other targeted assistance on a case-by-case basis, subject to project completion and liquidation requirements; it also committed to consider cancer-center, special-needs-school, classroom, and Pangasinan hospital-equipment requests.

Outcome PAGCOR answered the principal questions and made several conditional commitments, but most project assistance remained subject to letters, coordination, project completion, and liquidation. The remittance report, cancer-center assistance, special-needs support, classroom support, and Pangasinan equipment assistance were not yet finally delivered or approved during the hearing.

PAGCOR data submissions and supporting budget documentation

Committee members sought documentary support for PAGCOR's remittances, school-building allocations, revenue mix, and the effects of Casino Filipino privatization on UHC funding. PAGCOR said its school-building agreement covered 125 buildings and roughly about 1,500 classrooms at a total cost of about 7.5 billion, with close to about 3.5 billion earmarked for down payments. It maintained that it remitted its shares to the National Treasury, while the National Treasury was responsible for transferring the relevant 50% to PhilHealth or the UHC fund. PAGCOR cited 2025 National Treasury remittances of more or less 50 billion, implying 25 billion for UHC, and estimated privatization proceeds at roughly 25 billion to 30 billion after revisions, with retirement obligations estimated at about 28 billion to 30 billion. Members also requested detailed revenue lists, including projected Casino Filipino revenue of 9 to 10 billion, licensed-casino revenue of about 31.5 billion, and digital e-games revenue stated as 38,000,000,000 to 40,000,000,038. PAGCOR committed to provide the requested records and computations, generally within forty eight hours, but the committee ended the briefing before the submissions could be examined.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to obtain the records and computations needed to evaluate PAGCOR's proposed budget, including remittances, fund utilization, revenue by source, school-building allocations, and the fiscal effects of privatizing Casino Filipino. It also sought documentation on the Universal Health Care and Philippine Sports Commission remittance bases and on PAGCOR's regulatory and social-civic programs.

PAGCOR maintained that it was current and compliant in remitting its statutory shares to the National Treasury and PSC, while the National Treasury was responsible for the downstream PhilHealth or UHC remittance. It said school-building and social-civic programs were being implemented through DepEd and LGU agreements, and it undertook to submit remittance records, revenue lists, fund-utilization information, and privatization-related computations.

Outcome PAGCOR answered portions of the committee's questions but was required to submit substantial remittance, utilization, revenue, and privatization documentation. The briefing was terminated and the documentary issues were left for follow-up rather than resolved during the hearing.

FY2027 budget reductions in health, education, social protection, and agriculture

DBM initially explained that lower social-sector allocations reflected continuing 2026 infrastructure allocations, spillovers, and agency implementation capacity rather than zero funding. Congressman Arnan Panaligan challenged reductions in agriculture, health, social services, and education even as the proposed budget rose from about 6.7 trillions to 7,200,000,000,000. Representative Percival Sindania focused on the health allocation, which fell from approximately PHP 458 billion to PHP 362.7 billion, and was told that the change mainly reflected Facilities Enhancement Program utilization, retained medical assistance, an additional 14,000,000,000 PhilHealth subsidy, and the one-time return of 60,000,000,000 to PhilHealth. Representative Chel Diokno challenged reductions affecting education, SUCs, TESDA, health, PhilHealth, and DSWD, while DBM cited absorptive capacity, implementation status, and one-time expenditures. Jokno also questioned the 3.99% education computation, and DBM said it included national, Bangsamoro, local-government, and SUC-generated funds and undertook to provide a detailed breakdown. The chair directed the requested health reconciliation, while Jokno's call to reprioritize frontline-sector funding remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why proposed FY2027 allocations for health, education, skills development, social protection, and agriculture were lower despite a larger overall budget, and whether the reductions reflected actual service cuts or one-time 2026 expenditures and agency absorptive capacity. Members also questioned the basis for the education-sector computation and requested reconciliations of the affected appropriations.

DBM maintained that the apparent reductions in frontline-sector budgets did not generally represent unilateral cuts in services. It attributed them to agency absorptive capacity, implementation status, infrastructure-project timing, one-time 2026 expenditures, the return of the 60,000,000,000 PhilHealth fund balance, and the inclusion of other education-related funding sources in the 3.99% computation.

Outcome DBM provided explanations centered on absorptive capacity, one-time allocations, and funding-accounting differences, but members continued to question whether core frontline services were being underfunded. The committee accepted commitments for a health-sector reconciliation and a detailed education computation; the broader reprioritization issue remained open.

PhilHealth subsidy and universal health-care financing

Rep. Iris Marie Montes asked how much of the proposed budget would expand UHC financing and services and whether PhilHealth would receive funding beyond member contributions and sin-tax shares. DBM cited about 362.73 billion for the health sector, including about 270.98 billion for DOH and about 74.45 billion for PhilHealth, and confirmed that the PhilHealth subsidy came from sin-tax collections. Rep. Percival Sindania later questioned a decline from roughly 458 billion to 362.7 billion in the functional health allocation and asked whether the decrease represented actual service cuts. DBM attributed the change to agency utilization, the Facilities Enhancement Program, medical-assistance treatment, an additional 14,000,000,000 subsidy for expanded zero-balance billing, and the one-time return of 60,000,000,000 to PhilHealth. Chel Diokno also cited substantial reductions in DOH and PhilHealth budgets and urged reprioritization of health services. The chair directed the DBCC to submit a reconciliation of health-related appropriations for 2025 to 2027, leaving the sufficiency of the overall financing unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how much of the proposed 2027 budget would expand universal health-care financing and service capacity, particularly through PhilHealth, and whether reductions in health-sector appropriations reflected real service cuts or one-time adjustments. Members also asked how the proposed allocations would affect out-of-pocket spending and frontline health services.

DBM maintained that the apparent decline in health-sector appropriations was driven substantially by changes in utilization, one-time 2026 items, and the 60,000,000,000 return of a PhilHealth fund balance rather than a uniform reduction in services. It also stated that PhilHealth would receive an additional 14,000,000,000 in subsidy to expand zero-balance billing, while medical assistance was retained at the 2026 net level.

Outcome The agency explained the apparent health-sector reduction as largely reflecting one-time and utilization-related factors, while citing an additional 14,000,000,000 PhilHealth subsidy and expanded zero-balance billing. The committee directed the DBCC to submit a detailed 2025–2027 reconciliation, but the broader question of whether health financing was sufficient and whether out-of-pocket costs would rise remained open.

Unprogrammed appropriations, including 111,984,000,000 in operations

Members questioned the inclusion and scale of unprogrammed appropriations, including the 2027 operations item of about 111.984 billion and the 50 billion AFP modernization item for 2026. DBM said releases depended on triggers such as excess revenue and that foreign-assisted projects were placed in the item because loan agreements and required approvals were not yet certain. Laila Delima challenged the constitutional basis and identified about 57 billion for PDIC restoration, 42.553 billion for foreign-assisted projects, and 3.6 billion for risk management. Alan Teague asked about the 107.23 billion PDIC transfer and was told it had been treated as excess from the unrestricted portion of the Deposit Insurance Fund. DBM reported that proposed 2027 unprogrammed appropriations were 1.56% of the expenditure program and said there was no international maximum benchmark. The executive indicated that PDIC restoration could depend on excess revenue or a Supreme Court order, while DBM committed to provide project-level information before plenary.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the legal and fiscal basis for including unprogrammed appropriations, the projects and triggers covered by them, and whether the proposed amounts—particularly for foreign-assisted projects and PDIC fund restoration—were justified. Members also asked how the proposed level compared with historical levels and any applicable fiscal benchmarks.

The executive and DBM maintained that unprogrammed appropriations were justified for limited, necessary uses, particularly foreign-assisted projects awaiting approvals or loan agreements, PPP risk management, and partial PDIC fund-balance restoration. They said releases would depend on statutory or fiscal triggers such as excess revenue, and that the executive would comply with any Supreme Court ruling on constitutionality.

Outcome The committee received the executive's explanation of the limited proposed uses and fiscal triggers but did not resolve the constitutional challenge or establish an agreed maximum benchmark. DBM committed to submit project information, while the full PDIC restoration and the amount released for AFP modernization remained unresolved.

Agency unavailable · 2026-08-17 · unresolved

PDIC fund-balance transfer and restoration

Leila de Lima raised the constitutional and policy issue of placing PDIC restoration in unprogrammed appropriations. Rep. Alan Teague then asked Secretary Goh about the transfer, which was 107,230,000,000 pesos, its DOF origin, PDIC Board approval, and its effect on depositor protection. Secretary Goh said the amount came from an unrestricted or excess portion of the deposit insurance fund and was more than sufficient for insurance eventualities. DBM reported that FY2027 unprogrammed appropriations were 1.56% of the expenditure program and cited historical percentages from 2022 through 2026. Members questioned why the full transfer was not restored, while the executive said it had proposed 57,000,000,000 because of fiscal-space constraints and could restore the balance in two tranches or later. The Bangko Sentral governor did not finally endorse the amount and said PDIC consultation was required, leaving adequacy of the restoration unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the legal and fiscal rationale for placing PDIC fund restoration in unprogrammed appropriations, whether the 107,230,000,000 transfer had impaired PDIC's ability to protect depositors, and whether the proposed restoration was sufficient. It also examined the scale of FY2027 unprogrammed appropriations and the timetable for restoring the transferred amount.

The executive maintained that the transferred 107,230,000,000 was excess from the unrestricted portion of the deposit insurance fund and was considered more than sufficient for depositor-insurance eventualities. It proposed restoring 57,000,000,000 through unprogrammed appropriations, subject to available excess revenue capacity, with possible full restoration in two tranches and further restoration in a later year if needed.

Outcome The hearing established the executive's explanation that the 107,230,000,000 transfer was excess from the unrestricted portion of the deposit insurance fund and that 57,000,000,000 was the fiscal space available for partial restoration. Whether that amount was adequate and acceptable to PDIC remained open, with the Bangko Sentral governor saying consultation with PDIC was still necessary.

Debt service, deficit targets, revenues, and fiscal consolidation

Members questioned debt ratios, debt service, deficit discipline, revenue forecasts, and the credibility of the 2027 fiscal-consolidation path. Agencies reported a national-government debt-to-GDP ratio of 64.9%, debt service of about 1.1 trillion, and a 2027 deficit of about 3.304 trillion pesos, while explaining that lower growth assumptions reflected external shocks and weaker domestic conditions. DBCC officials said lower GDP assumptions would reduce revenues, and they attributed the 2026 shortfall of about 180 billion mainly to consumption taxes, including about 175 billion in VAT-related effects. The committee also challenged the 2027 revenue projection of about 5.2 trillion and the 101.5 billion privatization assumption, with DOF citing Semirara and CBK proceeds. DBM said contingencies included savings, flexible agency line items, early assistance for El Nino, and reprioritization during execution. The chair directed the DBCC to submit multiple downside scenarios and reconciliations, leaving the issue committed to further documentation rather than fully resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed budget's revenue, borrowing, debt-service, deficit, and privatization assumptions were credible and whether fiscal risks had been adequately planned for. Members also asked what spending was being displaced by debt service, how weaker growth would affect revenues and debt, and what contingencies would be available if collections fell short or external shocks occurred.

The DBCC and its component agencies said the lower growth, revenue, and deficit assumptions reflected updated macroeconomic conditions rather than a loss of fiscal discipline. They maintained that 2027 revenues could grow in nominal terms because of higher nominal GDP, while privatization proceeds, flexible agency spending, savings, and reprioritization would help manage fiscal and external shocks.

Outcome The agencies answered the principal questions but left several matters dependent on documents, including downside scenarios, forecast reconciliations, health-allocation details, and debt-financing breakdowns. The committee accepted the explanation that nominal growth supported the 2027 revenue increase and that privatization proceeds and budget reprioritization would provide flexibility, but continued to flag the risk of another shortfall.

Industrialization, manufacturing employment, and quality-job creation

Minority members questioned whether the 2027 budget would create quality jobs, citing a manufacturing-job target of 336 to 396,000 for 2025 alongside declines of about 177,000 in manufacturing employment and 226,000 in industry employment. DBM officials said better-quality jobs were generally wage-and-salaried positions and argued that recovery, infrastructure, energy, connectivity, and business reforms would improve employment. Congressman Arnan Panaligan pressed for a clear industrial policy, while the DBM responded that structural constraints had to be addressed before industry could become competitive. Representative Elijah San Fernando called for greater ambition and raised energy costs, including possible electricity VAT relief; economic officials said relief required replacement revenue. DEPDev also said industrial policy was reflected in the Philippine Development Plan and could work if basic constraints were fixed. The committee did not receive a firm estimate of 2027 industry jobs, and concerns about PACSILICA's strategic, environmental, and social implications remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the 2027 budget and the government's economic program had a credible industrial policy to reverse manufacturing and industry employment declines and create better-paying, higher-quality jobs. Members also asked whether energy costs, infrastructure, coordination, and the PACSILICA initiative would support industrialization.

The DBM and economic officials supported industrialization and higher-quality jobs but said the immediate priority was to resolve structural constraints, especially energy costs, infrastructure, connectivity, permitting, and coordination. They said industrial policy could support growth, including through high-value manufacturing and PACSILICA, but the 2027 job numbers had not yet been established.

Outcome The officials defended the budget's recovery and structural-reform strategy but did not provide a quantified 2027 industry-job estimate or a detailed, contested industrialization road map. PACSILICA was described as potentially supportive of industrialization, while Co's questions about its conditions and social and environmental costs remained pending.

Infrastructure allocation, project selection, and absorptive capacity

Members questioned whether the infrastructure increase was justified by implementation readiness, absorptive capacity, economic multipliers, and regional needs. DBM said the 2027 NEP infrastructure allocation was 4.4% of GDP and that PPP projects could move the ratio closer to the 5% benchmark; it also defended the DPWH increase as funding implementation-ready projects with greater multiplier effects. Members raised traffic losses of about 3.5 billion pesos a day, delayed foreign-assisted projects, right-of-way problems, and LGU permitting and political obstacles. DBM said right-of-way would now precede project approval, agencies were being required to coordinate with LGUs earlier, and DILG intervention could be sought. Rep. Nazal challenged whether SARO releases translated into actual implementation and requested detailed Fisaro project records, while the chair stress-tested the 2027 revenue and privatization assumptions. The hearing produced several commitments for documents and coordination, but did not fully resolve project execution, regional allocation, or financing-risk concerns.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether proposed infrastructure allocations were supported by implementation readiness, absorptive and monitoring capacity, sound project-selection criteria, regional equity, and credible financing assumptions. Members also asked whether delayed releases, local-government obstacles, and weak execution were reducing economic returns and contributing to underspending.

DBM maintained that infrastructure allocations and agency-level reductions were guided in part by absorptive capacity, implementation readiness, project evaluation, and expected economic multipliers. It said PPPs could lift infrastructure spending toward the 5% of GDP benchmark, right-of-way requirements had been moved ahead of project approval, and agencies retained primary responsibility for project implementation after allotment release.

Outcome The committee received explanations linking allocations and reductions to absorptive capacity, readiness, multipliers, and implementation status, but several issues remained open. DBM and related agencies undertook to submit project, execution, education-budget, disbursement, and delay-cost information, while LGU obstacles and the soundness of financing assumptions were left for further review.

Foreign-assisted projects, delays, and commitment fees

Rep. Edgar Erice requested a breakdown and status report for support to foreign-assisted projects, and DBM committed to submit it before plenary. Rep. Dadah Kiram Ismula asked about fees and penalties from delayed projects; DOF reported about 3.4 billion in commitment fees since 2022 during the Marcos administration, while clarifying that these were not technically penalties. Rep. Albert Garcia pressed for cumulative data on penalties and delay-related project costs, and DBM said delays more commonly produced cost overruns, with some projects potentially doubling in cost. The agencies identified right-of-way acquisition as a principal cause of delay and said ICC now required it before project approval. Leila de Lima challenged the placement of about 42.553 billion in foreign-assisted-project support in UA, while the executive said the amount covered loan proceeds for projects still awaiting approval or loan signing. The Supreme Court issue and comprehensive penalty and cost data remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how foreign-assisted projects were being programmed, monitored, and delayed; whether delays caused commitment fees, penalties, or cost overruns; and what documentation and corrective measures the executive agencies would provide. It also examined why support for foreign-assisted projects was placed in unprogrammed appropriations and how the executive would respond to constitutional challenges.

The agencies said commitment fees were distinct from penalties: DOF had incurred commitment fees when foreign-assisted projects did not proceed, while contractual penalties could apply under implementing agencies' contracts. They said delays were commonly reflected in cost overruns, especially where right-of-way acquisition was incomplete, and that loan-proceeds components of projects still awaiting approval or loan signing were placed in unprogrammed appropriations while government counterpart funding remained programmed.

Outcome The committee received the DOF's figure for commitment fees and the agencies' distinction between commitment fees and contractual penalties, but no total for project-specific penalties or cost overruns was submitted during the hearing. DBM committed to provide the foreign-assisted-project breakdown before plenary, while the constitutional issue involving UA and the status and cost consequences of delayed projects remained open.
