Regional equity and Mindanao's proposed budget share

Rep. Romeo Momo first argued that regional allocation criteria should account for infrastructure deficits, land area, and road length, not only per capita funding. Rep. Jila then questioned the gap between RDC priorities and the central budget process, while DBM and DEPDev officials described ongoing efforts to harmonize planning and budgeting. A DEPDev official said about 30% to 35% of RDC priorities were reflected in the GAA, compared with 50% in the NEP. Rep. Rufus Rodriguez challenged Mindanao's 15.1% share, citing its 22.3% population share, 18% to 19% contribution to gross national product, and seven of the country's 10 poorest provinces. DBM said Mindanao had the highest average increase outside NCR from 2026 to 2027 and that centrally managed funds might not yet be attributed to the region. Rodriguez requested an increase to at least 20%, and DEPDev confirmed receipt of the supporting RDC resolution, but no increase was agreed to.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether Mindanao's 15.1% share of the proposed regional budget was equitable given its population, economic contribution, poverty levels, and development needs. Members also examined whether regional development priorities were being incorporated into the national budget and whether the share could be increased before approval.

DBM and DEPDev said they were working to improve regional allocation by prioritizing RDC-endorsed projects, strengthening the planning-and-budgeting linkage, harmonizing calendars and submission systems, and identifying centrally managed funds that could benefit Mindanao. They did not commit to a specific increase to Mindanao's 20% request, but characterized the review as ongoing and confirmed receipt of the Mindanao RDC resolution.

Outcome DBM and DEPDev acknowledged the regional-equity concern, confirmed receipt of the Mindanao RDC resolution, and undertook continuing evaluation and process improvements. The requested increase from 15.1% to at least 20% was not resolved during the hearing.

Rep. Jila raised the need for a genuine bottom-up process linking barangay, local, provincial, and regional priorities to agency ceilings and the national budget. DBM and DepDev said they were harmonizing planning and budgeting calendars and portals, but acknowledged that only about 30% to 35% of RDC priorities appeared in the GAA, compared with 50% in the NAP. Rep. Albert Garcia connected weak regional planning and connectivity to traffic losses, migration to Metro Manila, and delayed foreign-assisted projects; DBM answered that mass transit, regional connectivity, and right-of-way reforms were priorities. Rep. Rufus pressed for proactive DBM engagement with RDCs and a 20% Mindanao budget share, while DBM cited a 10.6% increase in one Mindanao region and said the allocation issue remained a work in progress. Senior Vice Chair Albert Garcia later questioned bottom-up budgeting, meritocracy, CREATE MORE, and local PPPs; officials described ongoing performance reforms, cited registered investments of about 1.9 trillion, and reported about 50 LGU PPP proposals and three awarded local PPP contracts. The hearing produced commitments on calendar and planning reforms, right-of-way sequencing, and submission of comparative PPP and delay data, but did not resolve the regional allocation gap.

The committee sought to establish whether bottom-up and top-down budgeting processes adequately incorporated priorities identified by local and regional development councils into agency ceilings, the national investment program, and the General Appropriations Act. Members also examined whether regional connectivity, Mindanao's budget share, local government PPPs, and related planning and investment systems were sufficiently decentralized and demand-driven.

DBM and DepDev said they were working to strengthen the connection among RDC investment programming, agency budget submissions, national planning, and the GAA, including through harmonized calendars, portals, and a budget code. They acknowledged that regional priorities were not consistently carried through to the GAA, while arguing that centrally managed items and recent increases, particularly in Mindanao, required more accurate attribution and further evaluation.

Outcome The agencies acknowledged that regional priorities were substantially diluted between the NAP and the GAA and committed to improve planning-budgeting integration, local calendars, and project attribution. Mindanao's requested 20% share, cumulative delay data, and pre-PPP Code comparisons remained open for further evaluation or submission.

Rami Salamat asked about underspending and LGU obstacles; Secretary Kim reported a midyear 2026 program of 3.176 against actual disbursement of about R3.175, or about R1 billion short, and agreed to submit department-level figures. Rep. Allan Ty examined LGSF releases, including PHP57.872 billion for 2026, almost 54 billion released by July 31, and a little over 7 billion remaining. The hearing also covered savings allocations, including about 6.1 billion identified under the 2026 GAA, although one 2025 savings figure was garbled and required further verification.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the NTA and other LGU transfers were distributed equitably and released under the law, particularly in light of differences between cities and municipalities. Members also examined LGSF availability and releases, savings and unused appropriations, underspending, and obstacles created by LGUs in implementing nationally funded projects.

DBM said NTA distribution followed the Local Government Code and that municipalities generally received lower shares because of the statutory formula, although they had greater NTA dependence. It said additional transfers were justified for lower-income LGUs and devolved functions, while LGSF releases reflected programs such as RISE; it also said releases, savings, and implementation problems were governed by statutory rules and would require coordination with DILG and other agencies.

Outcome The existing NTA formula and the legal framework for additional LGU transfers were explained but not changed. DBM committed to provide written underspending data and to coordinate with DILG on remedies for LGU-related implementation obstacles; the savings figures were discussed and partially confirmed, but some figures remained unclear.

Budget execution rules under NBC 595, SAROs, SAAs, and NCAs

Rep. Roberto Nazal Jr. questioned whether NBC 595 imposed release conditions beyond the veto message and why specific DPWH projects required SAROs or additional internal allotment documents. DBM said NBC 595 requirements were intended to establish implementation readiness, and that a SARO provided obligational authority while an NCA concerned cash disbursement. DBM deferred questions about withholding SAAs and project-level implementation to the concerned departments, while acknowledging that cash availability should not prevent procurement or obligation. Rep. Rami Salamat raised underspending and LGU permitting or political obstacles; DBM said 2026 midyear disbursement was about 1 billion below program and undertook to provide departmental figures and consult DILG. Rep. Allan Ty then examined LGSF releases, including about 54 billion released as of July 31 and a little over 7 billion remaining, and questioned savings declarations ranging from about 12.87 billion for FY 2025 to about 6.1 billion under the 2026 GAA. The committee obtained commitments for documents and verification, but the precise savings figures and whether delayed obligations became manufactured savings were left open.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish the legal and administrative basis for release conditions under NBC 595, and to clarify the respective functions of SAROs, SAAs, allotment authority, and NCAs. Members also examined whether delayed project awards, LGU permitting obstacles, and declarations of savings contributed to underspending or created manufactured savings.

DBM maintained that NBC 595 release requirements were intended to verify implementation readiness for projects not vetted during the NEP or projects with changes, increased allocations, or special-provision requirements. It stated that SAROs provide obligational authority, SAAs concern internal allotment and suballotment, and NCAs concern cash disbursement; project implementation and internal SAA issuance generally remained with the implementing agency. DBM also stated that savings must derive from released allotments and be based on projects or PAPs that were abandoned, completed, or discontinued.

Outcome DBM answered the general distinctions among SAROs, SAAs, allotment authority, and NCAs, but deferred responsibility for internal SAA issuance and project implementation to the concerned departments. The committee required documentary follow-up on SARO projects and underspending, while the precise FY 2025 savings figure and the possibility of manufactured savings remained unresolved.

DPWH right-of-way, permits, and delayed project implementation

Rep. Mark Kawanko asked whether right-of-way could be funded and acquired before civil works because rising land values and delayed acquisition made projects less implementable. DBM said DPWH's right-of-way budget was a lump sum prioritized by DPWH, supported higher levels in the NEP, and was often reduced before enactment; no specific advance-funding mechanism was settled. DBM also said local autonomy constrained national support for acquiring land for barangay facilities and open spaces. Rep. Rami Salamat linked public-works underspending to LGU requirements such as building, location, and demolition permits and asked for a remedy when LGUs blocked projects. DBM said permits were not required before allotment release, emphasized early coordination for 2027, identified the Anti-Red Tape Authority and DILG as possible avenues, and committed to confer with DILG. The committee requested written department-level disbursement data, including a 2026 midyear shortfall of about 1 billion, while the proposed deemed-approval and other budget remedies remained unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how right-of-way could be funded and acquired before civil works, whether barangay land and open-space needs could be supported, and how permitting and local-government barriers could be prevented from delaying DPWH projects. Members also sought the executive's remedy when LGUs withheld or delayed required permits and coordination.

DBM said DPWH right-of-way funding was proposed as a lump sum and prioritized by DPWH, while DBM supported higher right-of-way levels but said they were often reduced in the enacted GAA. It said early LGU coordination and securing necessary permits during 2027 budget preparation should reduce implementation delays, but acknowledged that further recourse for LGU obstruction required coordination with DILG.

Outcome The committee received DBM's explanation that right-of-way funding was a DPWH-prioritized lump sum and that DBM supported higher allocations, but no decision was made to permit district-specific advance right-of-way items or national acquisition of barangay land. On LGU permitting, DBM undertook to coordinate with DILG and work with the member, while the proposed budget remedy and the broader question of LGU obstruction remained open.

Confidential and intelligence funds and DBM review authority

Renee Co asked DBM to identify agencies legally authorized to receive confidential and intelligence funds and to explain whether DBM could deny requests based on mandate and physical and financial plans. Secretary Kim said the 2027 proposal retained the same agencies as the 2026 NEP, listed the covered agencies, and said requests were evaluated against the agency's mandate and the governing joint circular. Rep. Ko raised concerns about the Office of the President's confidential-expense increase from 500 million in 2016 to 2.5 billion and sought greater accountability. Rep. Antonio Tinio questioned the roughly 10.8 billion total and the Office of the President's roughly 4.56 billion allocation, then pressed whether confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings. DBM answered that eligible expenses could be augmented subject to the general provisions and GAA approvals, but the Chair required a written explanation. DBM also explained that LGU allocations were reviewed for peace-and-order resolutions and other requirements, while actual use was subject to COA post-audit.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish which agencies were legally authorized to receive confidential and intelligence funds, how DBM evaluated requests, and whether confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings. Members also asked how DBM reviewed LGU confidential-fund allocations and whether the Office of the President's confidential-fund level was justified.

DBM said it evaluated confidential-fund requests against the requesting agency's legal mandate, applicable joint circulars, physical and financial plans, and GAA requirements. It stated that LGU allocations were reviewed for documentary and statutory compliance, while actual utilization was subject to COA post-audit; it also maintained that eligible confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings subject to required approvals.

Outcome DBM stated that it could review and reject or exclude requests that failed mandate, documentary, or legal requirements, and that eligible confidential and intelligence expenses could be augmented from savings subject to GAA requirements and approvals. The classification and augmentation issue remained subject to the written explanation requested by the Chair.

Electricity costs, VAT, transmission, and energy-sector regulation

Rep. Sergio Dagooc linked high electricity costs to household burdens, structural market problems, renewable-energy delays, transmission needs, and layered taxes, while agencies cited about 5.3% as the national-average share of household spending devoted to electricity. The agencies supported stronger ERC and PCC coordination and said EPIRA reforms were being pursued sequentially. Rep. Mark Kawanko pressed for advance and higher right-of-way funding and argued that electricity generation had a high multiplier effect, citing Vietnam's 68,000 megawatts against the Philippines' 22,000 megawatts. Rep. Elijah San Fernando asked about reducing VAT on electricity, and DOF said it would be neutral if replacement revenue were identified. Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez separately argued that VAT should not apply to system loss; the BIR said the charge was taxable because it was bundled into distributors' gross sales but reported that the ERC had a draft regulation under preparation. The committee requested the World Bank report and accepted commitments for further data, meetings, and regulatory work.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why electricity costs were high, how regulation, transmission constraints, taxes, and system loss affected consumers and industry, and what reforms or administrative actions could reduce those costs. It also examined whether right-of-way and electricity-generation investments should receive greater public support and whether VAT on electricity or system loss could be removed.

The agencies and economic managers said high electricity costs reflected structural market issues, project and transmission delays, coordination problems, and the tax and subsidy structure. They supported stronger ERC-PCC coordination and higher right-of-way funding, while maintaining that VAT reductions required replacement revenue; the BIR and ERC were nevertheless working administratively to address VAT on system loss.

Outcome The committee received agency explanations and several reform positions, but no final decision was taken on EPIRA amendments, electricity-tax restructuring, government ownership, or higher right-of-way allocations. VAT on system loss was left to an ongoing BIR-ERC regulatory process, while the World Bank report and additional data were to be submitted or discussed further.

Revenue measures, tax exemptions, and proposed new taxes

Rep. Iris Marie Montes established that the PhilHealth subsidy was tied to the sin-tax allocation, while Rep. Percival Sindania pressed officials on falling revenue forecasts and the fiscal cost of tax exemptions or reductions. Officials said the Progress bill included personal-income-tax and MCIT relief alongside eight revenue-enhancing measures intended to offset the lost revenue. The effective VAT rate was described as about 6% despite a statutory rate of 12% because of exemptions. Minority Representative Sarah Elago raised additional taxes on tobacco, plastics, sweetened beverages, alcohol, luxury assets, and billionaires; the last proposal was left for internal study. Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez argued that electricity system loss should not be subject to VAT, and the BIR said it was working with the ERC on draft regulations and public consultation. The committee directed the DBCC to submit several fiscal and revenue reconciliations, while the system-loss issue remained under agency action.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether proposed tax exemptions, tax reductions, and new revenue measures were fiscally sustainable and whether replacement revenues had been identified. Members also asked how revenue assumptions, tax reforms, and VAT treatment would affect public services, taxpayers, and fiscal consolidation.

The agency position was that tax removals or exemptions should proceed only when replacement revenues were identified, because the proposed national budget had to be funded. Officials said the Progress bill paired revenue-eroding relief measures with eight revenue-enhancing measures, while the BIR and ERC were pursuing a regulatory solution to VAT on electricity system loss rather than relying necessarily on new legislation.

Outcome Officials maintained that tax relief or tax removal required replacement revenue, while the Progress bill was presented as pairing exemptions with new revenue measures. The billionaires-tax proposal remained for internal study, and VAT on electricity system loss remained under BIR-ERC regulatory work rather than being resolved during the hearing.

Creative-industries digital VAT earmark

Representative Javi Benitez raised the gap between the creative economy's reported scale and proposed cultural-agency budgets, then pressed the agencies to implement the statutory 5% digital-VAT earmark. He cited BIR-certified collections of about 6.36 billion for August to December 2025 and a creative-industries share reported at about 318.08 million, although parts of the certification were unclear in the transcript. The DOF official confirmed 318,000,000 for the cited period and gave a running figure of 5% of 9,400,000,000, without fully explaining the calculation. Benitez asked whether a special account had been created and whether the share would flow as automatic appropriations. DBM Secretary Kim said the agencies were establishing the UACS code and would consult with DOF and other agencies on the proper booking and fund arrangement. The chair ended the exchange by saying the committee would monitor creation of the fund, leaving the automatic-appropriation issue unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the statutory 5% share of incremental digital VAT collections had been collected, accounted for, and earmarked for the creative industries. It also sought commitments on the creation of the special account and whether the funds would be treated as automatic appropriations or require annual appropriations.

The agencies confirmed a 2025 creative-industries share of 318,000,000, while the DOF official stated a running figure of 5% of 9,400,000,000 without elaboration. DBM said it was working with DTI, DOF, and other agencies to establish the UACS coding and finalize the proper booking and arrangement of the Creative Industry Development Fund, but did not definitively resolve whether the share would be automatic appropriations.

Outcome The agencies acknowledged the cited 2025 share and committed to work on the account, UACS coding, and legal and accounting treatment of the fund. Whether the share would be automatically appropriated and the complete current collections figure remained unresolved, subject to interagency finalization and committee monitoring.

Negros Island regional offices, plantilla positions, and funding

Deputy Speaker Chedeng Alvarez raised concerns that, more than two years after Republic Act 12,000 was signed, the Negros Island regional structure still lacked fully established offices, staffing, vehicles, and funding. DBM said it had prioritized the region and reported that 30 agencies had approved plantilla positions and offices as of 07/28/2026, with eight additional requests under evaluation. Alvarez questioned whether delays came from central or regional offices, and DBM said requests had to be endorsed by agency heads at the central office. BLGF reported an interim head, vehicles, proposed funding, and consideration of a Dumaguete City satellite office, while the Bureau of the Treasury said it would review the regional-office proposal. Alvarez requested budget and staffing breakdowns and a definite implementation timeline, and DBM committed to submit them through the committee within one week. The matter therefore landed as a commitment, with several organizational and funding issues still unresolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish why Negros Island regional offices, plantilla positions, vehicles, and funding remained at different stages of evaluation or approval, and whether delays originated with agency central offices or regional offices. It also sought the status of staffing and the timeline for fully operationalizing the Negros Island region.

DBM said it had prioritized proposals supporting the establishment of Negros Island regional offices, including offices, vehicles, equipment, and staffing, and said 30 national government agencies had approved plantilla positions and offices as of 07/28/2026, with eight additional requests under evaluation. BLGF said it had an interim head, vehicles, and proposed funding, while the Bureau of the Treasury said it would review the creation of a regional office because of its budget and organizational implications.

Outcome The issue was not fully resolved during the hearing. DBM committed to submit the requested budget, staffing, and implementation information within one week, while the Treasury review and the status of remaining agency proposals remained open.

The executive branch, through DEPDEB and DBM, said the FY2027 budget should combine fiscal discipline with investments that restore growth, protect vulnerable households, strengthen health and social services, improve food security, and address implementation bottlenecks. DBM maintained that the 7,200,000,000,000 pesos NEP reflected deliberate prioritization within limited fiscal space and would emphasize implementation-ready programs.

Outcome The committee received the executive branch's economic context and DBM's presentation of the proposed FY2027 NEP, including its fiscal framework and priority allocations. No member interpolation or contested issue on the topic occurred in the provided transcript.

Fiscal consolidation, deficit reduction, and spending compression

Secretary Frederic Diko presented fiscal consolidation as a strategy combining stronger revenue collection with better-targeted spending, with the deficit-to-GDP ratio projected to fall from about 5.4% in 2026 to 3.5% by 2030. Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan questioned whether the improvement instead reflected compression of spending, citing declines in revenue and disbursement ratios to GDP. The agency answered that revenues were expected to grow by about nine and a half percent annually and expenditures by 5% to 6% annually in absolute terms, even if both declined relative to GDP. Libanan also highlighted interest payments of 1,114,000,000,000 and their size relative to basic-education funding. The agency attributed the interest burden to debt-financed deficits, citing borrowing of about 1,600,000,000,000 pesos in 2026 and approximately 1,700,000,000,000 pesos the following year, with interest payments of approximately 1,000,000,000,000 pesos and 1,100,000,000,000 pesos, respectively. The agency reaffirmed its commitment to fiscal discipline, but the potential effect of spending compression on priority services remained contested.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the projected reduction in the fiscal deficit would result mainly from stronger revenue collection or from compressing government spending. Members also questioned the level of interest payments and their implications for fiscal discipline and future borrowing.

The agency said fiscal consolidation would not require shrinking revenues or expenditures in absolute terms. Revenues were projected to continue growing, while expenditures would also rise but more slowly relative to GDP; reducing the deficit was necessary to contain debt and interest costs.

Outcome The agency answered that both revenues and expenditures would continue to grow in absolute terms, while their ratios to GDP would decline as part of fiscal consolidation. The concern about whether spending compression could affect priority services was raised but not definitively resolved.

Public debt and projected interest payments of about 1.114 trillion

The DOF presented fiscal consolidation and debt sustainability as necessary responses to inherited debt and continuing borrowing needs. Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan questioned whether the projected deficit reduction relied mainly on compressing spending, noting that revenue and disbursement shares of GDP were also projected to decline. The DOF answered that revenues and expenditures would continue growing in absolute terms, while their GDP shares would fall, and said expenditures would grow by about 5% to 6% annually. Libanan then highlighted total interest payments of 1,114,000,000,000 and compared them with basic education budget figures. The DOF said borrowing was about 1,600,000,000,000 pesos in 2026 and approximately 1,700,000,000,000 pesos in 2027, with interest payments of approximately 1,000,000,000,000 pesos and 1,100,000,000,000 pesos, respectively. The exchange ended with the agency reiterating fiscal discipline, but the minority's concern about the effect of debt service on program spending was not resolved.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the projected reduction in the deficit would result mainly from compressing government spending rather than improving revenue effort. It also examined the scale of interest payments, borrowing, and debt-service costs relative to the national budget and domestic principal.

The DOF maintained that fiscal consolidation was necessary because deficits were financed through debt, and higher debt generated higher interest payments. It said revenues and expenditures would continue growing in absolute terms, while their shares of GDP would decline, and projected interest payments of approximately 1,000,000,000,000 pesos in 2026 and 1,100,000,000,000 pesos in 2027.

Outcome The agency explained the relationship between deficit, borrowing, debt, and interest payments, and defended fiscal consolidation as necessary to contain future debt-service costs. Libanan's concerns about spending compression and the size of interest payments remained contested, with no additional document or corrective calculation provided.

Rep. Ryan Recto raised concerns that the projected revenue growth from 2026 to 2030 was optimistic and asked whether it included the progress bill's revenue loss and proposed excise-tax increases. The DOF stated that the submitted revenue projections excluded both the revenue-enhancing and revenue-eroding effects of the proposed progress-bill measures. It said the ultimate revenue outcome could not yet be determined because the legislature had not finalized the tax rates and other provisions, particularly for excise taxes.

Outcome The DOF confirmed that the proposed revenue-enhancing and revenue-eroding measures were not included in the submitted revenue projections. The final fiscal effect remained dependent on legislative deliberations and the rates ultimately enacted.

Inflation targets, external risks, and contingency subsidies

The BSP reported that inflation had risen to 7.2% in April 2026 before easing to 6.2% in July, and projected averages of 6.4% in 2026, 4.5% in 2027, and about 3.1% in 2028. It based the 2027 budget on headline inflation of about 4% to 5% and Dubai crude oil of roughly 70 to 90 per barrel, while warning that risks remained tilted upward. Secretary Balisacan said elevated inflation threatened recent poverty gains and called for targeted and timely assistance to vulnerable households. Representative Ryan Recto challenged the inflation path as potentially too optimistic in light of the Middle East conflict, trade uncertainty, underspending, and capital-flow risks. He also cited a 105 pesos Dubai crude scenario and the possible risk to 1,400,000 Filipinos. A DBCC budget official answered that regular 2027 budget line items could be mobilized for targeted subsidies and fuel assistance, but no specific amount or operational contingency plan was committed.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the BSP's inflation assumptions for 2026–2028 were realistic given oil-price, Middle East, trade, capital-flow, and domestic implementation risks. It also sought to determine whether the DBCC and the budget contained contingency measures or targeted subsidies if those risks caused renewed inflation and threatened vulnerable households.

The BSP said inflation was elevated and risks remained tilted to the upside, but its projections were regularly updated and supported by a 3% target with a plus or minus 1% tolerance range. The DBCC budget official said existing regular budget line items in the 2027 budget could be mobilized for targeted assistance and fuel subsidies if another oil crisis occurred.

Outcome The BSP defended its inflation projections as regularly updated forecasts rather than fixed promises, while acknowledging significant upside risks. The DBCC identified existing 2027 budget line items as a possible source of targeted subsidies and fuel assistance, but no specific contingency amount or detailed trigger mechanism was presented.

Infrastructure investment and implementation capacity

Secretary Arsenio M. Balisacan and Acting DBM Secretary Kim Robert C. De Leon both linked infrastructure execution to economic growth and warned that spending increases alone would not ensure results. DBM proposed capital outlays of about 1.16 trillion, up 13.8%, and Build Better More infrastructure investment of about 1.47 trillion, also 13.8% above the fiscal year 2026 GAA infrastructure level. Rep. Ryan Recto questioned whether the increase could be implemented without recurring underspending, citing a 27.33% shift of resources from GOCCs to DPWH and the economy's two point three percent second-quarter slowdown. Secretary De Leon answered that 2027 infrastructure projects had complete documentary requirements, allowing agencies to begin early procurement before budget enactment. He said this would permit immediate award and implementation after passage of the budget. He confirmed that early procurement would become standard operating practice in the coming years, although actual resolution of underspending remained dependent on agency execution.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish whether the proposed increase in infrastructure and capital-outlay spending could be implemented effectively despite recent underspending and procurement bottlenecks. Rep. Ryan Recto specifically asked what mechanisms would prevent underspending and whether early procurement would become a continuing practice.

DBM maintained that higher infrastructure allocations were being screened against documentary completeness, implementation readiness, absorptive capacity, and past performance. It said early procurement could address delays by allowing agencies to begin procurement before budget enactment, and confirmed that this mechanism would continue as standard practice in the coming years.

Outcome The committee received DBM's explanation that early procurement, enabled by completing documentary requirements before budget enactment, would address procurement-related implementation delays. DBM confirmed that the mechanism would continue as standard practice, but the broader question of whether the larger infrastructure budget would eliminate underspending remained subject to implementation.

Differences between NEP and GAA levels for foreign-assisted projects

Antonio Tinio raised the issue by alleging that differences between NEP and GAA levels could create fiscal space for insertions. He cited a 2026 DOTR foreign-assisted-project NEP of about 135 billion against a GAA level of about 64 billion. DBM Secretary Kim Robert C. De Leon said the NEP amounts were based on evaluated requirements and agency proposals, and attributed discrepancies partly to delays in implementing foreign-assisted projects. He also explained that DPWH foreign-assisted projects were ordinarily tagged under the relevant central office. Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish why proposed NEP amounts for foreign-assisted projects were substantially higher than prior GAA levels, and whether the difference created fiscal space for budget insertions. It also sought to determine whether the lower GAA levels reflected legitimate implementation and absorptive-capacity considerations or budget padding.

DBM stated that NEP amounts for foreign-assisted projects were based on its evaluation of project requirements and the agencies' proposals, not simply on an effort to create fiscal space for insertions. It attributed differences between NEP and GAA levels in part to delays in project implementation and explained that DPWH foreign-assisted projects were normally recorded under the respective central offices.

Outcome DBM gave a general explanation that implementation delays and central-office tagging accounted for the differences, but it did not provide a project-by-project reconciliation of the 135,000,000,000 NEP and 64,000,000,000 GAA figures. The insertion or budget-padding allegation therefore remained contested and was not fully resolved in this exchange.

Electricity prices and their effect on inflation

Rep. Salvador Pleyto raised the effect of rising electricity rates on households and on the prices of goods and services. An agency official said electricity accounted for 5.3% of average household spending, or about 17,057 pesos per year, while the BSP's detailed response on electricity's CPI treatment was partly unclear. Rep. Ryan Recto questioned whether the projected decline in inflation was too optimistic amid domestic and external risks. The BSP cited projections including 6.4% average inflation, a 3% target with a plus-or-minus 1% tolerance range, and regular Monetary Board updates. Recto also raised Dubai crude assumptions of 70 to 90 pesos against a cited 105 pesos and warned that 1,400,000 Filipinos could fall below the poverty threshold. A budget official said regular 2027 budget lines remained available for targeted subsidies and fuel assistance if another crisis occurred.

Questions and agency response

The committee sought to establish how rising electricity prices affected household spending, production costs, and inflation, and how the BSP's inflation targets accounted for domestic and external risks. Members also asked whether the government had contingency measures if energy-price shocks worsened.

The BSP presented inflation projections and said forecasts were updated at each Monetary Board meeting, with a 3% average-inflation target and a plus-or-minus 1% tolerance range. The budget side said existing regular line items in the 2027 budget remained available for mobilization, including targeted assistance and fuel subsidies, if another energy-price crisis occurred.

Outcome The BSP defended the inflation framework as a regularly updated projection, but Rep. Recto's concern that the targets might be too optimistic was not fully resolved in the transcript. The budget official stated that existing 2027 budget lines could be used for emergency energy-related assistance.

Economic growth, employment, and poverty-reduction assumptions

DepDev Secretary Arsenio M. Balisacan presented the economic basis for the proposed 2027 budget, reporting strong longer-term growth but a recent slowdown. He cited weaker domestic demand, a contraction in investment, elevated inflation, and confidence and governance concerns, while noting that employment had fallen by 166,000 and unemployment had risen to 4.2%. He reported that poverty incidence had declined from eighteen point one percent in 2021 to nine point seven percent in 2025, lifting 8,800,000 Filipinos out of poverty. Balisacan projected growth of 5% to 6% in the next two years, inflation of 4% to 5% in 2027, and a return to the 2% to 4% target range by 2028. He identified targeted assistance, accelerated infrastructure, implementation-ready social and productive investments, and structural and legislative reforms as the response. The matter remained informational, with no recorded committee question or unresolved disagreement.

Questions and agency response

The committee was seeking the socioeconomic basis for the proposed 2027 national budget: the causes of slower growth, the effects on employment and poverty, and the growth, inflation, and employment assumptions guiding budget priorities. It also sought to establish which structural reforms and public investments DepDev considered necessary to restore inclusive growth.

DepDev said the economy had achieved significant growth, employment, and poverty-reduction gains but had recently lost momentum because of weaker demand, confidence problems, inflation, and structural constraints. It maintained that restoring growth required coordinated execution, high-impact public investment, protection for vulnerable households, and legislative and structural reforms.

Outcome DepDev presented the growth, employment, poverty, and inflation assumptions and linked them to budget priorities and structural reforms. No committee challenge, document request, or specific agency undertaking was recorded in the provided stretch.

House budget transparency and pre-plenary treatment

Independent Representative Toby Tiangco asked why the House budget did not receive the same pre-plenary review as other departments and sought equal treatment in the interest of transparency. The committee chair and Kim Robert C. De Leon said that the House budget had historically proceeded directly to plenary, while some other agencies and SUCs followed the same practice. They did not reject the request, but said the decision required House leadership. Tiangco cited House-budget figures including about 30 plus billion, 35,000,000,000, 17,000,000,000, 27,000,000,000, and 10,000,000,000, although several comparisons were unclear in the transcript. Members proposed referring the concern to the Committee on Appropriations and possibly taking it up in plenary. The chair committed to raise the matter with House leadership, but no final ruling or approval was recorded.

Questions and agency response

The committee was trying to establish whether the House of Representatives was legally or constitutionally exempt from pre-plenary budget deliberations. Representative Toby Tiangco also sought to determine whether the House budget would undergo the same transparency review as the budgets of other departments.

The committee's stated position was that the House or Congress budget had historically proceeded directly to plenary, as had the budgets of certain other agencies, SUCs, and executive offices, and was not necessarily exempt by a specific ruling established in the exchange. Committee officials supported transparency in principle but said they lacked authority to decide immediately whether a pre-plenary hearing would be held and would refer the request to House leadership.

Outcome The request for equal pre-plenary treatment was referred for consideration by the Committee on Appropriations and House leadership. No final yes-or-no decision or ruling on the point of order was recorded before the requested suspension.

Agency unavailable · 2026-08-16 · informational

Regional and local government allocations and barangay development program

Acting DBM Secretary Kim Robert C. De Leon presented the regional and local-government components of the proposed FY 2027 budget. He said local government units would receive about 1.533 trillion, including a proposed NTA of COP 1,320,000,000,000, roughly P129.3 billion above the current-year amount. He reported that about 4.603 trillion, or 63.9% of the proposed national budget, would be directly allocated to the regions, with allocations for the National Capital Region, Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao. He also identified 115,620,000,000 pesos for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and 58,530,000,000 for the Local Government Support Fund. The latter included LGU financial assistance, the Growth Equity Fund, and the barangay development program. The presentation was informational, with no recorded committee objection or follow-up action.

Questions and agency response

How did the proposed FY 2027 National Expenditure Program distribute resources among regions, local government units, and barangays, and what funding was provided for local-government support and development programs?

The DBM presented the proposed allocations as a deliberate effort to direct a substantial share of national resources to regions and local governments. It emphasized that the NTA, Bangsamoro funding, Local Government Support Fund, Growth Equity Fund, and barangay development program were intended to support devolved services, local infrastructure, social services, and community development.

Outcome The DBM completed its presentation of the regional and local-government allocations, including the proposed funding for the barangay development program. No committee challenge, amendment, document request, or separate undertaking on this topic was recorded.
